name: Mississippi Today
title: Fitch unveils plan for how Mississippi will spend $189M Meta settlement
description: Attorney General Lynn Fitch discusses her 2027 campaign for governor during an event at the Mississippi Republican Party headquarters in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026.
text:
Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch has unveiled a plan for how Mississippi can spend $189 million of national Meta lawsuit funds, directing over $18 million a year to be split among three state agencies for the next decade. 
The plan arrived in a consent decree that lawyers for the state filed Monday in Hinds County Chancery Court. Fitch drafted the plan as Meta, the corporation that runs Facebook and Instagram, prepares to pay billions of dollars to states after attorneys general accused the company of endangering children across the country with their social media platforms. 
States argued the company turned its platforms into “addiction machines,” targeting children during vulnerable life stages. Despite the settlement, Meta and other technology giants have denied the allegations against them and that they have any liability to states. The California-based company is represented in Mississippi by the powerful and politically connected law firm Butler Snow. 
The settlement agreement allows the attorney general to set the parameters for spending the money. Legal experts, mental health advocates and state lawmakers told Mississippi Today that Fitch’s plan could impact the health of children in the state for years to come. Here is what’s in it: 
How the money will be spent 
Mississippi will be able to spend its portion of the $17-billion national settlement over 10 years. The state’s share currently stands at $189 million, but it could go up to $270 million if the other tech companies ensnared in litigation — Snap, TikTok and YouTube — also agree to settlements with states’ attorneys general. 
The plan Fitch’s office filed directs $18.8 million in payments to be made per annual installment from Meta. That works out to just under $189 million over 10 years, which is the whole settlement. 
Starting in January 2027, Fitch set these parameters for the spending each year over the next decade: 

$6.8 million to the Mississippi Department of Mental Health for “mental health programs targeting but not limited to youth 12 through 18 years of age, including through cooperative programs with Mississippi K-12 schools.” For the remainder of 2026, Fitch directed all payments to be made directly to this department for the same purpose.
$6 million to the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks for “new playgrounds, parks, sporting courts or fields, or other outdoor recreation facilities, or improvements thereof, across the State of Mississippi, including through cooperative programs with Mississippi K-12 schools and local governments, targeting but not limited to youth 12 through 18 years of age.”
$6 million to the Mississippi Department of Education for “afterschool and school break learning opportunities and programming across the State of Mississippi, in cooperation with the Mississippi Department of Human Services.”

Meta will pay Mississippi an additional $6.1 million from a connected settlement involving Cambridge Analytica, a now-defunct British political consulting firm that allegedly harvested the personal data of tens of millions of American Facebook users without their consent before the 2016 federal election. All the money from that part of the settlement agreement will go to the Mississippi Department of Mental Health for youth mental health programs, Fitch’s office told Mississippi Today. 
All of the money will be deposited into the Attorney General of Mississippi Contingent Fund, a special state fund that holds money the AG’s office receives from legal judgments. 
How much control will lawmakers have on the spending?
Although the national settlement assigns spending decisions to attorneys general such as Fitch, the Mississippi Constitution gives the Legislature authority to spend most public money. Lawmakers have asserted that authority with both tobacco and opioid settlement funds. 
In her consent decree, Fitch decided which agencies will get the settlement money, how much money they’re getting and what sort of programs the agencies must use. But her office said the lawmakers have the authority to determine what specific programs will get funded. 
“The Legislature still directs how the money will be spent, and we will work with them on possible funding ideas in the upcoming session,” MaryAsa Lee, a spokesperson for Fitch, told Mississippi Today. “Ultimately, the Legislature decides how the funds will be appropriated.” 
Lawmakers could, for example, create new mental health programs targeting children between 12 and 18, or fund new playgrounds to be operated by the Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks, Fitch’s office added.  
Fitch’s plan also says the “parameters and structure” of the spending decisions made by lawmakers should be established “in consultation with the Governor of Mississippi and the Mississippi Attorney General.” 
Fitch’s office told Mississippi Today the consultation will involve meetings between lawmakers and the offices of the governor and attorney general about future legislation appropriating the settlement money. The legislation will ultimately not require any sort of specific written approval from either the governor or attorney general, they added.   
But the provision gives Fitch influence over the specific spending decision lawmakers could make in the future.  
Fitch, a Republican, is running for governor and has touted her efforts to protect children from large technology companies. 
In the upcoming legislative session beginning in January, there will be two initial payments the Legislature can spend, Fitch’s office said. 
State has a youth mental health crisis
Under the settlement, Meta also agreed to implement new safety standards on Facebook and Instagram. Those standards include setting daily time limits on platform use by children, restricting children’s access during school hours, requiring age verification and creating a range of content controls. Some experts have said the required platform changes are drawn from research findings, while others have questioned whether the changes will be effective.
Mississippi continues to face a youth mental health crisis. Roughly 31,000 children in the state between the ages of 12 and 17 have seriously considered suicide, according to the National Alliance on Mental Illness in 2025. The alliance also found that Mississippi only has about one school psychologist for every 10,000 public school students.
The consent decree filed by Fitch’s office said Meta violated the Mississippi Consumer Protection Act by designing its social media platforms to “entice, engage, and ultimately ensnare youth and teens.” Meta “misled the public about the dangers of its platforms and ignored the damages these platforms have caused to the mental and physical well-being of Mississippi’s youth,” the lawsuit argued.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Public has until noon Thursday to submit comments on 6 RI inspector general finalists
description: The public has until noon Thursday to send written comments on the six candidates vying to become Rhode Island’s first inspector general to the five-member commission who will be interviewing them. But the search panel has yet to decide whether it will post those comments online. A decision is on the agenda for the Inspector […]
text:
The Independent Man stands atop the State House marble dome on Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)The public has until noon Thursday to send written comments on the six candidates vying to become Rhode Island’s first inspector general to the five-member commission who will be interviewing them.
But the search panel has yet to decide whether it will post those comments online. A decision is on the agenda for the Inspector General Independent Advisory Commission’s meeting at 2 p.m. Thursday at the State House. The agenda was posted Tuesday.
Given the nature of the job, increasing government transparency, accountability and efficiency, the comments should be made public, Steven Brown, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union of Rhode Island, said.
“Clearly this information should be public,” Brown said in an interview. “Public bodies of all kinds make that sort of correspondence public.”
The commission consists of Attorney General Peter Neronha, Secretary of State Gregg Amore, General Treasurer James Diossa, Rhode Island Ethics Commission Executive Director Jason Gramitt of the and Will Fletcher, president of the Association of Inspectors General. The commission has voted on every action it has taken since its short search for the newest statewide position created by the General Assembly began in July.
Tim Rondeau, a spokesperson for the attorney general’s office, said the panel has “been posting everything we’ve received thus far,” including the resumes of all 33 people who applied during the 17 days the job posting was online.
Only eight of the 33 had certification from the Association of Inspectors General, a requirement set in the fiscal 2027 budget that created the position. From there, the panel narrowed down six contenders for the position: Stuart Robinson, David Harper, Mark Priebe, Jim Kirdar, Steven Kreuger, and Thomas Whetstone.
Interviews with the six finalists will be held Thursday, Sept. 24. The agenda posted Wednesday afternoon notes a possible vote on the three names the commission must forward to Gov. Dan McKee by Sept. 28.
The governor will then have 90 days to send his nominee to the Rhode Island Senate for advice and consent.
The job posting crafted by the commission following its July 29 meeting allows interviews to be held in person or via video conference. Candidates who travel to attend an in-person interview may be eligible for reimbursement of reasonable travel expenses. 
A five-year term comes with the position, with the inspector general eligible for reappointment for one additional five-year term. The annual salary range set by the commission is $175,000 to $225,000.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: State colleges, preK-12 schools must implement AI guardrails before July
description: The body regulating Florida public schools and state colleges Wednesday approved what the Florida Department of Education calls “one of the most comprehensive, parent-centered AI frameworks in the country.” The State Board of Education policies require public school districts and charter school governing boards to amend their internet safety policies to incl[...]
text:
The Turlington Building, which houses the Florida Department of Education, stands in the foreground, with the Tallahassee skyline, including the Capitol building, beyond. Photo taken from the FAMU campus on Dec. 31, 2024. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)The body regulating Florida public schools and state colleges Wednesday approved what the Florida Department of Education calls “one of the most comprehensive, parent-centered AI frameworks in the country.”
The State Board of Education policies require public school districts and charter school governing boards to amend their internet safety policies to include specific guardrails and directives related to AI by July 1. 
“We are neither going to one extreme, i.e. banning AI, nor are we going to the other extreme, which is just unfettered access,” Education Commissioner Henry Mack said during the board’s meeting in Winter Haven.
DeSantis administration moving to regulate AI from pre-K to Ph.D.

Districts and charter schools, at a minimum, must make policies to “protect students, parents, and instructional personnel from unlawful, deceptive, unsafe, or unauthorized uses of artificial intelligence systems, services, applications, and tools used in connection with educational programs and operations in Florida public schools,” according to the public school rule. 
The idea, the rule states, is to “ensure that any approved use of artificial intelligence protects education records and student information, while supporting student achievement, civic literacy, academic excellence, and workforce preparedness.”
More specifically, schools will have to notify parents when teachers approve an AI instructional tool for use, including the name of the platform and classes in which it would be used and the nature of student interaction.
The policy must include a process for parents to object to AI use and provide alternatives to the tool.
“Florida will not outsource childhood to a chatbot,” Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a news release following the meeting. “We welcome tools that help teachers teach and students learn. We will not accept tools that hide from parents, harvest student data, grade kids in secret, or pretend to be a friend. In this state, a teacher stands in front of the class, a parent has the last word, and a student still has to think.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Schools will be required to conduct additional reviews for AI tools used in PreK-5 to ensure they are age-appropriate. 
The rule looks to protect the teaching profession from being replaced by computers. It calls to “ensure that the use of AI instructional tools is limited to supplementing, and not replacing, the professional judgment of teachers and the primary right of parents to direct the upbringing and education of their children.”
Further, the policy must ensure AI is “accurate, transparent, viewpoint neutral, accessible to students and educators with disabilities.”
State colleges
The board approved a similar rule for the state college system, directing the 28 boards of trustees to create policies “that provide for the use and limitations of use of artificial intelligence tools in order to ensure quality of education for students, efficiency of operations, and a safe learning environment for the whole college community.”
“The rule that you accepted is not a prohibition, it empowers faculty to decide what to do, it allows the instructor to explicitly permit it or prohibit it with respect to their assignments,” Mack said of the college-level policy. 
“I just think it’s a great thing that we put the guardrails, but the guardrails are so nuanced that it allows for flexibility and innovation and faculty ownership in a way that does not compromise or usurp the faculty’s ability to teach what they want.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Right to Life Michigan says it opposes constitutional convention after DeBoyer comments on abortion
description: Right to Life of Michigan, the state’s foremost anti-abortion group, came out on Wednesday against convening a constitutional convention as a way to impose new abortion limits. Amber Roseboom, president of Right to Life Michigan said Wednesday that the organization opposes a constitutional convention, which Michigan voters will consider on the Nov. 3 ballot.[...]
text:
Participants take a photo at the Michigan March for Life outside the Michigan State Capitol on Nov. 8, 2023. Right to Life of Michigan also announced it was filing a lawsuit to overturn Proposal 3. (Photo: Anna Liz Nichols)Right to Life of Michigan, the state’s foremost anti-abortion group, came out on Wednesday against convening a constitutional convention as a way to impose new abortion limits.
Amber Roseboom, president of Right to Life Michigan said Wednesday that the organization opposes a constitutional convention, which Michigan voters will consider on the Nov. 3 ballot. The statement came days after state Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay Township), the Republican lieutenant governor nominee and running mate to U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township), suggested that Republicans could re-introduce limits on abortion via a Michigan constitutional convention.

“While we recognize and applaud the ongoing debate around this issue, RLM is opposed to opening the state constitution to a convention at this time,” Rosboom said in a statement. “Moreover, even if a constitutional convention were to be called through passage of the question this year, any recommended changes from the delegates would go before the citizens for a popular vote before being ratified. The citizens of our state continue to hold the power. Anyone suggesting otherwise is either misinformed or being intentionally dishonest with voters” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
DeBoyer’s remarks became public after The Detroit News obtained a recording from a Saturday event in Battle Creek. DeBoyer did not dispute the statement, but he walked back the sentiment, saying that the issue was “settled,” similar to language used by James in 2024 in his re-election bid for Congress, when he said, “the fact of the matter is that abortion is enshrined in our (state) constitution.”
Michigan Democrats pounced on DeBoyer’s comments in an attempt to infuse abortion policy into the 2026 election cycle even though abortion is  not explicitly on the ballot this year.
A constitutional convention to limit abortion rights? Democrats push back on DeBoyer suggestion

“Sadly, the Democrats are now using the Constitutional Convention question to wrongly suggest that abortion is on the ballot,” Roseboom said. “The Democrats have more than demonstrated they have no solution to the outsized economic strains their failed leadership has placed on Michigan families. If they care about the future of Michigan, it’s high time they focus on that.”
What is a ‘Con-Con’?
Every 16 years, the question of whether the state should rewrite its constitution appears on the ballot for voters to either approve or reject. Informally known as a “Con-Con,” the measure has automatically appeared on the state’s ballot beginning in 1978 and is enshrined in the Michigan Constitution’s Article XII, Section 3. Michigan has rejected the convening of a Con-Con for decades. The measure has appeared on ballots only three times in the state’s history — in 1978, 1994 and 2010.
What’s a Con-Con? Michigan voters will decide if they want to rewrite the constitution in 2026.

If approved in 2026, a special primary and then general election for delegates would have to be held, with one delegate elected on a partisan ballot in each of the 110 state House and 38 state Senate districts. 
The convention would then convene in October 2027, with no limit on how long it would last, although for comparison the convention that produced the current constitution began in October 1961 and lasted for 10 months before adopting a proposed constitution on Aug. 1, 1962. 
State voters then approved that document in April 1963, and it has been unchanged via a constitutional convention since, although many other amendments have been made to the state constitution through ballot measures.
Among the most notable additions to the state constitution was the issue at hand — Proposal 3 of 2022, which enshrined reproductive rights after voters approved the measure with 56% of voters casting ballots in favor and with 43% of the state’s voters against.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Spanberger declares state of emergency as drought strains Virginia farmers
description: Virginia farmers struggling with drought-damaged pastures will be able to receive larger hay deliveries under a state of emergency declared by Gov. Abigail Spanberger Wednesday.   Spanberger’s Executive Order 21 temporarily exempts over-width hay deliveries from certain transportation restrictions, allowing hay to reach farmers more quickly to feed their liv[...]
text:
Dairy cows graze in Stanley, Va. (Photo by Parker Michels-Boyce/Virginia Mercury)Virginia farmers struggling with drought-damaged pastures will be able to receive larger hay deliveries under a state of emergency declared by Gov. Abigail Spanberger Wednesday.  
Spanberger’s Executive Order 21 temporarily exempts over-width hay deliveries from certain transportation restrictions, allowing hay to reach farmers more quickly to feed their livestock. Persistent drought conditions that began last winter have led to an estimated hay shortfall totaling 500,000 tons.
“This waiver will help us move critical hay resources more quickly so farms can prepare for the months ahead, feed livestock, and sustain their operations,” Spanberger said in a statement.
Although drought conditions have improved in some parts of the state since earlier this year, some regions have experienced losses of up to 70% losses in hay yields. Southern Virginia along the North Carolina border remains under emergency drought conditions, according to the Department of Environmental Quality.
The dry conditions have left pastures without enough grass for cattle, forcing farmers to tap into their hay supplies earlier in the grazing season than usual. That means they must purchase more hay heading into winter.
“Extreme drought conditions across the commonwealth have left cattle producers without the forage stocks needed to support many of our herds this winter,” Virginia Cattlemen’s Association Executive Director Brandon Reeves said in a statement.
While the order grants exemptions for over-width deliveries, gross and axle weight limits remain in effect.
“Farmers are very resilient and innovative, and this transportation waiver will shorten the timeline for hay deliveries and also save significant trucking costs for producers purchasing supplemental hay as part of their overall drought management strategy,” Dan Goerlich and Stephanie Cornnell with the Virginia Cooperative Extension said in a statement.
The emergency declaration allows state agencies to coordinate support for farmers, implement emergency plans and grant temporary waivers as drought conditions continue.
The executive order took effect immediately and will remain in place for 45 days unless amended or rescinded. The over-width waiver will begin Oct. 1 and last for 30 days.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Your Questions About Mississippi Data Centers, Answered
description: Site of Amazon's data center under construction in Canton on Saturday, Oct. 4, 2025.
text:
Mississippi Today has been reporting on proposed data centers across the state. State leaders say the industry is a key driver for Mississippi’s economic future.
In Mississippi and across the U.S., residents have voiced concerns about potential energy costs and water usage, as well as air and noise pollution from the generators needed to power data centers. At the same time, data centers represent a historic investment in the state that is fueling demand in the construction industry, paying millions in taxes to school districts and local governments. 
There are a lot of unknowns with data centers in Mississippi given how early the state is in the buildout. The first project was announced in 2024. Read our past reporting here.
Map of data centers in Mississippi: Confirmed and potential projects

Here are answers to some frequently asked questions about data centers:
Data Centers 101
What are data centers?
A data center is a physical space that houses equipment, such as servers and routers, needed to process, store and distribute data.
Data is essential to the way we use the internet today. When we log into our email or watch a movie on Netflix, we are generating and using data. That data is stored on servers inside data centers.
What is artificial intelligence, or AI?
Artificial Intelligence is a broad term meaning a computer or system that can perform tasks generally associated with human intelligence, such as problem solving, learning and decision making. 
Chatbots, such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude, are examples of generative AI. Generative AI doesn’t just recognize patterns, it uses that pattern recognition to produce new content, such as text and photos. 
In order to create new content, these models have to be trained on huge amounts of data. This is a time and energy consuming process that requires tens of thousands of computer chips. The chips are stored in data centers.
If data centers have been around for a long time, why are so many being built right now?
Generative AI requires a lot of computing power, and there’s not enough right now to support the current and anticipated demand. Tech companies are racing to build more data centers to train and deploy new AI models. 
The chips, physical infrastructure and construction of such a large number of data centers is expensive, which is why companies are spending hundreds of billions to build data centers.
So, why build a data center in Mississippi?
Data centers need a large amount of reliable power and land, and companies are looking to build them quickly. Mississippi offers all of the above. In addition, leaders at Amazon have said the partnership and collaboration with Entergy and state officials and lack of strict regulations have made the process of building the data centers here effective and quick. 
Mississippi has relatively few data centers, compared to other states. The 10 states with the most data centers have over 100.

Water & Environmental Impact
How much water do data centers need, and how will they impact our water supply?
The short answer is it depends on the facility.
Large data centers, which often need water for cooling, use up to 5 million gallons a day, or the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute. Yet some, such as Amazon’s planned facility in Clinton, will instead implement “air cooling,” meaning they won’t need large volumes of water. The company is also planning to use recycled municipal wastewater at its Canton data center in a partnership with Veolia. 
As far as where they get water from, a data center can either purchase water from a local utility or dig a well, in which case it would need a permit from the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality. 
Regarding other data centers coming to Mississippi, companies have not said much publicly yet about their water footprints, but this is something we’ll be focusing on in our ongoing coverage.
What noise and air pollution levels will nearby communities experience?
Noise and air pollution concerns come primarily from data centers that self-generate power. The most glaring example we’ve reported on has been xAI’s cluster of natural gas turbines in Southaven. Because those turbines operate in a state-sanctioned loophole that allows them to run without permits, there’s no official data on how much toxic emissions are coming from the facilities. The Southern Environmental Law Center argued in a lawsuit that the cluster is likely emitting harmful amounts of nitrogen oxides and formaldehyde.  
Moreover, Southaven residents for months complained about a constant humming noise coming from the facility. Mississippi Today reporters could confirm hearing the noise when visiting the area.
What are the primary power sources for data centers?
For the most part, data centers in Mississippi will source their power from whichever utility owns the service area for that facility, such as Entergy Mississippi and Mississippi Power. It’s hard to delineate which types of power go to which places, as utility companies blend power from an array of sources before sending electricity to an end user. Entergy has said that investments from data center companies such as Amazon will help the utility bolster its natural gas generation. Mississippi Power also successfully petitioned to keep an aging coal unit alive to power a data center in Meridian.

Impact on electric bills?
Will data centers drive up my utility bill?
Last year, Entergy Mississippi CEO Haley Fisackerly told Mississippi Today that customers’ electric bills will go up less than they would have without the arrival of Amazon’s data centers. Because of the immense amount of power Amazon will have to buy to run the facilities, Entergy will be able to use that revenue to make grid improvements it otherwise wouldn’t be able to, the company said. According to Entergy, customers’ bills were going to go up regardless as both prices and demand for gas are rising, necessitating new generation capacity. But limited information around Amazon’s projected energy use, as well as limited oversight approved by state lawmakers in 2024, makes it hard to verify those claims. A recent report from Synapse Energy Economics Inc. estimates that the data center projects have already increased rates for Entergy Mississippi’s residential customers by $10.60 a month.
How much power does a data center use?
According to research from the International Energy Agency, a typical AI-focused data center uses enough electricity to power 100,000 homes. Another report, from the Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, found that data centers accounted for over 4% of the country’s electricity consumption in 2023, adding that the number could reach as high as 12% by 2028.

Economic Impacts
How many jobs do data centers create?
Amazon has said its data centers across the state will create 2,000 jobs, AVAIO in Brandon said it will create at least 60 direct jobs, xAI in Southaven said the project will create hundreds of permanent jobs and Compass in Meridian is expected to create thousands of direct and indirect jobs. 
The projects also create new jobs in construction and other indirect jobs, such as, service providers, caterers, electricians and more
In other states, the number can range from 50 to 400. Critics say the number of jobs is relatively few, especially relative to the size of capital investment. But proponents say new jobs are new jobs, that these jobs pay well and that services/surrounding businesses benefit from the center which creates more jobs in the area.
What are the benefits of having a data center in a community?
Like many things, it is a benefits vs risks situation. How do governments and companies maximize benefits for the community and minimize risks?  
People often point to Virginia, given the large number of data centers built and operated in the state over the past 15 years. An important caveat is that the technology has significantly evolved since then. 
Here’s a story on how a community used tax revenue from data centers to create an affordable housing program.  
In Loudon County, Virginia, sometimes known as Data Center Alley, the economic developer who led the data center development told the Wall Street Journal that he estimated property taxes are down 48 cents on the dollar in the county and 45% of county revenue comes from data centers.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Mothers, reproductive rights group sue Oklahoma officials over abortion ban
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Two Oklahoma mothers, who said they were forced to leave the state in order to terminate unviable pregnancies, sued state leaders Wednesday, challenging the limits of the state’s abortion ban. Magon Hoffman and Sheena Hamlin each had to spend thousands of dollars to leave the state to receive abortion care after prenatal […]
text:
An abortion procedure room pictured on March 3, 2025 at Planned Parenthood in Columbia, Missouri. (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).OKLAHOMA CITY — Two Oklahoma mothers, who said they were forced to leave the state in order to terminate unviable pregnancies, sued state leaders Wednesday, challenging the limits of the state’s abortion ban.
Magon Hoffman and Sheena Hamlin each had to spend thousands of dollars to leave the state to receive abortion care after prenatal testing determined their pregnancies were unviable or had fatal diagnoses, according to the lawsuit filed in Oklahoma County District Court. Medical professionals warned both women that their pregnancies would result in either stillbirth or an agonizing death for their wanted children shortly after birth, the lawsuit states. 
The Center for Reproductive Rights filed the lawsuit on the mothers’ behalf against Attorney General Gentner Drummond, Oklahoma County District Attorney Vicki Behenna, Commissioner of the State Health Department Keith Reed, Executive Director of the State Board of Medical Licensure and Supervision Sandra Harrison, and Executive Director of the State Board of Osteopathic Examiners Steven Mullins.
Their lawsuit argues that Oklahoma’s abortion bans violate pregnant women’s right to “life and liberty, their substantive due process rights, and their rights to equal protection.” The state Supreme Court in 2023 affirmed Oklahomans’ right to life-saving abortion care, and the lawsuit asks the courts to apply the same rights to pregnancies with fatal fetal diagnoses.
Two Oklahoma doctors who specialize in obstetrics and gynecology and the Oklahoma Call for Reproductive Justice are also named as plaintiffs. 
Attorney General Gentner Drummond, a defendant in the lawsuit, gives a speech at the Edmond History Museum on Aug. 19, 2025, in Edmond. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Currently, Oklahoma only allows abortion in very narrow circumstances, to save the life of the mother.
At 14 weeks pregnant, Hoffman suffered heavy bleeding and learned she had a “huge blood clot,” which required bed rest, according to the lawsuit. After her baby’s growth looked unusual, at 19 weeks, she underwent an anatomy scan with a maternal-fetal medicine specialist. The specialist diagnosed her baby with anencephaly, and said it had a “tiny bit of brain floating around,” but “no skull” and had “no chance of survival,” according to the lawsuit. 
The specialist told Hoffman the baby would not survive, and she had two options, leave the state to obtain an abortion or continue the pregnancy to term. If she carried to term, it was possible she could deliver a child who might live for a few hours or days, but would “be blind and dying,” according to the lawsuit.  
She and her husband later decided to travel to New Mexico to terminate the pregnancy, but because her insurance would not cover an out-of-state procedure Hoffman had to pay $3,000 out of pocket for her care, according to the lawsuit. Hoffman also lost her job because of the time she had to take off for her abortion, the lawsuit says.
“Oklahoma turned the hardest day of my life into weeks of needless suffering on top of our grief,” she said in a statement. “I had to travel eight hours out of state to get care, far from my home, my family, and my support system when I needed them most. Oklahoma is failing families like mine.”
Hamlin said when she went in for a routine anatomy scan at 21 weeks, her doctor referred her to a high-risk pregnancy specialist for additional testing. The follow up ultrasound found that her pregnancy was “not compatible with life,” according to the lawsuit. It appeared her unborn child, who Hamlin had named Ellie, had a lethal condition that resulted in a “sac-like protrusion of the brain through an opening at the back of the skull,” kidney cysts, scar tissue in the liver, and extra fingers and toes, the lawsuit says.
The specialist said Ellie would likely die before being born, but Hamlin could try to carry the pregnancy to term. But because the child’s lungs would be so severely underdeveloped, Ellie would “suffocate as soon as the umbilical cord was cut,” according to the lawsuit.  
Hamlin and her husband decided they didn’t want their daughter to suffer, so they spent $4,000 out of pocket to travel to Illinois for abortion care. 
Oklahoma’s laws denied her family the “mercy” they wanted for their daughter, she said in a statement. 
“I should have been able to get the care I needed at home,” Hamlin said. 
Mullins, who heads the state’s osteopathic examiners board and is a defendant in the lawsuit, said he had not been served, but looks forward to “the defense of the laws of Oklahoma by the excellent lawyers employed by the Oklahoma Attorney General.”
A spokesperson for the Oklahoma Attorney General’s Office said they are still reviewing the lawsuit.
A spokesperson for the Oklahoma Health Department said they had not yet been served, but that the agency does not comment on pending litigation.
Oklahoma Health Commissioner Keith Reed, a defendant in the lawsuit, is pictured at a ribbon cutting ceremony in Oklahoma City on Feb. 27, 2026. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Harrison, who leads the state’s medical licensure board, also said she had not been served and had no comment.
The Oklahoma County District Attorney’s Office did not return a request for comment by the time of publication.
Nancy Northup, president and CEO of the Center for Reproductive Rights, said the pain these families have been put through because of Oklahoma’s abortion ban is “unthinkable.” 
“Forcing women to give birth knowing they won’t be bringing a baby home is pure cruelty,” she said in a statement. “Every pregnant person should get to decide what is best for their family based on their own beliefs, values, and medical circumstances. The government should have no place in that. We’re suing to hold the state accountable for the pain lawmakers have caused these families, and to make sure no other families suffer in this way.”
This year, state lawmakers further restricted access to abortion care when Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt signed a bill making it a felony to distribute abortion-inducing drugs. 
Oklahoma’s infant mortality rate in 2024 ranked sixth highest in the U.S., according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 
Dr. Elizabeth Pinard, an OB-GYN in Oklahoma City and a plaintiff in the lawsuit, said the state’s abortion bans have made her feel “helpless.”
“I don’t want to tell my patients to leave the state when I can easily give them the care they need right here in my office,” she said in a statement. “This is not how health care should work. My patients deserve access to all of their options for care, and the state needs to allow us to do our jobs.”
The Center for Reproductive Rights has filed similar lawsuits in Texas, Idaho and Tennessee, according to a news release. 
Reporter Barbara Hoberock contributed to this story.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: NDA secrecy for major projects hovers over Louisiana’s congressional elections
description: Congresswoman Julia Letlow, the Republican U.S. Senate candidate, doesn’t want to answer questions about the nondisclosure agreement she signed with a Meta company about Richland Parish’s $50 billion dollar data center project, said Jamie Davis, the Democratic candidate.
text:
Congresswoman Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, signed an nondisclosure agreement about the Meta data center project in Richland Parish in 2024. Her opponent in the U.S. Senate race, Democrat Jamie Davis, is trying to make her NDA into a campaign issue for voters. (Photo by Piper Hutchinson/Louisiana Illuminator)Jamie Davis believes there’s one specific reason Congresswoman Julia Letlow hasn’t agreed to appear in person with him for debates or any other events during their U.S. Senate race. 
Letlow, the Republican candidate, doesn’t want to answer questions about the nondisclosure agreement she signed with a Meta company about Richland Parish’s $50 billion dollar data center project, he said. 
“Any other questions I want to ask about Meta, she won’t be able to answer because she might break her NDA,” said Davis, the Democratic candidate. 
Letlow not only signed the NDA but also began buying stock Meta and Nvidia, a company that makes computer equipment for data centers, in the months that followed, according to reporting from Gulf States Newsroom. The congresswoman didn’t disclose the stock purchases publicly until more than a year after the federal deadline to do so. 
By signing the NDA, Letlow might have had access to information about Meta’s business operations and finances not available to the public. 
Letlow’s campaign spokesperson did not respond to multiple requests  this week for comment about the NDA. But in August, her congressional staff told Gulf States Newsroom she was unaware the Meta and Nvidia trades were happening on her behalf at the time. 
As Louisiana undergoes an industrial megaproject boom, the extent to which public officials are trading away public transparency for economic investment through NDAs has become controversial. 
Dozens of local and state elected officials signed NDAs related to economic development projects such as the SpaceX complex in Vermilion Parish, the Hyundai steel plant in Ascension Parish and data centers in other parts of the state. 

More than 100 employees in Gov. Jeff Landry’s office also signed blanket NDAs prohibiting them from talking about what they learn working for the governor. 

Landry and his administration have said the NDAs are necessary to attract global brands. But the agreements raise questions about whether government officials are free to share information about the projects’ impacts on resources such as water and the electrical grid.  
LSU political science professor Robert Hogan said backlash over NDAs is part of a broader “general distrust that people have of government” right now. 
“I do believe this could be a very effective issue at sowing seeds of doubt in the minds of voters about people who signed these,” Hogan said in an interview this week.

As the underdog in the Senate race, Davis is trying to make Letlow’s Meta NDA into a campaign issue and brought it up during a speaking engagement at LSU this week. 
Davis said he never signed an NDA when he was an elected member of the Tensas Parish Police Jury and wouldn’t sign one if he was elected to the Senate. 
NDAs could creep into competitive US House races
In addition to the Senate race, the NDA issue could come up in the U.S. House  races, including open races for the 5th and 6th congressional districts, where many of the closely guarded industrial projects will take shape. 

Four state legislators and the chair of the Board of Regents, which oversees state higher education, are among the nine candidates running to replace Letlow in the 5th District. 

Of the five major candidates, two said they signed NDAs as elected officials in order to receive information about economic development projects. 

State Sen. Stewart Cathey, R-Monroe, confirmed he signed an NDA to learn basic details about the Meta data center coming to Richland Parish from state Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois before the project was publicly announced. 
Even after he signed the agreement, Cathey said Bourgeois would only tell him it was a data center project and not the name of the company behind the site. He’s not sure if he would sign an NDA again if elected to Congress. 

“The only legislators who have not signed NDAs are people who weren’t asked,” Cathey said. 
State Rep. Gabe Firment, R-Pollock, said he signed an NDA required to attend a meeting about a data center under construction in Rapides Parish, but the information shared at the meeting didn’t turn out to be particularly confidential. 
“I would not sign one again,” Firment said. “A lot of people I represent and I may represent in the future are not comfortable with that.” 

State Rep. Mike Echols, R-Monroe is one of the three 5th District contenders who has not signed an NDA as an elected official. He said he also wouldn’t sign one as a member of Congress. 
“I want to be as transparent as possible. I don’t see value for me,” Echols said. 

State Rep. Pat Moore of Monroe, the Democratic Party-endorsed candidate, said she has not signed an NDA as a legislator and could not recall signing one while a member on the Ouachita Parish Policy Jury. 

Misti Cordell, a Republican from West Monroe who leads the Board of Regents, said she hadn’t signed an NDA while in her current public position.

But Moore and Cordell wouldn’t rule out signing NDAs if elected to Congress. 

Cordell said she would make sure any agreement she signed didn’t require her to shield information about what might hurt the public. 
Moore said she wouldn’t personally benefit from any information she received through an NDA. 
“If there was confidential information that I could not disclose, I would not do anything to profit off of it,” Moore said. 
Two legislators are also among the 10 candidates running to replace U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields, D-Baton Rouge, in the 6th District. Fields decided against running again after state lawmakers redrew the district’s lines to make it harder for a Democrat to win. 

State Sen. Rick Edmonds, R-Baton Rouge, said he has signed one NDA with the Louisiana Economic Development agency. He said he couldn’t say whether he would sign any if elected to Congress because he doesn’t know entirely what the position would entail yet. 

State Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, did not return phone calls seeking comment on his policy regarding NDAs. It’s not clear whether he has signed one as an elected official. 

Two Democrats in the race, Pat Forbes and Lindsay Garcia, have not held elected positions previously and said they would not sign NDAs if elected to Congress. 
“I don’t think NDAs have any place in government,” said Forbes, who led disaster relief efforts as the head of the state Office of Community Development for several years.

“There is a distinct irony in you serving the interest of the public while keeping the public in the dark,” said Garcia, a community organizer and former teacher who graduated from Southern University Law Center last year.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Remembering veterans on Agent Orange Awareness Day and beyond
description: Agent Orange Awareness Day, though not an official federal holiday, is observed in the Beehive State and the rest of the country each year on August 10. That specific date was not arbitrarily chosen. According to the Blinded Veterans Association, the U.S. began spraying Agent Orange in Vietnam on August 10, 1961. Although its use […]
text:
Vietnam veterans affected by Agent Orange chemical exposure pose for a photo with the Rivetin' Rosie's Project at the Utah Capitol on Feb. 12, 2026, the day they were recognized by the Utah Legislature. Hannah Turk, a Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation board member, is at the far left. (Photo courtesy of Hannah Turk)Agent Orange Awareness Day, though not an official federal holiday, is observed in the Beehive State and the rest of the country each year on August 10.
That specific date was not arbitrarily chosen. According to the Blinded Veterans Association, the U.S. began spraying Agent Orange in Vietnam on August 10, 1961.
Although its use was intended to save American lives, the herbicide turned out to be extremely harmful to humans and the environment. That was because Agent Orange contained the toxic chemical dioxin.
Dioxin was a consequence of Agent Orange production. According to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, dioxin was an unwelcome byproduct of the chemical’s manufacturing process. 
As a result of exposure to Agent Orange and similar toxic herbicides, hundreds of thousands of Vietnam veterans have died from one or more illnesses associated with those chemicals. 
In Sunset Veterans Park, the Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation has been increasing public awareness of the tragic cost of using toxic chemicals during the war in Southeast Asia. 
Since last November, the foundation has been actively engaged in building one of the largest Agent Orange memorials in the United States. 
A number of organizations have been helping support the foundation throughout its ambitious mission. Among them is the Rivetin’ Rosie’s Project. 
In observance of Agent Orange Awareness Day, the organization shared a message on its Facebook page paying homage to victims of Agent Orange exposure and reminding that its effects continue today. 
The group also supported the Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation earlier this year. On Feb. 12, patriotic members showed up at the Capitol in Salt Lake City for a ceremony honoring Vietnam veterans exposed to Agent Orange and similar toxic herbicides.
They were in attendance to support Hannah Turk, a Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation board member, who helped facilitate the event. Hannah is also a co-founder and vice president of the Rivetin’ Rosie’s Project. 
The veterans at the ceremony and all Utah veterans exposed to Agent Orange were recognized with an official citation, which was read aloud by Rep. Tyler Clancy on the floor of the House of Representatives.
The presence of members of the Rivetin’ Rosie’s Project made the event even more memorable by evoking a nostalgic glimpse of a bygone era — a time when millions of American women symbolized by Rosie the Riveter helped the U.S. win WWII. 
As a Utah veteran, it is heartening to know that organizations like the Rivetin’ Rosie’s Project are striving to make a positive difference in the lives of veterans on special occasions like Agent Orange Awareness Day and other important times throughout the year.
One of those times is right around the corner, as October marks Agent Orange Awareness Month. It was established because a one-day observance did not seem like an adequate amount of time to increase awareness of the toxic chemical, and the month includes events that recognize veterans harmed by exposure to Agent Orange and similar toxic herbicides.
October also seems like an appropriate time for Utah lawmakers to consider joining the growing number of legislators in more than a dozen states who have officially recognized the Orange Heart Medal. 
While the medal is not yet an official federal award, it is nevertheless an extremely meaningful and well-deserved tribute to veterans who sustained internal injuries from exposure to Agent Orange.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Former Indiana utility regulator calls firing a ‘fishing expedition,’ denies spending allegations
description: Andy Zay rejected allegations he misspent campaign money — and said he settled because he didn't have the time or money to continued the lawsuit.
text:
Former utility regulator Andy Zay speaks with the Indiana Capital Chronicle on Tuesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Despite agreeing to settle his contentious lawsuit against the state, fired Indiana utility regulator Andy Zay maintains that his dismissal was manufactured to change the outcome in a now-pending review of a $71 million electricity rate increase for AES Indiana.
In an interview with the Capital Chronicle, Zay rejected the Braun administration’s allegations he misspent campaign money from his previous role as a state senator — but said he agreed to the $625,000 settlement because he didn’t have the time or money to see the lawsuit through.
“I never would have done anything to embarrass the administration, the (Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission), the work that we were doing,” he said Tuesday. “… They were on a big fishing expedition to move myself on, to get somebody in that would vote for the appeal, and I think that played out very publicly.”
Griffin Reid, a spokesperson for Gov. Mike Braun, slammed Zay’s remarks.
“Hoosier ratepayers should rest easy knowing they no longer have to guard their wallets from Andy Zay’s terrible judgment,” Reid said, in response to a request for comment from the Capital Chronicle. “This latest unhinged rant is just another sad chapter in his failed career in public service.”
The five-member IURC plays a key role in determining how much Hoosiers pay for electricity, natural gas, water and more.
Zay was one of three commissioners who voted in June to approve a $71 million base rate increase on AES Indiana customers.
AES Indiana’s downtown Indianapolis headquarters are pictured Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Braun — who previously appointed Zay to the commission as chairman — denounced the rate decision, demoted Zay and called for a redo. Indiana Utility Consumer Counselor Abby Gray filed a petition asking regulators to reconsider or rehear the case.
“Honestly, there wasn’t much new,” Zay said of the petition. “It was a lot of the stuff in the main case carried forward and repeated.”
“The problem, at that point, was if we don’t set the guardrails, if we don’t protect the IURC, we’re going to be looking over our shoulder on every decision we make,” he said. “And our intent at that point was just to stand by the order.”
A denial was finalized for consideration at an upcoming meeting.
“On Monday we (published) the agenda, the governor found out about noon, and I was fired at 3:35,” Zay said.
“I feel it’s greatly compromised now,” he said of the commission. “I think they are beyond the … mission of the IURC, they’re beyond statute with the political influence.”
Campaign finance allegations disputed
Zay filed a lawsuit alleging the firing was illegal — commissioners can only be dismissed “for cause” under Indiana law — and motivated by the Braun administration’s desire for control over the AES rate case.
Braun’s legal team fired back with allegations that Zay improperly used about $3,000 in campaign funds to give utility-themed ties and scarves emblazoned with his initials to commission staffers after he’d left the Indiana Senate.
Zay, a Republican from Huntington, resigned on Jan. 8 from the Senate seat he’d held since 2016 and began work at the IURC on Jan. 12.
Braun names 3 new utility commissioners, creating Senate GOP vacancy

But Zay said he made the purchase before switching jobs, even though the credit card statement didn’t come until Feb. 1. He provided the Capital Chronicle with a credit card statement showing the spending went through before he started at the IURC.
“I already had somebody announced to run against me in that seat in the primary, so I had some money,” he told the Capital Chronicle. “… And once (the appointment) was announced, I knew that hard deadline.”
He has been designing custom ties and scarves for about seven years and has cycled through a variety of symbols over that time, like the state flower. Zay said he considered an education theme when he began designing his latest order in November or December, but chose energy after hitting five years on the Senate utilities committee.
“I had a lot of campaign stuff left over, and I worked with my general counsel,” Zay said. “She said, ‘No, don’t hand them out, but have them there as surplus. And if people want to grab them, offer that to them. And that’s exactly how they were done.”
Fifty scarves and 50 ties, worth about $30 each, went up for grabs.
Zay shuffled through papers during this week’s interview, looking through other transactions made just before his departure from the Statehouse: tenderloins at Loughmiller’s Pub for Senate commerce committee members to celebrate the chamber’s passage of his state sandwich bill, a farewell dinner with his Senate staffers at St. Elmo Steak House.
There was another, too: a $15,000 donation to a Braun-aligned campaign fund.
“To show I was a team player, and knowing I couldn’t access my campaign money, I made a pretty good donation to the governor at that time, and that check didn’t clear (until after the job switch) either,” he said. “But, you know, it was kind of interesting that that didn’t come up in the conversation.”
‘Fighting the bank’
Despite his denial of the campaign finance and other claims, Zay agreed to settle with the state.
He received $485,000 in pay and benefits through the end of his expected four-year term on the utility commission, plus $140,000 in legal expenses.
“I’m fighting the bank, so to speak, and going against the house,” Zay said. “And, you know, I didn’t know what to do at that point. And I think there were a lot of wrongs, which has been pretty clearly delineated in litigation, but to take it all the way would have been very difficult.”
Zay plans to lay a low during his statutory yearlong “cooling-off” period from any lobbying work involving the Statehouse and the commission. He said he is watching his son’s football season at the University of Toledo and expecting a fifth grandchild while thinking about what’s next.
The IURC is scheduled to meet Thursday afternoon for a prehearing conference and preliminary hearing in the AES Indiana case.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: After gas companies’ appeal, PURA again orders rate cuts
description: The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority ordered rate decreases for customers of two CT gas companies, following a lengthy legal battle.
text:
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority ordered rate decreases for customers of two Connecticut gas companies on Wednesday, following a lengthy legal battle in which regulators admitted making procedural errors under former PURA chief Marissa Gillett.
Those errors forced a judge to toss the authority’s original 2024 decision cutting rates for the two companies, Southern Connecticut Gas and Connecticut Natural Gas, by a combined $35 million.
On remand, however, PURA ordered even larger cuts totaling $37 million, or about 4.2% of current revenues. Much of the reduction was due to regulators’ determination that the two companies must return $120 million in past overcollections to customers by Nov. 30, 2027. PURA also approved a return on equity of 9.20% for both companies.
“PURA was right from the start to slash these rates,” Attorney General William Tong said in a statement Wednesday. “Connecticut families cannot afford to bankroll padded profits and unsupported and unnecessary expenses.” 
Tong added, “CNG was over-collecting millions of dollars from Connecticut families before they had the gall to ask for more. PURA got this one right.”
Both SGC and CNG are subsidiaries of Avangrid, which also owns the United Illuminating electric company based in Orange. 
Angela Baccaro, an Avangrid spokeswoman, said in a statement on Wednesday that the decision to cut the companies’ revenues would play a “significant role” in their ability to make future investments in the state’s gas infrastructure.
“We are reviewing PURA’s decision and are disappointed that it does not meaningfully resolve the concerns raised by the Superior Court, which found clear evidence of prejudice and bias against CNG and SCG and concluded the companies had not received the fair legal process required by law,” Baccaro said. “This final outcome remains largely unchanged from the original decision and leaves critical issues unresolved, despite their significant operational, financial, and customer impacts.”
Neither PURA nor Avangrid immediately released a bill impact assessment on either decision Wednesday. 
Both of the remanded rate cases were approved by a 3-0 vote of the authority on Wednesday morning. PURA Chairman Thomas Wiehl, who worked on the previous applications of SCG and CNG while serving as an attorney for the state Office of Consumer Counsel, recused from both decisions.
Vice Chair David Arconti, who previously worked as a lobbyist for United Illuminating, also signaled his intention to recuse from both dockets, Wiehl said. Arconti did not participate in Wednesday’s meeting. 
One of the commissioners who supported the decisions, Janice Beecher, defended the authority’s handling of the remanded cases. Each of the commissioners involved, she said, took a fresh look at cases before issuing their final decision.
“The new findings are not tweaks, they reflect our judgement of the facts and issues of this case,” Beecher said.  
Gillett, the former chair, stepped down in October after facing growing scrutiny from lawmakers and utility officials over her leadership of PURA. Within weeks of her departure, attorneys representing the authority in the appeal of SCG and CNG’s rate cases conceded that Gillett had violated the law by appointing herself “presiding officer” over matters before PURA, without a vote of her fellow commissioners.
Gillett also faced allegations that she deleted text messages with lawmakers to hide her involvement in drafting an op-ed that was harshly critical of the state’s utility companies, including Avangrid and Eversource. Gillett denied the allegations.  
The judge overseeing Avangrid’s appeal of the original SCG/CNG cases, Matthew Budzik of the New Britain Superior Court, also referred two attorneys representing PURA to the Statewide Grievance Committee to determine whether they misled the court during the effort to uncover Gillett’s personal phone records.
An attorney for the Grievance Committee, which reviews ethics complaints against lawyers, said in an email Wednesday that there was no public resolution to either referral.

title: Hunters, anglers and nearly everyone else supports the roadless rule
description: The roadless rule is the single most important regulation that benefits hunting and fishing in America. The rule has been in place for 25 years, a habitat-enhancing force of nature since I started hunting elk some 20 years ago, with nearly universal popularity from the start. As Trout Unlimited President and CEO Chris Wood explained, […]
text:
A view of Oak Flat Trail in Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park, Montrose County, Colorado, in 2012. (Photo courtesy of NPS)The roadless rule is the single most important regulation that benefits hunting and fishing in America. The rule has been in place for 25 years, a habitat-enhancing force of nature since I started hunting elk some 20 years ago, with nearly universal popularity from the start.
As Trout Unlimited President and CEO Chris Wood explained, “1.6 million comments with 93% in favor came when the Roadless Rule was originally established in 2001.”
The roadless rule is a U.S. Forest Service policy that protects 58.2 million acres of roadless areas in national forests and grasslands from being sold for timber, roadbuilding, mining, or oil-and-gas drilling. The rule itself doesn’t prohibit hunting, fishing, motorized recreation, or other public uses — it regulates land management options in these areas. It places limits on industrial logging and mining, and the associated road-building those activities require.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While serving as chief of the U.S. Forest Service, Mike Dombeck was struck by the Roadless Area Conservation Rule (i.e., “roadless rule”) support.
“We are hard-pressed to think of many other policies carried on through six presidents — three Republican and three Democratic,” Dombeck and Chris Wood said in a September 2025 Seattle Times opinion piece. “The roadless rule’s staying power reflects its popularity.”
Unfortunately, last summer the Trump administration announced its intention to rescind the rule. The move is wildly unpopular among hunters, anglers, and nearly everyone else. During the 2025 public comment period, out of 625,930 comments received 99% opposed repealing the roadless rule. As hunters know from boots on the ground experience, roadless areas protect some of the best elk, mule deer and black bear habitat in Colorado and the country.
However, two states — Colorado and Idaho — have their own roadless rules, which are not currently being considered for rescission. A recent analysis by onX Hunt Maps looked at hunting and other recreational opportunities in roadless areas. Here’s a snapshot: 58% of roadless rule areas overlap elk habitat; 78% overlap black bear habitat. In Wyoming, 99% of roadless rule areas serve as elk habitat; in New Hampshire, 97% protect black bear habitat; and in Arizona, 96% serve as mule deer habitat.
In addition, the nation’s 370,000 miles of existing national forest roads (the Earth’s circumference is only 24,000 miles) have a $10-billion-plus maintenance backlog. We don’t need more roads. Also, roadless areas include 17,715 miles of hiking and biking trails, 7,201 miles of full-size motorized trails and roads, nearly 1,500 miles of mapped backcountry ski routes, and 3,000 climbing areas. From the sounds of it, there’s something for everyone in roadless areas.
The onX analysis also shows that a mere 3% of the country’s historical wildfire ignition points over the past 50 years occurred within roadless areas. The rule explicitly allows for wildfire suppression and fuel reduction, including road construction in emergency situations. Studies have also shown that 90% of all wildfires start within a half mile of a road, likely due to increased human interaction.
In addition, these lands were never roaded for a reason. They’re often steep, rocky and have marginal timber values. There’s simply no way to build more roads and make timber sales pencil out for the American taxpayer. That’s why Taxpayers for Common Sense is one of the biggest supporters of the roadless rule. “Repealing the 2001 Roadless Rule risks billions in new taxpayer liabilities from subsidized road construction and money-losing timber sales,” the organization says.
“Roadless areas pay for themselves through hunting, fishing and recreation dollars flowing into gateway communities every year,” said Devin O’Dea, Western conservation and policy manager for Backcountry Hunters & Anglers. “This isn’t fixing a broken system — it’s bulldozing one that already works, putting productive fish and wildlife habitat at risk while undermining the outdoor recreation economies they support.”
“Roads fragment habitat, disperse wildlife, and push elk and deer onto private land, out of reach for the average hunter,” BHA explained in a Sep. 6 Instagram post. “This isn’t a bureaucratic footnote — it’s wholesale elimination of protections for the backcountry habitat hunters, anglers, wildlife, and rural communities depend on,” said Ryan Callaghan, BHA president and CEO. In 2025, we fought like heck to keep our public lands from being sold off, but the war continues.
“There is a war being waged against public lands on a scale we haven’t seen in ages, where … the idea of shared ownership by all (is) replaced by profit and privilege for a few,” New Mexico BHA board member Kyle Klain wrote in the Winter 2026 Backcountry Journal. “BHA is one of the few groups willing to meet those pressures head-on, without apology.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Seven rural community colleges receive $5.93 million for healthcare training
description: Seven community colleges in what the Virginia Community College Association dubs the state’s “rural horseshoe” have received $5.93 million to train more healthcare workers.  Virginia has so far disbursed $122 million of its $198 million in Rural Health Transformation Fund money to organizations around the state. Associations, foundations and the state Health[...]
text:
A healthcare worker training mannequin rests in a bed in a classroom at Eastern Shore Community College. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Seven community colleges in what the Virginia Community College Association dubs the state’s “rural horseshoe” have received $5.93 million to train more healthcare workers. 
Virginia has so far disbursed $122 million of its $198 million in Rural Health Transformation Fund money to organizations around the state. Associations, foundations and the state Health Department have been fielding applications from interested parties. 
Virginia’s blueprint for using the funding is divided into several goals, including addressing healthcare workforce challenges, investing in telehealth, mobile clinics and upgraded healthcare technologies, and supporting chronic disease management and “food as medicine” programs. 
Because community colleges can serve as an entry point for aspiring medical professionals, the RHTF funding for rural colleges is intended to help grow the healthcare workforce in areas of the state that have experienced shortages. 
For Patrick & Henry Community College, the funding means it can add a part-time Licensed Practical Nurse program and a program designed to help LPNs become registered nurses. 
The college already had a full-time LPN program but identified a need among  working parents seeking to enter the field.
“Nursing school is no joke to begin with,” Patrick & Henry President Greg Hodges said. “When you couple that with trying to work and raise a family, that’s very, very challenging. So those students who want to continue to work full time and go to school part time now have that opportunity here.”
The college already partners with Sovah Health Martinsville to provide  students with the clinical hours required as part of their curriculum. But Hodges noted the rural nature of surrounding areas and said students who don’t remain  nearby after earning their degrees can fill positions at other rural hospitals. 


Awardees:

Germanna Community College
Laurel Ridge Community College
Mountain Gateway Community College
Patrick & Henry Community College
Paul D. Camp Community College
Rappahannock Community College
Virginia Highlands Community College



Just as healthcare access more broadly has been a challenge in rural areas, Virginia officials have also noted behavioral health hurdles in those regions. 
Mountain Gateway Community College will be using its RHTF award to expand instruction for future behavioral health workers, said Ben Worth, the college’s vice president of academic affairs. 
“Primarily, we’re talking about bachelor’s-level and master’s-level degrees,” he said of many mental health professions. But the state’s Transfer Virginia program ensures that community college students’ credits can count toward those degrees when they transfer to other institutions. 
That is why Worth said the RHTF can help the college prepare future psychologists and social workers in the region. The funding will support hiring instructors and launching a dual-enrollment program for high school students seeking a head start on earning the degrees they need to enter the workforce. 
“Partly, it’s awareness — making sure (high school students) are aware that there are huge careers out there,” he said. 
Worth added that the college will also focus on existing healthcare workers who lack a bachelor’s degree “so they can do that coursework while they’re still employed, and then earn degrees that can allow them to move up the ladder.”
He said the college’s focus on bolstering the behavioral health workforce also stems from conversations with regional community service boards and hospitals that expressed a need. 
“When we think of healthcare, we don’t always immediately think of mental health needs and behavioral health needs,” Worth said. “So I’m really glad to see that it was included in the list of eligible programs that can be funded through the rural health initiative.”
With the next phase of funding to be announced by the end of next month, the selected community colleges can begin putting their share to work. 
Virginia health leaders, lawmakers share enhanced healthcare resources for rural communities

There are 18 community colleges within the rural horseshoe, which stretches from Virginia’s Eastern Shore in a crescent through Southwest and Southside Virginia and into the mountain region near Winchester. 
Ten colleges applied during the first wave of funding, and seven received awards.
With applications for the second phase of funding having closed on Sep. 14, the Virginia Community Colleges Association anticipates that the next wave of grants will continue to focus on nursing, behavioral health and physical therapy assistants programs. It will also focus on expanding or establishing radiologic technology, sonography and dental hygiene programs. 
As RHTF money continues to roll out around Virginia, patients and providers are bracing for additional strains stemming from other federal actions. 
When Congress created RHTF last summer it also passed H.R. 1, a reconciliation bill that will remove 5,800 lawful immigrants from Medicaid next month and put about 300,000 Virginians at risk of potentially losing coverage by next year. 
Changes to hospital funding mechanisms also stand to strain hospitals as free clinics and other safety-net providers prepare to take on patients who cannot always afford to pay for care. 
The law can also shift more of the cost of funding the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program to states. So far, more than 100,000 Virginians have lost SNAP benefits, which help low-income people and people with disabilities who cannot work stretch their food budgets.  
Virginia Secretary of Health and Human Resources Marvin Figueroa has emphasized that while the RHTF can help alleviate longstanding rural healthcare challenges, it may not be enough to counter certain ripple effects from the reconciliation bill. 
Worth noted that some Mountain Gateway students come from low-income backgrounds, so “SNAP benefits are really important for them.” 
“Food insecurity, housing insecurity, access to transportation, access to childcare,” he said. “Those are all significant needs for some of the students that we serve, and so anything we can do to try to help address that is important.”
Hodges noted “concerns down the road” about the potential impact of H.R. 1 on healthcare. 
For now, he said, the RHTF “gives us a prime opportunity to innovate, to maximize our technology base, and really come out of this.”
