title: Fed raises interest rates for first time in 3 years, battling persistent inflation
text: WASHINGTON — The Federal Reserve raised interest rates Wednesday for the first time in three years as inflation continues to dog the economy, largely driven by soaring gas and fuel oil prices while the war in Iran drags on.The central bank’s Federal Open Market Committee voted 12-0 to increase its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, reaching the new range from 3.75% to 4% and making the cost of borrowing more expensive for Americans.The committee released an upbeat statement touting economic growth at “a solid pace.”“While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little,” according to the statement released Wednesday afternoon.“Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability,” the statement continued.Trump campaign for lower ratesPresident Donald Trump publicly pressured and name-called Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s predecessor Jerome Powell for months for not lowering interest rates. The public attacks escalated into a federal probe of Powell and the Fed for costly renovations at the Fed’s headquarters in Washington. The administration eventually dropped the investigation.The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The interest hike comes less than a week after the government’s latest consumer price index revealed the cost of food, energy, housing and other goods and services rose 0.4% from July to August. The cost of all items over the past year has risen 3.4%.Soaring gas pricesSpiking energy prices caused by the war in Iran were the main driver behind higher costs. Gasoline alone rose 3.9% over the month of August. As of Wednesday, Americans were paying an average of nearly $4.37 a gallon at the pump, according to AAA. Diesel prices reached a record high of $6.31.The price of a barrel of oil surged above $100 in recent days, including Wednesday afternoon, when it reached $105, as fighting flared in the Middle East. The United States and Iran continue launching rockets in the Strait of Hormuz, where one-fifth of the world’s petroleum traveled prior to the war. U.S. Central Command claimed Sept. 8 that it “destroyed” five Iranian crude oil carriers as part of its naval blockade aimed at damaging Iran’s economy.The conflict spilled over in July into another key waterway for Saudi Arabian oil exports. Iran-backed Houthi rebels restarted an assault on commercial vessels in the Red Sea for the first time since 2024, and are fighting for control of the Bab al-Mandab strait. The group also directly struck targets in Saudi Arabia, a U.S. ally, beginning in July, and is threatening more strikes, according to Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree. The United Nations Security Council is warning of the likelihood of a humanitarian crisis.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Supreme Court denies death row inmate’s appeal of incompetence
description: Steven Bixby, 59, received a pause in receiving a death warrant to hear claims of delusions and bizarre beliefs.
text:
The state Supreme Court turned down a last-ditch appeal from inmate Steven Bixby, pictured in a Greenville courtroom on Friday, Aug. 22, 2025. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — The state’s highest court turned down a last-ditch effort Wednesday for a death row inmate to avoid execution.
The one-line order could open the door for Steven Bixby to receive a death warrant as soon as Friday. The last execution the state carried out took place in November 2025.
Death row inmate convicted of killing 2 cops is competent for execution, SC judge says

Bixby’s attorneys could attempt to appeal the decision at the federal level. Whether they will do so is unclear. Bixby’s lead attorney did not immediately respond to a call requesting comment.
Bixby, who was convicted in 2007 of gunning down two police officers during a 13-hour standoff in his parents’ Abbeville house, ran out of normal appeals before the state resumed executions in September 2024.
Initially among five inmates slated for back-to-back executions, Bixby’s attorneys asked for a pause in his case, arguing he wasn’t competent to face the death chamber.
Bixby, 59, maintained during a two-day hearing in August 2025 that he did nothing wrong and a judge might still overturn his death sentence. He also told his attorneys he saw an angel at the crime scene, found special significance in numbers and believes most laws are unconstitutional, according to court filings.
Inmates must have a grasp on reality and the ability to communicate with lawyers to face the death chamber, the state Supreme Court has previously ruled.
Bixby met those benchmarks, even though his beliefs were sometimes atypical, making him competent for execution, a circuit court judge ruled last year.
Delusions or political opinions? SC judge to decide if inmate is competent for execution

Bixby’s attorneys then asked the state Supreme Court to weigh in, arguing the judge put too much belief in the state’s experts and didn’t address the full incompetence claim.
The court denied the appeal Wednesday.
If he received a death warrant, Bixby would be the eighth man executed since the state resumed the process in September 2024, following an unintended 13-year hiatus.
He’s one of 21 people on South Carolina’s death row. One inmate who received a death warrant in South Carolina is housed in California for crimes committed there.
One other inmate, Gary Terry, is also awaiting a decision from the court as to whether he is competent for execution.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont administration signals universal free school lunch is still on the menu
description: Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz told CT superintendents the Lamont administration wants free breakfasts and lunches for all public school students.
text:
Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz told Connecticut superintendents on Tuesday the Lamont administration wants free breakfasts and lunches for all public school students by next year. 
Legislators in the General Assembly called for exactly that during the 2026 legislative session, but the proposal didn’t make it into the final budget. What did was a narrower $12 million proposal from Gov. Ned Lamont: free breakfasts for all, and free lunches for students currently paying a reduced price.
“The governor and I are looking forward next year to add universal lunch, as well,” Bysiewicz told school leaders, drawing applause. “Because our students can’t learn without food in their stomachs.”
Schools have long offered free meals to students who qualify, but proponents of universal programs argue the restrictions on eligibility create problems. Some students from low-income families avoid taking free meals out of shame; if everyone eats for free, proponents say, that stigma goes away. Other students come from families that don’t qualify but are still struggling financially; with universal free meal programs, that’s no longer an issue.
Further complicating matters is the erosion of SNAP benefits since the passage of 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Enrollment in SNAP is one way families qualify for free school meals, and losing SNAP eligibility can bump families off the free meal list. A July report found nearly 18,900 Connecticut children have lost SNAP benefits since the bill was signed into law.
Bysiewicz told The Connecticut Mirror that concerns about affordability are a factor in the universal lunch conversation.
“It’s a major priority for the governor and I to lower costs for families, and if families don’t have to worry about providing breakfast and lunch for their kids, that’s a big thing,” Bysiewicz said.
The state’s free breakfast program is now in effect, though just weeks into the school year, it’s too early to say what kind of impact it’s having or how well that $12 million allocation is covering the cost. Bysiewicz said the administration still has to work out what adding universal free lunch would cost the state, too, before announcing a concrete proposal.
The Republican challenger in this year’s gubernatorial election, Sen. Ryan Fazio, expressed surprise that the Lamont administration is signaling a desire to pursue universal free lunches.
“I guess I would ask what his rationale is,” Fazio said. 
He expressed a degree of skepticism toward the idea, though he said he’s open to proposals.
“I’m for free and reduced [price] meals for … low and middle-income students. I don’t want middle-class taxpayers paying to subsidize the meals of millionaires’ kids,” Fazio said.
Bysiewicz said she hopes this year’s successful passage of the universal breakfast program will make it easier to get a lunch program over the finish line in 2027.
“Sometimes it takes good ideas a little while to happen, and sometimes good ideas happen in phases,” she said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: A data center in the tiny town of Walls? Officials eye rezoning 1K acres
description: Site of the state's mega center, which includes the Amazon data center currently under construction in Canton, Saturday,  Oct. 4, 2025.
text:
An application to rezone over 1,000 acres from agricultural to light-industrial use is facing intense public scrutiny in the small town of Walls. 
While there appears to be no project at this stage, some believe that the town wants to attract a data center. But residents say the larger question is why a rezoning this large is needed.
Rep. Dan Eubanks, a Republican from Walls, wrote on social media that the town is “wanting to put another massive data center right in our back yard.” 
Eubanks said that he’s for more economic development in the area but cautioned that it should not be done “at the expense of the residents.” 
In a letter to the town’s planning director, a representative for the land owner wrote that the rezoning would help attract economic development to the property which will in turn bring jobs and contribute tax dollars to the city. 
The rezoning has attracted so much attention in the majority-Black town of 1,400 that a planning commission meeting scheduled for Sept. 22 was moved to a larger venue, Walls Elementary School, in anticipation of a crowd. Some residents have expressed concern about how a data center or other industrial development would fundamentally change the small town’s character.
Walls resident Emily Harris said she was devastated when she learned of the rezoning, which is about a mile from her home. She and her family moved to Walls for the opportunity to own land in a rural, quiet community. 
“We are not against progress,” Harris said, “Growth is a wonderful thing if we do it smart.”
She and other residents have said they want more information about a potential project.
Residents questioned why the rezoning is coming so quickly after the town approved its comprehensive zoning plan earlier this year and if there has been sufficient change in the past few months to warrant rezoning.
The specter of Elon Musk’s SpacexAI looms large in Walls, which is near the company’s growing data-center operations in Southaven and Memphis. Harris has been to Southaven and has heard the noise that residents of Southaven have been living with for over a year. 
Members of the Walls Board of Aldermen did not respond to requests for comment, but on social media the town wrote that the rezoning was “to create a potential path to economic development” and encouraged residents to attend the meeting to gather facts, ask questions and express concerns.

name: Delaware
title: Katz, Arminio Give Delaware GOP Two Distinct Federal Campaigns
description: Senate nominee emphasizes affordability and unity; House nominee centers campaign on restoring economic growth and ending overseas wars DOVER, Del. — Delaware Republicans selected two candidates with unconventional political backgrounds Tuesday, hoping Dr. Mike Katz and Dr. Joe Arminio can expand the party’s reach and make the state’s federal races more comp[...]
text:
Photo: Delaware LIVE photo take a Katz Headquarters on 9/15. Dr. Mike Katz is pictured with his wife moments after announcing his victory.
Senate nominee emphasizes affordability and unity; House nominee centers campaign on restoring economic growth and ending overseas wars
DOVER, Del. — Delaware Republicans selected two candidates with unconventional political backgrounds Tuesday, hoping Dr. Mike Katz and Dr. Joe Arminio can expand the party’s reach and make the state’s federal races more competitive in November.
Katz, a physician, business owner and former Democratic state senator, captured about 77% of the Republican vote for U.S. Senate, according to unofficial election returns. Arminio, a political scientist, author and educator, won approximately 48% in the three-way Republican primary for Delaware’s lone U.S. House seat.
Katz will face Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Coons, while Arminio will challenge Democratic U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride. Both Democratic incumbents begin the general election with Delaware’s recent voting history on their side, but the Republican nominees bring approaches that differ from those of traditional GOP candidates.
Katz wins with coalition message
Katz’s decisive victory over John Shulli affirmed the Delaware Republican Party’s decision to endorse a candidate who has belonged to three political parties.
Katz represented northern New Castle County in the Delaware Senate as a Democrat from 2009 to 2013. He later became an independent and ran for U.S. Senate in 2024 before joining the Republican Party for the 2026 campaign.
Instead of avoiding that history, Katz incorporated it into a campaign centered on “people over party.” His campaign argues that Republicans cannot win statewide in Delaware without attracting independents and some Democrats who are dissatisfied with the cost of living, government performance and the direction of the state.
In his primary victory speech, Katz said he heard similar concerns while speaking with voters across the political spectrum.
“Delaware families are facing an affordability crisis,” Katz said. “The cost of housing, food, health care, energy and simply raising a family has become too high.”
Katz presented himself as a physician and business operator who would bring a problem-solving approach to Washington. His platform emphasizes reducing federal spending, cutting regulations, lowering energy and housing costs, expanding health care access and protecting Delaware employers.
“Leadership is not about talking about problems,” Katz said. “Leadership is about solving them.”
Katz said his medical and business experience taught him to examine evidence, bring people together, make difficult decisions and accept responsibility for the results. He argued that government should operate with the same accountability.
“Public office is not about power or titles, and it should never be about the person holding the office,” Katz said. “Those entrusted with public office — our public servants — work for you.”
His platform also includes traditional Republican positions on border enforcement, public safety, gun rights, election laws and women’s sports. Katz said those principles would not prevent him from working with people outside his party.
“We can stand firmly on our principles and still work with people who disagree with us,” Katz said. “I will work with anyone who is willing to work with me to solve problems for the people of Delaware.”
Coons, meanwhile, is seeking a third full term and won about 78% of the Democratic primary vote against three challengers. He enters the general election with the advantages of incumbency, a substantial campaign organization and more than a decade in the Senate.
Arminio campaigns on two sweeping ideas
The House primary produced a different message.
Arminio defeated attorney John Whalen III and Earl Cooper, the candidate endorsed by the Delaware Republican Party at its state convention. Unofficial returns showed Arminio with about 48%, Whalen with 32% and Cooper with 20%.
The result demonstrated that the party endorsement was not decisive for Republican voters in the congressional contest.
Arminio is a Wilmington native who holds a doctorate in political science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He has taught at American University and Lincoln University and has worked on national defense and public policy issues.
He built his campaign around two sweeping ideas: stopping what he calls America’s “endless wars” and returning the country to economic growth comparable to the 1950s.
Arminio argues that the two issues are connected. He says stronger domestic growth and a less interventionist foreign policy would allow the country to direct more attention and resources toward American families, communities and businesses.
His foreign policy proposal, which he calls “The Grand Bargain,” would reduce American involvement in overseas conflicts and pursue negotiated settlements in Europe and the Middle East. Arminio argues that the United States should avoid prolonged foreign entanglements while maintaining enough military and economic strength to deter adversaries.
Arminio has presented voters with detailed explanations of both proposals through campaign materials, policy documents and public appearances. Whether those plans would produce the results he promises — and how they would affect economic growth, national security and America’s alliances — will likely become central questions in the general election campaign.
Following his primary victory, Arminio said Republican voters had endorsed a campaign focused on developing substantial solutions rather than relying on slogans.
“I am grateful Republican voters endorsed a campaign committed to doing the hard work required to solve the issues facing our communities,” Arminio told Delaware LIVE. “I thank my two opponents for stepping forward and offering their ideas. I echo Delaware Republican Party Chairman Gene Truono’s call for unity. Now is the time for Delawareans who want change to come together and work to defeat U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride in November.”
McBride, who was unopposed in the Democratic primary, is seeking a second term in the House.
Can Republicans make Delaware competitive?
The nominations give the Delaware GOP two candidates who can argue that they are offering something different from standard party politics.
Katz is campaigning as a coalition-builder with experience in medicine, business and more than one political party. Arminio is offering detailed but unconventional plans intended to reshape American economic and foreign policy.
Those differences could help Republicans generate attention and focus the general election on affordability, government spending, energy costs, health care, economic growth and America’s involvement in overseas conflicts.
However, making Delaware competitive will require more than distinctive biographies and policy proposals.
Democrats have held Delaware’s U.S. House seat since 2010. McBride won the 2024 election with 57.9% of the vote, compared with 42.1% for Whalen. Republicans have not won a Delaware U.S. Senate election since William Roth’s reelection in 1994. Coons won his most recent election in 2020 with 59.4% of the vote.
The last Republican elected to federal office from Delaware was former U.S. Rep. Mike Castle, who won his final House election in 2008 and served until 2011. Castle was known as a fiscal conservative and social moderate who regularly attracted voters outside his party.
Katz used his victory speech to make a similar appeal beyond the Republican base.
“Ultimately, there are no Republican families, Democratic families or independent families,” Katz said. “There are Delaware families. We are neighbors. We are one community. We share a future and a responsibility.”
Katz and Arminio will now have to demonstrate that their messages can reach voters beyond the Republican primary. The November campaigns will test whether Delaware voters see their unconventional backgrounds and policy plans as credible alternatives or continue the state’s long pattern of supporting Democratic candidates for federal office.

name: Michigan Advance
title: ‘Facts first, conclusions second’: House committee begins review of ballot measure procedures
description: Michigan Rep. Mike Harris (R-Waterford Township) introduced a new House Select Committee, established to examine the rules and procedures of the Board of State Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections, specifically the sampling process used to verify signatures for ballot initiatives, at a first hearing of the committee on Tuesday afternoon. Harris’ approach,[...]
text:
Rep. Mike Harris (R-Waterford Township) introduces the purpose of a new House select committee, which he is chairing, to examine the sampling procedures used by the Board of State Canvassers and Bureau of Elections to determine the qualifications of ballot initiatives. Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)Michigan Rep. Mike Harris (R-Waterford Township) introduced a new House Select Committee, established to examine the rules and procedures of the Board of State Canvassers and the Bureau of Elections, specifically the sampling process used to verify signatures for ballot initiatives, at a first hearing of the committee on Tuesday afternoon.
Harris’ approach, he said in an introductory statement, is “facts first, conclusions second.”
“That standard will apply to everyone,” he continued. “It applies to the petition proponents. It applies to the Bureau of Elections. It applies to the Board of State Canvassers. It applies to outside organizations, and I hope the members sitting on this committee take that standard to heart.” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The committee was established after the Board of State Canvassers deadlocked on a vote to approve a ballot petition that would have established strict voter ID laws in the state. Because the canvassers could not come to a majority vote, that means the measure will not be on the November ballot. 
The decision was made on the margin of just a handful of signatures. In a sample of 1,000 votes, the petition was just three valid signatures shy of the needed margin. 
“We are not here to decide whether we agree with the proposed amendment,” Harris said. “We are not here to relitigate a political campaign, and we are not beginning this investigation with a conclusion about whether anyone did anything wrong. We are here because the Michigan House of Representatives determined that the rules, procedures, and practices used in this process deserve serious thought and oversight.”
Citizens-only voting petition sponsors look to 2028 after initiative fails before state canvassers

Earlier this year, a different ballot proposal, Michiganders for Money Out of Politics, did meet the threshold of valid signatures, though also by a small margin in the 1,000-vote sample. 
Some Republicans, including House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township), have alleged that conservative-leaning ballot measures have been treated unfairly in the signature verification process, but Harris said that he is going into his role as chair of the new committee as “very open-minded and unbiased.”
“I think that’s part of why I’m chairing this committee, that and my investigative background,” he said. “That is truly the role that I’m going to take, despite anybody else’s comments. My focus here is to get to the facts and understand the process.”
Harris said that the committee has invited representatives of both ballot measures to appear before the committee, though he noted that the scope of the committee would not be limited to those two petitions and would also include previous ballot measures.
New House committee to examine signature verification sampling process for ballot initiatives

Rep. Denise Mentzer (D-Mount Clemens), the minority vice chair of the committee, said that she did not personally have any concerns about what she saw with the state’s recent ballot measures, both this year or in past election cycles, but added that she believes it is good for government to regularly check itself and to make sure that the processes are functioning correctly. 
“I’m looking at the process. Is the process that was followed correct? Is the process the same as what’s been followed in other instances of constitutional ballot questions?” she said. “If the process is correct, as Chair Harris said, we’ve got no issue, right? If the process needs tweaking, we will figure that out as we review things. My goal isn’t to say whether the ballot initiative was correct or fair or whatever. I don’t care about the ballot initiative. I am here to look at, was the process followed appropriately and properly? That’s it.”
Following the hearing, Harris told reporters that he does not have any “predetermined outcomes on what we’re thinking for policy yet,” and that the outcome of the committee will be determined by what it finds.
“My goal by the end of this year is to make sure that we have a report that we submit to the body that has recommendations and findings on what we saw,” Harris said. “If everything’s working great, that’s what the report will show. If there’s what we think are inadequacies or things that are failing the citizens of the state of Michigan, we’ll report that as well, and there may be policy recommendations that come with that.”
Mentzer said that, if Democrats retake control of the state House in 2027, she would enthusiastically take over leadership of the committee to continue its work.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: State Treasury flagged $1.4B in improper payments; lawmakers say greater oversight needed
description: A pair of state lawmakers want to expand efforts to track improper payments by state agencies by requiring them to review and assess programs that fall outside of federal oversight of wasteful spending.
text:
State Treasurer Stacy Garrity announced Wednesday details on her office’s efforts to curb waste as it processes payments for more than 70 state agencies. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Captial-Star)Pennsylvania’s fiscal watchdog halted about 20,000 improper state government payments worth $1.4 billion last fiscal year.
State Treasurer Stacy Garrity announced Wednesday details about her office’s efforts to curb waste as it processes payments for more than 70 state agencies.
“During the last fiscal year, Treasury processed more than 21 million payments totaling $145 billion,” she said, noting that’s a payment ever three seconds.”As demonstrated by the results of the Payment Production and Improper Payments report, Treasury does not provide an automatic rubber stamp when payments are requested.”
A pair of state lawmakers want to expand efforts to track improper payments by state agencies by requiring them to review and assess programs that fall outside of federal oversight of wasteful spending.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“At a minimum, we must hold state government to the same level of responsibility which we hold ourselves to in our own personal finances,” state Sen. Kristen Phillips-Hill (R-York) said.
She noted the lawmakers spend a lot of time debating the budget, often facing disagreements within their own parties.
“But one thing that we should all agree on is … every single cent that we send out should be done properly. It should be transparent, and we must be accountable to the people,” Phillips-Hill said.
Phillips-Hill and Sen. Chris Gebhart (R-Lebanon) said they plan to introduce legislation that would require agencies to perform a review and assessment of each program that is not already subject to the federal Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 to determine which programs are vulnerable to improper payments.
Additionally, each agency would be required to perform the assessment every two years and post it to a publicly accessible website with detailed information on each agency’s improper payment assessment.
Garrity, who is also the Republican nominee for governor, noted her office released the first ever public report on payment production and improper payments for the 2024-2025 fiscal year.
This year’s edition, for the 2025-2026 fiscal year, shows the Treasurer’s Office saved taxpayers $75 million by preventing payments that were directed to ineligible recipients, addressed incorrectly, duplicates, not supported by a contract or had other procedural and technical errors.
Garrity noted that while the value of the flagged payments was $1.4 billion, the savings were less because the majority went through after the errors were corrected.
Over the last five years, she said, the Treasurer’s Office has stopped nearly 120,000 improper payments totaling $5.5 billion with a savings of more than $325 million.
According to the report, the departments with the largest share of flawed payments are Revenue, at 49.9%; the Liquor Control Board, at 19.8%; Human Services, at 7.3%; the Pennsylvania State Employees Retirement System, at 5.9%; and Transportation at 4%.
While the process usually goes largely unnoticed, this year her office determined that it could not authorize more than $1 million in payments for security upgrades at Gov. Josh Shapiro’s private Montgomery County home. 
The security measures were installed at Shapiro’s Abington residence after state police recommended them following the April 2025 arson attack on the official Governor’s Residence in Harrisburg.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“My team and I did our due diligence and made our decisions as required by state law,” Garrity said. “After extensive back and forth with Pennsylvania State Police, as a result of Treasury’s inability to legally make this payment, the Attorney General issued a settlement agreement, and that was to save taxpayers’ costly litigation.”
Gebhard said Pennsylvania has a mixed track record of preventing improper payments. In 2019, the federal government found Pennsylvania had an error rate of 14% in Medicaid payments. That improved in subsequent years, he noted.
And he noted the commonwealth was cited in a 2024 report by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General for improperly claiming $551 million in Medicaid funds for its school-based health programs.
Commonwealth agencies are required to report improper payments only when they involve federal funds. Gebhard said the legislation he and Phillips-Hill are proposing would address that limitation.
In addition to biennial reporting, each program would be designated as having low, moderate or high risks for improper payments. For high-risk programs, agencies would be required to identify flawed payments and error rates and create a corrective action plan, Gebhard said.

name: National
title: FDA acknowledges estrogen patch shortage, says it’s working to increase supply
description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says it’s helping manufacturers increase the supply of estrogen-based hormonal patches and acknowledged a current nationwide shortage as more women seek hormonal therapies for symptoms related to menopause. In a release earlier this month, the FDA said it is expediting actions to increase supply, and said all six manufac[...]
text:
Women take photos at a Women’s History Month event in the East Room of the White House in March 2025. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration this month acknowledged a nationwide shortage of estrogen-based hormonal patches, which are prescribed for women experiencing symptoms related to menopause. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says it’s helping manufacturers increase the supply of estrogen-based hormonal patches and acknowledged a current nationwide shortage as more women seek hormonal therapies for symptoms related to menopause.
In a release earlier this month, the FDA said it is expediting actions to increase supply, and said all six manufacturers are working to expand capacity and prioritize production of the patches.
Shifting attitudes on menopause drive lawmakers to push for new protections

“The FDA views increased interest in menopause treatment as an important development for women’s health and is working closely with manufacturers to help ensure that the supply of estradiol patches keeps pace with demand,” the release said.
Menopause typically occurs between the ages of 45 and 55, according to the National Institute on Aging, when a woman stops having menstrual periods. That hormonal change can cause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, bone density loss, insomnia and more. Estradiol transdermal patches worn on the skin can replace estrogen lost through menopause and reduce those symptoms for some women.
Stateline reported in May that more awareness of menopause and its effects was leading to more states introducing legislation around the topic to mandate more insurance coverage for treatment and to create more workplace accommodations. At that time, the FDA did not list the patches in its list of shortages — this month marks the first time the agency has acknowledged a shortage. The American Society of Health-System Pharmacists first noted a shortage in January, two months after the FDA removed the treatment from its longtime “black box” warning status.
As of May, the National Menopause Foundation said more than 60 pieces of legislation related to menopause had been introduced nationwide this year. Twenty-six, and 26 states have enacted menopause-related laws since 2019, and more bills are expected to be introduced in the upcoming 2027 legislative sessions.
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Researcher tells New Mexico lawmakers more funding needed for Holloman Lake wildlife PFAS testing
description: While previous testing showed plants and wildlife near Holloman Lake in the south-central part of New Mexico contain some of the highest levels of toxic contamination ever recorded, some samples remain untested due to lack of funding, a state university researcher told lawmakers on Tuesday. Experts believe the leading cause of contamination at Lake Holloman[...]
text:
An undated photo of PFAS-laden foam on Holloman Lake, documented by New Mexico environmental officials. High levels of forever chemicals have contaminated the area surrounding Holloman U.S. Air Force Base, including record-setting levels of contamination in wildlife and plant samples. (Courtesy of New Mexico Environment Department)While previous testing showed plants and wildlife near Holloman Lake in the south-central part of New Mexico contain some of the highest levels of toxic contamination ever recorded, some samples remain untested due to lack of funding, a state university researcher told lawmakers on Tuesday.
Experts believe the leading cause of contamination at Lake Holloman — a man-made, wastewater lake outside of Holloman Air Force Base — comes from firefighting foam containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, PFAS, being used on base from the 1970s until 2019. PFAS exposure is linked to kidney and reproductive cancers, decreased fertility, fetal developmental delays, disruption of immune responses and liver functions in people. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Last year, the New Mexico Environment Department released a report that revealed levels of PFAS wildlife at Holloman Lake. Samples taken from the carcass of dead animals had toxic concentrations of PFAS 2.5 million times greater than the federal standard set by the Environmental Protection Agency. These so-called “forever chemicals” bind to other molecules in the body and build up over time, a process called bioaccumulation, and can move through the food chain when the animal is consumed by a predator. 
But some samples have not been collected and others not tested due to a loss of funding, Jean-Luc Cartron, a research biologist from the University of New Mexico, told lawmakers in the interim Military and Veterans Affairs committee on Tuesday. Cartron and his team have been conducting research on PFAS toxicity of Holloman Lake water, soil, plants and wildlife since 2021.
Oryx, which are frequently hunted in the Tularosa Basin, emerged as an animal of concern. Researchers found that a herd of oryx would stay the night at Holloman Lake and samples taken showed slight contamination levels. Hunters in the state could potentially harvest the contaminated animals, Cartron said. 
Cartron advised hunters during his committee presentation to refrain from eating liver, where PFAS tend to bioaccumulate more. Once researchers complete the study, he said, guidelines for hunters can be put in place in partnership with the New Mexico Department of Wildlife and Department of Health, which previously released a health advisory for hunters that ate waterfowl between 2010 and 2024 from Lake Holloman.
But many more oryx samples remain in cryopreservation, unable to be tested due to lack of funds. Since the beginning of the investigation in 2021, which led to initial findings being published in a 2024 report, “limited funding” has prevented the team from completing the toxicity study, Cartron said, adding that a mix of private and university funds kept the research going.
Cartron urged the Legislature to support the toxicity surveillance research with funding in the next legislative session starting in January. He estimated that with proper funding, the final report could be published in a year.
“It’s important to know where there are hot spots of contamination, just like we would want to know if  an infectious agent presents a threat to any communities,” he said. “That requires some funding.”
The New Mexico Environment Department has been in litigation with the U.S. Department of Defense since 2016 and seeks all past and future clean-up costs and all natural resource damages under an EPA rule that forces polluters to pay the clean up costs of contamination.
Committee Chair Sen. Harold Pope (D-Albuquerque) expressed his appreciation for the researcher’s work and underscored its importance. 
“It’s always concerning when we talk about our wildlife that migrates and the effects on the folks who eat the meat and what it can do to our body,” he said. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Mississippi Today
title: LSU sack leader Princewill Umanmielen is served in $550K lawsuit filed by Ole Miss
description: Clemson quarterback Tait Reynolds (2) is sacked by LSU defensive end Princewill Umanmielen (1) in the first half of an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026 in Baton Rouge, La.
text:
LSU sack leader Princewill Umanmielen has been served legal papers related to a July lawsuit filed by the University of Mississippi which alleges that the former Rebels edge rusher owes Ole Miss $550,000 because of his decision to transfer to the rival Tigers.
Records filed in Lafayette County Circuit Court in Mississippi indicate that papers were served on Tuesday, just five days before No. 7 LSU was slated to visit No. 8 Ole Miss in a game immersed in hype stemming from coach Lane Kiffin’s decision to leave Mississippi in favor of LSU last Nov. 30.
A person familiar with the situation said Umanmielen was served outside LSU’s football operations complex. The person spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because university officials have not commented publicly on the lawsuit between Ole Miss and two former players who are now at LSU, and who allegedly failed to compensate Ole Miss for their departure as required by revenue-sharing agreements they signed in early January.
The other is offensive lineman Devin Harper, who allegedly owes Ole Miss $400,000.
While legal issues between Ole Miss and Umanmielen have gone unresolved for months now, the timing of papers being served, first reported by ESPN, will only further pump up the intrigue surrounding Saturday night’s game in Oxford, Mississippi.
It will mark the first time Kiffin has returned to Oxford since being showered with insults by angry Rebels fans as he arrived at a small airport to catch a private plane to Baton Rouge.
Kiffin persuaded four players and host of assistant coaches and other staff to follow him to LSU, including linebacker TJ Dottery and Winston Watkins Jr., Dottery is LSU’s leading tackler through two games and Watkins Jr. leads LSU in yards receiving so far this season.
College athletes have been able to transfer far more freely in recent years without having to sit out a year, as was once required by the NCAA. There have been scattered disputes between players and their former schools over compensation agreements. Earlier this year, Washington quarterback Demond Williams Jr. said he would return to the Huskies after his school was reportedly prepared to pursue legal options to enforce his lucrative name, image and likeness contract.
Ole Miss has said revenue-sharing agreements signed by both players included a provision requiring them to compensate the university with a predetermined amount if they departed before fulfilling their commitment.
“The University of Mississippi has a responsibility to enforce its contractual terms, and this position is consistent with the actions of other institutions in the current landscape of college athletics,” the Ole Miss statement said. “The university attempted to amicably resolve this matter prior to filing.”
Kiffin left Ole Miss following its regular-season finale against Mississippi State in late November. Kiffin initially asked to continue coaching the Rebels in the College Football Playoff after he’d accepted the position at LSU, but Ole Miss declined and appointed then-defensive coordinator Pete Golding as Kiffin’s replacement. Golding coached Ole Miss to the national semifinals.
Umanmielen had nine sacks and 13 tackles for loss as a junior last season for the Rebels. Harper was a freshman reserve in 2025, appearing in six games.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: State workers union ratifies contract, over a year after previous contract expired
description: The union for Maine executive branch employees has ratified a new contract, after 20 months of negotiations and over a year after the previous contract expired.  The contract will expire June 30, 2027, and includes a 4.5% pay increase effective Sept. 1 and a lump sum payment to union members of $2,000 to be paid […]
text:
Passersby honk at Winnie Malia (right) and other state employees chanting along State Street in Augusta on Sept. 26, 2023. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)The union for Maine executive branch employees has ratified a new contract, after 20 months of negotiations and over a year after the previous contract expired. 
The contract will expire June 30, 2027, and includes a 4.5% pay increase effective Sept. 1 and a lump sum payment to union members of $2,000 to be paid in October. 
Mark Brunton, president of the Maine Service Employees Association, SEIU Local 1989, said in a statement that the union will continue to push for a job classification study for state employees. 
“Our members stood united in these negotiations. Together, we refused to accept earlier offers that management had billed as its ‘last, best and final’ offer,” Brunton said. “This ratified contract is progress, but our work continues. We’re taking the gains we won together and organizing for the fights ahead.”
The contract also includes a $2,000 childcare reimbursement, three additional days of military leave and an expansion of bereavement leave. 
“We commend MSEA members’ ratification of these new contracts, which demonstrates the Mills administration’s commitment to providing competitive wages and benefits for State of Maine employees,” Elaine Clark, commissioner of the Maine Department of Administrative and Financial Services, said in a statement. 
The agreement comes after the union in June accused the Mills’ administration of negotiating in bad faith. Union leaders said after negotiations proceeded to arbitration, the administration refused to accept recommendations from the independent panel. 
That panel had recommended a 2.5% increase in the first contract year, a 3% increase in the second year and a $1,250 bonus. The ratified contracts offer a 4.5% raise rather than the 5.5% from that report, but the bonus payment for workers is larger. 
The Mills administration has been at odds with the union for years over the ‘pay gap’ between public and private sector workers. State employee wages have lagged behind equivalent private sector jobs, and the union has argued that the gap has led to chronic understaffing at Maine agencies.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Ethics complaint filed over Defense Secretary Hegseth’s Iowa State Fair fundraiser with Rep. Nunn
description: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing an ethics complaint filed by a group of former national security officials who are questioning if his August appearance at U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn’s Iowa State Fair fundraiser violated federal ethics restrictions. The Steady State, a nonpartisan organization comprised of 430 former national security, intelligence, di[...]
text:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gave a speech supporting U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn's 2026 reelection campaign at JR’s Southpork Ranch at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing an ethics complaint filed by a group of former national security officials who are questioning if his August appearance at U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn’s Iowa State Fair fundraiser violated federal ethics restrictions.
The Steady State, a nonpartisan organization comprised of 430 former national security, intelligence, diplomatic, military and law enforcement officials, asked the U.S. Office of Special Counsel Friday to investigate whether Hegseth violated the Hatch Act during his appearance supporting Nunn on Aug. 17, 2026.
Hegseth joined Nunn at the JR’s Southpork Ranch at the Iowa State Fair for “Operation Top Nunn: Salute to the Troops.” The Fair fundraiser was a rescheduled event, as Hegseth was originally supposed to join Nunn in Iowa in March. The March event was cancelled shortly after two Iowa soldiers were killed in an Iranian strike on a Kuwait facility on March 1.
At the fundraiser, Hegseth said, “according to the lawyers, I’m only here in a personal capacity today.” But those with The Steady State argue the Defense Secretary’s appearance could violate the Hatch Act, a longstanding federal law that limits partisan political activities for federal employees.
One of the prohibitions in the Hatch Act bars Cabinet members from using their authority or influence to impact the results of an election. The complaint asks the OSC to investigate whether Hegseth violated this rule and used his position as defense secretary “by invoking his position, his Department’s budget request, and his access to the President while urging the audience to return the incumbent to Congress,” according to the complaint.
At the fundraiser, Hegseth rallied support for Nunn’s reelection as he faces Democratic Iowa Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott for the 3rd District seat.
“President Trump needs the type of leaders who understand why a $1.5 trillion dollar budget, a one-time generational investment, is what is necessary to ensure that my kids and your kids, that your grandkids and my grandkids, live in a free country, defended by the most powerful military in the world,” Hegseth said, calling for Iowans to vote for Nunn.
The complaint also calls for the investigation of whether Hegseth’s trip involved the use of government funds. A news release on the complaint references a social media post from a Washington Post reporter that stated while a Pentagon official said Hegseth traveled to Iowa in his personal capacity, “because of Hegseth’s role, he used taxpayer-funded military aircraft for the trip.”
Information about the travel — including what government resources were used, whether travel costs were reported under the Federal Election Campaign Act or were reimbursed and the itinerary of Hegseth and the aircraft — was requested by The Steady State to be part of the OSC investigation. The Steady State emphasizes the complaint “does not assert that reimbursement did not occur,” according to a news release.
A Pentagon official reiterated in a statement that Hegseth attended the event in Iowa in his personal capacity, adding, “Department staff are not involved in, nor privy to, the details of events that Secretary Hegseth attends in his personal capacity. Therefore, we have no comment.”
Nunn’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment on the complaint. But Democrats argue Nunn should provide more answers about the event and Hegseth’s involvement.
Zach Schenkman, Trone Garriott’s campaign manager, said in a statement, “the reporting on Zach Nunn and Pete Hegseth’s fundraiser continues to unearth new questions that Zach Nunn needs to answer.”
“Who paid for that flight? Did Pentagon lawyers sign off before the Secretary of Defense got on a stage and asked donors to send Zach Nunn back to Washington?” Schenkman said. “Iowans paid for that plane one way or the other, and they are owed an answer.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Residents push back against planned Nashville ICE coordination center
description: Dozens of residents packed the Nashville Metro Council on Tuesday to speak against plans to establish a national immigration enforcement support center in Nashville.  One after another, Nashville residents took to the podium during the meeting’s public comment period to say they opposed the coordination center. “We are here to protect our community from a […[...]
text:
Protester against and Immigration and Customs Enforcement national support center in Nashville packed the Nashville Metro Council meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 15.  (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee LookoutDozens of residents packed the Nashville Metro Council on Tuesday to speak against plans to establish a national immigration enforcement support center in Nashville. 
One after another, Nashville residents took to the podium during the meeting’s public comment period to say they opposed the coordination center.
“We are here to protect our community from a system that doesn’t reflect the morals and ethics of our city,” said Alexandra Van Zeelandt, who criticized ICE’ mass arrest and deportation policies.
“Our city protects its people, all of them, and we expect the same from anyone who chooses to operate here,” she said.
Federal documents show Alaska-based Koniag Services landed a government contract of up to $63 million to provide “services in support of enforcement and removal operations” in Nashville, effective Aug. 6.
The services include a 24/7 operation to coordinate with local police and sheriffs across the country who have entered cooperative agreements with the federal government to enforce immigration laws. 
The contract, which originally listed the small Middle Tennessee town of Adams, Tenn. as its place of performance, was later edited to say the center will be located in Nashville, listing a zip code that corresponds to the Donelson neighborhood. No specific location has been publicly revealed. 
Rick McKinney joined scores of residents who protested plans for a national Immigration and Customs Enforcement support center in Nashville on Tuesday, Sept. 15. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
The call center was not part of the meeting’s agenda and council members took no action Tuesday. 
A Koniag representative has not responded to the Lookout’s questions in recent weeks, and did not respond again on Wednesday. In August, a spokesperson said the company was “not at liberty to discuss this very recently awarded contract at this time.”  The company has posted more than two dozen job listings for a Nashville call center, which list government security clearances as an employment requirement.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement also declined to answer questions about the center’s physical location or plans, citing security concerns.
It is unclear how elected council members could legally intervene to prevent the ICE center’s presence in Nashville. A spokesperson for Mayor Freddie O’Connell told the Lookout in late August that he was “still in the process of getting a consistent depiction of what is planned.”  The Lookout sought additional information from the mayor Wednesday.
ICE changes location of Tennessee call center site from Adams to Nashville

Nevertheless, speakers on Tuesday night urged council members to take action against the support center. Some speakers noted that an effort to establish a mass ICE detention center in Lebanon, Tenn. earlier this year was scrapped after strong community pushback.
Jennifer Berry, who identified herself as a longtime educator, told council members she was “deeply concerned about what we are teaching our children by potentially allowing a 287(g) ICE coordination center to operate in our community.”
Nashville children are already fearful of ICE’s power to separate them from their parents and families, she said.
“They do not need us to normalize surveillance, suspicion and the idea that some families are less deserving of safety and surveillance than others.”
The government’s description of the contract responsibilities, in a document published in November soliciting bids, describes an operation that would more closely integrate the work of local police and federal immigration authorities. The document says the support center’s primary function would be to operate a call center capable of handling an estimated 6,000-7,000 daily inquiries from law enforcement agencies across the nation. The document also describes providing local law enforcement with “targeting focus and material” to locate immigrant children.
“They are building infrastructure to surveil our neighbors, share information about our neighbors and ultimately remove our neighbors from families and their communities,” Luis Mata, communications and deputy director for the Tennessee Democratic Party, told councilmembers.
“Someone’s father or mother doesn’t come home. A child loses a parent. Your favorite small business closes down. That is what all this infrastructure eventually touches.”

outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: US House to leave for campaign break without action on AI, affordability
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. House is expected to depart Wednesday evening for a seven-week campaign break after spending less than two weeks in session during August and September.The extended “district work period” is intended to give incumbents from both political parties time to meet with constituents and fundraise back home before voting in this year’s midterm elections ends on Nov. 3. House Republican leaders hope that more time campaigning will help some of their most vulnerable members secure reelection, allowing the party to hold onto its majority for another two years. Less time on Capitol Hill also means less time voting on potentially divisive issues. Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, for example, would have been able to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday had the House remained in session. Despite the somewhat limited time in session, Speaker Mike Johnson said Tuesday he believes Republicans have accomplished much during their nearly two years with unified control of government. But he brushed aside requests to keep the chamber in session to address warnings from several executives about artificial intelligence.The Louisiana Republican pointed to a bipartisan task force that issued a 273-page report in December 2024, saying those recommendations meant lawmakers would not be “caught flat-footed here.” “We’ve been working on this for years and we’re right there where we need to be,” Johnson said.Moments later, however, he added Congress cannot apply those recommendations to draft legislation to regulate AI because “nobody in the room knows yet what that should look like.”“Why? Because we don’t have the latest information,” Johnson said. “We are not in the … frontier labs who have taken this technology many steps further than even when our own report was published.” He argued that instead of Congress debating legislation, the executives of AI companies should instead “self-police” and “self-regulate.”“They don’t need the government to tell them to slow it down,” Johnson said. “If they want to slow it down, they should.”‘Nothing’ done, Dem leader saysHouse Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries sharply disagreed with Johnson and Republicans' approach, saying Wednesday that there was considerable work left to do, despite the planned recess. “They have decided to cancel votes and run out of town without providing any relief to hard-working American taxpayers,” he said. “Republicans have done nothing to lower the high cost of groceries,” he continued. “Nothing to make healthcare more affordable, nothing to end the reckless war of choice in Iran, nothing to lower gas prices, nothing to stop the violent mass deportation machine, nothing to hold the Trump administration accountable for the unprecedented corruption unleashed on the American people.” Jeffries questioned why Republicans haven’t been able to improve the economy and lower prices for everyday Americans, despite having made it a central campaign promise during the last election cycle. “For two years, Americans have been wondering — were MAGA Republicans lying, indifferent, or are they just incompetent?” he said. “We now have an answer: It’s all of the above.”Long lame duckThe House will return after the election for two weeks in November and three weeks in December. That will give lawmakers a total of 27 weeks in session this year, though those are rarely the type of five-day weeks most Americans are used to. House lawmakers often take their first vote of the week on Monday evenings around 6:30 p.m. and their last vote of the week on Thursday morning, before many walk down the steps of the Capitol to cars waiting to take them to the airport. Some weeks are shorter, giving House lawmakers a total of 72 days in session so far with 20 more days of voting on Capitol Hill scheduled before the end of the year. An American with four weeks of time off a year spends about 48 weeks or 240 days at work, significantly more than the United States House of Representatives dedicated to debating and voting.Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that Americans in the private sector with more than 20 years of experience get, on average, four weeks of paid vacation a year.

title: New Mexico Forward Party asks US Supreme Court to intervene in ballot access lawsuit
description: New Mexico’s nascent minor political party is asking the nation’s highest court to put its two statewide candidates on the Nov. 3 general election ballot after a U.S. District Court judge and the U.S. 10th Circuit Court of Appeals denied the party's request to put two of its statewide candidates on the ballot. The state's current ballot access laws leave "vo[...]
text:
Former presidential candidate Andrew Yang and New Mexico Forward Party Chair Bob Perls pictured on April 10, 2026, during an announcement of the New Mexico Forward Party’s creation. In a Sept. 15, 2026, filing, party officials asked the U.S. Supreme Court to place its candidates on the general election ballot. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)New Mexico’s nascent minor political party is asking the nation’s highest court to put its two statewide candidates on the Nov. 3 general election ballot.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
New Mexico Forward Party Chair Bob Perls, a former state lawmaker, is seeking to run for the U.S. Senate against incumbent Democrat Ben Ray Luján and Michael Vigil is seeking to run against incumbent New Mexico State Auditor Joseph Maestas.
While the state Forward Party successfully fielded candidates for several local races, neither Perls nor Vigil acquired the more than 14,000 signatures needed for minor party candidates to make the ballot. They subsequently sued New Mexico Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver in U.S. District Court, alleging that she was enforcing discriminatory ballot laws that require them to gather far more than the roughly 2,500 and 2,350 signatures that Democratic and Republican candidates need, respectively.
U.S. District Court Judge Margaret Strickland denied their motion to place them on the ballot, but did not immediately rule on their broader case. Perls’ attorneys appealed her decision to the U.S. 10th Circuit Court of Appeals.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez filed a brief in support of the party’s appeal last week, writing that political candidates of all parties “should compete on a level playing field in New Mexico’s elections. Today, they do not.”
However, the appellate court upheld Strickland’s ruling in a Tuesday filing.
Perls’ attorneys subsequently asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene.
In the filing addressed to Justice Neil Gorsuch, Forward Party officials argue that New Mexico has the most stringent requirements for minor party candidates in the country. Both Perls and Vigil gathered more signatures than major party candidates are required to, they wrote, alleging that the current requirements deprive their constitutional rights.
“We are asking the court to address rules that, in our view, place an extraordinary burden on a newly qualified party and its statewide candidates, leaving voters without real options on their ballots,” Perls said in a statement.
State Forward Party attorneys asked the Supreme Court to issue a decision no later than Friday, so state election officials can print ballots bearing its candidates’ names in time for early voting to begin in early October.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Appeals Court okays auditor appointing elections board members
description: The General Assembly did not violate the constitution when it transferred Board of Elections appointments from the governor to the state auditor, a split Appeals Court panel decided.  The legislature passed a controversial law after the 2024 election transferring Board of Elections appointment power to newly elected Republican state Auditor Dave Boliek, taki[...]
text:
North Carolina State Board of Elections members, left to right, Jeff Carmon, Chairman Francis DeLuca, Stacy "Four" Eggers, Siohban Millen, and Robert Rucho, May 7, 2025. (Photo: Lynn Bonner)The General Assembly did not violate the constitution when it transferred Board of Elections appointments from the governor to the state auditor, a split Appeals Court panel decided. 
The legislature passed a controversial law after the 2024 election transferring Board of Elections appointment power to newly elected Republican state Auditor Dave Boliek, taking that power away from Democratic Governor-elect Josh Stein.
 In the decision issued Wednesday, the Appeals Court overturned the ruling of a three-judge panel that had sided with Stein. 
Stein contended that the law stripping his appointment powers prevented him from performing his constitutional duty to ensure all laws are followed. 
In a majority opinion Judge April Wood wrote that the separation of powers was not violated because the legislature assigned Board of Elections duties to another member of the executive branch. 
“… We cannot hold that the reassignment of duties from the Governor to the Auditor results in a plain and clear violation of the separation of powers,” Wood wrote. “Whether the General Assembly should be allowed to reassign these duties from a public policy standpoint is not for this Court to decide.”
The board is apolitical, Wood wrote, and “should not, nor is it designed to, effectuate the policy preferences of any elected or appointed official.”
New Republican majority on the NC elections board replaces the executive director

Judge Valerie Zachary concurred. Both Wood and Zachary are Republicans. Judge John Arrowood, a Democrat, dissented. 
The appeals court had allowed the law to take effect even as the three-judge panel found portions of the law to be an unconstitutional violation of separation of powers and before the appeals court made a decision about the lawsuit’s merits.  
Boliek took control of state Board appointments and county board chair appointments. The state and county boards flipped from 3-2 Democratic majorities to 3-2 Republican majorities. 
Arrowood wrote in his dissent that enforcing election laws is a core power of the governor, requiring some control over the Board of Elections. 
The supposed apolitical design of the election boards should not be a factor in deciding that the law is constitutional, Arrowood wrote. 
When Republicans took the majority in the state board, they replaced the executive director with Sam Hayes, a former counsel to Republican House Speaker Destin Hall. Boliek hired a former N.C. Republican Party Executive Director, Dallas Woodhouse, to work with counties on early voting plans. 
Additionally, the board has eliminated Sunday early voting hours in some counties, eliminated polling places at some college campuses, and moved to make it easier to reject absentee ballots, Arrowood wrote. 
“These actions all appear to be designed to make it more difficult for citizens, who have historically voted in favor of candidates not favored by the majority of the members or the Legislature or the Auditor, to vote,” Arrowood wrote. “None of these actions appear designed to promote boards of elections free from political influence or interference.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: South Lyon City Council directs staff to examine impacts of canceling Flock contract
description: SOUTH LYON — Members of the South Lyon City Council met this week to discuss whether it should renew a contract for a set of automated license plate reader cameras located along 10 Mile Road. But the discussion held Monday resulted in the South Lyon City Council directing its staff to examine the legal and […]
text:
Flock license plate reader camera in South Lyon on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)SOUTH LYON — Members of the South Lyon City Council met this week to discuss whether it should renew a contract for a set of automated license plate reader cameras located along 10 Mile Road.
But the discussion held Monday resulted in the South Lyon City Council directing its staff to examine the legal and financial impacts of canceling the contracts for Flock cameras that were approved for installation in 2025. 
The initial request for cameras came from South Lyon Police Department Chief Bonnie Unruh, Hometown Life reported. While law enforcement officials say the cameras can be used to help locate missing persons and stolen vehicles, civil rights advocates like the American Civil Liberties Union have raised concerns over how the data these cameras collect is being used and stored.
Of note, 22 police and sheriff’s department officials across the country have been arrested, fired or placed on leave following a USA Today investigation into alleged misuse of the technology. In one case, a former Florida Police Officer was charged with four felony counts of accessing a computer network without authorization after allegedly using the service to search a woman’s license plate at least 189 times over a period of eight months. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On its website, the South Lyon Police Department states that it uses the cameras “to capture objective evidence without compromising on individual privacy.” 
“The South Lyon Police Department utilizes retroactive search to solve crimes after they’ve occurred,” the website reads. “Additionally, the South Lyon Police Department utilizes real time alerting of hotlist vehicles to capture wanted criminals.”
The department’s Flock transparency page says license plate and vehicle data is stored only for 30 days. The Michigan Department of Corrections, Livingston County Sheriff”s Office, Oakland County Sheriff’s Office, Oak Park Department of Public Safety and police departments in Brighton, Farmington, Hazel Park, Lathrup Village, Milford, Novi, Southfield, Troy, Waterford Township and Wixom have all been granted access to the data from South Lyon’s cameras.
Monday’s meeting was meant to address community stakeholder concerns, drawing South Lyon locals and residents of neighboring townships to the community’s city and school administration building this week to discuss the contract’s renewal.
Councilmember Lisa Dilg said she had previously supported the installation of Flock cameras, but had changed her stance.
“I had not done enough research into the experiences of other communities, the broader privacy questions surrounding the license plate reader technology, or the ways this data could potentially be accessed or used beyond our own police department,” Dilg said. “I should have. That was my responsibility as a council member, and I apologize to the residents for not doing the due diligence that I should have done.”
The South Lyon City Council during a meeting on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Councilmember Alex Hansen put forth a motion to cancel the city’s Flock contract, remove the cameras, request reimbursement for any unused credits, and requested an affidavit from Flock stating any and all data related to the city asset line has been deleted.
However, South Lyon Mayor Stephen Kennedy raised concerns about the potential legal and financial ramifications that could result from Hansen’s motion, suggesting there may be a benefit in speaking with the city’s attorney and its finance director.
After further discussion, Hansen eventually withdrew his initial motion and made another motion to direct the city’s finance director, and the city attorney, to look into the Flock contract and examine if there were any implications — financial or otherwise — for canceling the contract for discussion at the council’s next meeting.
The motion passed with unanimous support.
Residents overwhelmingly opposed the contract’s renewal
Several residents of South Lyon and its neighboring communities spoke out against renewing the city’s contract with Flock, pointing to privacy and safety concerns, as well as the growing opposition to the cameras in other Southeast Michigan communities.
Julielyn Gibbons, a 46-year-old South Lyon resident, raised concerns about the lack of legal guardrails at the state and national level dictating how data collected by automated license plate reader companies is used.
License plate reader searches by Grand Rapids PD point to need for guardrails, legal advocates say

“It’s not the South Lyon Police that I’m worried about,” Gibbons told council members. “It’s bad actors sharing data that is not theirs to share.”
Ryan Mathewson, another resident, directed his comments to individuals who wrote off concerns about the cameras by saying residents “have nothing to hide, but you still have something to protect.”
“This was never about doing something wrong,” Mathewson said. “It’s that there’s now a permanent, searchable record of everywhere you drive, time-stamped, stored where you can’t see it and can’t delete it.”
Mathewson added that the data collected by license plate readers creates a map of someone’s life, and warned that companies stockpiling that data are ripe for a breach.
“It’s not a question of if, but when,” Mathewson said.
Amy and Jeremy Pavlov, who live in Green Oak Township, are just a stone’s throw away from one of the city’s Flock cameras. Jeremy Pavlov said the cameras had changed his feelings about coming into town, describing it as a big “you’re kind of not welcome” sign.
While other community members had raised concerns about the accuracy of the license plate readers, pointing to instances across the country where individuals were detained when a camera misread their license plates, Amy Pavlov argued that the issue is the surveillance itself.
She also noted that there are other license plate reader companies outside of Flock, voicing opposition to any contracts the city might consider with an automated license plate reader company.
At least once councilmember stood up for Flock
However, one council member, Margaret Kurtzweil, made it clear that she would not support canceling the Flock contract, offering a lengthy argument against the concerns raised during public comment. 
Kurtzweil questioned why opponents focused their ire on Flock, rather than types of video surveillance present in other settings. She pointed to federal court cases which had upheld the use of automated license plate reader cameras under the Fourth Amendment; and discussed different responses various lawmakers and leaders at the state and national level had made in response to concerns around Flock.
Council Member Margaret Kurtzweil at a meeting of the South Lyon City Council on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
 
Councilmembers Thad Bogert and Michael Squires voted against the motion to place license plate readers within the community. Bogert responded to Kurtzweil by noting that the difference between Flock and other types of surveillance cameras is that the city council holds control over the license plate reader cameras.
Bogert told his fellow council members that he understands the appeal of the technology, but that his role on the council goes beyond asking whether a technology can be useful. 
“I also have to ask what powers are we giving government, what infrastructure are we creating, and what those powers could become in the future?” Bogert said.
Bogert later noted that although there will always be a compelling reason to give government one more tool in the name of public safety, elected officials hold the responsibility of deciding where that line should be.
“For me, continuously collecting, collecting, and creating searchable records of the movements of people who are not suspected of committing a crime crosses that line,” Bogert said.
The City Council’s next meeting is scheduled for 6:30 p.m. on Sept. 28.
