name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Ideas on healthcare affordability differ among 6th District candidates
description: Candidates in Louisiana’s 6th Congressional District agree healthcare coverage affordability is a major public concern, but they have drastically different proposals for fixing the problem.
text:
Candidates for Louisiana's 6th Congressional District seat disagree on how to make health insurance more affordable and what types of rules should be applied to the government-sponsored Medicaid program. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger/States Newsroom)Candidates in Louisiana’s 6th Congressional District agree healthcare coverage affordability is a major public concern, but they have drastically different proposals for fixing the problem. 

Four major candidates are competing to be the next U.S. House member from the Baton Rouge area in the Nov. 3 election. Incumbent Cleo Fields is stepping down after the state legislature created new district boundaries last spring to make it harder for a Democrat to retain his seat. 
The two leading Democratic candidates in the race said reinstituting government subsidies for health insurance plans sold through the Obamacare exchanges would be a priority if they were elected. 

“I would reverse the cuts to the Affordable Care Act subsidies,” said Pat Forbes, a retired state employee who helped lead Louisiana’s disaster recovery efforts as the longtime head of the state Office of Community Development.
People who don’t receive health insurance through an employer, but don’t qualify for plans like Medicare or Medicaid, can purchase coverage through the government-run marketplace. 

During President Joe Biden’s term, the federal government increased subsidies to make the Obamacare plans more affordable. But those subsidies expired at the end of 2025, with President Donald Trump firmly against keeping them in place, and prices for the coverage skyrocketed.

Like Forbes, community organizer Lindsay “Rubia” Garcia said she would work to bring the subsidies back if elected. 
But she eventually wants to move to a taxpayer-funded national health insurance plan, sometimes referred to as a “Medicaid for All” strategy. Under that structure, every citizen would get access to government-sponsored health insurance, regardless of their age or economic status. 

“Healthcare is a human right in the United States,” said Garcia, a former teacher who graduated from Southern University Law Center in 2025. 
Unlike the Democratic candidates, Republican state Sen. Rick Edmonds of Baton Rouge said he would not favor restoring higher subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans. 

Instead, Edmonds said he would support giving Americans direct access to funding to cover their medical costs through expanded health savings accounts to help offset the cost of care for people with high deductible insurance plans.  

This idea, which is popular among conservatives, was pushed by outgoing U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-Baton Rouge. Trump also floated a similar plan last week when he promised to send $500 rebate checks to people enrolled in Obamacare. 
“I am a strong proponent of the open market,” Edmonds said. 
The other notable Republican candidate in the race, state Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, did not return several phone calls and text messages over the past week asking for an interview about his healthcare priorities. 

Medicaid work requirements 

Another difference between the Democrats and Edmonds is their opinion on work requirements that take effect in January for certain low-income Medicaid recipients. 

In 2025, Trump and Congress enacted new rules that will require many Medicaid enrollees to earn at least $580 per month or complete 80 hours of volunteer work or school each month to retain their benefits.
Forbes and Garcia said they would work to repeal the work requirements, while Edmonds said he is in favor of the new restrictions. 
Forbes said the requirements mean more citizens will go without healthcare and be unable to work as a result of an illness. It will lead financially vulnerable medical providers, such as rural hospitals, to close because they will have to treat more uninsured patients who can’t cover their bills, he said. 

Garcia said working people shouldn’t make so little money that they qualify for Medicaid. If someone is working full-time, they should make enough to afford a private insurance plan, she said. 
“I’m for people working, and when they are working, earning a livable wage,” she said. 

Edmonds said the new work requirements will incentivize low-income people enrolled in the Medicaid program to get new job training. If they gain a new skill, they might be able to find employment that allows them to pick up private insurance, he said. 
“We want to push people to have a great job,” Edmonds said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: National
title: More states embrace ‘50-50’ child custody in divorce cases
description: A growing number of states are making an equal split between parents the default child custody option in divorce cases. Louisiana and Mississippi this year joined at least five other states that have adopted the so-called 50-50 standard — four of them since 2021, as more legislators rework divorce-related laws that remained mostly unchanged for years. The […[...]
text:
A mother holds hands with her son on a swing set. At least seven states have passed laws making equally shared parenting time the legal default in child custody cases.
(Photo by Troy Bennett for Maine Morning Star)A growing number of states are making an equal split between parents the default child custody option in divorce cases.
Louisiana and Mississippi this year joined at least five other states that have adopted the so-called 50-50 standard — four of them since 2021, as more legislators rework divorce-related laws that remained mostly unchanged for years.
The 50-50 custody issue does not break down cleanly along partisan lines: The Mississippi bill was sponsored by Republicans, the Louisiana legislation by Democrats. Both states’ laws explicitly codify a custody guideline that many courts in other states follow.
Supporters say a formal 50-50 custody standard makes divorce proceedings more equitable for fathers — who historically have been awarded less custody time than mothers — and encourages them to maintain an active role in their children’s lives.
And it can reduce friction between separating parents by signaling they’re both starting the custody process on an equal playing field, said Don Hubin, board chair of the National Parents Organization, an advocacy group that has pushed for more states to adopt legal presumptions of shared parenting.
Without that presumption, Hubin said, one or both parents may feel like they have to paint each other in a bad light in order to ‘win’ more time with their children.
“It’s not just about the practice of shared parenting, but about the law signaling to parents that this is going to be the outcome unless something special is going on in your case,” he said. “It reduces the anxiety of the parents, which reduces the conflict between the parents.”
But critics say the standard might harm vulnerable women and children by making it more likely that children must spend time with a parent who isn’t safe. They fear that for women in abusive marriages, the knowledge they would have to cede 50% of their child’s time to an unsafe parent could push them to remain in a marriage just to protect their children.
Kimberly Rummage, who lives in Kentucky, calls her state’s 50-50 custody standard “absolutely diabolical.” She’s had a lengthy battle in court with her ex-husband over custody of their child.
“I think that parents should have to prove why they get that 50-50,” she said. “You should have to show what you’ve done in that child’s life, what you know about that child, how you’ve participated and supported that child.”
Some critics also argue that the 50-50 standard doesn’t account for the needs of children at different ages. Mississippi state Rep. Dana McLean, a Republican, warned her colleagues the state’s new law could harm breastfeeding infants who need to spend most of their time with their mothers during their first months of life.
Mississippi’s new law requires family courts to use equally-shared parenting time as the default in custody cases. Parents seeking more time must present evidence showing why a 50-50 split isn’t in their child’s best interest. It also changes how child support is calculated: The new formula for 50-50 custody can lower child support payments for the parent with the lower income.
Louisiana’s new law says child custody “shall” be divided equally, rather than “should,” which was the language under the previous law.
In both states, as in others that have adopted the 50-50 standard, a judge can override the rule if the court finds credible evidence for awarding more time to one parent.
But in Mississippi, several judges spoke against the bill before it passed, saying the old system — in which custody was awarded on a case-by-case basis using a specific set of factors — was the most fair.
At least five other states have similar laws, and all were approved with bipartisan support: Kentucky (2018), Arkansas (2021), West Virginia (2022), Florida (2023) and Missouri (2023).
Effects on divorce rates
Proponents of 50-50 laws say one positive side effect is that they could save some marriages. In Kentucky, the state’s divorce rate dropped 25% between 2016 and 2023, compared with an 18% decline nationwide.
But Krista Westrick-Payne, one of the researchers who studied the rates, told Stateline it’s impossible to tie Kentucky’s drop directly to the state’s 2018 50-50 custody law because too many other factors in that timeframe influenced it.
“There’s no one cause, no one single driver for these rates,” said Westrick-Payne, who is the assistant director of the National Center for Family & Marriage Research at Bowling Green State University in Kentucky.
The data shows that factors like state laws or local economic conditions tend to have a minimal effect on whether a couple divorces, she said.
“The more significant things that affect whether or not a couple decides to divorce have much more to do with their relationship and their personal situation.”
Divorce becomes next battleground as states debate family values

Westrick-Payne said she believes divorce and custody-related law should be crafted with the effects on individuals and families in mind, rather than as a way to affect widescale, population-level changes.
“When it comes to something like divorce, something that’s so personal, I think the focus needs to be more on the individuals going through it,” she said, “as opposed to some big policy to affect just whether somebody divorces or not.”
A growing effort
Hubin expects to see more states moving to codify the equal custody presumption in their laws in the coming years, as parenting norms change and more households become dual income. Fathers have taken on more caregiving responsibilities than a generation ago, he said.
“Fathers who’ve been involved with their kids, they’re not happy with being consigned to an ‘every other weekend’ visitor in their kids’ lives,” he said.
Nationally, mothers of children under 6 spend about seven and a half hours a day with their children, compared to a little over five hours for fathers, according to the latest available data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The time gap shrinks as kids get older: Mothers spend 3.8 hours a day with their teens and fathers spend about 3 hours.
Earlier this year, a 50-50 custody bill in Oklahoma, sponsored by both Republicans and Democrats, sailed through the House but died on the Senate floor. Similar bills have been proposed in Alabama, Idaho, Indiana and North Carolina.
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: As drought expands across central NH again this fall, in some places it never fully went away
description: It’s been more than a year since all of New Hampshire was completely drought-free, and despite some spring and summer rain, drought has returned to a central swath of the state as fall approaches. Meanwhile, in some parts of the southeast and Seacoast, it never went away. That’s despite last winter’s snowfall totals, which were […]
text:
Grasses and brush go to seed in a field in Concord on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. A swath of New Hampshire is back in drought this fall, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)It’s been more than a year since all of New Hampshire was completely drought-free, and despite some spring and summer rain, drought has returned to a central swath of the state as fall approaches. Meanwhile, in some parts of the southeast and Seacoast, it never went away.
That’s despite last winter’s snowfall totals, which were close to typical by historical standards, scientists said. Yet that snow contained less water, reducing its mitigating effect on the drought. It’s an example of how stretches of more “normal” conditions are not always enough to overcome impacts from increasingly extreme weather — a pattern that tracks with scientists’ understanding of how climate change manifests in New Hampshire, according to State Climatologist Mary Stampone.
“What we’re seeing when we get these multi-year drought periods is that, you know, the amount of snow we get or the way we get our precipitation in the winter isn’t enough to help us recover from the previous season’s drought,” Stampone said.
As of early September, more than half of New Hampshire was experiencing moderate drought, while about 41% was abnormally dry, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor.
The extent of drought in New Hampshire as of Sept. 8, 2026. (Graphic courtesy U.S. Drought Monitor)
The area in drought as of Sept. 8 stretches across central and eastern New Hampshire, while the North Country and southwestern New Hampshire are listed as “abnormally dry,” a condition on the edge of drought. An area of southwestern New Hampshire along the Vermont border, representing approximately 4% of the state by land area, is experiencing typical conditions.
The last time New Hampshire was entirely drought-free was last summer, according to the Drought Monitor’s metrics — which are informed by a net of local measurements of precipitation, stream flow, reservoir levels, temperature, soil moisture, and more. The summer of 2025, indeed, began with plentiful rainfall, Stampone said. But that gave way to a hot and dry stretch in mid- and late summer; by Aug. 12, 2025, “moderate drought” had set in in eastern New Hampshire.
A month later, a portion of central New Hampshire entered “extreme drought.” That condition, shown in the red on the Drought Monitor map, continued to expand until it peaked at about just over half of New Hampshire in mid-October 2025.
New Hampshire drought map released on Oct. 21, 2025. Red areas show “extreme drought,” dark orange areas “severe drought,” and light orange areas “moderate drought.” (Graphic courtesy U.S. Drought Monitor)
The abrupt plunge into severe drought conditions is characteristic of how scientists believe climate change manifests in New Hampshire, with both rain and dry weather becoming more concentrated. Increasingly extreme fluctuations in conditions, linked to climate change, allow droughts to take hold quickly and ultimately reach greater intensity, Stampone said. 
“It’s not that these droughts are unheard of for New England. We have a highly variable climate, but what’s different today … is this increase in intensity that we’re seeing, that tends to happen in late summer,” she said.
The snow that accumulates on the ground throughout New Hampshire’s winter typically trickles into groundwater aquifers as it melts, making it an important factor in an area’s emergence from drought conditions. 
Last winter’s snowfall was promising in some ways, totaling, in inches, near historical averages across much of New Hampshire, according to Eric Kelsey, a snowpack researcher and research associate professor with Plymouth State University. 
But there was a catch: That snow, he said, was “dry.”
Scientists call the amount of water contained in snow “snow water equivalent,” or “SWE,” often pronounced “swee,” for short. Wetter, denser snow has a higher SWE measurement, while fluffier snow has less. When it comes to determining the effect of snowfall on groundwater, this is a crucial measurement.
Last winter’s total snow water equivalent across the state was well below historical averages, ranging between about 50% and 75% of those benchmarks in most places, Kelsey said. Thus, from a drought perspective, the snowfall brought less relief.
“It was a drier winter, if you will, even though there was plenty of snow on the ground,” Kelsey said. That’s somewhat rare, he said, “especially these days.”
Nonetheless, more plentiful rainfall in the spring and summer made up for that, alleviating drought conditions in much of the state, with the exception of the portions of southeastern counties that remained in drought. In some parts of central New Hampshire, rainfall totals approached two times average levels in late spring, Kelsey said. 
This helped reduce that area’s rain debt for a time. But following what has become a pattern of shifting extremes, drought and dry conditions have returned relatively quickly to a swath of the state this fall, though conditions are less severe than they were at this time last year.
Prolonged dry periods without relief increase the chances that areas could rapidly enter severe drought conditions, Kelsey said.
“It causes stakeholders to be on heightened alert constantly, you know, where the situation isn’t dire, but the drought’s at a point where it could only take another month or two of really dry conditions to make it a really bad drought,” he said. 
Effects of drought in New Hampshire include strain on farmers and the large population of residents who rely on wells for their drinking water. About 250 people have reported a dry well to the New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services over the last year, according to the department, which reopened its Emergency Drought Assistance Program in 2025. 
The department approved 60 emergency assistance projects to move ahead, with about half completed at this time, said Water Division Assistant Director Ted Diers. The department expects to spend all of the $1.8 million that was allocated to this phase of the program on those projects, he said; there are still more applications pending before the department, he added, for which there are not currently enough funds allocated to the program to complete.
“At this time, it does not appear likely that the program will be opened to new applications,” he said in an email.
Meanwhile, 88 public water systems across the state and two municipalities have outdoor water use restrictions in place, according to the department.
This fall’s drought is not as extreme as last year’s was at this point, but it remains unclear when relief could come.
Hard-hit areas of New Hampshire are contending with a precipitation deficit of about 10 inches, an amount that would need to arrive before frost sets in and makes it more difficult for that water to permeate the ground, Stampone said. And low water tables in the southern portion of the state are attributed to a much longer-term precipitation deficit, according to NHDES. 
This year’s snowfall has the potential to be impactful on these conditions, and will set the tone for how much relief may come in spring, Stampone said.
Another area for hope is the outlook for New Hampshire’s awe-inspiring, tourism-driving fall foliage, which can sometimes be impacted by severe drought as dry leaves fail to display their vivid colors. 
The North Country and mountains have milder dry conditions, with less of a precipitation deficit than some other portions of the state, Stampone said — so it’s quite possible that the leaves will still put on their show.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: EPA backs Indiana coal combustion residual program takeover
description: Officials insisted that state control over disposal permits for toxic coal byproducts will be better for public health and the environment.
text:
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Deputy Administrator  David Fotouhi announces the proposed approval of Indiana's coal combustion residuals permit program during a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana’s proposed takeover of toxic coal byproduct permits is ready for approval, federal officials announced Tuesday. If finalized, the program would be the largest in the country.
“Giving states the lead … helps ensure that those who understand local conditions the best, and their local energy needs, are in the driver’s seat to oversee the process,” U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Deputy Administrator David Fotouhi told reporters at an Indianapolis news conference.
Coal combustion residuals, or CCR, are primarily produced by burning coal in power plants.
The powdery fly ash, glassy boiler slag and other byproducts contain dangerous contaminants like mercury, cadmium and arsenic. 	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The EPA regulates CCR disposal in most states. Under President Donald Trump, the agency is increasingly encouraging states to take responsibility instead. Indiana is the 10th state with proposed or final approval for CCR disposal units, according to the EPA.
Fotouhi and state leaders maintained the move would improve health and environmental results.
“Let me be very clear: this step reinforces, not weakens, safeguards for human health and the environment,” Fotouhi said. “It allows Hoosiers to decide what is best for Indiana.”
Gov. Mike Braun similarly said Indiana’s approach “strengthens environmental safeguards and keeps permitting decisions here at home,” adding that a state-run program will offer “greater control, transparency, and accountability in how coal ash is managed.”
“Our program gives us stronger tools to prevent groundwater contamination, protecting drinking water where these impoundments are, and it gives us agility in terms of staying on top of it,” he said, but didn’t offer examples.
Indiana Gov. Mike Braun speaks at a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Braun last year issued an executive order banning new state environmental regulations that are more stringent than federal versions unless explicitly required by law or deemed necessary by the governor’s office. Such “no more stringent than” limits are also scattered through Indiana law.
Asked how the state would improve outcomes given those restrictions, Braun responded, “To just assume that there would be anything being laxed or done at a lower level of concern or quality would be a bad assumption.”
The Indiana Department of Environmental Management would oversee the CCR program. The agency estimates that 100 CCR units across Indiana would require permitting under the proposed rule.
The takeover has been in the works for years.
IDEM staff wrote the regulations between 2021 and 2024, and the Indiana Environmental Rules Board gave final approval in late 2025, according to slides presented at the board’s August meeting. The program includes requirements for design, operation, groundwater monitoring, closure, recordkeeping and financial assurance, according to a news release.
The state submitted its CCR application t0 the EPA in June. The proposed rule will be published in the federal register on Wednesday, kicking off a 60-day public comment period.
Indiana Department of Environmental Management Commissioner Clint Woods listens during a news conference on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
IDEM anticipates federal approval as soon as February or March, according to the slides.
Once approved, CCR units have 180 days after the new program goes into effect to submit applications for permits. IDEM will have to approve or deny applications for new CCR units or major changes within one year. Minor changes have a 180-day deadline for the agency.
The state program will come with an estimated $1.3 million in personnel costs — inspectors, engineers, geologists and more — along with equipment, training and conference expenses.
IDEM is already “moving forward with staffing,” per Braun.
The program will mostly be funded by permit fees, with supplemental income from federal grants and state coffers, IDEM Commissioner Clint Woods said.
“I think we will continue to advocate with EPA to ensure (that), because we have the biggest program in the country, that resources ought to come to us, and we ought to get our fair share,” Woods said. “… In the past, those have been divided for states that have a lot fewer coal combustion residual sites. … Insofar as there are federal resources available, we’ll continue to advocate that Indiana needs to be at the front of the line, considering how robust and well-run this program will be.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Congressional Black Caucus conference begins amid concerns over Callais, Voting Rights Act
description: The Congressional Black Caucus Foundation conference is typically “a big homecoming,” but this year's event could be the last for some caucus members, as changes to the Voting Rights Act have put Black representation on Capitol Hill under threat.
text:
Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-4th) at a November 2025 news conference. Ivey, who will co-chair this year's Congressional Black Caucus Foundation conference, said caucus members are angry over Supreme Court changes this year to the Voting Rights Act that could cost up to 20 members their seats this fall. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-4th) says the annual Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s legislative conference is typically “a big homecoming,” but this year’s event could be the last for some members at a time when Black representation is under threat on Capitol Hill.
The conference that starts Wednesday comes just months after the U.S. Supreme Court’s April ruling in Louisiana v. Callais gutted racial protections in the Voting Rights Act, saying states’ use of race-based redistricting amounts to an “unconstitutional racial gerrymander.”
Analysts have said the seats of as many as 20 members of the 62-member Congressional Black Caucus could be threatened this year, as Republican states have rushed to redraw congressional boundaries less favorable to minority voters.
“We’re all angry about what happened with the Voting Rights Act. We’re all angry about what the Trump administration’s done,” Ivey said in an interview Monday.
“The Republicans’ goal at the federal and state level is to dilute Black votes so Blacks can’t [vote for] the people they want to represent them in Congress,” said Ivey, who will serve as honorary co-chair of this year’s conference with Rep. Alma Adams (D-N.C.).
A proud history and a cloudy future: Congressional Black Caucus hit by Supreme Court ruling

Callais will be just one of at least 100 panels at the 55th annual conference, which runs through this weekend, with sessions on voting, election integrity and fighting for representation in the Black community, among others.
A Thursday panel to discuss Callais and the Voting Right Act will hosted by Rep. Cleo Fields (D-La.), who announced in July that he would not seek reelection to Congress, after the Louisiana Legislature redrew Fields’ district to make it more favorable to a Republican candidate. Fields will instead run for a vacant Louisiana state Senate seat after the death of Sen. Larry Selders.
Ivey acknowledged a few other caucus members have been affected by redistricting, including Rep. Shomari Figures (D-Ala.). The Alabama Legislature redrew Figures’ district to decrease the Black voting age population from nearly 49% of the district to 39%.
“But the key piece right now is to beat them [Republican candidates] at the ballot box,” Ivey said.
“We can still win a lot of those races, in part because Trump is so deeply under water. Also in part, because there’s a lot of African American voting blocs,” he said. “If we turn out and, as they say, ‘Show up and show out’ like we did for [former President Barack] Obama in 2008 and 2012, we can still win those races.”
A ‘silver lining’
Besides the more than 60 members of the Congressional Black Caucus, thousands of other elected officials, business and community leaders are expected to be in attendance at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center. This year’s theme, “Rooted, Ready & Rising,” coincides with the 50th anniversary of the nonprofit caucus foundation that conducts policy research and implements programs.
This is the second year a Maryland lawmaker will serve as an honorary co-chair, after freshman Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) co-chaired last year with Rep. Joe Neguse (D-Colo.). Alsobrooks and Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) made history last year when they became the only two Black women to serve at the same time in that chamber.
Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), right, was honorary co-chair of the 2025 Congressional Black Caucus Foundation conference, with Rep. Joe Neguse (D-Col.). (File photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Sessions at this year’s conference will touch on the Trump administration’s continued push to eliminate various diversity programs, on protecting civil rights among the future of artificial intelligence and closing the racial wealth gap.
At least one session will feature an intimate conversation Friday with civil rights icon Andrew Young, who worked alongside the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. to help pass the 1964 Civil Rights Act and the 1964 Voting Rights Act.
Young resides in Georgia, one of nine states featured in a report called “Accelerating South” that highlights how the region has emerged as a center for political capital, economic investment and migration. Howard Franklin, president and CEO of Ohio River South, will be at this week’s conference in D.C., where he plans to distribute copies of the report.
“The silver lining I see for this reapportionment is that CBC has had upwards of 60-plus seats they could guarantee African American candidates,” Franklin said. “Now you will see a number of those seats [in jeopardy] and force some of the members to get better at communicating to voters that look like them.”
Other panels, events
The panels won’t strictly focus on the November general election and voting disenfranchisement.
Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Florida) is scheduled to have a fireside chat Thursday with producers and songwriters Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis. A few of the artists they worked with include Janet Jackson, New Edition and Rod Stewart.
Of course, a gathering with thousands of people won’t just be a bunch of panel discussions.
Receptions will be held throughout the city, such as one hosted Thursday by the Greater Washington Region Clean Cities Coalition, in partnership with EVNoire, on “Clean Mobility and Energy.” The reception will honor seven people for their work to advance transportation and energy that include former CBC Chair and Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), Virginia House Speaker Don Scott (D) and Maryland Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain.
Besides urging Congressional Black Caucus members to push for more funding for energy and transportation to help underserved communities, coalition CEO and Executive Director Antoine Thompson said caucus members need to work to make Justice40 federal law. It was a Biden-era promise to make sure at least 40% of investments in clean energy and transportation go to disadvantaged communities.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“We need to negotiate that and make sure it’s embedded as a law, so that no other president can come in and just dismantle programs that are designed to help people,” Thompson said. “I think that would be one thing that we’d love to see the CBC to take advantage of.”
Ivey plans to host a panel Friday to encourage more Blacks into the space exploration field, with retired NASA astronauts Jeanette Epps and Victor Glover slated to appear.
While the conference will celebrate Black achievement, talk of the looming elections — and how Democrats can take control of at least one of chamber of Congress to rein in President Donald Trump (R) — won’t be far off.
Ivey pointed to Trump’s promise at last week’s GOP midterm convention in Dallas to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate in November.
“Essentially a bribe effort. If you vote for us, we’ll pay you. I think people see past that, okey-doke,” Ivey said. “I can’t wait for us to get the gavel so we can make sure there’s full investigations and full accountability on this type of misconduct.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: So, you want to be a journalist in Indy? Here’s what you need to know.
description: WFYI newscaster and reporter Samantha Horton remembers how hard it was to establish her journalism career in Indiana. A former college athlete, she wasn’t daunted by the long hours, but says the low pay and sudden schedule changes were tough to manage. “I lived with roommates and, at times, worked a second job to have […]
text:
(Courtesy banner)WFYI newscaster and reporter Samantha Horton remembers how hard it was to establish her journalism career in Indiana. A former college athlete, she wasn’t daunted by the long hours, but says the low pay and sudden schedule changes were tough to manage.
“I lived with roommates and, at times, worked a second job to have enough to cover necessary costs and try to save,” she said. “That was a tough balance with irregular work hours and not disrupting the others I lived with.”
Horton landed her first job in Evansville in 2015. She said she was idealistic about working in radio, thinking she could avoid the sexism her colleagues faced in television. 
Now, with 11 years of experience under her belt and a job as a host and correspondent at WFYI, she’s considered a veteran in the industry. Horton is a bit of an exception. Locally, out of the dozens of young journalists who start entry-level jobs, few manage to hang on for 10 years. Many of them quit or end up laid off. 
In a 2024 report, the Center for Innovation and Sustainability in Local Media found among 600 current and former journalists surveyed, heavy workloads correlated with leaving the field. Professionals working 51-60 hours per week saw a 24% leaving rate compared to a 15% retention rate.
Horton even left journalism for a year and came back. 
How did she persevere when so many entry-level journalists leave the profession? Horton says she tapped into her own curiosity. She learned to be open to fair feedback on her work and to show up in the community, earning the trust of her peers and the audience. She leaned on her editors, who pushed her to refine her reporting and storytelling. As she improved, her desire to stay in the job grew.
“What has helped me survive the 10-year mark is the support systems I have made in the industry as well as those outside, in my personal life,” said Horton. “Being curious of the world with the desire to tell people’s stories and hold those in power accountable for their actions are what keep me wanting to come back each day.”
Getting a journalism job is easier than keeping it
Many reporters don’t make it to the 10-year mark in the profession before washing out. In addition to pressures of the work, they contend with a volatile industry: shrinking newsrooms, dwindling resources, and the possibility of news organizations shutting down altogether. Yet, the journalism school at Indiana University, the Media School, persists, enrolling a steady 225 students. 



Here is a list of the major internships and fellowships at Indy-area news outlets (applications for those listings without links open later this year):

The Pulliam Journalism Fellowship (IndyStar) in news and sports reporting, visuals, and photojournalism
Indianapolis Press Club Foundation scholarships and internship opportunities
The Journalism Academy for Writing and Storytelling Fellowship(JAWS at The Indianapolis Recorder)
WFYI internships
Do317 Media Internships on LinkedIn
WTHR internships
WISH-TV internships
FOX59/CBS4 and WRTV internships
Indianapolis Monthly
Indianapolis Business Journal
WIBC
Mirror Indy Youth Reporter and Photojournalism internships



When I spoke to journalism educators about the future their graduates are facing, educators said many entry-level reporting positions are open to recent graduates but that the industry makes it hard for journalists to thrive deeper into their careers.

Editors and news directors told me that cub journalists need more support these days than they once did. Younger workers are more self-conscious about looking foolish. (And not without reason. It’s not unusual for a powerful person to publicly mock journalists for doing their jobs.)

These fledgling reporters are stepping into a world where social media and AI are transforming the journalism landscape. Has journalism education kept up with the times? What does it take for a reporter to land their first job in Indy? To thrive in the market? 

IU professors described the journalism profession’s retention problem.

“What I’ve observed is that people enter journalism and they leave within five to ten years because of the lack of fair compensation, lack of leadership opportunities, the volatility of the industry,” said Suzannah Evans Comfort, associate professor at the Media School at IU. “So people are hiring, but they want to hire cheap. They rarely, in my observation, hire mid-career people. I think that’s pretty rare.”

It’s in local newsrooms that those who were journalism majors or in other disciplines find good entry-level opportunities, Evans Comfort told me. Entry-level journalists often arrive in newsrooms with rough edges on their storytelling and critical thinking skills. Cub reporters and producers receive a lot of feedback from their bosses and editors, which helps them improve, but once they’ve gotten some experience under their belts, it’s hard to find mid-career jobs that meet their needs. 

CJ Hoyt, news director for FOX59 and CBS4, agrees that some new professionals leave in the first five years, but says it’s understandable.

“This is a stressful environment,” he said. “Frankly, it’s not for everyone. There are people who find out this business is not what they expected. I suppose that happens in most every industry. There are also people who develop skills in our industry that can apply in other industries where they might find more normal schedules or better pay.”
Tech skills are desirable, but fundamental journalism skills are more important.
Student journalists are already adept at navigating new technology, adapting to social media platforms and using AI. Professors teach journalism students the basics of accuracy, fairness, and neutrality as the first step in their education.

“We ensure that students have the basic elements of journalism first before they engage with technology of any kind,” Evans Comfort said. “That technology changes, but the fundamentals of journalism do not.” Evans Comfort instills in her students an understanding of the ethical issues new technology presents. 

Taeyoung Lee, an assistant professor in IU’s Media School, encourages her students not to become overly dependent on platforms or constantly chase shortcuts, whether for social media or AI search. 

“In my Social Media and Journalism course, I teach students how journalists and newsrooms can use social media effectively for news promotion, newsgathering, and audience engagement,” Lee said. “Social media offers enormous opportunities, but I also describe it as journalism’s ‘frenemy’ because of challenges such as misinformation, loss of control over news distribution, and growing distrust in news.”

Elaine Monaghan, professor of practice and program director for journalism at IU Bloomington, said it’s not a question of whether future journalists will use AI and other emerging technologies. “The question is whether they will understand those tools well enough to use them ethically, transparently, and in service of the public interest,” she said. “That’s where journalism education comes in.”

Students hone their skills with the fundamentals of journalism in class and at an array of student and other media, including the Indiana Daily Student and the on-campus television station. Through the Michael I. Arnolt Center for Investigative Journalism at IU, students work on stories with media partners like the Associated Press, Reuters, USA Today, and the Indiana Capital Chronicle. They learn how to make records requests at the state and local level and learn how to make FOIA (Freedom of Information Act) requests. 

For instance, IU students partnered with Indiana Capital Chronicle staff to produce this investigative story on state spending for the “contentious technology park,” The Limitless Exploration/Advanced Pace (LEAP) Research and Innovation District in Boone County. 

Evans Comfort calls the next generation “driven” and “inspirational” in their dogged pursuit of the profession, despite challenges. In 20 years, not much has changed in what students face; it’s only gotten more complicated, she said. Students must stand up to doubtful parents who urge them to pick more lucrative paths and must understand the industry’s rocky footing and uncertain future.
Getting practice 
Although some news outlets have reduced the number of interns they use, the Media School at IU creates opportunities for students to flex their classroom knowledge, Jill Bland, career services specialist for the Media School, told me. 

“We’re super aware of the changing landscape and are trying to find innovative ways to help students get experiences,” Bland said. She makes sure students know how to market themselves for internships and prospective jobs by highlighting skills with social media, content creation, and other strengths.

This fall, IU added Indiana Newsroom, a grant-funded initiative designed to solve two problems at once: News organizations’ need for more local news and students’ need for practical experience. While student reporters aren’t paid a fee, their stories are published and circulated statewide by media partners. Max Jones, a 49-year veteran of the newspaper industry, is the instructor, editor and program director.

Recently, the university has placed students at the Herald Times, WISH-TV, Indianapolis Monthly and Hoosier Illustrated.

Have a news tip?

WFYI’s Horton said the key to her endurance was landing a job in a newsroom that aligned with her personal values. “The industry isn’t for the faint of heart, and with layoffs becoming more common,” she said. “I think it’s okay to take some time away to reset.”
Horton stepped away from journalism in 2023, after a negative experience with an editor in another market. She said she was burnt out and needed time to process her experiences in the news industry before deciding whether she wanted to return. In her early years, she found the editing process brutal and said that there was a steep learning curve that felt overwhelming.
“Edits to my stories were tough,” Horton said. “You put so much time into writing something and then an editor tears it apart.”
She had to learn how to deal with factual and subjective critiques of her work. The factual criticism, such as getting a name or number wrong, she learned to accept and appreciate as helpful, although frustrating. The subjective critiques, about her word choices, voice or appearance, she found harder to endure.
“Receiving critiques can make it difficult to keep wanting to do this work,” Horton said. “Yet every so often, when you get an email, a call or a comment out in the field from someone thanking you for a story and what you do is what I have come to focus on and build my confidence to keep going.”
She finally landed at WFYI through connections she made in her first journalism job. Sarah Neal-Estes, WFYI’s news director, became familiar with Horton’s work and mentored her along the way.
“Her mentorship and the care she has for her newsroom made it easy for me to want to come work for her,” Horton said. “I like to believe my body of reporting and her knowing my work ethic and drive helped me land at WFYI in the role I am in today.”
If Horton could give advice to her younger self, or to new reporters, she’d recommend building a support system in the industry, being kind to yourself when long hours feel overwhelming and bleed into your personal life, and finding a newsroom that values your work and pays you fairly for it.
“I believe that mission can only go so far without having people you work with to support you and friends and family understand the demands the job can have with long hours and unexpected time working to cover breaking news,” she said. “Finding a newsroom where you are paid for your experience and are able to make a living is how the industry prevents losing more reporters who have to make tough decisions between living costs and their passion for news.”

title: Everyday increases cost Maine households $4,300 since Trump returned to office
description: You’re not imagining it: everyday costs are going up. From gas to groceries, heating oil to healthcare, Mainers are paying substantially more for goods and services than they were a year ago. The average Maine household has paid an average of $4,300 more for goods and services since President Donald Trump began his second term, […]
text:
Across the country, food costs have increased by 4% since 2024, the Joint Economic Committee found. That means an average household has to spend an extra $310 for groceries compared with two years ago. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)You’re not imagining it: everyday costs are going up. From gas to groceries, heating oil to healthcare, Mainers are paying substantially more for goods and services than they were a year ago.
The average Maine household has paid an average of $4,300 more for goods and services since President Donald Trump began his second term, according to an analysis released last week, which attributes much of that increase to the war in Iran, tariffs and rising healthcare costs. 
The left-leaning Maine Center for Economic Policy (MECEP) released a summary of cost increases last week, relying on analysis from Democrats on the U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee and other sources that have tracked price increases due to Trump administration policies.
Healthcare is the biggest variable: since Congress allowed enhanced premium tax credits for marketplace health plans to expire at the beginning of this year, some families saw much more than the average $4,300 increase, while those with employer-sponsored health insurance have not seen such dramatic price hikes.
But other increases — such as gas, which now costs more than $4 per gallon, and heating oil, which is now $5.15 per gallon — are more ubiquitous, and expected to add more than $2,000 to household budgets by the end of the year.
“These are very clear examples of policy decisions being made by this administration that are ultimately going to serve to increase cost on everyday items for most, if not all people,” said Garrett Martin, president and CEO of MECEP.
Mainers are feeling the impact of these rising costs just two months before the November midterm elections, with affordability seen as a central issue for candidates and voters. Congressional Democrats have pointed to the figures as evidence that Trump has failed to deliver on his campaign promises to lower costs.
“I think Mainers recognize that decisions that are being made in Washington are having a direct impact on their household budgets,” Martin said. 
“The question I think they’re going to be asking themselves this election cycle is, who are the people who are most likely to help address those concerns.”
Healthcare price hikes 
Many Mainers are already dealing with high healthcare costs due to the combined impact of cuts and eligibility changes to Medicaid, higher health insurance premiums, and the loss of the enhanced premium tax credits.
Combined with the closure of rural hospitals and decreasing access to primary care, it has created what Martin called “healthcare shrinkflation, where you’re paying more but getting less out of it.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The cost of health insurance is going to continue increasing next year. The Maine Bureau of Insurance last month announced an average rate increase of 14.8% for the individual market and 13.5% for the small employer market for 2027, which is comparable to the national 15% increase in insurance costs. According to the bureau, higher rates are reflective of increased utilization of services, increasing costs for prescription drugs and more expensive provider contracts.
But the impact of the expired subsidies is also apparent in the projected 2027 rate hikes “due to expected continued decline in enrollment by healthier and younger members,” Bureau Acting Superintendent Tim Schott told Maine Morning Star in June. 
Increased everyday expenses 
Across the country, food costs have increased by 4% since 2024, the Joint Economic Committee found. That means an average household has to spend an extra $310 for groceries compared with two years ago. 
Gas price increases are perhaps the most apparent impact of the Iran war. The MECEP analysis estimates people across the state have spent an additional $393 million on gas since the beginning of the war in late February, costing the average family in Maine an additional $706.
The war is also partly to blame for an increase in fertilizer costs, which jumped up by 52% since the war started, forcing farmers to choose between paying more or using less, threatening crop yields and pushing up food prices.
Tariffs’ toll
Trump’s on-again-off-again trade war has also impacted household ledgers, MECEP found, though the impact is not as clear. Maine’s largest trading partner, Canada, imposed retaliatory tariffs last week on a host of materials and products that are expected to hit Maine goods by an estimated $170 million.
MECEP collected price increase data from various sources that demonstrate the tariffs will add an estimated $1,100 to the average family’s costs over the next 12 months.
That includes price increases for new and used cars — that cost about $1,200 and $1,300 more respectively — and clothing, which has gone up by more than 4%.
Housing also costs more, both to buy and build. People looking to buy a new home will now face a mortgage rate of more than 7% and companies building homes have to reckon with construction materials that cost 15% more, adding about $11,000 to the average new home cost.
Manufacturing costs overall have been impacted by both the war and the tariffs, with construction materials such as steel, copper and aluminum costing about 50% more, raising prices on everything from beer to fire trucks to equipment. Diesel has increased 60% and jet fuel is up 56%, raising costs for several industries including trucking, farming, and air transport.
“Our concern both with the tariffs and with the war is that it’s not clear what the plan is for this administration,” Martin said.
“So these things could persist well into the future, or they could certainly change overnight. But the pattern has been that they have not changed for the better.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania is building more EV chargers. Will drivers come?
description: An electric road trip across Pennsylvania—a state that’s spending big on its charging network—shows early promise.
text:
The author’s Chevrolet Bolt charges at an Applegreen Electric station at a Pennsylvania Turnpike rest stop near Newburg in July. (Photo by Kyle Bagenstose/Inside Climate News)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. 
As I drove 500 miles across Pennsylvania and back in a little blue Chevrolet Bolt EV, a charging station near a dumpster at the back of a Pizza Hut parking lot proved to be a convenient stop. But after spending two hours charging there on back-to-back days and encountering more feral cats (four) than other drivers (one), I started to wonder about its overall utility.
It’s an important question, because the charging station was subsidized with $705,000 in federal taxpayer money, part of $4.5 billion being spent across the country through the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program, a Biden-era pot of money to install thousands of EV fast chargers nationwide.
Just up the hill from the quiet Pizza Hut station was a Tesla supercharger station constructed with no such subsidy. It was crowded with drivers like Levi Morgan, a western Pennsylvania resident who stopped there amid a six-hour drive to Virginia with his family of five. For him, the company’s robust network was a major selling point, and he actually welcomed having to stop and charge every now and then.
“I know some people want to drive eight hours straight or whatever. We would never do that with kids,” Morgan said, adding that Tesla chargers seemed to be everywhere. “For us, they’re there anytime we need it.”
Cats lounge on the pavement in front of an EV charging station near Bedford, Pa. (Photo by Kyle Bagenstose/Inside Climate News)
At first glance, the contrast between the two charging stations would seem to lend credence to criticisms of the NEVI program. The Competitive Enterprise Institute, a libertarian think tank, opined in a report this year that “the private market is already responding to consumer demand for EV chargers far more efficiently than NEVI has,” and called for the program’s abolition.
The U.S. Government Accountability Office has also faulted the program for a lack of clearly-defined performance goals, at a time when the country’s EV market is floundering and the usefulness of federal investment is up for debate.
But transportation experts like Nick Nigro, founder of the research firm Atlas Public Policy, recommend staying the course. For one, he said, the economics of charging stations are different from gas stations and don’t rely as much on the regular coming and going of vehicles. More importantly, he added, NEVI wasn’t designed to meet or spur current EV demand, but instead help the United States build infrastructure for a future of electric transportation.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Despite shifting policy priorities among federal lawmakers, who have already rescinded $500 million from NEVI and don’t plan to add any new money during the next five-year transportation funding cycle, Nigro believes that an electrified future is still to come. Even in Pennsylvania, where EV adoption is lagging, as the state ranks just 29th in electric vehicle ownership per capita.
“Just like when we built the national highway system, just like when we built the electrical grid, the federal government was seeing the future and trying to make it possible for Americans to get there more quickly,” Nigro said. “A lot of these stations along highway rest stops, in today’s EV market, are not going to be frequently visited because we don’t have thousands and thousands of electric vehicle drivers crisscrossing the country… but we will.”
Pennsylvania is perhaps the best test case for what federal dollars can buy. The $16.2 million in NEVI funding it spent by the end of 2025 puts it ahead of every other state, according to the Sierra Club. That made it one of few bright spots in a rollout often criticized for being too slow, as just 25 chargers were installed nationwide between the program’s creation in 2021 and the time Biden left office in early 2025.
Colton Brown, alternative fuels infrastructure coordinator for the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation, said that Pennsylvania alone has since eclipsed that mark, using its NEVI dollars to underwrite 40 charging stations in operation along highway corridors in the commonwealth, with construction of another 39 underway.
Pennsylvania has also received a total of $77 million in NEVI funding thus far, most of any state. That means much more charging infrastructure will soon follow, including the installation of chargers at every turnpike rest stop from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh. The state is already considered “fully built out” along its highways under NEVI guidelines, Brown said, allowing it to be among the first to move onto a second, community-charging phase in which funds will subsidize chargers within cities and towns.
Many EVs, like the 2017 Chevrolet Bolt, are not compatible with Tesla Superchargers, the nation’s largest network of charging stations. Experts say that’s why federal funding for EV charging has focused on stations that are compatible with all makes and models. (Photo by Kyle Bagenstose/Inside Climate News)
As in the U.S. as a whole, there are important climate stakes in Pennsylvania, which has the fourth-highest greenhouse gas emissions nationally. Its transportation sector accounts for about a quarter of those emissions, as Pennsylvania tailpipes spew out more greenhouse gases than the individual economies of 20 other U.S. states.
All of this makes the Keystone State, currently ranked just 32nd in public chargers per capita, a proving ground for what NEVI funding looks like in action. As more charging infrastructure is built, will the EVs come?
 Road worrier

To test out the current NEVI network in Pennsylvania, Inside Climate News spent five hours at four NEVI-funded charger stations spread out along the Pennsylvania Turnpike this July. A 2017 Chevy Bolt made an ideal test subject, as the vehicle’s maximum charging speed (55 kilowatts) is about three times slower than the now-industry standard of 150 kilowatts, and much slower than the more than 350 kilowatts newer top models can reach. The Bolt also only reaches its top charging speed when its battery is 10 to 50 percent charged, after which it drops precipitously.
That means the vehicle has little room for error on a road trip, and thus presents a worst case scenario for traversing Pennsylvania’s highways in an EV. To avoid being stuck charging for hours on end, a roadtripping Bolt driver needs to pull into a charging station near empty and leave when the battery is about three-quarters full. Hitting that window just right requires a robust number of chargers along the route. Too few, and the driver will be forced to stop at inopportune times and sit through longer charging sessions.
Or even worse: anxiously watching the car’s predicted range, switching off AC and slowing down, all to squeeze out the miles needed to make the next charging station. Such range anxiety is now at the top of the list of reasons consumers are wary of buying electric vehicles, Brown said.
“In the 2010s, purchase price was the number one thing cited holding people back,” Brown said. “Now in the past five years, reliable charging access has kind of become that number one.”
So how did the decidedly non-roadtrip friendly Bolt do on a 240-mile route from Philadelphia to Johnstown, Pennsylvania and back again?
Surprisingly well.
Heading west on the Pennsylvania Turnpike, the first planned stop was the conveniently located charger station behind the Pizza Hut near the town of Bedford. At exactly 200 miles away (near the end of the Bolt’s 240-mile range) and just off the exit for Johnstown, it was an ideal location to recharge a low battery.
But driving at highway speeds on a hot day, the Bolt’s battery started draining more quickly than anticipated, and reaching Bedford became a dicey proposition. Not a problem: more NEVI-funded chargers could be found at Turnpike rest stops 25 miles and 60 miles closer. A 20-minute charging stop at one boosted the battery from 20 to 50 percent, adding 65 miles of range, while allowing for a bathroom break and the consumption of an Auntie Anne’s soft pretzel. No other drivers were present.
Next up were two stops at the Pizza Hut station, one on the way to Johnstown, and one on the way back the next morning. On the second visit, another driver was there: Mary Peters and her husband, EV enthusiasts from Detroit who were driving 530 miles to Baltimore to trade in their electric Ford F-150 Lightning for a Volkswagen ID. Buzz, an electric minivan.
A less-than-scenic EV charging station at the back of a Pizza Hut parking lot near Bedford, Pa. (Photo by Kyle Bagenstose/Inside Climate News)
The couple has been “all EV” since 2022, she said, and used to experience range anxiety. But Peters works for an electric utility in Michigan and has firsthand knowledge of how many businesses are requesting connection to the grid to build chargers. The charger behind the Pizza Hut was a prime example—a station right where she needed it as she disembarked from the Pennsylvania Turnpike to head south into Maryland.
“I can tell you the infrastructure is growing,” Peters said. “It’s gotten a lot better… you can stop and charge at a fast charger for 30 minutes, and you’re out. We always time them around eating.”
The final scheduled stop was another NEVI-funded EV charger along the turnpike in Lancaster County, 150 miles east. But halfway there a detour to the state capital of Harrisburg was required, and the Bolt didn’t have enough power to make both.
This time there were no nearby NEVI stations to divert to. However, there were plenty of private options, and a quick stop at a charging station tucked aside a convenience store provided the needed boost. Later, a stop at the Lancaster charger finished the job. Once again, there were no other drivers present.
 Looking in the mirror

The trip may sound a bit chaotic, but the five-stop itinerary was due mostly to its fact-finding nature. Using a popular route-planning smartphone app for EV drivers, a straightforward trip could be done in two stops of about 50 minutes each, or three stops of 35 minutes.
That’s a long time to spend waiting for fuel. But the 2017 Chevy Bolt is not indicative of the EVs on the market today. A middle-of-the-road, newer electric SUV could do the trip in two stops of 30 minutes. Something really fancy could make do with two 10-minute stops, basically a gas-up-and-go experience, which the next generation of EVs are expected to finally match.
All three of these scenarios would involve a stop at a NEVI-funded charging station just off the Turnpike’s Blue Mountain exit, where Pennsylvania’s farmland meets the southern run of its Appalachian Mountains. Located outside a restaurant and ice cream parlor, the 10 chargers available there are drawing good reviews since opening in January 2026, the beneficiary of $811,000 in federal funding.
Brown, with Pennsylvania’s transportation agency, PennDOT, said the stop exemplifies exactly what the NEVI program required states to build with their federal dollars: high-quality, fast-charging, dependable stations located conveniently along highways.
“It essentially meant you have to have charging to a level that people can confidently travel the interstate highway system and have a place to charge when they need it,” Brown said, adding that a federal guidance that Pennsylvania followed— since scuttled by the Trump administration— required chargers to be placed no more than 50 miles apart.
He also said contrary to criticisms that NEVI is redundant, perhaps even wasteful compared to private industry, the program has proved essential to building out high-quality charging stops in Pennsylvania. There are over 2,000 EV charging stations in the state, and only 40 of them so far were built with the help of NEVI, he admitted. But only about 300 are fast chargers, and half of those are Tesla, which are not compatible with many other makes and models. That leaves just 150 fast chargers for cars like the Bolt.
A crowded Tesla supercharger station near Bedford, Pa. (Photo by Kyle Bagenstose/Inside Climate News)
Whittle it down further to reliable stations where there are at least four charging cords, Brown said, and the NEVI program represents “a decent proportion of the stations that any vehicle can drive up to use.” And while some stations may appear underused, he added, they’re balanced by others. In total, the NEVI-funded network in Pennsylvania saw 30,000 charging sessions in Q2 2026 for the first time, an average of about eight sessions per station per day.
That’s closing in on the 10-per-day mark that Brown says is a typical break-even point for a charging station. NEVI subsidies already make that math better for developers, providing up to 80 percent of capital costs, which is typically the most expensive proposition for a would-be developer.
“We’re still at 1 percent to 2 percent of cars on the road [being EV],” Brown said, meaning developers have to be cautious. “It really helps to have that capital incentive.”
But it isn’t clear that Pennsylvania’s NEVI buildout has so far insulated it from a nationwide downturn in EV demand. Sales of plug-in electric cars in the state fell 3.1 percent between Q1 2025 and 2026, according to the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, slightly better than the national average of 3.4 percent.
Still, experts say some of that has to do with a rush to buy EVs prior to the expiration of federal tax credits last year, and Pennsylvania remains committed to its plans. Now that the state is nearing completion on its highway buildout—the turnpike plans to have EV chargers at all 17 of its rest stops by next spring—it is moving on to providing funding for community charging. Brown said that will begin in the state’s heavily populated southeast, where EV adoption is highest, and owners often have to endure long queues at public charging stations. The state took community applications this summer and is actively scoring them based on factors like location and cost, with construction likely to start next year.
“For Pennsylvanians, you’re good [to drive an EV] within the state, and probably within most of our surrounding states as well,” Brown said. “Great progress has been made, and we’re going to continue.”
 A bumpy road in Washington

In the nation’s capital, however, continued support for EV charging remains precarious.
In an interesting twist, the slow, prescribed rollout of NEVI has actually helped protect it from Trump-era rollbacks, E&E News reported last fall. The program’s clearly delineated rules, approved by Congress, have made it difficult for the administration to exercise prerogative.
But the program hasn’t proven bulletproof. In 2025 it endured a funding freeze and a lawsuit, only to see Congress approve a $504 million rescission in NEVI funding in January 2026, dropping total funding from $5 billion to less than $4.5 billion. The rescission impacted 28 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, all of which had not yet received their full 2022 allotments, which became subject to rescission.
On a percentage basis, Atlas Public Policy found, hit hardest were states like Nevada, which Atlas calculated could lose a third of its total NEVI allotment, enough to threaten its ability to build out a highway network. In total dollars, Texas, Florida and Missouri lost the most, and the nation now stands to have 3,700 fewer fast charging ports after the rescission, Atlas estimated.
Linda Bailey, a transportation consultant and former technical assistance team leader in the federal office that administered NEVI, said it’s hard to say just how far the remaining funds will go. Quick-acting states like Pennsylvania are in good shape, she said. But lagging states now face a fear of further reductions, making it difficult to confidently invest.
She predicts rural states in particular may end up falling behind. And they’ll also have less help after Bailey’s former office, the Joint Office of Energy and Transportation, was hollowed out in the first months of the second Trump administration.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“It’s really tough to complete a federal grant program if the federal agency you’re working with doesn’t want to help,” Bailey said.
The storm clouds hanging over the program extend to next year, when Congress is set to determine the latest round of federal highway funding, which moves in five-year cycles. As presently written, the House’s BUILD America 250 Act adds no further funding for the NEVI program, while cutting a sister program, the Charging and Fueling Infrastructure (CFI) program, from $2.5 billion to $1 billion.
Some Pennsylvania political leaders are already rallying to the cause, with a collection of State Representatives and county and city executives in April penning a letter to Pennsylvania’s Democratic U.S. Senator, John Fetterman, urging him to prioritize NEVI.
State Rep. Madsen, a signee of the letter whose Harrisburg office became an impromptu stop on the Bolt trip, said his district is making progress on the clean energy transition, with the local Steelton-Highspire School District becoming a state leader in solar installation and school bus electrification.
Madsen’s House district has just one public charger, and he’s fielding calls from constituents asking for more. More federal funding will become even more critical in districts like his, he predicts, as adoption increases.
“Once EVs become cost effective and people can save money and they’re as efficient,” Madsen predicts, “You’ll see people make that transition.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: As Trump administration runs roughshod over Smithsonian, even Mark Twain would get canceled
description: Mark Twain once said of the praise he’d received: “I do love compliments, yet I’m often embarrassed to say what I think to the person when I get a compliment, I so often feel that they somehow, have not gone far enough.” Twain just may be correct. Earnest Hemingway once said of Twain that “all […]
text:
The National Museum of American History sits on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. (Photo from National Museum of American History)Mark Twain once said of the praise he’d received: “I do love compliments, yet I’m often embarrassed to say what I think to the person when I get a compliment, I so often feel that they somehow, have not gone far enough.”
Twain just may be correct. Earnest Hemingway once said of Twain that “all modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain called ‘Huckleberry Finn.’” Twain created the nation’s plainspoken, irreverent, and quintessential voice.
Critics consider “Huckleberry Finn” one of the most resounding antiracist novels by an American, and as such, Twain poses a conundrum for people trying to hide elements of the nation’s racial past and present. Namely, will they have to cancel this archetypal American?
Earlier this month, Lonnie Bunch, who has led the Smithsonian Museum Institution since 2019, announced his retirement. His exit follows White House accusations the National Museum of African American History and Culture was “divisive and race-centered.”
Uh, yeah. It is a Black museum detailing the Black experience. Were they shocked to find Black history there?
Interestingly, the accuracy of the exhibitions wasn’t challenged.
News of Bunch’s departure landed hard on those of us who have met him. He is revered in and beyond the museum world, and he served with honor and warmth.
The Trump administration has argued that museum content should be told “in a way that is inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic,” according to the Associated Press.
The Smithsonian system operates outside the executive branch. A board of regents that included Vice President J.D. Vance and Supreme Court Justice John Roberts, exercised oversight of Bunch. The Trump administration has scrutinized Smithsonian museums since last year, seemingly pushing a whitewashed version of American history and culture.
President Trump also recently stripped Confederate criticism from a memorial.
Given these encroachments, a classic line from Twain comes to mind: “Politicians and diapers must be changed often, and for the same reason.”
The question again becomes, what happens to the author of one of the most powerful American antiracist novels? What happens to the man who confronted slavery, brutality and moral hypocrisy in his work?
Really, who is more American than Mark Twain?
Consider how Twain loaded down many of his white characters with horrible character flaws. Huck’s father was a violent alcoholic who beat Huck. Twain describes him as, “a fish-belly white, a tree toad white, a sick white.”
Jim, the lead Black character, served as a kind of moral compass in the novel. He was Huck’s only role model.
Readers follow Huck deep into his own psyche as the boy wrestled with the internal work necessary for human growth and transformation. Huck remained in constant conversation with his conscience.
Twain helped shaped American literature, American humor and America’s understanding of itself. The speech of everyday Americans bloomed as he lifted their vernacular in his work.
Controversy has followed “Huckleberry Finn” in recent decades. Twain uses the N-word some 200 times in the book, and that fact has caused some school districts to avoid teaching it in classes, despite its antiracist aims.
This issue surfaced back in the late 1990s, while I worked at the Louisville Courier-Journal. My editor learned that the great novelist Earnest Gaines was speaking at public library and sent me there to ask Gaines his thoughts about Twain, Huck Finn, and use of the N-word.
Gaines grew up in rural Louisiana plantation quarters. His upbringing found its way into his novels that included “The Autobiography of Miss Jane Pittman,” “A Gathering of Old Men” and “A Lesson Before Dying.”
Gaines considered Twain important to understanding America and said Twain’s investigations of race placed him at least 100 years ahead of his time.
We’re left wondering what Twain might say about contemporary race relations, about politicians clinging to power into their 80s and 90s, about the current administration.
I’m guessing here, but maybe something like: “Some people bring joy wherever they go, and some people bring joy whenever they go.”
Mark McCormick is the former executive director of the Kansas African American Museum, a member of the Kansas African American Affairs Commission and former deputy executive director at the ACLU of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate.
