title: Arkansas pharmacies file lawsuit accusing PBM of underpaying them for medications
description: Twelve Arkansas pharmacies sued a pharmacy benefit manager in federal court Tuesday, alleging the company illegally underpaid them for tens of thousands of prescription medications. The complaint accuses St. Louis-based Express Scripts of violating a 2015 law that requires pharmacy benefit managers, also known as PBMs, to pay pharmacies at least the national[...]
text:
Prescription drugs sit on a pharmacist’s counter. (Photo by John Moore/Getty Images.)Twelve Arkansas pharmacies sued a pharmacy benefit manager in federal court Tuesday, alleging the company illegally underpaid them for tens of thousands of prescription medications.
The complaint accuses St. Louis-based Express Scripts of violating a 2015 law that requires pharmacy benefit managers, also known as PBMs, to pay pharmacies at least the national average of what drugstores pay wholesalers for drugs. The pharmacies that filed the suit include one run by Republican Rep. Brandon Achor and his wife. 
“The pharmacies had no practical choice but to absorb those shortfalls,” the complaint states. “Refusing or reversing a claim means turning away a patient who needs medicine.”
Pharmacy benefit managers negotiate prescription benefits among drug manufacturers, distributors, pharmacies and health insurance providers, and the biggest ones also own pharmacies and insurers.

Pharmacy Petition (Stamped) 
Express Scripts is one of the nation’s three largest PBMs, along with CVS Caremark and OptumRX, and all three are owned by much larger corporations that each also own some of the nation’s largest health insurers. The three companies manage 79% of prescription drug insurance claims for approximately 270 million people, according to a July 2024 Federal Trade Commission report.
Express Scripts did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday afternoon. 
The company is also among the five plaintiffs that sued Arkansas last year over its first-in-the-nation law banning PBMs from holding a permit to operate a drugstore. A federal judge blocked the law, saying it “likely violates” the U.S. Constitution’s commerce clause. The state appealed the ruling.
That law, Act 624, was one of several bipartisan 2025 measures the Legislature passed with the goal of increasing patients’ access to medication and helping independent pharmacies stay afloat amid PBM underpayments and competition from chain pharmacies.
Another one of those laws, Act 630, was also blocked in federal court in May. The Arkansas State Board of Pharmacy decided in July to not enforce the law, which would remove drugmakers’ power to limit which pharmacies can purchase their drugs.
The plaintiffs in Tuesday’s lawsuit cite another law that gives pharmacies the ability to sue PBMs that underpay them. The law entitles pharmacies to statutory damages of up to $10,000 per violation, in accordance with the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.
Pharmacy benefit managers will have to pay Arkansas drugstores dispensing fees under new rule

The plaintiffs also seek injunctive relief, a jury trial and payment of their attorneys’ fees.
Arkansas officials have taken several steps in the past few years to regulate pharmacy benefit managers. In 2024, a legislative panel approved an Arkansas Insurance Department rule requiring PBMs to include dispensing fees in their reimbursements to pharmacies for prescription drugs. A federal appeals court in August ruled that Arkansas can enforce this rule, upholding a dismissal of a legal challenge to the measure.
In July, Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin sued 22 defendants, including 13 drug manufacturers, alleging they violated the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act by undermining healthcare providers’ access to a federal drug discount program.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island archery hunters get earlier start under new deer rules
description: Rhode Island archery deer hunters started the season two weeks earlier in a larger portion of the state on Tuesday, a change supported by new data on the size of the deer population. The Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management (DEM) divides the Ocean State into four deer management zones for hunters. Archery season in […]
text:
A backyard camera captures several deer deer at 12:51 a.m. on Jan. 2, 2025, in Beechwood Estates in the Yawgoo area of Exeter. The town is located in Zone 2 where archery season started two weeks earlier. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island archery deer hunters started the season two weeks earlier in a larger portion of the state on Tuesday, a change supported by new data on the size of the deer population.
The Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management (DEM) divides the Ocean State into four deer management zones for hunters. Archery season in Zones 1 and 2 opened Tuesday for adults and runs through Jan. 31, 2027. (An archery hunting weekend for youth started on Saturday, Sept. 12.)
This marks a change in Zone 2, where archery season previously began Oct. 1. The zone covers much of western and southern Rhode Island, as well as Tiverton and Little Compton.
Zone 1’s archery season also began Tuesday. Its territory includes the state’s more developed and more densely populated urban corridor, including Providence, Warwick, Cranston and communities extending north toward Woonsocket. 
The additional time allowed hunters in Zone 2 this fall is part of a broader change to DEM’s regulations aligning archery, muzzleloader and shotgun hunting dates in Zones 1 and 2. The agency’s July deer program report noted that the respective start and end dates for these different modes of hunting are now the same across the two zones. 
Muzzleloader season lasts Nov. 7 through Dec. 4. Shotgun season begins a day later and lasts through the end of the year. 
Kim Keough, a DEM spokesperson, said the longer deer hunting season for archers in Zone 2 was requested in a survey of the state’s hunters. 
New data on the state’s deer population also gave a reason for the change, Keough said. The agency granted the hunters’ wish after an aerial infrared survey conducted last winter estimated a statewide distribution of 16 deer per square mile, with the distribution of deer across Zones 1 and 2 likely comparable. Tiverton and Little Compton had 17 deer per square mile.
Only about 8% of the state’s land area was surveyed in February and March 2025, while Colt State Park, Dutch Island and Patience Island were surveyed in their entirety. Colt State Park had a concentration of 70 deer per square mile, Dutch Island had 94 and Patience Island had 56.
The survey results released in February 2026. A helicopter equipped with an infrared camera flew in planned routes about a mile apart. The goal, the report recaps, “was not to produce a perfect count of every deer in the state…[but] to better understand how deer are distributed across Rhode Island and to see if the current hunting season structure should be modified.” 
The camera captured images about once every second along its routes. The resulting thousands of images were later reviewed by University of Rhode Island researchers who extrapolated estimates of the deer population from the visual data.
Warm-bodied deer sometimes appeared on the infrared images “as bright shapes against cooler ground,” the report reads, while noting that the conditions for photography were not always ideal. 
“In many images, deer did not stand out clearly from the background,” the report said, adding that the camera could not see through pine trees like it could deciduous trees like oaks, which offer better visibility when stripped of leaves in the winter.
“Therefore, it is likely that some deer were not counted as they were not visible to the camera.” 
The survey’s estimates were less than the range of roughly 18,000 to 21,000 deer in earlier population projections , Keough said.
DEM’s 2025-2026 deer report noted that the state’s hunters harvested 2,816 deer, which was only a 1% decline from 2,846 the previous year. 
Overall, the state’s hunters have harvested more deer annually since the 1970s: While 145 deer were harvested in 1976, the state’s harvests increased considerably until peaking at 2,937 in 2008.
Much of the state’s hunting activity was concentrated in Zone 2, which comprised the largest share of the state’s deer harvest, with 1,601 deer successfully harvested in Zone 2 last season. 
Zone 2’s popularity is largely due to its concentration of the state’s forested areas, much of which hosts the state’s public and cooperative hunting property.
Full hunting area maps for all four zones can be found on DEM’s website, as well as an interactive atlas.
 



 Breaking down Rhode Island’s Deer Management Zones

Zone 1: Barrington, Bristol, Central Falls, Charlestown, Cranston, Cumberland, East Greenwich, East Providence, Jamestown, Johnston, Lincoln, Middletown, Narragansett, Newport, North Kingstown, North Providence, North Smithfield, Pawtucket, Providence, Smithfield, South Kingstown, Warren, Warwick, West Warwick, Westerly and Woonsocket.
Zone 2: Burrillville, Coventry, Exeter, Foster, Glocester, Hopkinton, Little Compton, Portsmouth excluding Prudence and Patience islands, Richmond, Scituate, Tiverton and West Greenwich.
Zone 3: Patience and Prudence islands.
Zone 4: New Shoreham (Block Island). 
What’s changing: Zones 1 and 2 now share the same archery season, from Sept. 15 through Jan. 31. That’s an earlier start for Zone 2, which previously opened Oct. 1. Zone 3’s archery season has also been lengthened, beginning Oct. 19 and running through Jan. 31. Zone 4’s season is unchanged.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma board OKs unpermitted dam. Property owner offers his own solution.
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Residents of a drying up waterfront community expressed outrage Tuesday after a state agency allowed an unpermitted dam to remain upstream of their lake. After the meeting, one of the dam’s owners, former state Senate President Pro Tem Glenn Coffee, offered the residents $100,000 if they could raise $300,000 for seed money […]
text:
Tammy Cramer’s dock is now on dry land as lake levels have dropped at Cedar Lake near Hinton, Okla., Wednesday, July 15, 2026. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Residents of a drying up waterfront community expressed outrage Tuesday after a state agency allowed an unpermitted dam to remain upstream of their lake.
After the meeting, one of the dam’s owners, former state Senate President Pro Tem Glenn Coffee, offered the residents $100,000 if they could raise $300,000 for seed money to form a rural water district. They’d also have to agree not to sue him. 
The Oklahoma Water Resources Board approved a consent order with Coffee to allow the dams to continue holding water that Cedar Lake residents say used to fill their lake. State law allows a dam owner to seek a permit after construction.
Cedar Lake resident Mark Sullivan addresses reporters Tuesday following a meeting of the Oklahoma Water Resources Board in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)
Residents of the nearly 400-person lakefront community, located about 45 miles west of Oklahoma City,  blame the dams for the low lake level that has caused boat docks to become grounded, water wells to go dry and lower property values.
A report from the Oklahoma Water Resources Board blames the deterioration on a drop in aquifer levels related to homeowners’ domestic wells. 
Coffee, who serves as the Senate Republican Caucus senior legal consultant and is a former Oklahoma Secretary of State, said Tuesday that he blames the water drop on drought. An independent hydrologist report disagreed, saying the dams are a significant factor.
Residents packed the auditorium at the Oklahoma Judicial Center where the meeting was moved from its regular location at the Oklahoma Water Resources Board offices in Oklahoma City. Members of the Oklahoma Highway Patrol were on hand to provide security.
Residents were told in advance that they had no business before the board and would not be allowed to speak.
Cedar Lake residents Don Machacek, LaDeanna King and Patricia Sisson on Tuesday wait for a meeting of the Oklahoma Water Resources Board to begin in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)
But once the meeting began, one resident attempted to have the agenda item pulled out and heard separately from other items. He was not heard or recognized. The board’s agreement with Coffee was considered as part of a consent agenda, where multiple issues are taken up at the same time without any discussion.
“You guys have failed us,” one member of the audience yelled after the board declined to reconsider the vote.
“Whose money lines your pocket?” yelled another.
Residents want the dams removed on the Coffee family property or they want the family to release the water they say has been permitted to them for the lake.
“All Oklahomans lose today because anybody that wants to deprive their neighbors of water is free to do it, as long as people in that room are complicit in helping the rich and powerful do it,” said Mark Sullivan after the vote. He owns property at Cedar Lake, which is in Canadian County.
“This isn’t the end,” he said. “I mean, goodness gracious, a wrongdoing of this magnitude cannot be, you know, just passed over with a vote that says, ‘OK, hey, you get away with it today.’”
Some residents believe Coffee’s political status factored into the board’s decision.
In a statement after the meeting, the Oklahoma Water Resources Board said it is limited to ensuring the dam meets the safety criteria established in state law.
At its July board meeting, the Oklahoma Water Resources Board tabled action on the consent order until Tuesday.
Glenn Coffee, former Senate President Pro Tem, speaks Tuesday to reporters about a water dispute between his family and the residents of Cedar Lake. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)
Coffee waited until after the water board approved the consent order to announce his offer.
“Cedar Lake has an infrastructure problem,” Coffee said. “The problem is bigger than the dams.”
If the residents were to form a rural water district, they would be able to apply for grants, loans and other forms of assistance to solve long-term water problems, Coffee said.
Coffee said if he were to release water, it would only raise the Cedar Lake level one or two inches for a short period of time, something some residents dispute.
Coffee said he and his brothers own the property, which his father manages.
“We have a large family that uses it for recreation purposes, but it’s there primarily for watering the cattle and other purposes,” Coffee said.
Coffee said he wanted to turn the page and create solutions.
“I think if they are willing to come to the table with my family, lots of options are on the table, and I am not going to speculate on what those are,” Coffee said.
When told of Coffee’s offer Tuesday afternoon, Sullivan said it was “interesting,’’ adding that the offer was a wise decision.
He said homeowners would consider it.

name: VTDigger
title: Potential sale brings the former Sterling campus closer to new beginnings
description:
Sterling College and Headwaters Community Trust agreed on terms of a campus land sale, bringing the two groups closer to a deal.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Potential sale brings the former Sterling campus closer to new beginnings.
text:
The Sterling College campus in Craftsbury. Photo courtesy of Sterling College

When Sterling College graduated its last student in May, its trustees faced a hard question. With the school closing for good, what happens to the campus? 
This week, they got closer to an answer.
The former school and Headwaters Community Trust, an organization that provides affordable housing and land in the Northeast Kingdom, signed a sale purchase agreement. The two sides have not finalized the expected transition, but all that remains are standard due diligence practices for real estate transactions, according to Linda Ramsdell, the board president of Headwaters Community Trust.
“Sterling College is unique in their offering, and has a very special place in the world,” said Allison Hooper, chair of the Sterling College Board of Trustees. “And so this transition to Headwaters helps to perpetuate an opportunity to reinvigorate all of that ethos.”
Hooper declined to provide a sale price until the transaction is finalized.
Sterling, a small college that focused on environmental education and hands-on work experience, announced in November 2025 that it would close the school and held its last class in May. That left the board of trustees to find a new owner for the school’s roughly 165 acres and 26 buildings.
“Every year we had difficult times, and we managed to get through,” Hooper said. “And several years ago we considered closing, but we downsized the college, significantly downsized the budget and the curriculum, so we kept going, but the enrollment just was so low, it wasn’t a sustainable business model.” 
Sterling is the latest of seven small colleges that have shut down across Vermont in recent years, including the College of St. Joseph, Green Mountain College, Goddard College and Southern Vermont College. When a college closes in a rural area, it can be difficult to replace the economic revenue and reuse the real estate.
Vermont communities have mobilized to repurpose the former campuses. Southern Vermont College was temporarily obtained by Southwestern Vermont Health Care for COVID-19 testing and vaccination during the pandemic, and plans are now in the works to convert the campus into a luxury resort. In another instance, Green Mountain College may soon be repurposed for religious education.
By purchasing the former Sterling campus, Ramsdell said, Headwaters Community Trust can ensure it continues to meet the needs of the Craftsbury community.
Craftsbury Saplings, a local preschool, plans to remodel one of the campus dormitories and move their center onto campus. According to a Sterling College press release, the move would allow the center to welcome almost twice as many children as it currently does, as well as offer infant care.
The campus is ripe with opportunities for affordable housing projects and educational uses, both as a collaboration with the public school system and as a place for Sterling’s faculty to continue to teach through a different format than a traditional college, Ramsdell added.
The Sterling Institute, established by Sterling faculty and staff, hopes to provide an avenue for the faculty to continue educating on Sterling’s campus. It’s a non-credit educational program designed to continue the college’s legacy in hands-on learning and environmental stewardship after the closure. Hooper said she hopes this organization can continue to grow under the campus’ new ownership.
“It’s a competitive market for those activities,” Hooper said. “So I’m hopeful that the Sterling Institute will give itself enough of a runway to be able to realize their dream.”
Ramsdell said she’s eager to finish the acquisition process and start involving the community.
“A lot of people care deeply about this place,” Ramsdell said in the press release. “Our job now is to ensure the community has a voice in what comes next.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota recreational cannabis sales hit $150M one year in
description: Minnesotans bought over $150 million worth of recreational cannabis products in the first year of sales at state-licensed stores, the state’s Office of Cannabis Management said in a press release Tuesday. The state’s 90,000 registered medical cannabis patients also bought over $100 million of medicinal weed, adding to a total of at least $250 million […]
text:
Legal cannabis flower from RISE dispensary. Minnesotans have bought over $150 million worth of recreational cannabis products since non-tribal licensed businesses began selling them September 2025. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesotans bought over $150 million worth of recreational cannabis products in the first year of sales at state-licensed stores, the state’s Office of Cannabis Management said in a press release Tuesday.
The state’s 90,000 registered medical cannabis patients also bought over $100 million of medicinal weed, adding to a total of at least $250 million of cannabis sales since last September.
The state’s first non-tribal recreational marijuana shops opened about a year ago, two years after state legalization. Tribal nations were able to move quicker by opening stores on reservations and then negotiating compacts with the state to open off-reservation dispensaries.
Minnesota’s first non-tribal recreational dispensaries open two years after legalization

The number of businesses with adult-use, or recreational, cannabis retail licenses has grown to over 200, according to the office’s market dashboard.
More than 2 in 5 of all cannabis business licenses — including growing licenses — have gone to so-called social equity applicants, originally intended to include people from marginalized communities disproportionately impacted by the criminalization of marijuana. That includes people who were convicted of selling marijuana before it was legalized, or the parents or children of someone with a conviction. The Legislature expanded the definition of social equity so that it included more than one-third of all Minnesotans, according to a Reformer estimate.


The number of cannabis plants being grown by licensed cultivators has skyrocketed in the past year, from around 72,000 plants in inventories last September to around 486,000 plants currently.
The sales and plants numbers don’t include hemp-derived THC products, the low-dose edibles and drinks found in liquor stores and gas stations across the state. Those products were inadvertently legalized by Congress in 2018 and by the Minnesota Legislature in 2022. The industry is facing a possible extinction thanks to a federal ban set to begin in December.
Recreational and medical marijuana sales along with low-dose THC sales generated $45 million in tax revenue from last September to July, the Office of Cannabis Management said. As of a new law that took effect in July, Minnesota’s cannabis tax is 15%. After adding the state’s sales tax, the total tax rate for cannabis is around 22%, and higher in many metro cities.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Supreme Court to decide if governor overstepped sending National Guard to DC
description: Watchdog nonprofits argued Gov. Henry McMaster's deployment went beyond his powers in state law, but his attorneys disagreed.
text:
U.S. Army Spc. Zachary Benehaley, with the 4th Battalion, 118th Infantry Regiment, South Carolina National Guard, monitors a Metro platform at the Federal Center Metro Station in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 14, 2025. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Army National Guard/Sgt. Jalen Miller)CLEMSON — A legal challenge over Gov. Henry McMaster’s decision to send National Guard troops to Washington, D.C., could test the bounds of the governor’s power as the state’s commander in chief, attorneys argued to the state Supreme Court on Tuesday.
Arguments in the case, which a government watchdog group filed in January, came as 30 troops from the state remain in the nation’s capital as part of President Donald Trump’s “Operation Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful.” McMaster first sent troops to D.C. in August 2025, and the most recent deployment returned in August after three months.
Lawsuit claims SC governor illegally sent National Guard troops to DC

The next rotation of 300 soldiers, which will last six months, is scheduled to leave the first week of December, according to the governor’s office.
The Public Interest Foundation and American Civil Liberties Union told the state’s highest court Tuesday that McMaster doesn’t have the legal authority to send them there. McMaster’s attorneys disagreed, saying he has sweeping powers as the state’s commander in chief.
A similar legal challenge in West Virginia was dismissed in November 2025, after a circuit court judge ruled Gov. Patrick Morrisey acted lawfully. D.C.’s attorney general is suing to remove National Guard troops from the city.
Questions of authority
The decision on the governor’s authority over the National Guard will likely come down to how the five justices interpret two longstanding state laws.
Under those laws, the governor can deploy or activate the National Guard to stop “war, insurrection, rebellion, invasion, tumult, riot or a mob,” or when a “public disaster,” such as a natural disaster, takes place. He can also activate the guard to execute laws, including as requested by the president.
Neither law says anything about sending troops to other states or jurisdictions, attorneys said.
SC governor deploys troops to Washington at Pentagon’s request

“I will grant, of course, there’s nothing explicit in those statutes that says you may send the guard out of state,” said Grayson Lambert, the governor’s chief legal counsel, after questions about the interpretation from justices. “But there is nothing explicit in those statutes that says you can’t.”
McMaster’s deployment of the troops didn’t meet the requirements established in the law, said Allen Chaney, attorney for the ACLU. The offices of the governor and adjutant general said the soldiers’ mission involved supporting local law enforcement and maintaining safety for residents and visitors, but their work didn’t reflect that, Chaney said.
“Hundreds of South Carolina guardsmen spent the better part of this year in Washington, D.C., not repelling an invasion, putting down a riot or quelling a tumult but picking up trash, spreading mulch and patrolling subway platforms,” Chaney said.
Typically, the governor deploys the National Guard at the request of another state’s governor, Chaney said.
An interstate mutual aid network gives states a standing agreement to deploy troops during emergencies, such as natural disasters. No similar agreement existed in this case, and McMaster’s only justification for deploying troops came from the news release he put out announcing the mission, Chaney said.
If justices side with the governor, nothing will stop McMaster or a future governor from sending troops to any other city, Chaney said. Though this deployment came at the president’s request, the ACLU contended it failed to meet legal benchmarks.
“Here, the governor is asserting pretty generalized, implicit authority to send the National Guard to D.C.,” Chaney said. “If he is given that power, there is no check of consent.”
Chief Justice John Kittredge questioned where justices might draw the line on the governor’s authority. The state constitution puts the governor in charge of commanding the state’s militia, which suggests he has the authority to make decisions about how to use it, Kittredge said, adding that McMaster could have just as easily turned down Trump’s request.
“It’s a matter of discretion,” he said. “It’s that basic.”
That applies only after a situation meets the requirements set in state law, Chaney replied. Those laws are meant to create a check on the governor’s powers, keeping him from sending out soldiers whenever and wherever he wants, the attorney argued.
“We’re not asking the court, “Was this a good idea or a bad idea to deploy the National Guard to D.C.?’” Chaney said. “We’re asking, ‘Does the statute actually authorize the governor to deploy, under these conditions, the guard to D.C.?’”
The answer is yes, Lambert said.
“The governor is the commander in chief of the South Carolina militia, and he possesses broad constitutional and statutory authority to call out the militia,” Lambert said.
Legislators who passed that law clearly meant for the governor to have the authority to send troops to any other state, Lambert said.
He pointed to a separate law barring the State Guard, an all-volunteer force that assists the National Guard, from deploying across state lines. That specification would be pointless if legislators wrote their requirements for the state and national guards with the intention of working only within the state, he said.
Lambert pointed as far back as the Seminole, Mexican and Spanish-American wars of the 1800s as examples of governors using their authority to deploy the state militia, which eventually became the National Guard.
More recent deployments have used the same federal law used to send troops to D.C., Lambert said. Known as Title 32, the agreement requires the federal government to pay for the cost of deployment but allows the governor to keep control over the guardsmen.
Chief Justice John Kittredge questions attorneys during a state Supreme Court hearing in Clemson, S.C., on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (Screenshot of SCETV livestream)
Under those agreements, the state sent the National Guard to help with security missions in Atlanta during the 1996 Olympics and to provide security in D.C. during protests in 2020, Lambert said.
“There are 230-plus years of practice of the governor deploying the guard outside of South Carolina when the need arises and absolutely no pushback from another branch of government whose authority would theoretically be infringed by that,” Lambert said.
Because the state has done that before, though, doesn’t make it correct, said Justice George James.
“The fact that it hasn’t been challenged doesn’t make it legal,” he said.
That’s true, Lambert replied. But the multiple deployments without pushback from legislators suggest the governor could send troops to other states in similar instances under the boundaries legislators set, he said.
Justices gave no timeline on a decision Tuesday.
Broader legal questions
Much of Lambert’s argument centered around whether the watchdog groups had the right to sue.
South Carolina allows legal challenges under the “public importance exception,” which is meant to decide on matters that don’t actually harm anyone involved if they matter to the general public. The court can also take up cases for the sake of offering guidance for future laws and actions.
Justices shouldn’t take up those sorts of cases, including this one, and should instead hear only legal challenges from people directly affected, Lambert said.
If the Supreme Court were to agree, that could have major implications for how the court interprets the state’s laws, Kittredge and James said.
Cases where no one is directly hurt, such as violations of open meeting laws, would no longer come up, they said. Nor would environmental cases brought by nonprofits such as the Sierra Club, which isn’t involved with every piece of land it sues to protect, the justices said.
“Those would never have seen the light of day in a courtroom,” James said.
Just because no single person is harmed by a decision doesn’t mean it stops mattering to the people of the state, Chaney said.
“We are not suggesting that the abuse of the governor’s authority as commander in chief imposes no harm at all; merely that it’s a diffuse constitutional harm that’s borne by all citizens of the state,” Chaney said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: A new report highlights the scarcity of maternal care in rural NC
description: One in six North Carolina counties is a maternity care desert, with no birthing facilities or obstetric clinicians, according to a new report from the March of Dimes. About 61,000 women ages 18 to 44 live in maternity care deserts, and 4,000 babies are born each year to mothers who live in maternity care deserts. […]
text:
North Carolina's infant mortality rate declined in 2024, but racial disparities remained. (Photo: Getty Images)One in six North Carolina counties is a maternity care desert, with no birthing facilities or obstetric clinicians, according to a new report from the March of Dimes.
About 61,000 women ages 18 to 44 live in maternity care deserts, and 4,000 babies are born each year to mothers who live in maternity care deserts. Almost 67% of maternity deserts are in rural counties. Twelve percent of counties have only one obstetric clinician. 
Patricia Campbell, director of the March of Dimes’ maternal & infant health initiative, presented the report on access to maternity care to a committee of the N.C. Child Fatality Task Force focused on health during and around the time of birth.
On average, women in North Carolina travel 17 minutes to reach a hospital with labor and delivery services. However, women who live in maternity deserts travel nearly twice as long, she said.
The state’s infant mortality rate dropped to a historic low in 2024. But Black babies continue to die at a rate 3 times higher than that of white babies.
Eastern counties have the highest rates of infant mortality, said Kathleen Jones-Vessey, an epidemiologist at the N.C. Division of Public Health. Those counties also have some of the state’s highest rates of unemployment, poverty, and other non-medical factors related to health, she said.
The state has a goal in its Healthy North Carolina Plan of narrowing the racial disparity ratio to 1.5 by 2030, but it is moving in the wrong direction. 
NC’s child death rate is rising, with a big jump in teen homicides

Each state is getting federal money to help improve rural healthcare. 
The state Department of Health and Human Services is using its federal rural health transformation grant to help expand access to maternity care. 
North Carolina received $213 million in its initial installment. With that federal money, the state has set up regional “NC Roots” hubs connecting medical, behavioral and social services. 
Some of the work assigned to the hubs focuses on perinatal care, said Belinda Pettiford, section chief in the N.C. Division of Public Health. 
The hubs will develop plans to increase access to prenatal services, Pettiford said. “Our focus is around improving access in that first trimester, because our numbers in North Carolina are going in the opposite direction that we’d like them to go,” she said.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Another gubernatorial debate canceled due to GOP candidate Tom Tiffany declining to participate
description: Another planned debate between Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley has been canceled as Tiffany declines to participate in more than one debate ahead of the Nov. 3 election.  The planned debate was jointly sponsored by the Milwaukee County Intergovernmental Cooperation Council, TMJ4 and the University of W[...]
text:
(Photos by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Another planned debate between Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley has been canceled as Tiffany declines to participate in more than one debate ahead of the Nov. 3 election. 
The planned debate was jointly sponsored by the Milwaukee County Intergovernmental Cooperation Council, TMJ4 and the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee and was to be held at the UW-Milwaukee campus. 
“We are deeply disappointed that scheduling did not work out to make this happen,” the organizations said in a statement. “We hope that Wisconsin’s next governor will make local government a significant focus of his administration.” 
TMJ4 reporter Charles Benson said in a post on X that Tiffany had indicated he would only do one debate and Crowley was not available for the original date proposed by the channel, though his team was interested in finding another date for the debate. 
This is the second debate to be canceled after Tiffany declined to participate. The Wisconsin Broadcasters Association, which has hosted gubernatorial debates since 1990, canceled its proposed debate two weeks ago. Tiffany told conservative radio host Dan O’Donnell that he didn’t agree to the debate because he thought one debate was sufficient. 
“I had no time. There was lots of negotiations going on behind the scenes,” Tiffany said. “One debate is sufficient to be able to cover the issues that need to be covered.”
Crowley’s campaign manager Garren Randolph said in a statement that Crowley was looking forward to the debate. He criticized Tiffany, saying he is “refusing more debates because he doesn’t want to face voters and answer tough questions about his record of supporting an endless war that’s resulting in record high gas and diesel costs, as well as voting for every single one of Donald Trump’s tariffs that are crushing Wisconsin farmers and manufacturers, and driving up costs on everything from groceries to the new shoes parents are trying to buy for their kids as they go back to school.”
The Examiner has reached out to the Tiffany campaign for comment. 
Both candidates plan to participate in an Oct. 21 debate hosted by WISN-12. It will be moderated by WISN-12 reporters Matt Smith and Gerron Jordan and will cover topics including cost of living, taxes, immigration enforcement, data centers and election security.

text:
The Rhode Island Board of Elections met Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, to certify results from the state's Sept. 9 primary. (Screenshot)A review of three close primaries by the Rhode Island Board of Elections morning did not change the winner in any of them, Miguel Nunez, elections board director, told the panel Tuesday.
A rereading of flash drives holding vote totals from ballot counting machines concluded with identical margins of victory for Republican gubernatorial nominee Aaron Guckian and Democratic Providence City Councilor Justin Roias, Hunter said. A third review that involved recounting every ballot cast in a separate Providence City Council primary cemented Councilor Juan Pichardo’s victory, though the vote total changed slightly, Hunter said.
RI elections board rejects Pelino’s recount request in Republican gubernatorial primary

The elections board certified results for all of the Sept. 9 races, including those subject to recounts, at its Tuesday afternoon meeting. The 158,973 total ballots cast represents just over 20% of registered voters, the highest percentage of participation on record in a state primary in the last decade, according to historical data from the Department of State.
In 2022, the last primary election cycle that included state general officeholders, 137,686 voters cast ballots, equal to 17% of registered voters.
More than two-thirds of 2026 primary voters cast ballots on the day of the primary, followed by 18% who submitted mail ballots. The remainder voted during the 20-day early, in-person voting hours offered at designated sites in every municipality.
Two hours before the final certification, Guckian declared himself the victor of the GOP gubernatorial contest, thanking voters, election administrators and his campaign team while setting the stage for his general election race. 
“One party rule has not served Rhode Islanders well and we need to restore balance to state government. Families are being crushed by the cost of living, taxes, fees, energy bills, and a state government that now spends more than $15 billion a year,” Guckian, 50, of East Greenwich, said in a statement. “Rhode Islanders deserve better.”
The eight-paragraph press release did not mention his opponent, Elaine Pelino. Pelino, 72, of North Smithfield, lost the Republican nomination by 259 votes, but continues to protest what she claims is a lack of public notice and transparency in counting ballots.
“Conservatives have spent years saying election integrity matters,” Pelino said in a Facebook post Tuesday afternoon. “This is a chance to show we mean it in the unglamorous cases too: checking the math in a close race, even when the outcome isn’t a question of Democrat vs. Republican.”
The MAGA Republican candidate agreed with election administrators and good government advocates on one problem with the process: the late date of the state primary — second to last nationwide this election cycle — leaves little time to consider recount requests or other problems before certifying results and mailing general election ballots out to military and overseas voters. Ballots must be mailed by 8 a.m. Saturday to reach voters in time for the Nov. 3 election, Nunez said.
“The fix is structural: move the primary earlier so the count, the review, and any recount can happen without a stopwatch running,” Pelino wrote. “Rhode Island shouldn’t rush the process that decides who’s on the ballot.” 
Guckian did not respond to requests for comment on his opponent’s protests of the process.
A self-described compassionate conservative, Guckian now faces Democratic nominee Helena Buonanno Foulkes, and independents Ken Block, Jay Gotra and C.D. Reynolds in the general election. Much of Guckian’s messaging around fiscal responsibility and government efficiency echoes that of Block, a former Republican candidate, and Foulkes, who blasted Gov. Dan McKee for poor management of major projects like the Washington Bridge demolition and rebuild.
Preliminary public polling in the governor’s race shows Foulkes with a 20-point lead over Block, with the Republican nominee close behind. But,  one in five likely voters were still undecided as of the most recent survey, published on Aug. 27 by the University of New Hampshire.
In Providence, incumbents prevailed following reexamination of results in two tight Providence City Council Democratic primaries. 
A recount confirmed Councilor Juan Pichardo as the winner of the primary for the Ward 9 seat spanning Elmwood, South Elmwood and Roger Williams Park, defeating challenger Carmen Castillo. Pichardo initially led Castillo by nine votes, widening to an 11-vote margin following the recount, Nunez said. 
“Today is a victory for voters and working families for children,” Pichardo said in an interview. “Every vote counts. It’s not just a saying.”
Pichardo will face independent candidate Diego Tomas Morley in the Nov. 3 general election.
Castillo did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday.
A rereading of memory sticks also did not change the outcome for the Providence City Council Ward 4 primary, cementing Councilor Justin Roias’ 55-vote win over challenger Joseph Casoli for the seat representing the Wanskuck and Charles neighborhoods.
Casoli said in an interview Tuesday that he is still contemplating a write-in challenge against Roias in the general election.
Roias did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Elections board members Marcela Betancur and Randy Jackvony did not attend the meeting.

title: A constitutional convention to limit abortion rights? Democrats push back on DeBoyer suggestion
description: Michigan Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay Township), the Republican lieutenant governor nominee and running mate to U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) faced backlash from Democrats and reproductive rights groups after he floated the idea of re-introducing limits on abortion in Michigan via a constitutional convention. At a news conference Tuesday, Michigan Sen[...]
text:
Michigan House Oversight Committee Chair Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay Township) talks to reporters on continuing allegations of ethics violation by Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel. Dec. 16, 2025 | Screenshot Michigan Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay Township), the Republican lieutenant governor nominee and running mate to U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) faced backlash from Democrats and reproductive rights groups after he floated the idea of re-introducing limits on abortion in Michigan via a constitutional convention.
At a news conference Tuesday, Michigan Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks, Democratic lieutenant governor nominee, called the remarks shocking.   During a Saturday event in Battle Creek, DeBoyer proposed banning abortion after 12 weeks of pregnancy by enshrining those limits in the state constitution through a convention. The comments were first reported by The Detroit News. Michigan’s voters will decide in November whether to hold a constitutional convention in 2027.
“Sometimes, you have to say to yourself, ‘This might be our only way,’” DeBoyer said, according to the Detroit News. “It might be, and I don’t know that I’m going to vote yes on it. I’m just giving you the argument that it might be our only way to make some of these modifications.” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Asking an audience member about new restrictions on abortion, he continued on to say, “If I could get that pulled off today and get it reeled back to 12 weeks, would you support me?” 
DeBoyer, who described himself as “a staunch pro-life guy,” was met with a positive response. 
Although DeBoyer did not dispute the statement, he walked back the sentiment to the News, saying that the issue was “settled,” similar to language used by James in 2024 in his re-election bid for Congress, when he said, “the fact of the matter is that abortion is enshrined in our (state) constitution.”
Alyvia Bailey, a spokesperson for the James-DeBoyer campaign, reiterated the same message to the Michigan Advance and said, “The abortion issue has been settled by the people of Michigan.” Bailey added that further back-and-forth on the topic was a distraction from other campaign issues. 
However, Brinks (D-Grand Rapids), the Democratic Party nominee for lieutenant governor, disputed that framing in a call with reporters. Brinks said that  “the reproductive freedom issue is clearly not settled so long as John James and Jay DeBoyer have a shot at becoming governor and lieutenant governor.”
Brinks said DeBoyer and James, and the GOP as a whole, were “clearly trying to say one thing and do another, or say nothing and then go after our rights.”
James’ vote record on reproductive rights has been celebrated by anti-abortion groups, and in his 2018 U.S. Senate bid, he compared abortion to “genocide.”
DeBoyer’s statements similarly drew the ire of reproductive rights organizations. 
“We need to believe John James and Jay DeBoyer when they tell us they are anti-abortion extremists,” said Shanay Watson-Whittaker, the director of Michigan campaigns for Reproductive Freedom for All, during the Tuesday press call. “Voters are watching, and they will hold DeBoyer and James accountable at the polls.”
Watson-Whittaker also warned that, while DeBoyer had floated the idea of putting in place abortion restrictions by way of a constitutional convention, she would expect them to “use any means possible” to do so if the constitutional convention ballot measure fails. 
“This is not the only avenue, we have to stay vigilant,” Watson-Whittaker said.
Dr. Melissa Bayne, an OB/GYN in west Michigan and member of the Committee to Protect Healthcare’s Reproductive Freedom Taskforce, called the comments “deeply disturbing.”
“Not only does DeBoyer’s plan fly in the face of Michigan voters, who spoke loudly and clearly when they passed the Reproductive Freedom for All amendment, but it’s downright dangerous,” Bayne said. “We’re seeing how abortion bans in other states are harming women’s health and even taking their lives. Ignoring the will of the voters to once again ban abortion in our state would lead to preventable deaths here too.”
Bayne added that “John James and Jay DeBoyer should stick to politics and leave medicine to the physicians.”
Paula Thornton Greear, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Advocates of Michigan, said DeBoyer suggesting a constitutional convention as a way to restrict abortion access “is deeply concerning.”  
“Michiganders deserve leaders who respect the rights they secured at the ballot box, not ones who look for new ways to take those rights away,” Greear said. “Rep. DeBoyer may now say that abortion rights are ‘settled’ in Michigan, but his recent comments tell a different story.”
In a Facebook post, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer said “Michigan voters already made reproductive freedom a constitutional right. Now Republicans want to overturn your rights and overrule your vote.”
A spokesperson for Right to Life of Michigan did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication. This story will be updated when a response is received.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Some New Mexico agencies improved on opioid fund spending after early struggles, state auditor says
description: New Mexico state agencies failed to spend roughly a quarter of the millions of dollars in opioid settlement funds they received in the 2024 fiscal year, according to a new report from the New Mexico State Auditor’s Office.
text:
A new report the New Mexico State Auditor’s Office released Sept. 15, 2026, found that state agencies failed to spend nearly a quarter of the $21 million they received in opioid settlement funds in fiscal year 2024, but have since greatly improved. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico state agencies failed to spend roughly a quarter of the millions of dollars in opioid settlement funds they received in the 2024 fiscal year, according to a new report from the New Mexico State Auditor’s Office.
The state agencies, along with local governments, began receiving opioid litigation settlement payments in 2023 intended to compensate communities for the harms caused by the prescription opiate manufacturers, distributors and pharmacies in creating and exacerbating a national epidemic. The edipemic remains acutely felt in New Mexico, where the drug overdose death rate has been one of the highest in the nation for most of the last two decades.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The funds will ultimately total more than $920 million in New Mexico, including more than $344 million that is designated for local governments and more than $328 million for state agencies. 
The state auditor’s office, in a report released Tuesday, examined how seven state agencies used approximately $54 million they received in opioid settlement funds over the last three fiscal years. 
The state agencies received the funds to pay for a range of services related to opioid addiction. 
The Health Care Authority, for example, received funding for housing assistance, telehealth services and community behavioral health clinics. The state Health and Corrections departments also received funds for the provision of overdose reversal drugs to rural areas and opioid replacement drugs to state prisons. 
In New Mexico’s 2024 fiscal year, which runs between July 1, 2023, and June 30, 2024, the seven public entities returned more than $5 million of $21 million they received, an indication that they were unable to spend roughly 24% of the funding they received within required time periods, according to the report. 
The New Mexico Children, Youth and Families Department, the state’s child welfare agency, failed to spend any of the $2 million it received that year in funding aimed at improving monitoring and adherence to plans for families raising infants exposed to opioids. 
The CYFD did not respond to the auditor’s office about why it failed to spend those funds, according to the report. A CYFD spokesperson also did not respond to Source NM’s emailed request for comment Tuesday. 
New Mexico local governments lag in spending opioid settlement funds, new report finds

However, the state auditor noted that many of the entities that received funding may have failed to spend it all that fiscal year as they worked on “new initiatives that required hiring staff, establishing contracts, developing partnerships, or building service capacity.”
The report also notes that the agencies and UNM vastly improved their spending in the two subsequent fiscal years. In fiscal years 2025 and 2026, the entities spent all but approximately 1% of the roughly $32 million they received. 
State Auditor Joseph Maestas, in a statement Tuesday, said the improvements since 2024 are “encouraging signs that state agencies are learning, adapting, and improving how they deploy opioid settlement funds.”
Maestas’ report is the second in recent weeks from the auditor’s office evaluating opioid settlement payments. The first focused on local governments and found that almost half of them had failed to report any spending by July of last year.

title: New Mexico’s largest electric provider, private equity firm propose revised merger terms
description: The parent company of New Mexico’s largest electric provider and the private equity firm looking to acquire it on Tuesday asked state regulators to approve a revised merger application that company officials say would help the company invest in New Mexico’s aging electric grid and give customers direct rebates. The proposal includes $220 million in direct cu[...]
text:
TXNM Energy Inc., the parent company of New Mexico’s largest electric provider, and the private equity firm vying to acquire it on Sept 15, 2026, proposed a revised merger, which company officials say would enable them to modernize the state’s aging grid and give customers direct rebates. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)The parent company of New Mexico’s largest electric provider and the private equity firm looking to acquire it on Tuesday asked state regulators to approve a revised merger application that company officials say would help the company invest in New Mexico’s aging electric grid and give customers direct rebates.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The draft application, which would require New Mexico Public Regulation Commission approval, says the companies would issue $220 million in direct customer rate credits. In a statement, PNM’s parent company, TXNM Energy Inc., and private equity firm Blackstone Infrastructure noted that amount is more than double the amount of rate credits proposed in their initial merger application.
The proposed revisions also include $40 million for workforce and economic development initiatives; $25 million for virtual infrastructure upgrades; and $15 million for PNM’s Good Neighbor Fund, which provides bill payment assistance to low-income households.
It also includes commitments to keep PNM’s New Mexico headquarters and to keep in-state leadership and management officials.
“Our focus has been and will continue to be on serving our customers with safe, reliable, affordable energy,” Don Tarry, PNM and TXNM president and CEO, said in a statement. “These enhanced commitments put real dollars back in customers’ pockets, protect the people who do this work every day and keep PNM locally managed and locally rooted — while giving us the capital to build the grid New Mexico needs.”
PNM, private equity firm extend merger deadline to mid-2027 after regulators deem stock sale illegal

The proposal comes amid legal and public pushback to the proposed merger, and follows regulators’ finding earlier this summer that the two companies violated state law by conducting a $400 million stock sale in 2025 without first gaining PRC approval. 
Regulators ordered the two sides to reverse the sale.
After paying back Blackstone, TXNM announced it intended to once again sell $400 million worth of company stock. The pending private equity takeover’s opponents called on state leaders to buy the shares and give the state government more control over its largest electric company. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, however, has consistently opposed that proposal.
The revised application announcement also comes less than a week after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez sent a letter to Tarry alleging that numerous customers have complained about the company’s practice of issuing expensive monthly bills based on “estimated” electricity consumption, rather than a meter reading.

title: Attorney general defends Trump blast at US Supreme Court over vote-by-mail ruling
text: The Trump administration will comply with the U.S. Supreme Court’s order this week blocking new restrictions on mail voting for this year’s elections, but President Donald Trump was right to attack the ruling, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said during a wide-ranging White House press conference Tuesday.Concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence are overstated, military action in Iran is not a war and the justices wrongly decided the case in which the Justice Department argued in defense of a U.S. Postal Service rule overhauling vote-by-mail requirements before the election, Blanche told reporters during a roughly half-hour briefing in the White House Rose Garden.Blanche, who was Trump’s personal attorney before joining the government, began the press conference praising federal prosecutions of terrorism and election fraud suspects. But he quickly transitioned into a broad defense of recent Trump actions and administration policies.The Trump administration will continue prioritizing “election security” ahead of this year’s midterms, despite its setback at the Supreme Court on the proposed mail voting regulation, he said. “Of course we're going to comply with the Supreme Court's decision, as we always do,” he said. “That doesn't mean that we're not going to do everything in this administration that we can to make sure that there are free and fair elections,” he added. “There's this constant pressure and this effort by the media and mostly by Democrats that somehow doing that is a bad thing. Everybody should want that.”Trump’s morning Truth Social post articulating regret over nominating some Supreme Court justices who have ruled against him was “what a democracy is about,” Blanche added.“As far as President Trump's Truth about about the justices, he is very frustrated, and … he has every right, and, indeed, he should communicate his concerns with the Supreme Court whenever he has them,” Blanche said. “I am also upset about the Supreme Court decision. But the idea that President Trump shouldn't be allowed to communicate to the American people his frustration, I don’t share that.”While opining on a host of issues, Blanche declined to comment on potential criminal investigations, including when asked about Minnesota Democratic U.S. Rep Ilhan Omar and longtime public health official Anthony Fauci.AI as campaign issueAnxiety about artificial intelligence “conveniently became a flashpoint this week,” Blanche said, suggesting Democrats sought to ramp up discontent ahead of Nov. 3 midterm elections to determine control of Congress.Asked about how AI should be regulated and if development should be slowed, Blanche said the Department of Justice’s mission is to prosecute, not regulate. But he echoed Trump’s comments this week that U.S. companies should press forward with the technology to remain competitive with China.Political figures from both parties have commented on AI policy following a call by the chief executives of top companies for a development slowdown amid disclosures the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity.“When the leaders of the top AI companies are sounding the alarm about the potential for imminent threats, we need to take them seriously,” Hawaii Democratic Sen. Brian Schatz said Tuesday. “This is an emergency, and we need to treat it like an emergency. If the risk of AI is anywhere near the level that it has been characterized to be, then we have an obligation to act on a bipartisan basis immediately.”In the Rose Garden, Blanche questioned whether Democrats were raising the issue in good faith or for an electoral advantage.“Every Democrat senator suddenly races to a microphone to talk about AI after being eerily silent for months and months and months,” he said. “So to talk about the timing of this as being nothing but an effort to to influence the midterms, I shouldn't have to say that out loud. Of course, that's what it is. And that shouldn't be what drives the decisions that we're making around AI. We can't lose the AI race to China, right?”Hegseth ‘phenomenal’Asked about the articles of impeachment Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced Tuesday against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, objecting to continued military action in Iran even after the House passed a resolution calling for an end to the war, Blanche said Hegseth was doing “a phenomenal job.”The Justice Department ensures that all Defense Department activity is lawful, Blanche said. He added that the conflict should not be categorized as a war.“You called it a war,” he told the reporter who asked about the impeachment. “I disagree with that characterization, as does most of Congress.”Ariana Figueroa contributed to this report.

name: VTDigger
title: Hundreds of layoffs announced at the 2 largest healthcare networks Vermonters rely on
description:
Dartmouth Health is cutting over 420 positions while University of Vermont Health lays off 199 staff.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Hundreds of layoffs announced at the 2 largest healthcare networks Vermonters rely on.
text:
TeleED hub: Alison Kapadia, MD, and Daryl Holthoff, RN, providing emergency care to patients via the TeleED hub. Photo courtesy of Dartmouth Health

Hundreds of layoffs are underway at the two major healthcare networks Vermonters rely on.
Facing similar financial challenges, both Dartmouth Health and the University of Vermont Health network announced the cuts Tuesday ahead of the Oct. 1 start to hospitals’ fiscal year. 
UVM Health is in the process of laying off 199 staffers, according to a letter that network CEO Steve Leffler sent employees Tuesday. 
The layoffs include the closure of two patient care units, according to a separate release from the hospital.
The cuts at UVM Health are expected to save $16.8 million, the network said Tuesday.
Across the Connecticut River, 124 Dartmouth Health employees learned that their positions are being terminated, according to a release Tuesday from the New Hampshire-based hospital network. The network canceled an additional 303 open positions at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, New Hampshire, and at its clinics in the region.  
Vermonters rely heavily on care from Dartmouth Health, which includes the medical center, Mt. Ascutney Hospital and Health Center in Windsor, Southwestern Vermont Medical Center in Bennington and six other New Hampshire hospitals. About 40% of Dartmouth Hitchcock’s patients are Vermonters, said Audra Burns, a spokesperson for the network.
Hospitals across the nation are struggling to find financial stability. The costs of drugs, supplies and salaries are increasing, but the number of patients who seek out care and pay for it is shrinking. 
Dartmouth Health
Earlier this year, Dartmouth Health began to interrogate spending in light of its financial challenges — but Tuesday marked the first major layoffs.
An early sign of change came this summer when the network confirmed its intention to close its Tele-ICU and Tele-ED services, which the network had identified as unsustainable without outside investment.
Those telehealth services are among the three programs the network said it would eliminate as part of Tuesday’s layoffs.
Dartmouth Health also wants to end a collaborative group it has run for 17 years across community hospitals, behavioral health centers and home health agencies throughout northern New England, called the New England Alliance for Health. 
Additionally, the network plans to close an employee training program and instead outsource it. 
The cuts include an effort to consolidate executive roles and administrative positions, according to a press release.
Dartmouth Health’s staff reductions are part of a larger plan to curb spending and increase revenue. The network emphasized work it’s already done to reduce the amount it spends on temporary traveling clinicians and on sending its own staff to conferences. The network also stressed Tuesday its efforts to review operating costs like contracts and supplies, and its efforts to expand staff capacity to care for more patients. 
In April, the hospital system created a new office specifically to address the organization’s financial health. The next month, Dartmouth Health told its bondholders that it had operated at a $63.5 million loss between October 2025 and March 2026, according to reporting by the Valley News. 
“The employees affected by these changes have made meaningful contributions to Dartmouth Health, our patients and our communities,” Dr. Joanne Conroy, Dartmouth Health’s CEO and president, wrote in the Tuesday release. “Some have spent many years serving this organization. The decision to eliminate a position or program does not diminish the value of the work these colleagues have done and the contributions they have made.”
UVM Health 
UVM Health is no stranger to cuts. The Tuesday layoffs are the latest in a long series of expense reduction measures, including job cuts, that the hospital has already taken. 
“This is not the first or the last step we’ll need to take to make our health system more sustainable,” Leffler wrote in his Tuesday letter to staff.
Annie Mackin, a spokesperson for the hospital group, said the network had been in the process of figuring out how to best make these reductions well before the Green Mountain Care Board’s Monday ruling for the hospital to cut its revenue even further. 
The layoffs span all six hospitals in the network’s New York and Vermont footprint, including at Helen Porter Rehabilitation & Nursing and the network’s Home Health and Hospice Services, a release from the hospital detailed. 
UVM Medical Center now intends to close a general medicine unit and care for those patients on a similarly equipped floor. It is also consolidating an alternative care unit. Mackin said those moves were possible because the unit has had lower numbers of patients recently. UVM Medical Center has also pushed to reduce patients’ lengths of stay, she said. The layoffs at UVMMC account for 118 of the total positions affected.
At Central Vermont Medical Center in Berlin, three mental health technicians are among the 24 total positions being cut. The total includes patient safety attendants, who sit and observe patients who are at risk of harming themselves. Earlier this year, UVM Medical Center significantly reduced how many of those safety observers work in that hospital. Central Vermont Medical Center plans to re-post 11 of those roles with changed responsibilities.
UVM Health has also consolidated or cut 28 positions in human resources, information technology and community health. The changes are designed to reduce duplication across the health system, a release from UVM Health said, rather than eliminate the services altogether.
A joint press release from the Vermont Federation of Nurses, which includes nursing staff across UVM Health, and Health Professionals & Support Staff United — the union of technicians, nursing assistants and others — estimated that about 90 union members were among those laid off. 
“We are deeply concerned by these decisions — above all for the safety and wellbeing of our patients,” the release said. “Management has yet to provide plans for how quality patient care will continue to (be) delivered to our community. These cuts to care come after years of exorbitant costs to Vermonters, and million dollar salaries for executives. If UVM Health is serious about fiscal sustainability, they would reverse short-sighted cuts to patient-facing roles, and partner with our unions to champion systemic healthcare reform.” 
The two unions have an all-day bargaining session with the hospital scheduled for Wednesday, following the expiration of both unions’ contracts.
The layoffs will take effect by the end of October, Leffler wrote in his letter to staff.
