name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Trump aims to shore up support for Whatley in NC with Wednesday visit
description: North Carolina’s open Senate seat could be key to majority control of the upper chamber.
text:
North Carolina Republican Senate hopeful Michael Whatley (R) speaks alongside U.S. President Donald Trump at the Rocky Mount Event Center on Dec. 19, 2025 in Rocky Mount. (Photo by Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)President Donald Trump is visiting North Carolina on Wednesday to campaign with Republican U.S. Senate nominee Michael Whatley.
It’s a sign the party is concerned about its prospects in the purple state. 
Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee and the North Carolina Republican Party, continues to trail Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper in recent polls and fundraising. 
Whatley said on social media that he’s “thrilled” to welcome Trump to his home of Gastonia. 
“President Trump needs an ally in the Senate and North Carolina needs a fighter,” Whatley posted. “That’s why we will win on November 3!”
North Carolina’s open Senate seat, soon to be vacated by retiring GOP U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis, could be key to majority control of the upper chamber. Cook Political Report rates the race as “lean Democrat.”
At the moment, Republicans hold 53 seats, while Democrats have 45. Two independent senators caucus with the Democrats.
‘Garbage and lies’: Senate candidate Michael Whatley lashes out at media as campaign flounders

In addition to the Tar Heel State, Republicans are looking to defend competitive open seats in Iowa and Texas — states that haven’t historically needed much GOP attention — and back their incumbents in Alaska, Maine, and Ohio. They’re also eyeing pick-up opportunities in Michigan, New Hampshire, and Georgia. 
North Carolina has some of the country’s most expensive media markets in Charlotte and the Raleigh-Durham area. Both parties may need to spend significantly more than expected, which may leave them needing to triage their resources. 
“The Republicans can still hold the majority in the Senate even if they lose North Carolina,” UNC Charlotte political science professor Eric Heberlig told NC Newsline. “That’s part of their calculations as well: Where do they think they have the best chance of mitigating any losses?”
A presidential visit shows the importance of the Senate contest on the national scene, according to Heberlig. 
With Trump’s approval rating hovering around 35% in North Carolina, his appearance in Gastonia is unlikely to win Whatley many swing voters. But Heberlig says that’s not the main goal. 
The aim, he says, is to mobilize the GOP’s base, especially low-propensity voters who may not be familiar with Whatley and may not turn out to vote in the midterm.
“If you’re the Republican, what you need to do is hold those Republican voters who have voted for President Trump, who have voted for Thom Tillis and Ted Budd. You just need to get them to pull that ‘R’ lever again,” Heberlig told NC Newsline. 
Trump’s visit could also help boost GOP turnout in a scandal-ridden western North Carolina congressional district.
GOP U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards abruptly dropped his reelection bid in the state’s 11th Congressional District last month, leaving party leaders scrambling to find a replacement. Earlier this month, the U.S. House voted to censure Edwards for inappropriate conduct. 
The NCGOP selected state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to replace Edwards on the ballot. She’ll face Democrat Jamie Ager, a fourth-generation farmer from a political family, in November. Cook Political Report rates the seat as “lean Republican.”
Former Gov. Roy Cooper centered his general election kickoff event in Raleigh on March 4, 2026 on policies he said would make food and grocery prices more affordable. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)
While Democratic candidates have performed well recently in North Carolina for state-level positions, it isn’t always the same case for federal contests.
The Tar Heel State last elected a Democratic U.S. senator in 2008, when Barack Obama became the first Democratic presidential candidate to win North Carolina in 32 years. No Democratic presidential or senatorial candidates have won North Carolina since.
On the other hand, Cooper is the best-known U.S. Senate candidate Democrats have fielded in decades. He’s won numerous statewide elections as a two-term governor and four-term attorney general. His 16-year tenure in that office was the longest in North Carolina history. 
“Having a candidate such as Roy Cooper, who’s won statewide multiple times, helps a lot there because it’s somebody that voters have already voted for, has name recognition, has a positive image, so that gives you a good foundation to build on,” Heberlig said.
Ahead of the rally, North Carolina Democratic Party chair Anderson Clayton said the event indicates the GOP is worried. 
The party also gave Whatley the spotlight last week with a speaking slot at its midterm convention in Dallas. 
“It just goes to show you right now how scared Republicans are in this state,” Clayton said. “They’re treating every single county like it matters, and so are we in North Carolina.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Democrat Rob Sand calls for prioritizing public safety as property tax growth slows
description: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand said Tuesday he would work to ensure resources are protected for Iowa law enforcement and other public safety officials if he is elected in 2026. Sand was joined by law enforcement officials, prosecutors, and other public safety workers at a campaign event at the Des Moines Firefighters Local Four union […]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand was joined by local law enforcement officers and Iowans working in the court system for a campaign event Sept. 15, 2026 in Des Moines. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand said Tuesday he would work to ensure resources are protected for Iowa law enforcement and other public safety officials if he is elected in 2026.
Sand was joined by law enforcement officials, prosecutors, and other public safety workers at a campaign event at the Des Moines Firefighters Local Four union hall, who spoke about the reasons why they supported the Democrat for Iowa governor in 2026. Sand said as Iowa communities work through the implementation of Senate File 2472, a property tax law signed by Gov. Kim Reynolds in May, the top funding priority “has got to be public safety, firefighters, first responders, police officers, sheriff’s departments.”
“These are the folks that are making sure that when you call 911 there’s somebody who can get there, and get there quickly,” Sand said. “And so that should be that should be the first group of people that we’re listening to, and the first group of people where, even if we’re only a short time into our experience in this new law, if we’re hearing from them something consistently, that’s the first place where we should be willing to listen to that and make changes based on what we’re hearing.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Democratic candidate’s comments come as Iowa local governments like Des Moines are preparing to make reductions to account for budget gaps due to the new property tax law.
The event came a day after Sand’s campaign announced a slate of endorsements from 60 Iowans involved in public safety work, including former Attorney General Tom Miller — for whom Sand worked as an assistant attorney general before becoming state auditor — Iowa Professional Firefighters Association President Ryan Hanghian, as well as several county attorneys and county sheriffs.
Former Marshalltown Police Chief Mike Tupper said he met with Sand when the auditor came to Marshalltown at least once a year to speak with members of the community — conversations where Tupper said he “learned firsthand that Rob supports public safety.”
“Public safety is a high priority for him, and he worked it, he lived it,” Tupper said. “He was in the trenches with with law enforcement. He understands law enforcement, and he wants to make sure that we have the safest state in the country. He’s very intentional about building relationships with law enforcement and focusing on public safety, and we’ve all saw his work in the state auditor’s office.”
Des Moines Local 4 Firefighter President Joe Van Haalen thanked Sand for supporting firefighters as they advocated to pass House File 969, a law expanding disability and death benefits for firefighters, emergency medical services responders and law enforcement officers from the current 14 cancers covered to all types of cancer.
“Throughout our work to pass our cancer legislation, Rob was there to offer encouragement and advice, and quite simply, he cared about what we were doing and pushed us forward,” Van Haalen said. “Today, Rob is here to talk about something that affects every Iowan, regardless of where they live or how they vote — keeping our communities safe and making sure that people we depend on in an emergency have the resources, support, and leadership that they need.”
Sand said the cancer coverage law should have been a “20-minute conversation,” and was an example of an issue he would work to move forward if elected governor.
“If you want people to do public service work, they’re willing to sacrifice … the way people do when they run into a burning building, when they move into a situation where they know someone’s got a gun and they’re angry, the least that we can be doing is making sure that the exposure that they have to risk is something that we recognize, respect, and cover,” Sand said. “Because the bottom line is they’re still going to be taking risks. They’re risking life and limb on our behalf. The easiest thing for us to do is to say that if it’s some long- term chemical exposure because of the work that you do, that’s a no brainer. That obviously we should be covering that. So at the end of the day, a lot of this just comes down to having a conversation and listening to people.”
Sand also said he wanted to bring the attitude of public safety and law enforcement work to the governor’s office if elected.
“That attitude that I’m talking about is the one where … you might have a ‘D’ or an ‘R’ after your name on the ballot, but you don’t ask people when they call 911 whether or not they’re a Democrat or a Republican,” Sand said. “You go and you help them out, and it doesn’t matter,  because you’re there to serve the public. And I want that attitude that you find in law enforcement, that you find in public safety, that you find from firefighters across the state, that you find from first responders across the state — I want that attitude to be found in the Capitol building in Des Moines. I am sick and tired of a politics that feels like it’s two private clubs beating up on each other, when fundamentally it is supposed to be about public service, and working together for the good of all and the good of anyone.”
In a Monday news release, Sac County Attorney Ben Smith, a Republican, said he supported Sand for governor because “he has the experience and judgment to keep our communities safe.”
“As a conservative Republican, I won’t agree with Rob on every issue,” Smith said in a statement. “On law enforcement, though, I don’t have to guess where he stands. He’ll fight for the men and women who run toward danger so the rest of us don’t have to, putting public safety ahead of politics.”
Sand is running against Republican Zach Lahn in the general election. Lahn’s campaign announced Tuesday an endorsement from the National Rifle Association Political Victory Fund. In a news release, Dan Capodilupo, a spokesperson for Lahn’s campaign, criticized Sand as a candidate who “likes Gun Control.” Sand hunts using firearms and has regularly said he supports the 2nd Amendment.
“Zach Lahn is a rock solid Second Amendment defender and that’s why the NRA endorsed him today,” Capodilupo said.

title: Federal judge ends North Carolina mental health settlement after 14 years
description: A federal judge on Monday ended nearly 14 years of court oversight of North Carolina’s program to help people with serious mental illness move from institutional settings into community housing.  U.S. District Judge James C. Dever III approved a request from North Carolina and the U.S. Justice Department to end the 2012 settlement. The program, […]
text:
People rally for mental health care funding at the Pennsylvania Capitol in 2022. Federal Medicaid cuts could threaten already-struggling psychiatric units at hospitals across the country. (Photo by Amanda Berg for Pennsylvania Capital-Star)A federal judge on Monday ended nearly 14 years of court oversight of North Carolina’s program to help people with serious mental illness move from institutional settings into community housing. 
U.S. District Judge James C. Dever III approved a request from North Carolina and the U.S. Justice Department to end the 2012 settlement. The program, known as Transitions to Community Living, was created as part of the agreement.
In their filing, both sides agreed North Carolina had substantially complied with the deal and that court oversight should end early.
The settlement followed a federal investigation into North Carolina’s practice of institutionalizing people with serious mental illness in adult care homes. It required the state to provide housing, mental health services and employment assistance to help people who were able to live in the community to do so.
The agreement was supposed to end in July 2020. The state and Justice Department modified the agreement six times, extending the deadline and removing requirements the state had completed. The latest extension set a July 1, 2027, deadline.
The state says more than 4,150 people now have stable housing through the program and more than 6,700 have been diverted from adult care homes.
Advocates for people with disabilities say they’ll be watching closely to make sure the state maintains its efforts. 
“North Carolina cannot afford to lose the progress it has made under this settlement,” Virginia Knowlton Marcus, CEO of Disability Rights North Carolina, told NC Newsline. 
Marcus said the group appreciates the state’s renewed commitment to community living but will continue monitoring the state’s progress.
But the state still has work to do. That’s according to the court-appointed independent reviewer tasked with monitoring North Carolina’s compliance.
In a report filed in January, reviewer Martha B. Knisley said the state continued to struggle to provide supported housing, mental health services and employment. She said the state did not meet any new major requirements during the 2025 fiscal year.
Knisley was particularly critical of the state’s progress in moving people from adult care homes into supported housing. The settlement called for 2,000 people with serious mental illness living in adult care homes to receive supported housing in communities. As of January, the state was providing those slots to 1,022 people, up 22 from the previous year. 
Knisley described the states’ progress in 2025 as “negligible.” She also found the state was not meeting some requirements for mental health services and supported employment.
For this Mama Bear, home is a right worth fighting for

The state, however, had surpassed several of the settlement’s broader goals. By June 2025, it had provided housing services to 3,998 people, above the 3,000 target. It also exceeded targets for Assertive Community Treatment and supported employment.
North Carolina and the Justice Department acknowledged the remaining gaps, but said they did not outweigh the state’s overall progress, according to the joint filing.
NCDHHS said the state will continue the work through its broader efforts to provide community-based housing and services.
“For almost 15 years, our mission has been to provide the right services at the right time so people with disabilities can live, work and receive treatment in the communities of their choice,” NCDHHS Secretary Dev Sangvai said in a statement.

title: Hagley Car Show Spotlights American-Made Classics
description: 30th annual show celebrates nation’s 250th anniversary with rare vehicles from independent automakers WILMINGTON, Del. — Hundreds of classic vehicles will roll into Hagley Museum and Library on Sunday, Sept. 20, as the Hagley Car Show celebrates its 30th anniversary and America’s 250th birthday. text:
30th annual show celebrates nation’s 250th anniversary with rare vehicles from independent automakers
WILMINGTON, Del. — Hundreds of classic vehicles will roll into Hagley Museum and Library on Sunday, Sept. 20, as the Hagley Car Show celebrates its 30th anniversary and America’s 250th birthday.
The rain-or-shine show will run from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. in the fields surrounding the first du Pont family home. Thousands of automobile enthusiasts are expected to attend.
This year’s theme, “American Independent Automakers,” will spotlight companies that competed outside Detroit’s “Big Three” of Ford, General Motors and Chrysler. Featured manufacturers will include AMC, Packard, Studebaker and Hudson.
Classic cars of all makes and models, dating from the early 20th century through 2001, will fill the main show field.
Rare vehicles highlight American innovation
Among the lesser-known automobiles scheduled to appear is a 1940 Graham Hollywood Supercharged Sedan.
Graham-Paige was founded in 1927 after three brothers purchased the Paige-Detroit Motor Car Co. for $4 million and invested an additional $4 million in the business. The company introduced innovations including shatterproof windshields and its distinctive “shark-nose” body design before automobile production ended in 1940.
The featured field will also include a rare 1963 Kellison J-3 Roadster. Its aerodynamic fiberglass body reflects the aviation background of company founder Jim Kellison, a former Air Force mechanic who drew inspiration from fighter jets and Italian sports cars.
The vehicles represent a period when smaller manufacturers tested new designs and technologies while competing against the nation’s dominant automakers.
30 years of automotive history
Hagley launched the car show in 1996 as “100 Years of Cars,” commemorating the Duryea brothers’ first production run of gasoline-powered vehicles in 1896.
Three decades later, the annual event has grown into a gathering for collectors, families and automobile enthusiasts from across the region.
Visitors can walk among rows of vintage vehicles while listening to music from different motoring eras. A parade featuring some of the show’s most distinctive vehicles will begin at 11:30 a.m.
Food trucks will offer meals and refreshments throughout the day.
Admission is sold by the carload and must be purchased in advance. Passes will not be available at the gate. General admission is $30 per vehicle, while Hagley members pay $25.
To Go Box:

What: Hagley Car Show
When: Sunday, Sept. 20, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.
Vehicle parade: 11:30 a.m.
Where: Hagley Museum and Library, 200 Hagley Creek Road, Wilmington
Admission: $30 per carload for the general public; $25 per carload for Hagley members
Tickets: Advance purchase is required at hagley.org/carshow, the Hagley Visitor Center or the Museum Store through Saturday, Sept. 19. No tickets will be sold at the gate.
Arrival: Visitors must enter through Hagley’s main entrance off Route 141 and arrive no later than 1 p.m.
Weather: The show will be held rain or shine.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Republican AG nominee proposes criminal charges against men for unwanted pregnancies
description: Republican attorney general nominee Alan Gordon said he’s confident in his legal analysis of the 19-page plan he unveiled Tuesday in his campaign’s first press conference at the Rhode Island State House. “I ran it through three AIs,” he told the only reporter who showed up. His idea: to criminally charge men whose consensual sex […]
text:
Alan Gordon, the Republican nominee running for Rhode Island attorney general, stands next to a statue of 19th century antislavery activist and women’s suffragist Elizabeth Buffum Chace on the second floor of the State House on Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Republican attorney general nominee Alan Gordon said he’s confident in his legal analysis of the 19-page plan he unveiled Tuesday in his campaign’s first press conference at the Rhode Island State House.
“I ran it through three AIs,” he told the only reporter who showed up.
His idea: to criminally charge men whose consensual sex results in an unwanted pregnancy. 
“Where a man has accidentally, recklessly, or even deliberately caused such profound changes to a woman’s body, he’s going to have to answer for that,” Gordon, 56, said while standing near a statue of 19th century antislavery activist and women’s suffragist Elizabeth Buffum Chace.
Gordon argues that an unwanted pregnancy amounts to unlawful bodily harm whatever the outcome — whether birth, miscarriage, or abortion. So his plan would let prosecutors pursue felony charges under existing Rhode Island assault and battery statutes.
First-time offenders would be eligible for diversion rather than traditional incarceration under Gordon’s proposal. He envisions a residential program where participants would receive vocational, educational and personal-development training.
Rhode Island’s felony assault law covers conduct that causes serious bodily injury, while the criminal-negligence statute cited by Gordon applies when a person causes serious bodily injury through criminal negligence. But neither law specifically identifies pregnancy as bodily harm.
AG candidates show mostly subtle differences in first public forum

Gordon was unopposed in the Sept. 9 Republican primary that saw contested races for governor and the 2nd Congressional District. Gordon received 20,288 votes, according to unofficial results from the Rhode Island Board of Elections. 
Approximately 23,000 ballots were cast in the GOP’s gubernatorial contest between Aaron Guckian and Elaine Pelino. Just over 15,000 votes were cast in the Republican race to represent Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District where Vic Mellor defeated Dr. Stephen Skoly.
Kim Ahern received 46,025 votes in the four-way Democratic AG race that drew 126,718 ballots.
Gordon came to the State House with his cousin and campaign manager Anne Armstrong, who said she sent the campaign’s proposal to a former Roger Williams University School of Law professor for vetting. The professor did not immediately respond when Rhode Island Current reached out with a request for comment.
However, Steven Brown, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union of Rhode Island, offered a blunt assessment, calling Gordon’s idea “too ridiculous to warrant any comment.” 
Jocelyn Foye, director and co-founder of the Womxn Project, said the proposal was simply “a publicity stunt.”
“It would be nice to see him work on real issues that affect people’s day-to-day lives,” Foye said in a phone interview. “People are genuinely getting rounded up for reasons that aren’t legal.” 
Gordon said his proposal latches on to his Democratic opponent’s idea to create a “reproductive justice unit” in the attorney general’s office. 
Ahern’s team wants to focus on protecting reproductive rights through litigation, public education, a legal helpline and coordination with advocacy groups. 
“I have to be honest about having sort of stolen their idea of a reproductive justice unit,” Gordon said. “She’s got a good idea, and I’m not going to oppose it just because I’m her political opponent.”
Gordon had hoped Ahern would stop by the State House to debate him on the finer points of his policy proposal. Ahern’s campaign confirmed an invite was received, and described her Republican opponent as “staunchly anti-choice and opposed to abortion under any circumstances.”
“Kim believes defending reproductive justice means protecting a woman’s right to choose whether, how, and when to start a family, not prohibiting access to critical care,” spokesperson Josh Block said in an emailed statement.
Gordon acknowledged he personally opposes abortion, but would enforce “the law of the land” if elected.
Gordon referred to himself as a “longshot RI GOP AG candidate” in a Sept. 10 press release ahead of Tuesday’s press event. A canon lawyer is trained in the legal system governing the Catholic Church. He previously ran for attorney general as an independent in 2018 and is seeking the office this year as a Republican. 
Gordon’s campaign website states he received an accelerated Honors LL.B. law degree from the University of Buckingham in England in 2012, “graduating at the top of his class in Criminology and Criminal Justice.” He received a self-designed Bachelor of Arts degree from The Pennsylvania State University in 1992, with a concentration focused on the legal and public policy issues surrounding cannabis reform.
The GOP’s nominee “has never taken the oath required for admission to the Rhode Island Bar,” according to his campaign biography.
His Democratic opponent, Ahern, who most recently chaired the state’s Cannabis Control Commission, served nine years as a special assistant attorney general under three attorneys general: Peter Neronha, Peter Kilmartin and Patrick Lynch. She later served as deputy counsel to former Gov. Gina Raimondo and deputy chief of staff to Gov. Dan McKee
Early voting begins Oct. 14 ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Board appoints Nonya Thrasher as superintendent of Hazlehurst public schools
description: Hazlehurst school board President Paul Rhodes, board Secretary Oscar Tanner and Superintendent Nonya Thrasher are pictured at a meeting on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026.
text:
Nonya Thrasher, who has led Hazlehurst City School District as interim leader since June, is now the permanent superintendent. 
Hazlehurst City School District Superintendent Nonya Thrasher Credit: Courtesy: Nonya Thrasher
The school board voted 3-2 Tuesday to appoint Thrasher and offer her a one-year, $130,000 contract. Darryl Hilliard Jr., Gloria Sandifer and school board President Paul Rhodes supported Thrasher’s appointment. Corey Murray and Oscar Tanner III voted no. 
Rhodes said there was no reason why the board offered Thrasher a one-year contract instead of a longer one.
Thrasher had served as the district’s director of accountability, compliance and accreditation since July 2023. Before working in Hazlehurst, she was superintendent of Claiborne County School District during the COVID-19 pandemic. 
With Hazlehurst, Thrasher inherits a district in crisis. The Mississippi Department of Education may take over the district by December if it does not clear outstanding accreditation violations. In March, the state Board of Education rejected the district’s corrective action plan to address those violations. 
For nearly a decade, the state Education Department has downgraded the district’s accreditation to probation. The agency previously took over the district from 2008 through 2014.
Before Thrasher took over as the interim leader, district facilities needed maintenance, its dysfunctional special education department failed students, and poor administrative oversight allowed for poor recordkeeping. 
The district has received a “C” rating on the state accountability system the past two years. Both its high and middle schools earned “D” accountability ratings in the 2024-25 school year.
As Hazlehurst schools’ accountability chief and later, interim superintendent, Thrasher reduced the number of accreditation violations from 11 to two since January.
Her predecessor, Cloyd Garth, left the district on June 5. The school board would not confirm if Garth resigned or was fired. He had failed to act on state education department reports that detailed problems in the district’s special education department. The district’s graduation rate for disabled students dropped to 17% last year, the lowest in the state.
Thrasher hired a new special education director over the summer and told Mississippi Today on Tuesday that clearing remaining violations is a top priority. Hazlehurst schools still face another threat: consolidation with the Copiah County School District. Lawmakers have been meeting to discuss school district consolidation ahead of the 2027 session. Consolidation bills introduced last session failed. 
Thrasher plans to meet with lawmakers next month.“We want to avoid consolidation if at all possible,” she said.
Rep. Greg Holloway, D-Hazlehurst, looks over a document during a meeting of the House Select Committee on Consolidation at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Democratic Rep. Greg Holloway of Hazlehurst, the Copiah County board of supervisors and other local leaders have expressed support for Thrasher. Hazlehurst residents also rallied for Thrasher in recent weeks. District alumni, parents and community members posted messages of support on Facebook and circulated posters and flyers listing her qualifications.
Rhodes said Tuesday community members have recently approached him in Walmart to voice their support for her.
Thrasher said she is heartened by the support as a Hazlehurst resident.
“I’m ready to get the job done,” she said. “I have been overjoyed, overwhelmed and overloved by the community, but I have always worked in this community long before sitting in this seat. Whatever we need to do to move this community forward, I have always been in the forefront to make that happen.”
Rhodes feels optimistic, too. He said he believes Thrasher will help the district better serve students and improve academic standards.
“I believe we reached that point to where we can now move forward, straighten things up and educate our kids,” Rhodes said, “which is the reason why we’re here.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT prison watchdog DeVaughn Ward announces early departure
description: Ward’s appointment made him CT's first correction ombuds since the office shuttered in 2010. He plans to step down early, on Oct. 16.
text:
Connecticut’s independent prison watchdog DeVaughn Ward said Tuesday he plans to leave the post next month and join a personal injury law firm.
Ward’s appointment in September 2024 made him Connecticut’s first correction ombuds since the office shuttered in 2010 to cut costs. His term was slated to end in January 2027, but according to the press release announcing his departure, Ward’s last day will now be Oct. 16.
In a phone interview, Ward explained that the timing of his early departure was dictated by the needs of the law firm he’ll be joining. He expressed hope that the announcement of his upcoming departure might speed up the process of selecting his successor.
“It has been an honor being able to serve the incarcerated population in Connecticut,” he said. “I’m very proud of the work that we’ve done, and I’m very much looking forward to the next chapter.”
The next ombuds will serve in the post for four years. The state legislature passed a law last year extending the term length of the appointment.
Ward said his main accomplishments as ombuds were obtaining increased funding for the office and bolstering its statutory authority.
The Office of the Correction Ombudsman initially had an annual budget of $400,000 and Ward was its sole employee. 
“It really didn’t speak to the challenge that was laid out for the office in terms of providing oversight over all the correctional facilities and the dozens of halfway houses we have here in the state,” he said.
Since Ward began urging lawmakers to increase the office’s funding, its annual budget has tripled, surpassing $1.2 million. Ward now works with four staff members, and he said the office will expand to 10 or 11 staff members by the end of 2026.
Ward also pushed for necessary “statutory tools” for the office, such as subpoena power and the ability to carry out unannounced prison inspections and use electronic devices to document prison conditions. 
His office released regular reports on its findings, including a March report that spurred the Connecticut legislature’s elimination of medical copayments for incarcerated people and the Department of Correction’s planned rollout of healthcare reforms.
Before assuming the role of ombuds, Ward worked as a criminal law and personal injury attorney and litigated high-profile cases against Connecticut’s Department of Correction. He secured settlements in lawsuits alleging inadequate medical care in Connecticut prisons, including a class-action lawsuit filed by incarcerated residents who said they were denied treatment for Hepatitis-C.
Cindy Prizio, executive director of Connecticut civil rights group One Standard of Justice, praised Ward’s performance as ombuds. She described him as a “strategist,” highlighting his successful lobbying efforts to increase the office’s funding.
“I’m just delighted with his track record,” Prizio said. “I don’t think anyone could have come in and done a better job than he did.”
But Barbara Fair, who runs the criminal justice advocacy group Stop Solitary CT, expressed frustration about what she described as a lack of transparency from Ward’s office. (Fair previously applied for the ombuds role and was ranked second in early 2024 by the Correction Advisory Committee, which reviews applications for the role and presents the governor with three finalists.)
She noted that at the start of Ward’s tenure, she’d urged him to hold regular meetings to keep community members informed about his work. The office scheduled its first public town hall for Sept. 23, two years after Ward assumed the role. 
Ward said he spent most of his term getting the office up and running by hiring staff, visiting Connecticut’s 13 correctional facilities and investigating complaints from incarcerated people. 
“I was really heavily focused on the operational needs of the office, and I think now we’ve reached a point where the operational capacity of the office is stabilized, and I think now we actually have something to talk to the community about,” he said. 
Fair, whose advocacy group opposes strip searches and solitary confinement, said Ward did not respond promptly to her questions about what his office was working on.
For example, Fair said she repeatedly asked Ward if he had set up confidential drop boxes for prisoners to submit complaints to his office. She said she only learned that these drop boxes were being implemented in Connecticut prisons in Tuesday’s press release announcing Ward’s departure.
Ward said the design for the drop boxes hadn’t been finalized until a few weeks ago and his office is in the process of installing them in Connecticut’s prisons.
“Barbara Fair is somebody who applied for this job, didn’t get it, and has been frustrated by my entire term,” he said. “I hope that she finds a way to work with my successor in a way that she could not find to work with me.”
Both Prizio and Fair voiced concerns about the timeline for finding Ward’s replacement, citing how lengthy the process had been just to place Ward in the role. 
After the law reestablishing the ombuds’s office passed in 2022, the Correction Advisory Committee posted the job application in June 2023 and later narrowed down the applicant pool to three finalists. Though the committee in January 2024 recommended civil rights attorney Ken Krayeske for the role, Gov. Ned Lamont instead appointed the third-place finalist, public defender Hilary Carpenter. 
Lamont faced fierce backlash following Carpenter’s appointment, and the legislature never confirmed her for the role. Instead, the governor and lawmakers formed an agreement that he would collaborate with the Black and Puerto Rican Caucus to appoint an interim ombuds that summer. The Correction Advisory Committee then reopened the hiring process for the permanent role that September.
Lamont announced Ward’s nomination as interim ombuds in August 2024, and Ward took office the following month. Ward was confirmed by the legislature as permanent ombuds in April 2025.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: New guidance limits voting disqualifications to murder, manslaughter convictions
description: Among Virginians who are no longer incarcerated, only those convicted of murder and voluntary or involuntary manslaughter remain disqualified from voting under new guidance from the Virginia Department of Elections.  The update comes days before early voting begins in the midterm elections, and months after a federal judge ordered the state to narrow how it[...]
text:
Among Virginians who are no longer incarcerated, only those convicted of murder and voluntary or involuntary manslaughter remain disqualified from voting under new guidance from the Virginia Department of Elections. 

The update comes days before early voting begins in the midterm elections, and months after a federal judge ordered the state to narrow how it determines voter eligibility under the Virginia Readmission Act. Among Virginians who are no longer incarcerated, only those convicted of murder and voluntary or involuntary manslaughter remain disqualified from voting under new guidance from the Virginia Department of Elections. 
The update comes days before early voting begins in the midterm elections, and months after a federal judge ordered the state to narrow how it determines voter eligibility under the Virginia Readmission Act. 
The act is part of a series of Reconstruction-era laws barring former Confederate states from disenfranchising residents except those convicted of felonies recognized as common law in 1870.  
The Department of Elections said it identified murder and the two types of manslaughter as disqualifying offenses “because they exactly match the elements of one of the offenses listed above.”
Other felonies recognized at common law included arson, burglary, escape and rescue from prison or jail, rape, robbery, larceny, sodomy and mayhem. 
Virginia’s chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union estimates that of about 250,000 Virginians who otherwise would not have been able to vote, only about 10% will now be sidelined due to their type of criminal offense. 
Although more people than believed may be eligible to vote in Virginia as early as by the end of the week, the path to that clarity was marked by confusion. 
After the court ruled in favor of the Virginia chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union in January, friction emerged with Attorney General Jay Jones’ office over which modern-day crimes aligned with the common-law offenses. 
By the time Virginia held its primary elections in August, there was confusion around applications and eligibility, prompting some would-be voters to sit out the election while others remained in registration limbo. 
Civil rights group files motion to speed up Va.’s reform of voter registration process for ex-felons

Last month, the federal district judge reaffirmed the ruling in favor of the ACLU and said the state had lagged, ”egregiously so,” in implementing the January decision. 
Jones’ office had initially sought additional time to comply with the January ruling so the state could develop guidance for registrars and determine which modern-day felonies might still prevent someone from registering to vote. 
For instance, illegally using tear gas appeared on a list of potentially disqualifying crimes issued by Jones’ office earlier this year, “even though tear gas was not invented in 1870,” ACLU attorney Eden Heilman said in an interview this summer. 
With the latest update, more people may be eligible to vote than previously anticipated. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger also restored voting rights to more than 60,000 Virginians with past felony convictions this summer. 
The move contrasts with the approach taken by former Gov. Glenn Youngkin, who shifted the process to an individualized petition system with little clarity about the criteria might be used to grant or deny restoration. 
Though the Readmission Acts lawsuit means some people with felony convictions should never have lost their voting rights, Virginia’s Constitution still disenfranchises others unless the governor restores their rights or grants them a pardon. 
One of three pending constitutional amendments could allow voting rights to be restored automatically once a person has completed their prison sentence, if voters approve it statewide this fall. 
The ACLU of Virginia, WilmerHale and Protect Democracy issued a joint statement Tuesday celebrating the outcome of their case and the updated guidance. 
“This victory is an enormous step towards ending felony disenfranchisement in Virginia, one that Virginians can advance even further at the ballot box this fall,” the joint statement reads. 
With early voting beginning  and Election Day set for Nov. 3, some people with past felony convictions will now be able to weigh in on the proposed amendments and participate in congressional midterm and local elections.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV voters will decide on proposed citizen-only voting constitutional amendment in November
description: West Virginia state code prohibits people who are not United States citizens from voting in elections. A measure on the ballot in the November election would take the prohibition further by adding it to the constitution.
text:
Jack Tomczak, vice president of outreach for Americans for Citizen Voting, and Sen. Patricia Rucker, R-Jefferson, spoke to reporters Tuesday in support of a ballot measure that would add an amendment to the state constitution prohibiting people who are not citizens of the United States from voting in West Virginia elections. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)West Virginia state code prohibits people who are not United States citizens from voting in elections. A measure on the ballot in the November election would take the prohibition further by adding it to the constitution. 
Sen. Patricia Rucker, R-Jefferson, a naturalized U.S. citizen and the lead sponsor of Senate Joint Resolution 9, which put the measure on the ballot, told reporters Tuesday citizen-only voting is a very important issue. 
“West Virginia already has in code that only citizens can vote in elections, but that isn’t enough,” Rucker said. “That’s law. Law can change, as we know. Every legislative session we have, we can change law.”
She said the state constitution is not clear: it requires voters to be citizens of the state, but does not specify that they be U.S. citizens. 
“This proposed amendment would ensure that no future Legislature could just simply change the election law with only a bill,” she said. “It also gives us greater authority to enforce the law we currently have in place.”
If the amendment is approved by West Virginia voters, that section of the state constitution would read as follows:
“Only citizens of the United States who are citizens of this state shall be entitled to vote at all elections held within the counties in which they respectively reside; but a person who is a minor, or who has been declared mentally incompetent by a court of competent jurisdiction, or who is under conviction of treason, felony or bribery in an election, or who has not been a resident of the state and of the county in which he or she offers to vote, for 30 days next preceding such offer, shall not be permitted to vote while such disability continues; and, a person in the military, naval, or marine service of the United States shall not be deemed a resident of this state by reason of being stationed therein.”
Besides Rucker, Senate Joint Resolution 9 was also sponsored by Sens. Chris Rose, R-Monongalia; Darren Thorne, R-Hampshire; Amy Grady, R-Mason; Craig Hart, R-Mingo; Laura Chapman, R-Ohio; Senate President Randy Smith, R-Preston; Rollan Roberts, R-Raleigh, Eric Tarr, R-Putnam; Jay Taylor, R-Taylor; Charles Clements, R-Wetzel; Trenton Barnhart, R-Pleasants; and Mark Maynard, R-Wayne. 
The Senate and the House of Delegates both unanimously approved the resolution during the 2026 legislative session. 
The League of Women Voters of West Virginia opposes the ballot measure. A statement on the organization’s website said the proposed amendment is “completely unnecessary.” 
Likewise, West Virginia Citizens for Clean Elections, an organization that aims to “increase transparency and accountability in West Virginia elections,” also opposes proposed Amendment 1. 
“This unnecessary amendment perpetuates long-debunked conspiracy theories and scapegoats our immigrant neighbors to sow mistrust in our election results,” Julie Archer, coordinator for WVCCE, wrote in an email to West Virginia Watch. “West Virginia’s election process already includes strong safeguards to ensure only eligible citizens vote. Despite these safeguards, some politicians continue to spread falsehoods to undermine trust in our elections and justify restrictive voting policies that do more harm than good by disenfranchising eligible voters.”
Rucker was joined Tuesday by Jack Tomczak, vice president of outreach for Americans for Citizen Voting, an organization that works to pass citizen-only amendments around the country. 
Fifteen states have amended their constitutions to prohibit non-citizens from voting in local, state and federal elections, Tomczak said.
“In every state, it has passed with overwhelming support, and we anticipate that again here in West Virginia,” he said. 
Tomczak said the amendment would prohibit cities from allowing non-citizens to vote, as has happened in four other states.
Rucker said she’s unaware of non-citizens being charged with illegally voting in state elections but said while campaigning door to door, she had met some people who were registered to vote and did not realize that they were ineligible because they weren’t U.S. citizens. 
“I had to inform them of that,” she said. “So it was, in their case, inadvertent; (they) just didn’t understand. Some of them had … automatically checked a box at the DMV without understanding that the box says you must be a U.S. citizen.”  
A representative of Secretary of State Kris Warner’s office said that as the state’s chief election officer, Warner does not take a formal position on ballot issues or candidates. 
Constitutional amendments need a simple majority of more than 50% of votes in order to pass. The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham and Utah Gov. Cox discuss how to ‘disagree better’ across party lines
description: Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham levied criticism Monday against the National Governors Association, which she characterized as “feckless.” Lujan Grisham and Utah Gov. Spencer Cox also discussed how to dialogue constructively and reach bipartisan solutions.
text:
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, left, and New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, right, held a talk in support of bipartisan dialogue and healthy disagreement at the University of Michigan on Sep. 14, 2026. (Courtesy of Gov. Grisham's Office)Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham levied criticism Monday against the National Governors Association, which she characterized as “feckless.” 
Lujan Grisham said she has called its chair and vice chair and told them they are running an organization that has “zero courage.” Her comments, she said, stem from her frustration with the NGA’s lack of action on immigration reform “since its inception.” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, a Republican, called Lujan Grisham’s comments “fair,” but said he still thinks the NGA, for which he formerly served as chair, is an important organization. And Lujan Grisham said she’s stayed on the NGA, despite being “mad” at it, because of her respect for Cox.
The discussion about the NGA unfolded on stage at the University of Michigan in a conversation titled “Disagree Better,” moderated by Lynette Clemetson, director of the university’s Wallace House Center for Journalists. The pair had a similar public conversation last year at the University of Notre Dame in Indiana following the assassination of rightwing commentator Charlie Kirk. The most recent discussion follows publication this month of Cox’ book, “Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt.”
Lujan Grisham and Cox also worked together as chair and vice chair, respectively, of the Western Governors’ Association, which bills itself as a regional organization that advocates for bipartisan solutions, and which Lujan Grisham highlighted on Monday as a group that has helped create national policies.
The NGA, on the other hand, emerged as a topic when moderator Clemetson asked for examples of how Lujan Grisham and Cox had navigated disagreements.
“If we’re going to continue to let the federal government indiscriminately separate children and attack families, then I’m not in,” Lujan Grisham said about the NGA inaction on federal policy, adding that she thinks the organization is unable to take the initiative on the issue due to governors’ fear of federal backlash.
The Democratic governors of Kansas, Minnesota and Michigan all cut ties with the National Governors’ Association in 2025 over similar concerns.
Cox called Lujan Grisham’s comments a “fair argument,” but noted that he remained with the NGA to improve the organization in ways that “she would agree are better for our country.” Lujan Grisham said she did not pull her membership like other governors due to her trust in Cox.
When the governors were asked about a time when the other helped change their mind on an issue, Cox cited New Mexico’s universal childcare policy, saying that he is “challenging his priors” and “open” to the idea of pursuing the policy in Utah.
In response to the same question, Lujan Grisham said that she “looks to Utah and gets advice” from Cox and Utah First Lady Abby Cox on possible solutions to New Mexico’s challenges with public safety and child well-being. The state moved from last to 49th in the nation in child welfare earlier this year. 
“I need to keep doing things differently until we resolve those risks for every single child and every single family,” Lujan Grisham added.
The good natured conversation between Lujan Grisham and Cox, despite disagreements, highlighted the namesake of the event.
“We have had this toxic divide in our country where we don’t just disagree with someone—we detest them,” Cox said, adding that democracy thrives with willingness to have conversations across the aisle.
Of her colleague, Lujan Grisham said, “We need more people like Spencer Cox out in the world — folks interested enough to open the door to conversations about areas or subjects that we may not inherently agree with.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Group renews petition effort to put transgender sports on next year’s ballot
description: The group aiming to limit what sports and school facilities transgender students can access is renewing its signature collection effort, aiming to get a referendum question on next year’s ballot. The initiative was first approved by the Maine Secretary of State’s Office to appear on the November ballot. But following a legal challenge questioning the […]
text:
A canvasser with the Protect Girls Sports campaign looks on as a voter signs a petition to restrict transgender students’ access to sports and school facilities at the Green Ladle culinary school in Lewiston on Nov. 4, 2025. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)The group aiming to limit what sports and school facilities transgender students can access is renewing its signature collection effort, aiming to get a referendum question on next year’s ballot.
The initiative was first approved by the Maine Secretary of State’s Office to appear on the November ballot. But following a legal challenge questioning the validity of hundreds of signatures collected by the group, Protect Girls’ Sports, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and the Maine Supreme Judicial Court ultimately determined that the initiative did not clear the threshold.
The group appealed to federal court, but announced Monday that the final ruling would not be released in time for the midterms. Instead, Protect Girls’ Sports is turning its attention to gathering 5,000 more signatures, although it needs only about 532 more to qualify. 
“Now is your chance to make sure Maine girls can access bathrooms, locker rooms, and sports free of males,” said the announcement calling for volunteers.
Protect Girls’ Sports did not respond to requests for comment on the renewed signature collection effort.
The citizen initiative titled “An Act to Designate School Sports Participation and Facilities by Sex” had been largely funded by Republican megadonor Richard Uihlein. If passed, it would mandate schools to restrict trans students from playing on sports teams, using bathrooms or locker rooms aligning with their gender identity. 
Following national scrutiny by President Donald Trump’s administration and several failed legislative attempts at passing similar bills, the referendum sought to ask voters whether to change the Maine Human Rights Act, which protects against discrimination based on gender identity.
However, the initiative was not questioned because of the restrictions it aimed to pass. After Bellows announced in March that Protect Girls’ Sports had collected enough signatures to qualify for the Nov. 3 ballot, three Maine voters filed a lawsuit challenging the validity of those signatures. 
The court remanded the matter back to the secretary’s office, which held a hearing where both sides presented evidence of the signature collectors’ practices, many of whom were paid workers from out of state.
Through the hearing, a pattern of negligence emerged. Bellows announced in May that the ballot initiative would no longer qualify— a determination that in June was backed up by a Cumberland County Superior Court judge. 
Protect Girls’ Sports appealed that decision to Maine’s highest court, which after hearing oral arguments on July 1 came to the same conclusion.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Leake County schools released from decades-long desegregation order
description: Will Russell, superintendent of Leake County School District, speaks during a meeting of the House Select Committee on Consolidation at the Capitol in Jackson, Miss., Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026.
text:
After more than half a century, Leake County schools have been released from a federal order that monitored and prevented racial discrimination within the district. 
That means a judge will no longer oversee Leake County School District to ensure Black  students get equal access to a quality education. 
U.S. District Court Judge Daniel Jordan approved the order’s dissolution on Sept. 3. Officials announced the decision Monday night on Facebook.
“This historic milestone reflects our continued commitment to providing every student with an equitable, high-quality education,” the post reads. 
Leake County schools Superintendent Will Russell said Tuesday that it’s been an arduous process, and the decision reflects the work of the community and past district leaders. 
“I just want to congratulate everyone who’s been part of this effort,” he said.
The U.S. Department of Justice has been monitoring Leake County schools for decades, after parents of Black students brought a discrimination lawsuit against the school board in 1963. The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi imposed a formal desegregation order in 1969, ordering Leake County schools to halt discriminatory practices and practice mandatory reporting to ensure no school within the district was racially identifiable.
Justice Department officials closed two Leake County schools in 2011 and reassigned students and faculty to promote equity after they found four schools were still racially divided.
Monte Ladner, former Leake County superintendent, said Tuesday the district had little choice but to comply at the time. 
“We weren’t given much of a choice on how we got back in compliance,” he said. “Even if we suggested something different, their reaction was ‘no.’”
In a Sept. 14 Facebook post, the Leake County School District announced a judge’s decision to end its decades-long desegregation order. Credit: Leake County School District
That lack of community input about the school closures was devastating, Russell said. 
“It was just one of those hard things to accept even though it was the right thing to do,” he said. 
The district has made strides since then. Last year, each school reached the standard the court established to determine racial balance.
The school district consolidated its high schools this school year due to declining student enrollment. Russell prefers to call that “realignment” because of the community’s negative memories of the 2011 school closures. 
Board attorney John Hooks argued in a July 28 court filing the merger will ensure equity. Ladner agreed Tuesday and said the merger will make it easier for the district to provide equal opportunities to students. 
Leake County schools have lost about a fifth of their students over the past decade. The district enrolled 2,369 students last year, about a 19% decrease from 2015-16. 
“It’s great to get out from under this order,” Ladner said. “It gives the district some flexibility now in moving forward. This reflects the work of this administration and others before that tried to better the district. It’s very positive and will benefit students and parents alike.”
Leake County is the third Mississippi school district to be released from such an order in two years. Rankin County School District was released from its desegregation order in July, and Copiah County School District in August 2025. 
Under President Donald Trump, the Justice Department has signaled increasing willingness to release school districts from desegregation orders. 
Twenty-seven Mississippi school districts remain under desegregation orders. 
Russell is confident Leake County schools will maintain its progress without federal oversight. 
“We’re in a good place to keep it going and make sure we’re equitable across the board with student achievement,” he said. “I don’t see us slipping back into this concern again.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. announces two measles deaths, bringing total to four in ongoing outbreak
description: State Department of Health officials said Tuesday the dead include an 18-year-old from Mifflin County, according to the county coroner, and a 40-year-old Jefferson County woman,  who died Saturday. Both were unvaccinated, the department said.
text:
A sign at a University of Utah health clinic warns visitors about the spread of measles. Under the Trump administration, federal health officials have cut back the number of recommended vaccines, and more states are offering exemptions for parents who don't want to vaccinate children entering public schools. (Photo by McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)Two more Pennsylvanians have died after becoming infected with measles, health officials said, bringing the number of deaths in the commonwealth attributed to the virus to four.
State Department of Health officials said Tuesday the dead are an 18-year-old from Mifflin County, according to the county coroner, and a 40-year-old Jefferson County woman,  who died Saturday. Both were unvaccinated, the department said.
The deaths are in addition to two Lancaster County infants who died after exposure to the virus.
The Mifflin County Coroner’s Office said Tuesday a review of medical records indicated the teenager, who was not otherwise identified, died of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, which is a rare and severe neurological complication of measles.
Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong said in a Facebook post that the woman who died had tested positive for measles after being exposed to the virus by a close contact who had also recently tested positive. The woman suffered from a lung condition and was dependent on oxygen but would not have died without the virus, Furlong told The Guardian.
In a news release, the Health Department stressed that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the best protection against measles. Two doses of the vaccine provides lifetime protection at a 97% immunity rate.
“My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly-contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades,” Pennsylvania Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the MMR vaccine – which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades,” she added.
Measles is an airborne virus that spreads through breathing, coughing, or sneezing. It causes high fevers, coughs, and red, watery eyes, initially. That’s followed by a rash that begins at the head and progresses down the body three to five days after symptoms begin.
So far, the outbreak has sickened 693 people in 38 counties. According to the Health Department’s measles dashboard, last updated Monday, fewer than 1% of those infected were fully vaccinated and 133 people were hospitalized with complications of the virus. 
The deaths in Lancaster County were the commonwealth’s first fatal measles-related cases in 35 years and the first in the country this year. The virus had been considered eliminated in the United States, but has made a resurgence in the midst of a movement against vaccination over the past two decades. 
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control (CDC) lists 3,294 confirmed measles in 47 states in its latest update Thursday. 
U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime skeptic of vaccine safety, questioned the first reports of deaths in Lancaster County late last month. 
The outbreak comes as the CDC is changing the way it counts measles cases, according to reports. In a note on its website this month, the agency said it would use data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), drawing criticism from public health officials. That system is used to track long-term mortality trends. 
Previously it used the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS), which supplies the CDC with data directly from state and local health departments.  
The CDC’s measles webpage includes an asterisk for the number of measles deaths in 2026 with a note that the NCHS does not have death records from this year listing measles as an underlying cause. It also says it is working with a national council of epidemiologists to develop a standard definition of death due to measles.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Lawmakers seek solutions to lower cost of building homes in Oklahoma
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — State lawmakers on Tuesday turned their focus to policy ideas to lower the cost of building houses in Oklahoma.  Rep. Rob Hall, R-Tulsa, who requested the study, said he will file legislation focused on lowering the cost of building homes in Oklahoma as he said this has become a national issue.  He’s […]
text:
Members of the Oklahoma House vote on a bill on May 6, 2026 on the House floor. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — State lawmakers on Tuesday turned their focus to policy ideas to lower the cost of building houses in Oklahoma. 
Rep. Rob Hall, R-Tulsa, who requested the study, said he will file legislation focused on lowering the cost of building homes in Oklahoma as he said this has become a national issue. 
He’s not sure yet what shape his legislation will take, which is why he said he held an interim study focused on “conservative” and “free market principled” solutions to the housing crisis. 
“I think people are interested in it because it affects every single one of their constituents,” he said after the study Tuesday. “Everyone needs a place to live, and so whether you’re renting, buying, roommates, whatever the situation is, we all need a place to put our head at night.”
A myriad of policy proposals were discussed at Tuesday’s interim study before the House County and Municipal Government Committee. 
Hall said he’s most interested in permitting reform to streamline the timeline of building housing as well as reviewing, and possibly updating, Oklahoma’s building codes. 
He said when permitting battles get dragged out, the cost of delays are passed on to the consumer or home buyer. 
Hall said he wants to make the process for obtaining permits to build homes smoother, but also allow local governments to maintain control. 
Jaimie Cavanaugh, the senior state policy counsel at Pacific Legal Foundation, said government restrictions often inhibit property owners. The group is a national public interest law firm. 
She described several pieces of model legislation her organization has pushed across the country, including what she called the “Permitting Approval Timeliness Act.” The proposal would require municipalities to respond to permitting applications within a set period of time or else it would automatically be approved. 
Other suggestions from Cavanaugh’s group covered updating zoning requirements, removing limitations on the number of non-family members living together, and limiting who can object to developments.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa scientists push for more renewable energy to meet growing demands
description: More than 180 Iowa scientists and sustainability scholars from universities and other organizations across the state have asked Iowans to advocate for the deployment of renewable energy systems to meet growing electricity demand.  The 2026 Iowa climate statement, published Tuesday, says Iowa is at a “fork in the road” with one path continuing to develop […]
text:
Wind turbines near Ogden, Iowa on Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) More than 180 Iowa scientists and sustainability scholars from universities and other organizations across the state have asked Iowans to advocate for the deployment of renewable energy systems to meet growing electricity demand. 
The 2026 Iowa climate statement, published Tuesday, says Iowa is at a “fork in the road” with one path continuing to develop renewable energy sources and the other, building new fossil-fuel-generated power plants to meet growing energy demands.
“We have a choice to make, and we need to make it now,” the statement said. “Rapidly rising electricity demand calls for every stakeholder — from ordinary Iowans, to tech industry leaders, to local elected officials and utility company executives — to advocate for and adopt cheaper, cleaner, and more efficient ways of generating electricity and to push back against roadblocks designed to selectively hinder renewable energy.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
David Courard-Hauri, a professor of environmental science and policy at Drake University, said as the nation sees hotter summers, increasing patterns of drought, flooding and intense storm events and as the “proliferation” of data centers spreads through Iowa, it’s a “critical time to think carefully about how we want our energy future to look in Iowa.” 
Trump EPA to strip greenhouse gas limits for power plants, a key Biden climate policy

“As we expand generation capacity, do we want our electric utilities and the corporations building independent data centers to continue the path that Iowa has blazed in renewable energy, or do we go back to fossil plants with climate and health risks as well as price volatility that we’ve all been suffering from recently?” Courard-Hauri said in a virtual news conference Tuesday. 
Researchers on the call referenced a recently published report from the Iowa Environmental Council that found that the share of energy generated by coal increased in 2025 for the first time in several years. 
The report similarly called for greater adoption of wind, solar and battery infrastructure to meet 2050 carbon neutral goals. 
Utilities, which have continued to expand solar and wind projects in Iowa, said the Iowa Environmental Council report and climate goals don’t take into account the complex challenges of balancing electricity reliability, consumer cost and sustainability. 
The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, or MISO, reported in 2024 that peak load to the grid remained essentially flat from 2009 to 2024, but now the “pace and scale” of industry trends have caused peak load forecasts to have a “significant increase.” MISO attributes the increase in demand to growth in artificial intelligence and data centers, new or onshored industrial activities, electric vehicles and building electrification. 
The grid operator, which covers much of the Midwest and parts of the South, currently forecasts a 1.6% compound annual growth rate, which means by 2044,  the annual coincident peak demand is forecast to be 38% higher than what it was in 2024. 
Jacqueline Dowling, an assistant professor of civil and environmental engineering at the University of Iowa, said Iowa adopted “visionary policies” 20 years ago to make use of wind and solar energy. Iowa consistently ranks among the top states for renewable energy generation.  
“Continuing along the pathway toward a wind- and solar-dominated system will lead to health benefits due to cleaner air, electricity affordability benefits due to zero fuel cost resources and global climate benefits due to reduced carbon emissions,” Dowling said. “If we need to build a lot more electricity generation quickly, we should seize the moment and build clean, cheap, and secure energy.” 
An array of solar panels near Palo, Iowa, Sept. 8, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Iowa is also home to one of several previously shuttered nuclear energy centers that is being restarted with support from the U.S. Department of Energy. More than 90% of the energy generated from the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Linn County is slated to go to Google who is expanding its data center footprint in Iowa. 
Iowa utilities are also building new natural gas plants to help handle peak demand, though some energy groups fear the plants will need to operate more often to meet anticipated demands. 
Dowling said right now, utilities are taking an “all of the above strategy.” 
“They’re building everything,” Dowling said. “They’re building solar, restarting the nuclear power plant, also building new gas, and using our existing coal plants more.” 
Dowling said nuclear energy has a “lot of pros and cons” but “it is carbon free, reliable power” that can provide “firming” capabilities to help fill the gaps when the wind doesn’t blow or the sun doesn’t shine. 
“We would advocate for a wind and solar dominated system backed by carbon free, reliable power,” Dowling said. 
This is the 16th annual climate statement signed by various scientists across the state. Last year, the group looked at climate change and its impact on rising insurance prices. In 2024, scientists urged individual action that would help solve the climate crisis and curb climate anxieties. 
“As our climate continues to change, further investments in wind and solar power in Iowa will pay dividends in less expensive electricity and better health for generations to come,” the latest statement concluded. 
A full list of supporting scientists, researchers and their affiliated universities or organizations can be found at the bottom of the statement.
