title: Assistant principal at New Haven’s Hillhouse High charged with sexual assault of student
description: Asst Principal Daniel Bonet turned himself in after police issued a warrant alleging he sexually assaulted an underage student during school hours.
text:
A Hillhouse High School assistant principal turned himself in for arrest on Monday night after police issued a warrant alleging that he sexually assaulted an underage student on two occasions during school hours.
The school district had placed the assistant principal, Daniel Bonet, on administrative leave on Tuesday, May 26, as he faced investigations from both the New Haven Police Department and the state Department of Children and Families.
According to a statement from the NHPD on Tuesday, the police department received a call about the allegations four days prior, on Friday, May 22, which preceded Memorial Day Weekend.
Bonet, 49, is now facing charges of two counts of sexual assault in the second degree and two counts of sexual assault in the fourth degree. His bond has been set at $250,000.
According to the NHPD’s statement, the student “disclosed two separate allegations of sexual assault which occurred on consecutive days in Bonet’s office after he arranged to be alone with her while school was in session.”
Detective Mariah Miller of the Special Victim Unit “was able to corroborate the victim’s account with video surveillance from the school which corroborated her accounts” as well as “statements with witnesses and staff members,” according to the statement.
Bonet did not respond to a request for comment in time for the publication of this story.
His lawyer, Don Cretella, wrote in an email to the Independent, “I was in court today, representing Mr. Bonet at his arraignment. Unfortunately, the court did not lower his bond and it remained as set at the police department at 250,000 Mr. Bonet is attempting to make bail.”
“I just received a copy of the warrant and have not had a chance to thoroughly review it,” Cretella wrote. “Once I do, Mr. Bonet and I will begin his defense.”
“At this point, we have no indication” of allegations that Bonet assaulted other students, said NHPD spokesperson Officer Christian Bruckhart — “not to say that there are no other victims, but at this point we only know of one.”
Hillhouse Principal Antoine Billy sent a letter to families affiliated with the high school on Tuesday announcing that a warrant for Bonet’s arrest had been issued.
NHPS spokesperson Justin Harmon wrote in a statement that, “We are working with our school social workers and specialized staff to support our students and staff. JHHS [James Hillhouse High School] and NHPS are committed to maintaining a healthy and supportive school community. Support is available for any students and staff who need it.”
“Nothing is more important than the safety of our students,” Harmon wrote. “Hillhouse families with questions or concerns have been invited to reach out to the school.”
Harmon said that Bonet continues to be on paid administrative leave. “We always put people on paid administrative leave when an allegation is made,” Harmon said. “What will happen next is currently being worked out.”
Mayor Justin Elicker said in a statement on Tuesday that “the allegations of sexual assault and the arrest of this school administrator are extremely disturbing and rightfully shock the conscience of every student, parent and educator at the Hillhouse High School community. Our schools must always be safe and supportive places where our students can learn, grow and thrive.”
“This individual will be held accountable for their actions to the fullest extent of the law,” Elicker wrote, “and New Haven Public Schools will be there to support this student and the larger school community during this difficult time.”
This is not the first time Bonet has been placed on leave while helming a New Haven public school. In January 2019, he was placed on temporary leave from his role as principal of John C. Daniels School due to allegations of staff harassment and non-compliance with DCF reporting mandates, allegations he denied. When Bonet was cleared to return to work, he was transferred to the assistant principal role at Hillhouse in August 2019.
The RAINN National Sexual Assault hotline provides resources for teens and families about how to recognize grooming and child sexual assault, and about how to support loved ones and community members through those experiences. The hotline is available 24/7 for survivors and loved ones who want to speak to a trained listener. Call (800) 656-HOPE or text HOPE to 64673.
This story was first published Sept. 15, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: In New Hampshire’s 1st District, DiLorenzo and Shaheen face off in a consequential race
description: After winning their respective primary elections last week, Republican Anthony DiLorenzo and Democrat Stefany Shaheen will face off in November’s general election to see who will represent New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. Both candidates call Portsmouth home and both present themselves as centrist options within their parties. DiLorenzo is a car d[...]
text:
Left: Anthony DiLorenzo speaks to supporters in the Music Hall Lounge in Portsmouth after winning the Republican nomination for New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District in the Sept. 8, 2026, primary. Right: Stefany Shaheen speaks to supports at an election results watch party in Portsmouth on Sept. 8, 2026. (Photos by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)After winning their respective primary elections last week, Republican Anthony DiLorenzo and Democrat Stefany Shaheen will face off in November’s general election to see who will represent New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District.
Both candidates call Portsmouth home and both present themselves as centrist options within their parties.
DiLorenzo is a car dealer with over a dozen locations who self-funded much of his campaign and earned the endorsement of President Donald Trump. He tried to paint himself as a pragmatic businessman from humble beginnings who can use his business acumen and previous successes to solve problems in Congress.
Voters hold signs of support for Maura Sullivan at primary watch party at To Share Brewery in Manchester after the Sept. 8 primary. Hours later, they learned that Stefany Shaheen had beaten their preferred candidate in the primary. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“My opponents talk about what they are going to do,” DiLorenzo said to a crowd of supporters in Portsmouth immediately after The Associated Press called his victory. “I want to talk about what I’ve done: building businesses, creating jobs, and giving back to my community — something I’ve done for over 35 years.”
Shaheen, the daughter of U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, served on the Portsmouth City Council and worked as a consultant for a Manchester biotech firm. Like many Democrats this cycle, she’s sought to center Trump, who has historically low approval ratings and has lost New Hampshire in three consecutive presidential elections. At an election watch party a couple blocks away from DiLorenzo’s, Shaheen echoed that messaging in a speech to supporters as election results were trickling in in her favor.
“This race has always, from day one, been about tackling the challenges that matter most to New Hampshire families,” Shaheen said. “It has meant the need and the focus to tackle and take on Donald Trump and his disastrous corruption, his endless war, his attacks on small business with these disastrous tariffs, the skyrocketing costs families are facing in New Hampshire and across the country.”
However, she suggested that messaging must go further.
“But let’s just be clear: It’s not enough to stop Trump’s damage,” Shaheen continued. “We have to do better than that. We have to give a reason for people to feel motivated and inspired and ready to show up between now and November, and that’s what we will do.”
The district covers the eastern half of the state, including Manchester, the Seacoast, and much of the Lakes Region. Since 2018, Chris Pappas has held the seat, but the Manchester Democrat is now his party’s nominee for New Hampshire’s open U.S. Senate seat. 
DiLorenzo beat out a slew of other conservatives including Hollie Noveletsky, who owns Novel Iron Works in Greenland and was once chair of the New Hampshire Republican Party, and State Rep. Brian Cole, who represents Manchester in the State House. DiLorenzo won with 51.7% of votes (per the AP as of Tuesday when 99% of votes had been counted) compared to Noveletsky’s 26.2% and Cole’s 14.1%. Two other candidates, Melissa Bailey and Lindsey Anderson, took less than 5% each.
DiLorenzo has dismissed questions about his lack of legislative experience: “I have exceptional experience, all sorts of different ranges of experience.”
Stefany Shaheen hugs her daughter at an election results watch party in Portsmouth soon before The Associated Press called the primary election for her. In the early hours of the next day, Sept. 9, 2026, she was declared the winner of the Democratic primary for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
He also said he doesn’t plan on changing his campaign messaging much for the general election. During the primary, DiLorenzo weathered attacks from fellow Republicans that he wasn’t sufficiently conservative on issues such as abortion, where he opposes federal legislation on the issue, and immigration, where he’s suggested openness to pathways for citizenship.
Throughout the primary, though, the Republican candidates struggled to differentiate themselves.
“How do you break out from that field, right?” Noveletsky said in an interview. “When we’re all Republicans and we’re all really philosophically similar.”
In order to earn her spot on the general election ballot, Shaheen fought off another centrist, Marine Corps veteran Maura Sullivan, and a host of progressives led by Hampton Select Board member Carleigh Beriont. She walked away with 36.9% of the vote, narrowly edging Sullivan, who won 34.8% of the vote. Beriont took 22.5%.
GOP congressional candidate Hollie Noveletsky (foreground left) peeks over the shoulders of supporters at a TV displaying partial election results at a watch party at Novel Iron Works in Greenland on Sept. 8, 2026. Soon after, her opponent Anthony DiLorenzo was declared the victor. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Shaheen promised to fight for a single-payer Medicare for All system like many of her primary opponents. She also opposes the Trump administration’s tariff policies and, as the mother of a diabetic daughter, wants to make insulin prices a priority.
If elected, DiLorenzo would be the first Republican to represent New Hampshire in Congress in over a decade. Before Pappas first won the district in 2018, the seat had flipped between Republicans and Democrats in five consecutive elections. Political observers are now wondering whether the district soured on Republicans or if Pappas was a uniquely strong candidate. This election could provide insight into that question, but it will also have ramifications nationwide as the two parties battle for control of the House of Representatives.
“We all know the map to a Democratic Congress runs through New Hampshire,” Shaheen said. “And it runs through the 1st District, running through communities like Rochester and Merrimack and Derry.”
Shaheen is trying to extend the tenure of her politically powerful family. Her mother, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, announced her retirement last year after 18 years in Congress. Before that, she was governor of New Hampshire for six years. If elected, the younger Shaheen will be sworn in at the same time her mother leaves office. The candidate is also the daughter of Billy Shaheen, an attorney and Democratic Party operative who was involved in helping Jimmy Carter win New Hampshire’s 1976 primary election and the White House. Since that 1976 election, he’s been a player in New Hampshire Democratic politics. With that, Stefany Shaheen has faced accusations of nepotism throughout her bid for Congress.
DiLorenzo is likely to highlight that dynamic over the next several weeks.
“Growing up in a working-class family, we often sat around the kitchen table talking about things, and I often dreamed about being successful,” DiLorenzo said. “And I never, ever imagined that I’d be up on stage talking about running for Congress. It’s a great country, America.”
Anthony DiLorenzo celebrates his primary victory as confetti flies over him in the Music Hall Lounge in Portsmouth after the Sept. 8, 2026, election for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Bishop William Barber, NC faith leaders call for ‘conspicuous courage’ to combat voter confusion
description: One month before early in-person voting begins in North Carolina, civil rights leader and Repairers of the Breach President Bishop William Barber said voters should not fall victim to the confusion surrounding voting in the midterms. The Trump administration asked the U.S. Supreme Court to approve the president’s executive order restricting mail-in voting ah[...]
text:
Bishop William Barber, president of Repairers of the Breach and founder of the Moral Monday movement (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)One month before early in-person voting begins in North Carolina, civil rights leader and Repairers of the Breach President Bishop William Barber said voters should not fall victim to the confusion surrounding voting in the midterms.
The Trump administration asked the U.S. Supreme Court to approve the president’s executive order restricting mail-in voting ahead of the midterm elections, directing the postal service to refuse to deliver mail ballots to certain voters. Late Monday, the high court kept in place a lower court’s order blocking President Donald Trump’s plan to place new restrictions on mail ballots ahead of the Nov. 3 elections.
Voting rights advocates remain concerned that Homeland Security and ICE may dissuade some individuals from showing up at the polls.
Trump has called voting by mail a “hoax,” and he and Republican supporters claim more restrictions on it are needed to prevent election fraud in November. However, Trump himself regularly votes by mail, and study after study has found that mail-in voting fraud is extremely rare.


Upcoming election dates:
Oct. 9: Voter registration deadline.
Oct. 15: In-person early voting begins; same-day registration available. Vote Early in Person.
Oct. 20: Absentee ballot request deadline
Oct. 31: In-person early voting ends (3 p.m.).
Nov. 3: Election Day.
Source: NC State Board of Elections


Barber, founder of the Moral Monday movement, told reporters at a Monday press conference at Raleigh’s Martin Street Baptist Church this was all about creating confusion.
Trump won North Carolina in 2024 by 183,000 votes, but Barber said 1.2 million poor and low wage workers stayed on the sidelines and did not vote. If just 15% of the voters who didn’t cast a ballot two years ago were mobilized to vote in the midterms, the entire outcome could shift, said Barber.
Barber said extremists trying to cling to power are trying to sow confusion into the election process, even as North Carolina absentee ballots are being mailed out, in hopes that some potential voters will become discouraged and decide not to vote.
“What they’re doing is creating confusion where there has been no confusion. That’s what’s going on,” said Barber. “It’s not good for North Carolina. It’s not good for democracy. And lastly, they’re creating confusion that’s so bad that they’re hurting their own people.”
Barber said the only way to push back against the confusion surrounding the mail-in voting rules and other changes is to vote early and, if possible, in person.
More absentee ballots in NC in danger of being tossed under new directives

Barber and faith leaders announced in early August plans to mobilize 1,000 marches to the polls. Their goal is to engage with 5 million low-wage voters and at least 1 million Black men, particularly in the South. As of Monday, they had 320 marches organized in 23 states.
Rev. Dr. Hanna R. Broome said the country is facing a moral crisis when people in power try to make it harder for eligible voters to participate.
“You are telling somebody their voice is too much trouble to count,” said Broome. “And here’s what people behind these attacks are counting on – that no one will call it what it is. This is evil.”
Broome said the best way to combat that strategy  is to make a plan to vote, and volunteer to lead a local march to the polls.
Rev. Dr. Hanna R. Broome. (Photo: Repairers of the Breach video stream)
“Anyone  – your church, your organization, fraternity, sorority, lodge, barbershop, hair salon, or family reunion – can march or caravan to the polls,” said Broome.
Barber said the hope is that five people can organize 50, and that 10 people might have the power to encourage 100 more to vote. He calls such visible demonstrations “conspicuous courage” that will inspire infrequent or anxious voters to cast a ballot this fall.
Even though early voting hours and Sunday voting hours may shift in some counties this fall, he said voters must remain determined and vote en masse.
“What we’re not going to do is retreat,” said Barber. “Don’t you get weary. Know what side you’re on. You’re on the side of democracy.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trump administration helps announce Hitachi Energy plans for $528M transformer factory in Copiah County
description: Gov. Tate Reeves says he believes Mississippi's SNAP payment error rate will fall below 8% before the end of September. Reeves also says workforce development should be part of efforts to reduce dependence on federal assistance.
text:
Hitachi Energy is investing $528 million to build a new transformer factory in Copiah County, with plans to create 654 jobs. 
Gov. Tate Reeves announced the development on Tuesday morning from the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston, alongside President Donald Trump administration leaders. 
Federal leaders emphasized that the Zurich-based company’s investment is a part of Trump’s “energy dominance” agenda and goal to bring back American manufacturing.
“This is bigger than just one factory announcement,” said U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, chairman of the National Energy Dominance Council.  “This is about America’s determination to build the infrastructure to win the intelligence race, to power the next generation of American manufacturing and to bring prosperity and affordability to American citizens.”
Reeves said: “This administration is doing the work to bring back jobs to America because in Mississippi just like in America this what we do. We make stuff. We build stuff.”
The plant would be Hitachi Energy’s largest investment in America and is part of the company’s total $1.5-billion investment across the U.S. to increase production of transformers and other grid infrastructure to meet energy demand. The company is a subsidiary of multi-billion dollar Japanese firm Hitachi, Ltd.
Trump has said that he wants the U.S. to be the leader in energy production and exports. 
According to the company, the transformers produced in Mississippi will bring additional capacity to help growing demand for electricity. Consulting company Mckinsey has estimated that the U.S. demand for power will increase by 3.5% annually through 2040. 
“America needs more affordable, reliable and secure electricity generation, and this new investment by Hitachi will help make that happen,” said Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “The Trump Administration welcomes today’s announcement of a Hitachi transformer manufacturing facility that will provide jobs to local Mississippi communities while also helping improve electricity reliability and affordability for millions of Americans.”
Hitachi Energy has been in Mississippi for 70 years, but this investment would double the size of its existing operation. The company will build the new factory on a 45-acre site at the Copiah County Industrial Park in Gallman. Construction is expected to begin later this year with production to start in 2029.
Reeves called it a historic day for the U.S., Japan and Mississippi, emphasizing Mississippi’s existing relationship with other Japanese companies such as Toyota and Nissan. 
“Hitachi could’ve picked any state in the country. They chose Copiah County. They chose Mississippi,” Reeves wrote on social media.

title: State Land Office says New Mexico’s renewable energy brings in revenue, offsets environmental harm
description: Renewable energy projects leased on state land are expected to bring in billions of dollars for New Mexico in the years to come, State Land Office officials told legislators Monday. The 55 active green energy projects, such as solar and wind farms, brought in $8 million in revenue this year, a 1,287% increase from 2019, […]
text:
New Mexico State Land Office officials shared projected revenue from renewable energy sources such as solar with legislators during the Sept. 14, 2026, meeting of the interim Revenue Stabilization and Tax Police committee meeting.  (Photo by Anna Padilla for Source New Mexico)Renewable energy projects leased on state land are expected to bring in billions of dollars for New Mexico in the years to come, State Land Office officials told legislators Monday.
The 55 active green energy projects, such as solar and wind farms, brought in $8 million in revenue this year, a 1,287% increase from 2019, they said. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Around 12% of all land in New Mexico is managed by the State Land Office, which offers bonds for leases of the land for various projects: energy, commercial development and agriculture. The office generated $16 billion in eight years.
Though the renewable energy revenue may seem small now compared to the $3.1 billion that went into the state permanent fund last year from oil and gas revenues, the projected revenue on just existing leased projects, not including pending or future leases, will bring in $2.5 billion by 2040, State Land Office Deputy Commissioner Sunalei Stewart told lawmakers on the interim Revenue Stabilization and Tax Policy Committee during their meeting at the state Capitol.
Moreover, Stewart said, those renewables will offset air pollution equivalent to the carbon emissions of 380 million barrels of oil.
Stewart said the long projection time stems from renewable energy projects having a different life span when compared to oil and gas projects. While oil and gas leases generate massive revenues in the short term and decline over a long period, renewable energy leases are “the inverse,” Steward said, due to the “initial phase” of building renewable energy: securing the capital, acquiring the lease for the plant site and building the infrastructure. 
The long-term nature of building renewable energy infrastructure left some lawmakers concerned about the possibility of energy developers failing during the long lifespan of solar and wind farms, which would leave the state with the decommission costs. 
“I think you’re putting us at risk,” Sen. George Muñoz (R-Gallup) said.
Steward noted that the State Land Office’s lease agreements include decommissioning costs.
The state is also planning to expand the geothermal energy sector. In May, the State Land Office published a new rule that would allow for larger projects to be developed on state lands. Last year, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham touted the state as a potential leader for geothermal energy, following a report about its potential here.
“New Mexico is primed to attract additional renewable energy business,” Steward told state lawmakers. “We’re beginning to see the state investment council do more renewable energy investments because they’re seeing the value in it.”

name: Delaware
title: Officer’s quick response removes loaded handgun from Glasgow High
description:
The Delaware State Police arrested a 17-year-old Glasgow High School student, from Newark, Delaware, on firearm and related charges after a loaded handgun was discovered in his backpack Monday afternoon. […]
The post State Police Arrest Glasgow High School Student After Loaded Gun Found in Backpack appeared first on Delaware State Police - State of Delaware.
text:
Photo caption: Delaware State Police released this photograph of the loaded handgun investigators said was recovered from a 17-year-old Glasgow High School student’s backpack.
The incident demonstrates the value of having trained law enforcement officers inside schools, where an immediate response can prevent a dangerous situation from escalating.
NEWARK, Del. — A Delaware State Police school resource officer deserves credit for helping bring a potentially dangerous situation at Glasgow High School under control Monday and removing a loaded handgun from the building.
The officer was already inside the school when a hallway fight was reported at about 1 p.m. Sept. 14. Working with school staff, the officer separated the students and began investigating what had happened.
That investigation led to the backpack of a 17-year-old student from Newark. Police said the student had removed the backpack before the fight and that the officer learned it allegedly contained marijuana.
A search uncovered a loaded handgun and a small quantity of marijuana, according to Delaware State Police.
The student was taken into custody and transported to an area hospital for treatment of injuries sustained during the fight. Police described the injuries as not life-threatening and said no other injuries were reported.
After being discharged, the student was taken to Delaware State Police Troop 2 and charged with possession of a firearm by a person under 21, possession of ammunition by a person under 21, possession of a firearm in a safe school zone, possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony and possession of marijuana by a person under 18.
Four of the five charges are felonies.
The student, whose name was withheld because he is a juvenile, was arraigned by Justice of the Peace Court and committed to the Delaware Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families in lieu of an $87,000 cash bond.
Officer’s presence made a difference
It is impossible to know what might have happened if the backpack had not been searched or if the loaded handgun had remained inside the school. What is clear is that the school resource officer was in the building, responded immediately and had the training and legal authority to investigate.
The result was not merely an arrest. It was the removal of a loaded firearm from a school before the situation became more dangerous.
The incident offers a practical reminder of why trained officers belong in schools. Their presence provides an immediate response to violence, allows suspicious behavior to be investigated and creates a visible warning that weapons and criminal activity can be detected.
Deterrence does not mean every student will follow the law or that no weapon will ever enter a school. It means increasing the likelihood that violations will be discovered and addressed quickly. At Glasgow High, that system worked.
Research on the overall effects of school resource officer programs remains mixed, and properly trained officers must avoid becoming involved in routine disciplinary matters that belong with educators. But federal research also recognizes that school officers can support safety through law enforcement, problem-solving, community relationships and crisis response.
The National Institute of Justice has found that school resource officers often perform several overlapping roles in maintaining a safe learning environment. Justice Department-supported research has also documented cases in which officers intervened before planned school violence could be carried out.
Those broader debates should not obscure what happened Monday. A fight drew an immediate response. An officer followed the evidence. A loaded handgun was found. Students and staff were protected from the risk posed by a firearm inside their school.
That is public safety at its most direct, and it is why the officer’s work should be recognized.
To Go Box

What happened: Delaware State Police said a school resource officer recovered a loaded handgun and marijuana from a 17-year-old student’s backpack.
Where: Glasgow High School, 1901 S. College Ave., Newark.
When: About 1 p.m. Monday, Sept. 14.
Student’s status: The student was committed to the Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families on an $87,000 cash bond.
Learn more: Read the Delaware State Police report and review the National Institute of Justice’s research on school resource officers.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Republicans warn of the red menace, even as Comrade Trump breaks out the Marx-Engels playbook
description: President Donald Trump speaks at the Republican convention Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, in Dallas.
text:
A national trend of Republican candidates warning that Democrats are a bunch of Bolsheviks trying to turn the U.S. into the USSR has trickled down to Mississippi, with some of our GOP politicians warning of the red menace in the midterms.  
But Mississippi McCarthyites seeking reelection to Congress or other offices might want to look inward, to the current administration they appear to support without question. As they seek to root out socialists and communists on the Mississippi midterm ballot, Comrade President Donald J. Trump appears to have broken out the Marx-Engels playbook. He’s been pushing to seize the means of production, redistribute wealth and institute what appears to be socialist-leaning market and price controls.

“If you elect a Democrat, you’re going to elect a socialist party,” Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Ezell told Mississippi Today recently. “Anybody that votes for a Democrat, that’s what we’re going to get.”
But if Ezell’s Democratic opponent, state Rep. Jeffrey Hulum, is a fellow traveler, he must be one heck of an embedded sleeper agent. Retired Army Sgt. Maj. Hulum, a 22-year combat veteran, has shown no overt socialist or communist leanings in his nearly five years in the Legislature nor in his congressional race platform.  
That’s exactly what commie sleeper agents do. Better keep an eye on him.
But despite their vocal fears of the creep of socialism and communism into American government, Ezell and his fellow Republicans in Mississippi’s congressional delegation have been noticeably quiet about what critics and analysts have called “Trump socialism,” or “state capitalism.”
A Wall Street Journal column recently opined that Trump is “imitating the Chinese Community Party by extending political control ever deeper into the economy.” The libertarian think tank the Cato Institute has noted the “irony” of the Trump administration denouncing the left for socialism while it seizes federal equity stakes in private businesses and implements centralized planning. 
The Trump administration has taken federal government equity stakes in more than two dozen companies. It has converted federal grants into stock and taken “golden shares” of private companies. The federal government has created quite a venture investment portfolio, seeking control production in industries including nuclear power, semiconductors, steel, minerals and quantum computing.
The pretense for federal government control of private companies has been national security and to — kid you not — promote innovation.
Anyone who believes socialism or communism promotes product innovation should go out and buy a Lada automobile.
The real corker is the potential U.S.-Venezuelan oil “deal.” The term deal here means the U.S. taking another country’s oil production at gunpoint, ousting one dictator and installing another and cooking up a deal in secret without approval from the elected legislatures of either country for the U.S. government to seize more control of the global oil market.
But don’t worry, Trump is full of proposals to redistribute wealth to the workers, although his promised checks have a way of not ever showing up in the bank accounts of the proletariat.
Back home in Mississippi, our Republican politicians appear unperturbed and unimpressed by this. Instead, they are trying to create a new Red Scare for Mississippi voters to shun those commie Democrats in the midterms and next year’s statewide elections.
“We can’t let the radical Democrat socialist agenda take hold in Mississippi,” Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith recently urged.
“This November 3rd, we must rally and defeat the Marxist Communists, Democratic Socialists and Red-Green alliance …” wrote Republican Agriculture Commissioner and gubernatorial candidate Andy Gipson. “Standing with President Trump, we will never let the enemies of freedom win!”
There is an unprecedented shift from capitalism to some form of socialism that probably has Ronald Reagan rolling over in his grave. But it’s not being led by Mississippi Democrats.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Blaze engulfs vacant commercial building in Jackson; no injuries reported
authors: Aaron Lampley, Simeon Gates and Sophia Paffenroth
description: The Jackson Fire Department was dispatched to 1030 Mill Street at about 5:30 a.m., Tuesday, September 15, 2026 in Jackson, Miss.
text:
An early morning blaze engulfed the old Midtown Center located on Mill Street in downtown Jackson Tuesday, causing extensive damage but no injuries, fire officials said..
The Jackson Fire Department was dispatched to 1030 Mill Street at about 5:30 a.m. Crews arrived to heavy smoke and flames.
Division Fire Chief of Investigations Charles Felton confirmed the building was vacant and there were no injuries.
“At this time, I do not have any information as to how long it’s been vacant. We do know it’s been vacant for some time. But the definite time frame we do not have,” Felton said.
The cause of the fire is under investigation.
The fire broke out near a residential neighborhood and not far from the Midtown Head Start Center on East Fortification Street.
Luckily, the childcare facility was not in operation, said Nita Norphlet-Thompson, the executive director of the Mississippi Head Start Association. The building is under construction, according to Norphlet-Thompson.
“Currently, that center is under renovation and probably won’t be open until the 1st of the year,” Norphlet-Thompson told Mississippi Today.  
Capitol Police closed off nearby streets near the fire zone, as water from firetrucks slickened streets.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana continues gas tax reimbursements
description: The Indiana State Board of Finance on Tuesday approved its third round of reimbursements to local governments for losses incurred during the state’s gas tax suspension. The three-member board unanimously approved roughly $139 million in reimbursements from the State Highway Fund to replace July revenue from Indiana’s gasoline excise and use taxes. The State[...]
text:
The Indiana State Board of Finance on Tuesday approved its third round of reimbursements to local governments for losses incurred during the state’s gas tax suspension.
The three-member board unanimously approved roughly $139 million in reimbursements from the State Highway Fund to replace July revenue from Indiana’s gasoline excise and use taxes. The State Comptroller’s Office will begin distributing $46 million to counties, cities and towns this week, according to a news release from Gov. Mike Braun’s office.
“Indiana has enjoyed the lowest gas prices in the country all summer while continuing to make local communities whole, protecting local roads and infrastructure,” Braun said in the release Tuesday. “I want to thank the Board of Finance for their partnership in once again helping us keep that promise.”
The board previously approved reimbursements for losses incurred from April through June at its July and August meetings.
Indiana shifts $130M to replace road funding lost during gas tax holiday

Braun suspended Indiana’s gasoline use tax in April to provide relief for motorists as fuel prices escalated amid the war with Iran. He lifted the state’s gasoline excise tax the following month, both of which remain suspended through at least October 6.
The taxes are split between the Indiana Department of Transportation and counties, cities and towns to pay for infrastructure maintenance and repair.
Losses for local governments and the State Highway Fund are projected to reach $1.1 billion should the suspension remain in effect through Dec. 4.
Braun pledged to reimburse local governments for any losses incurred during the suspension, approved each month by the State Board of Finance, and intends to ask lawmakers to tap into the state’s $4 billion reserves to cover the state’s losses when legislators return in January.
“The Comptroller’s Office is committed to restoring funds to our local government partners and is prioritizing this distribution so critical operations can continue at a local level,” Comptroller Elise Nieshalla said in the release.
Treasurer Daniel Elliott added, “Indiana’s continued extension of the gas tax holiday is a reminder of what good fiscal stewardship and sound economic policies can allow us to do. I commend Gov. Braun for continuing his leadership on this issue and ensuring that Hoosiers have affordable fuel prices.”
The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline in Indiana hit $3.59 Tuesday, 17 cents higher than last week’s average but still lower than the national $4.32 average, according to AAA.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana can tell you exactly how long it jailed people it had no right to hold
description: The additional days people are kept imprisoned beyond what their sentences prescribe cost more than time.
text:
Razor wire and fencing surround the Orleans Parish Justice Center jail. (Richard A. Webster/Verite News)An Orleans Parish judge ordered Lisa Andres to be released from jail May 30, 2025, according to court records cited in a new lawsuit against the state. She was not. 
The Louisiana Department of Public Safety and Corrections secured the documents needed for Andres’ release Oct. 15 — 100 days after the judge’s order — according to a federal lawsuit from Andres and Jaren Brignac, who the state held nine days past his release date. Their complaint was filed Aug. 28 with the U.S. District Court in Baton Rouge. Gary Wescott, leader of the state prison agency, is the sole defendant in the case. 
The plaintiffs attorneys are seeking class-action status for the case, hoping that others held beyond their release date will join.
Andres and Brigan are not outliers. The corrections department’s own numbers, cited in the lawsuit, show more than 1,200 people have been held past their release dates from when Westcott took over the agency in August 2024 through 2025. The U.S. Justice Department found in 2023 that Louisiana’s failure to put adequate policies and procedures in place was causing systemic overdention.
With Andres’ paperwork in hand Oct. 15, the state corrections staff made its calculations that same day and released her the next. The other 100 days, the lawsuit says, “were spent waiting for someone to be required to begin it.”
Court records show Andres was on parole from two Orleans Parish convictions — theft and unauthorized use of a motor vehicle — and under probation in a third case. Police arrested her Dec. 30, 2024, on a single count of misdemeanor domestic abuse battery, which prosecutors later reduced to keeping a disorderly place. By the time she was released, she had spent 151 days in jail on a charge that carries a 90-day sentence.
The lawsuit says Westcott has never told his time-computation staff to handle people entitled to immediate release first, and it claims he has never set a deadline for finishing a release-date calculation. 
When asked about the lawsuit, a Department of Corrections spokesperson said the agency does not comment on pending litigation.
The additional days people are kept imprisoned beyond what their sentences prescribe cost more than time. Federal investigators have found the toll of overdetention includes job opportunities and family milestones. 
Andres, who lost her apartment while she was in jail, had to rely on a shelter once she was released, the lawsuit says.
Overdetention is not a recent development for the Louisiana Department of Public Safety and Corrections 
Its own review in 2012 found more than 2,000 people each year were held past their release dates, according to the lawsuit. A decade later, federal investigators found 26.8% of people Louisiana released from jails and prisons in early 2022 were held too long, at an estimated cost to the public exceeding $2.5 million a year.
A Louisiana Legislative Auditor’s report published in February found, for the fifth straight time, that the Department of Corrections had not made sure someone double-checked staff changes to prison release dates. Auditors recommended the agency follow its own policy requiring a second employee to check every change to an incarcerated person’s release date. Westcott’s response to the audit said his staff could not second-check every change to every inmate’s release date and still process new arrivals and clear releases on time.
Put another way, the department’s rule was changed to fit its staff. When those who set the standard lower it for themselves and demand the public meet it, a gap opens and respect drains through it. 
Louisiana holds the people it sentences to the letter of the law. Its corrections department holds itself to whatever its staff can manage. 
Questioned under oath in Humphrey v. Leblanc, another federal lawsuit over the same practice that has been pending since 2020, Westcott called overdetention “just the nature of sentencing sometimes” and said incarcerated people “would understand that sometimes, there are delays,” according to the complaint.
On the day Andres and Brignac filed their lawsuit, Attorney General Liz Murrill told WBRZ-TV it was “nothing more than an attempt at a money grab,” adding that her office spent years helping build a new system, and that calculating time is complex.
Andres and Brignac are asking for unspecified compensatory and punitive damages for themselves and everyone else the department held for too long, along with a court order requiring the state to stop holding people after their sentences. 
No check buys back 101 days. No settlement heals the fear, the doubt, the weeks of hearing, as Andres put it, that “everybody treated me like I was crazy” for knowing her own release date. Calling that a money grab is disrespectful. It reads the ledger and never looks at the person.
A calculation that takes one day cost Lisa Andres 101. The state calls the gap complexity and the nature of sentencing. Neither one moves a single sheet of paper.
Setting a deadline for finishing a release-date calculation would. Andres’ lawsuit asks for required releases 48 hours from the moment a person finishes serving the sentence a court handed down, the same limit the earlier overdetention suit asks. 
Setting this deadline requires no new system or an act of the legislature, and it wouldn’t cost the state a dime, the lawsuit argues. 
Westcott has had that authority for two years. He has not used it.

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye

• Faith leaders on Ohio Haitians. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Karen Kasler reports, “Faith leaders call on DeWine to help Haitians in Ohio facing ankle monitors, detainment.”
Faith leaders delivered a letter to Gov. Mike DeWine Friday, asking him to protect Haitians immigrants in Ohio who have lost temporary protected status.
Hundreds of clergy members signed the letter asking DeWine to forward on the letter to U.S. Sens. Jon Husted and Bernie Moreno and U.S. Reps. Mike Carey (R-15) and Mike Turner (R-10). It asks them take whatever action they can to help the tens of thousands of Haitians in Ohio, most in Springfield and Columbus. Temporary protected status (TPS) ended for Haitians in July, which ended their ability to live and work legally in the U.S. Some Haitians are now being detained, while others are ordered to wear GPS ankle monitors.
• Rural pharmacies. The Ohio Newsroom’s Kendall Crawford reports, “‘A financial lifeline’: Rural pharmacists hope federal funds can bridge healthcare gaps.”
A large federal grant could help better connect rural pharmacies with local physicians.
The Ohio Department of Health recently announced that $2 million from the Trump administration’s Rural Health Transformation fund will go to the Ohio Pharmacy Association.
The group aims to create a Health Information Exchange network that allows pharmacies to have access to patient medical history. That would help clear the way for small-town pharmacists to provide treatment, in addition to dispensing medication.
• Husted and Merrin at the Trump Fest in Dallas. Spectrum News’ Harri Leigh reports, “Why Husted and Merrin spoke at the GOP midterm convention.”
(T)wo Ohio Republicans in hotly contested races not only attended, but delivered speeches at the convention: former State Rep. Derek Merrin, who is challenging Rep. Marcy Kaptur in Ohio’s 7th District; and Sen. Jon Husted, who is fighting a comeback bid by former Sen. Sherrod Brown. Both of the races are considered toss-ups…
By speaking at the convention, both Merrin and Husted made a bet that tying themselves to the president would be a smart move in Ohio, a state that Trump won by a 12-point margin in 2024.
• Bankrupting the JFK memorial Kennedy Center and then extorting its future by tying it to Trump’s ego. The Washington Post reports, “Kennedy Center could close as early as Tuesday, warns of bankruptcy, documents show.”
Leaders of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, installed by President Donald Trump, say the center is on the brink of bankruptcy and argue that putting the president’s name on its facade — and thus ensuring his fundraising efforts — may be the only way to avoid imminent and “certain fiscal collapse,” according to documents obtained by The Washington Post…
Lawyers for Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), a Kennedy Center trustee who has sued to keep Trump’s name off the building, blasted the new proposal.
“This constant effort to add Donald Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center facade is the definition of insanity,” lawyers Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky said in a statement. “This is now the third attempt to deface this sacred memorial and turn it into a vanity project for one man’s ego.
“Worse still, now Trump is taking the Center hostage and threatening to in effect kill it unless he gets his way,” they added. “This has to stop.”
• Who among us hasn’t had their wedding funded by a Russian oligarch? ProPublica reports, “Donald Trump Jr.’s Bahamas Wedding Was Secretly Bankrolled by Russian Oligarch Close to Putin.”
The oligarch, Umar Kremlev, spent hundreds of thousands on expenses like renting out a private island. He appears to have met Trump Jr. only recently, but he attended the intimate wedding with a large group of other Russian guests.
• Elon. The Washington Post reports, “‘Musk’ film is almost four hours long, engrossing and terrifying. What to know.”
The documentary paints the tech titan as a power-hungry megalomaniacal con man with a God complex. Musk accuses the filmmaker of compiling “hit list” against him.
• We’ll meet again some sunny day. The Guardian reports, “AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?”
Does artificial superintelligence really pose a risk greater than nuclear weapons? Is there a significant chance of “a Chornobyl-sized catastrophe”. Might there even be a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” in the next decade?
These warnings were issued on both sides of the Atlantic about the potential impact of a technology that most people still think of as a more talkative search engine.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Secretary of state: No runoff elections for Mississippi’s federal midterm races
description: Voters headed to the polls Tuesday, March 10, 2026, in Jackson, to cast their ballots in the primary election.
text:
Mississippi does not hold runoffs for general elections for federal offices, Secretary of State Michael Watson is reminding voters. 
“Ensuring Mississippi voters and election officials have clear, straightforward information about how our elections are decided is imperative,” Watson said in a statement. “The requirements are not the same for every office, so we want to make sure candidates, election officials, and voters have trusted information prior to Election Day.”
Watson’s clarification comes amid a high-profile Senate race, with Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith facing two challengers: Democratic nominee Scott Colom and independent opponent Ty Pinkins. 

Runoff elections can be confusing in Mississippi because some offices require them, but others do not. There have been runoff elections in recent congressional elections. But those were either primary elections or special elections, not regular general elections.     
In 2018, a runoff between Hyde-Smith and Espy occurred after the two received more votes than former state Sen. Chris McDaniel. This was a special election after longtime Sen. Thad Cochran’s resignation. 
McDaniel also forced Cochran into a 2014 runoff in the Republican primary after neither gained an outright majority because of a third-party candidate, Thomas Carey. Cochran later defeated McDaniel in the runoff. 
But it’s long been the law in Mississippi that there are no runoff elections for general elections in federal races. The winner is required to win only a plurality of the votes, not a majority. 
Cochran famously became Mississippi’s first Republican U.S. senator since Reconstruction in 1978 without securing an outright majority. Cochran competed in the general election against Maurice Dantin, the Democratic nominee, and Charles Evers, an independent. 
Cochran received 45% of the vote, Dantin received 31%, and Evers received 22%. 
Mississippi requires candidates for the eight statewide state offices, judicial offices, and county offices to receive a majority. Only a plurality is required for candidates running for congressional, legislative, state district, and municipal offices.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: State-funded college scholarship successfully tackling WV teacher shortage
description: There was good news at the state Capitol on Tuesday: a competitive college scholarship is having great success at recruiting and retaining passionate public school teachers in West Virginia.   The Underwood Smith Teaching Scholarship requires recipients to teach in the state five years after completion of their degree and teach in an in-demand field, includi[...]
text:
West Virginia Higher Education Policy Commission Chancellor Sarah Tucker speaks about the success of the Underwood Smith Teaching Scholarship to the Joint Committee on Education at the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)There was good news at the state Capitol on Tuesday: a competitive college scholarship is having great success at recruiting and retaining passionate public school teachers in West Virginia.  
The Underwood Smith Teaching Scholarship requires recipients to teach in the state five years after completion of their degree and teach in an in-demand field, including elementary education, mathematics and special education. 
West Virginia has struggled to fill more than 1,000 certified teacher positions. 
West Virginia Higher Education Policy Commission Chancellor Sarah Tucker (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“So far, we have 42 Underwood Smith teaching scholars who are currently teaching in a West Virginia classroom in public education,” said Sarah Tucker, chancellor of the West Virginia Higher Education Policy Commission. “These students are serious. This is what they want to do for their vocation.”
Tucker presented scholarship information Monday to members of the Joint Committee on Education at the state Capitol in Charleston. 
Lawmakers revamped the teaching scholarship in 2019, providing up to $40,000 to high school students in West Virginia who desire to be teachers. The stackable scholarship can be combined with other awards, like the Promise Scholarship. 
The Underwood Smith Teaching Scholarship program receives an annual appropriation of $1.4 million from the Legislature that funds 25 students per cohort. 
“This presentation is really a victory lap for all of you,” Tucker told lawmakers. “I want to thank you for providing these students the opportunity you have provided them.”
Hundreds of eligible students have applied for the scholarship since 2024. It’s a four round-selection process in which a selection committee reviews the applicants’ GPA, test scores and an essay about why the student aspires to be a teacher. Twenty-five students are selected each year to receive the award. 
“I know we hear lots of negative things about West Virginia … These are amazing students, and we have hundreds of them that apply every year that all want to stay here and all want to teach and all want to do better for the state of West Virginia,” Tucker said.
The 42 scholarship recipients are currently working in 22 different counties around the state. 
As Underwood Smith Teaching scholars, students are provided with mentoring to help them prepare for their teaching careers. 
Tucker said that many students who didn’t receive the scholarship still went on to pursue a degree in education.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Public comment opens for planned New Mexico uranium mine as firm pledges not to leave behind ‘mess’
description: Leaders of a Colorado company seeking to open a uranium mine in New Mexico promised lawmakers at a recent legislative hearing that they won’t leave a “mess” behind if they are granted federal and state permits to extract the mineral over the course of two decades near Mount Taylor.
text:
Energy Fuels, Inc. submitted a finalized operations plan in May 2026 for how it would mine uranium near Mount Taylor, including pumping out water to access uranium ore. (Courtesy New Mexico Mining and Minerals Division)Leaders of a Colorado company seeking to open a uranium mine in New Mexico promised lawmakers at a recent legislative hearing that they won’t leave a “mess” behind if they are granted federal and state permits to extract the mineral over the course of two decades near Mount Taylor. 
Energy Fuels, Inc. has sought for more than a decade to establish the Roca Honda Mine within the Cibola National Forest boundaries in McKinley County. After a years-long hiatus, the company in late May submitted a 273-page “reclamation” plan to officials at the state Mining and Minerals Division, marking a significant step forward in the state’s permitting process, environmentalist groups said at the time. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Monday marked the first day of a 30-day public comment period as Energy Fuels seeks a federal permit for the mine from the United States Forest Service, which is preparing an environmental impact statement. The Forest Service’s announcement notes that the mine would operate, if approved, for approximately 21 years, of which 11 years would be mineral production and the rest would be spent reclaiming and monitoring the site.
Leaders of the company on Friday opened their presentation to lawmakers on the interim Radioactive and Hazardous Waste Committee with acknowledgments of uranium mining’s long-lasting impact on the environment and public health, as well as promises to do better than the companies that have left hundreds of abandoned uranium mines across the state.
“We understand why the history shapes the questions people are asking about Roca Honda today,” said Nick Martin, an environmental manager at Energy Fuels. “We’re not here to tell anyone that history didn’t happen, or those concerns aren’t legitimate. But you have our commitment that we’re not going to just stop at acknowledgment.”
Martin and other company officials said they are committed to adhering to all federal and state environmental requirements, as well as meaningfully listening to tribes about the potential cultural impacts of the mine on Mount Taylor, which several pueblos and the Navajo Nation deem sacred. 
Tribes and pueblos in the early 2000s successfully convinced the state to designate the mountain and outlying areas a “traditional cultural property,” an effort to protect it from mining.
Company representatives said they have already updated their proposed mine plans to avoid, as much as possible, drilling or other disturbances within the boundaries of the Mount Taylor Traditional Cultural Property designation. Nonetheless, the current plans include about 30 acres within the boundary for dewatering well pads and ventilation shafts. 
Sen. Crystal Brantley (R-Elephant Butte) said members of the public should be more open-minded to uranium production in the state, especially given the global energy demand and that mines in New Mexico and the rest of the country are preferable to mines that open in countries with fewer environmental regulations. 
Still, she said the concerns from communities historically impacted by uranium are “valid” and asked Energy Fuels to commit to cleaning up the mine site. 
“Do we have your commitment that you are going to participate in the reclamation, in the cleanup, to ensure that that doesn’t happen, what happened decades ago with mining projects?” she asked Misael Cabrera, the company’s senior vice president of regulatory affairs. 
“You have my absolute commitment that we will not leave a mess for the state of New Mexico,” Cabrera responded.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Number of West Virginia foster children decreasing, but hundreds of kids still going out of state
description: The number of West Virginia’s foster children is trending slightly downward but the state continues to send hundreds of children out of state.  There are 5,719 children in foster care and the number has declined from more than 7,000 children in 2020. West Virginia spends more than $60 million a year putting hundreds of foster […]
text:
The offices of the West Virginia departments of Health, Health Facilities and Human Services are located on Capitol Street in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)The number of West Virginia’s foster children is trending slightly downward but the state continues to send hundreds of children out of state. 
There are 5,719 children in foster care and the number has declined from more than 7,000 children in 2020.
West Virginia spends more than $60 million a year putting hundreds of foster children in out-of-state facilities across the country. At times, the state has removed children from facilities due to alleged dangerous conditions and abuse or educational deficiencies. 
Sen. Vince Deeds, R-Greenbrier
“Ultimately, we need to know where these children are going and why they are going out of state,” said Sen. Vince Deeds, R-Greenbrier. “ … I don’t feel that there’s a clear plan on how to bring them home and how to develop those facilities here.”
Members of the Legislative Oversight Committee on Health and Human Resources reviewed West Virginia foster care data Monday at the state Capitol during legislative interims.
Deeds stressed that foster children need to be close to home. The state Department of Human Services currently has children placed in facilities in California, Minnesota, Texas, Washington and more. 
“As soon as we uproot them and they and take them away from their community, away from their family and their extended family, their kinship family, then it is so hard for them to have that contact back home and be integrated back into their family,” Deeds said. 
As of June, 390 foster children were placed in out-of-state facilities. That number hasn’t decreased in line with the overall number of foster children. 
West Virginia Bureau of Social Services Deputy Commissioner Kendra Boley Rogers speaks to members of the Legislative Oversight Committee on Health and Human Resources on Monday, Sept. 14, 2026 in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“Our primary goal is to serve as many children in the community as possible,” said Kendra Boley Rogers, deputy commissioner for the state Bureau of Social Services. “What we’ve seen is that we have programs we need to build in West Virginia so we can keep our kids closer to home.”
West Virginia has 450 in-state residential beds for foster children, but it’s not enough to meet the demand, particularly for older children with behavioral challenges. As of June, 448 children were placed at in-state facilities. 
The state’s only psychiatric facility can hold 15 children, but is only serving about nine children due to staffing limitations.
Boley Rogers told lawmakers that the state lacks treatment options for children in care dealing with self harm, sexualized behaviors and mental health needs combined with autism.
While the number of in-state beds has been decreasing, Boley Rogers told lawmakers that DoHS is actively working on building new-in state options. It could involve both in- and out-of-state partners. 
“The department is reviewing plans to open new local (psychiatric residential treatment facility) programs to meet our children’s needs,” Boley Rogers said.
Without specific plans, Deeds said lawmakers need more information on whether the state has the infrastructure to care for the children in-state. 
“Until we have those healthcare providers to be able to take care of those kids, then we’re in a holding pattern. We’ll never be able to bring them home,” Deeds said. 
Earlier this year, Gov. Patrick Mrorisey proposed a $6 million “Bring Them Home” fund with the goal of bringing 380 foster children back to West Virginia. Lawmakers declined to fund the idea. The bill was short on details, and House of Delegates Finance Chairman Vernon Criss, R-Wood, told West Virginia Watch, “There was no appetite for it.”
Boley Rogers attributed the downward trend in the total number of foster children to the state’s progress on its substance use disorder crisis and safely reunifying more children with their biological families. 
“We have also seen a reduction in overdose deaths in West Virginia, so we feel like that’s a contributing factor in why we’re seeing some of these reunifications because we’re getting better with identifying the substance use disorder and providing the treatment and services to our families,” Boley Rogers said.
There has been a 23% growth in the state’s wraparound services, according to Boley Rogers, and those services are now supporting 1,900 children. These children are less likely to need to be admitted to a residential facility. 
West Virginia has 1,159 to 1,192 active foster homes. There is an ongoing need for families to accept older youth.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas authorities battling wildfire near Camden industrial park
description: Arkansas authorities are battling a wildfire that’s grown to more than 2,300 acres near a Camden industrial park where several defense contractors are located. Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders on Tuesday ordered the Arkansas National Guard to deploy two Black Hawk Helicopters with “Bambi buckets” that are used to drop water onto wildfires to assist in […]
text:
(Getty Images)Arkansas authorities are battling a wildfire that’s grown to more than 2,300 acres near a Camden industrial park where several defense contractors are located.
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders on Tuesday ordered the Arkansas National Guard to deploy two Black Hawk Helicopters with “Bambi buckets” that are used to drop water onto wildfires to assist in responding to the blaze.
Sanders also directed two bulldozers and a fire plow to respond to the wildfire. Ten Guard members will support the wildfire mission, according to a news release.
“We’re closely monitoring the ongoing fire at Highland Industrial Park in Camden,” Sanders said in a post on X Monday night. “State personnel are working to contain it and evacuate the area.”
Highland Industrial Park is home to several defense contractors, including Lockheed Martin and Raytheon. There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage to the facilities. Sanders said she appreciated outreach from the White House and Pentagon about the fire.
Hegseth touts Arkansas missile industry in speech at arms factory expansion site

The fire began on Monday and the cause is unknown, according to the state’s online wildfire dashboard. 
“The city of Camden is currently monitoring and assisting in the response to the devastating fire near the Highland industrial Park – the very epicenter of our local industry where countless of our citizens are employed,” Camden Mayor Charlotte Young said in a statement posted on the city’s Facebook page. 
The Arkansas Department of Emergency Management said Tuesday it activated the state emergency operations center in response to the wildfire, which will allow agencies to coordinate closely.
Temporary shelters had been set up in Hampton at Victory Baptist Church, the Hampton High School Library and Hampton First Assembly of God Church, according to the Calhoun County Sheriff’s Office.
Southern Arkansas University Tech evacuated students living on campus Monday night because of smoke from the wildfire. The students were given the all-clear to return to their dorms late Monday night. 
“Crews have been working extremely hard for many hours,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post Tuesday morning. “Please give them room to work and be patient as efforts continue.”
All of Arkansas’ 75 counties are at high risk of wildfires and burn bans are in effect in 68 counties, according to a map from the state Department of Agriculture.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida GOP endorses Amendment 3 — American Planning Association opposes
description: Seven weeks before the Nov. 3 election, Florida organizations are taking stands on Amendment 3, which, if approved by 60 % of the voters, would substantially reduce homestead property taxes while simultaneously reducing revenues for local government services. The Republican Party of Florida on Monday went on the record as supporting the proposal. “Floridians[...]
text:
The Florida Chapter of the American Planning Association says it supports tax relief but opposes how the proposal found its way on the statewide ballot. (Photo from APA-Florida chapter website)





Seven weeks before the Nov. 3 election, Florida organizations are taking stands on Amendment 3, which, if approved by 60 % of the voters, would substantially reduce homestead property taxes while simultaneously reducing revenues for local government services.
The Republican Party of Florida on Monday went on the record as supporting the proposal.
“Floridians work hard for what they have. Government should not spend it all and then come back for more,” said RPOF Chairman Evan Power in a written statement. “Amendment 3 puts money back in the pockets of people who own their homes.”
Additionally, the Florida GOP announced support for Amendment 1, intended to strengthen Florida’s rainy-day fund. Gov. Ron DeSantis does not support the amendment, labelling it “foolish” in a social media post.
Meanwhile, the Florida Chapter of the American Planning Association (APA Florida) is opposing the measure. The group says it supports tax relief but opposes how the proposal found its way on the statewide ballot.
“Our concern is that there was a decision made to put it on the ballot without any kind of analysis, without any kind of data to really make a well thought out informed decision,” said Allara Mills-Gutcher, president of the Florida Chapter, in a video interview with the Phoenix.
“We recognize that this [ballot] language was decided in about three days in early June and, since then, we have seen some data come out, looked at Florida TaxWatch’s website to show the implications of this per county, and we are really concerned about making a decision, especially a constitutional decision, without having that data before you make the decision.”
There are approximately 3,000 planners in Florida. While some are general planners, others concentrate on different silos like the environment, transportation, historic preservation, or, in the case of Mills-Gutcher, policy. Some are regional planners, others economic planners.
Comp plans
Florida law requires local governments every seven years to evaluate their comprehensive plans to reflect changes in state requirements since the last comprehensive plans were filed. Mills-Gutcher said she has looked at some communities that haven’t been financially able to evaluate their plans for 10 to 20 years. “So, it’s important to stay on schedule,” she said.
“The state produces that schedule, it’s on their website,” she added. “So, I believe that could be hindered just as we’re choosing between whether or not you’re going to supply your community with adequate police and fire services or work on your comprehensive plan. I would imagine that they would go with police and fire services.”
Amendment 3 would increase Florida’s homestead exemption for non-school property taxes from its existing $50,000 level to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with annual adjustments for inflation beginning in 2029.
The additional exemption would not apply to school district property taxes. According to the research arm of the Florida Legislature, passage of Amendment 3 could reduce revenues by as much as $12 billion annually. That means local governments would have to determine how to make up that funding, if at all.
‘In the background’
Planners are “kind of hidden in the background” until a major project like a data center surfaces, Mills-Gutcher said.
“We make sure that those roadway capacities are adequate. We make sure that water and sewer lines can handle the demand that has been created by additional development. When we update our comprehensive plans, we are required to look out and conduct the analysis for 20 years to make sure that our community can handle the increased population that is forecasted.”
That means adequate parks, emergency services, roads and sidewalks, Mills-Gutcher said.
“Those are some of the many things that we look at as planners when we’re formulating our analysis to create the policies and comprehensive plan that is the map of the growth of the community over the next several years.”
Momentum for passage of the amendment has increased this month. The Florida Realtors trade group announced last week that it had formed a Vote Yes on 3 campaign and put $10 million toward the effort. Also, Gov. DeSantis has said he will now help promote and campaign for the measure, after previously saying he didn’t intend to do so.

name: Mississippi Today
title: At Pride in the Park, Jackson’s Black LGBTQ+ community finds connection
description: Cyanne Herron waves her rainbow fan at Fondren Park during Jackson Black Pride's event on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026.
text:
Under the welcome shade of Fondren Park trees, dozens of LGBTQ+ friends and allies socialized and enjoyed barbecue with a drag performance at a local Black Pride event, organized by public health group My Brother’s Keeper. Then, they were called upon to provide the entertainment.
Jose Ramirez, left, attended Pride in the Park with Tony Patrick, right. They drove in on Patrick’s Kawasaki Ninja motorcycle. Sept. 12, 2026. Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
After some cajoling by repeat Jackson Black Pride host JStruktuur on Saturday, a few intrepid attendees stepped up to the open mic, which featured a $75 cash prize for the winner. First up was Tony Patrick, who sang Ed Sheeran’s “Thinking of You.” Patrick came to the event with Jose Ramirez, driving from an hour away in Scott County on his lime green motorbike. After hearing about Pride in the Park the night before at Shade, a LGBTQ+ bar and nightclub in Jackson, they decided to make another trip to the city.
Despite living in an environment that can feel “closed in,” Patrick said he feels comfortable expressing himself as a gay man.
“We’ll go right now to a club that we’ve never been to and hold hands,” he said.  ” If I love myself, there’s nothing nobody can do about it.”
Afterward, they were off to a birthday party, again traveling by motorcycle and hoping the rain would hold off. 
Next on the mic was Cyanne Herron, an artist, fashion designer and poet. Herron told Mississippi Today that she is still shy about sharing her poetry. When she found out about the open mic, her first reaction was, “ Don’t look at me.”
An hour later, wearing a bright yellow bandana and a shirt she painted herself, Herron sat on the steps on the Fondren Park stage and began reading from her phone. Friends who had encouraged her to speak cheered her on, including Landon Williams, a retail worker by day and drag queen by night. 
Herron and Williams first met at Shade, and at Saturday’s event, they caught up on his Batman-themed show hosted at the nightclub the weekend prior. Williams flipped through videos on his phone of a fellow drag artist performing stunts as DC antihero Harley Quinn, while he twirled his cape as Quinn’s paramour, Poison Ivy.
 ”Drag has saved a version of myself that was kind of scared,” Williams said. He’s 26, but remembers that at 18, he didn’t have public events like Pride in the Park to meet other members of the LGBTQ+ community. In January, he started doing drag after finding two drag mothers, or mentors, who gave him a makeup kit and his first wig. 
“When you want to show your confidence in a bold way, you kind of feel shy about wanting to put it out there like that because people might look at you a certain way,” he said. “ But it’s just like, why don’t I get to be bold in my confidence?”
“ I love that for you, actually,” Herron said. “ Because I feel like we all deserve, our last day on Earth, to at least have some type of thought in our consciousness that says that I actually was being myself while I was here.” 
Cyanne Herron, left, and Landon Williams discuss Williams’ recent Batman-themed show at the Shade nightclub on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026, during Pride in the Park in Jackson. Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
Connecting people to care
Aside from building a sense of community, Pride in the Park allowed attendees to connect with resources. Some partners, like MS Capital City Pride and the Transgender Resources, Advocacy, Networking and Services (TRANS) Program, have been at previous iterations of the event. Others, like Awakening Love, a Jackson-based, Black and trans-led organization with a drop-in center that offers health resources and regular social programming, were there for the first time. 
Monica Smith, a phlebotomist with Open Arms Healthcare, holds an HIV antibody test which she uses to do rapid screening for presence of the virus on Saturday Sept. 12, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
Love Latonia, the founder of Awakening Love who is herself a veteran drag entertainer and transgender woman, tabled a booth alongside her longtime friend, Aubrey Grayson. The two got to know each other through the Jackson nightlife scene, where Grayson loved the way her friend performed in drag shows. 
“It just drew me to her,” she said, turning to Latonia.  “And then you did my hair. Remember you did my hair?”
Latonia replied with an emphatic, “Uh-huh,” as they laughed together.
Grayson said she knew several of the people there but wanted to mingle in the crowd. “ I thought it was more important for me to come out here because I’ve never really been, and I just wanted to just see my community,” she said. 
Dana Brooks, owner of Trampz Smokin Grill, catered Pride in the Park in Jackson on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. Brooks’ business is named in honor of his late father, who died a few years after Brooks began his transition.   Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
Participants also learned about health resources and received HIV screenings through the Open Arms Healthcare Center, the clinical arm of My Brother’s Keeper. 
Inside an air-conditioned trailer several notches cooler than the humid 90 degrees outside, phlebotomist Monica Smith took finger pricks for about a dozen attendees throughout the day. With each blood sample, she then administered an HIV test. Seconds later, the appearance of a blue dot in the HIV test showed a positive or negative result. 
The mobile unit can be requested through Open Arms Healthcare to travel across Mississippi, and provides both screenings and information or referrals to PrEP, a prescription drug that prevents HIV.
Outside, the party wound down as the sun began to set. Dana Brooks, who owns a catering company and is a transgender man, started packing up the burgers and beans he supplied. Friends folded up their lawn chairs, and Taylor Turnage, running the vintage sports clothing pop-up booth, put away her wares. 
The open mic wrapped up, too, after announcing the winner: Cyanne Herron. 
This story was produced with support from the Sarah Yelena Haselhorst Fund for Health Journalism.
Drag queen Aphrodite Morningstar, center, performs at Pride in the Park on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. Credit: Anna Hu/Mississippi Today
