name: Alaska Beacon
title: Arctic climate report set for publication despite loss of federal support
description: The Arctic Report Card, the annual peer-reviewed analysis of climate in the circumpolar region, will continue even without federal government support, scientists announced. The American Geophysical Union, an organization representing tens of thousands of Earth and space scientists, announced last week that it has taken over as manager of the Arctic Report Ca[...]
text:
A polar bear walks onshore in Alaska on Sept. 6, 2019. This year's Arctic Report Card, to be issued under new management after the Trump administration pulled federal support, is set to include a chapter updating the status of polar bear populations. (Photo provided by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)The Arctic Report Card, the annual peer-reviewed analysis of climate in the circumpolar region, will continue even without federal government support, scientists announced.
The American Geophysical Union, an organization representing tens of thousands of Earth and space scientists, announced last week that it has taken over as manager of the Arctic Report Card after the Trump administration pulled support last month.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration was, until this summer, the agency that coordinated and published the annual report since the inaugural edition in 2006.
But the Trump administration has slashed funding for climate science work at NOAA and other federal agencies, and Trump himself has repeatedly referred to climate change as a “hoax.”
The annual Arctic Report Card is now one of several NOAA climate-related programs which the Trump administration has eliminated or reduced.
The report provides status updates for permafrost thaw, sea ice extent, air temperatures, wildlife patterns, tundra vegetation and other subjects. It places a heavy emphasis on Alaska. Researchers from UAF and other Alaska universities are prominent among the chapter authors, and in recent years the report has included analysis from Indigenous Alaska scientists and community members.
Under AGU oversight, the Arctic Report Card’s editorial team remains intact, with continued leadership by researchers from the University of Alaska Fairbanks and the University of Colorado. Rick Thoman of UAF’s Alaska Center for Climate Change Preparedness remains one of the three main editors. The other two are from the University of Colorado’s Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Science, which includes the National Snow and Ice Data Center.
In a statement, one of the Colorado-based lead editors said the Arctic Report Card’s survival was a victory against censorship of climate science.
“Beyond the importance of sharing this key science, the fact that we can pull together and ensure the Arctic Report Card goes forward is a sign that science won’t be stopped or silenced,” Matthew Druckenmiller, a senior NSIDC scientist, said in the statement. “When we come together, we have a powerful platform for robust observational evidence to inform global decisions – we are counting on that same spirit of support to help us close the remaining funding gap and secure the report card’s future.”
This year and beyond
The AGU will issue the 2026 Arctic Report Card at its annual conference in December, the same event at which NOAA issued past report cards.
Thoman noted that much of the work was already completed before NOAA announced its withdrawal from the project, so changes might not be obvious.
“I suspect 2026 will have a look and feel very similar to what we’ve done in the past,” he said.
This year’s report will include, along with the usual updates on ice, air temperature, ocean and tundra conditions, some special chapters of interest to Alaska, Thoman said.
One chapter will examine Indigenous wildfire management practices, and another chapter will examine wildfire patterns more broadly, he said. There will be a polar bear update, he said. And a chapter led by UAF geophysicist Andy Mahoney will examine changes in shorefast ice, the land-attached type of ice that is important to Arctic coastal communities.
Beyond this year, the shape of future Arctic Report Cards “is really not thought out,” Thoman said.
Some operation changes are already underway.
The editors and authors are no longer using archived data, images or other information from climate.gov, a NOAA climate information website that the Trump administration took down last year. Instead, they are using an alternative nonprofit site called climate.us.
That site was established and is maintained in part by some of the same NOAA scientists and staffers who had worked on climate.gov but lost their agency jobs. “They know what they’re doing,” Thoman said.
The editors will be turning to an international source, the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme of the eight-nation Arctic Council, for assistance with peer reviews. There might be similar outreach on other tasks, Thoman said. “There could be more robust international collaboration,” he said.
Trump administration policies on climate change
The end to NOAA support for the Arctic Report Card comes amid similar cuts.
Last year, for example, NOAA pulled its support for the National Snow and Ice Data Center’s satellite-based sea ice tracing program. The Colorado-based center switched to more reliance on satellite data from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, that nation’s counterpart to NASA.
Trump administration officials have expressed particular animus toward NOAA.
The Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025, a blueprint for a second Trump administration, recommended breaking up NOAA. The agency’s six science-focused divisions, which include the National Marine Fisheries Service and the National Weather Service, “form a colossal operation that has become one of the main drivers of the climate change alarm industry and, as such, is harmful to future U.S. prosperity,” Project 2025 said.
Russell Vought, the lead author of Project 2025, now heads Trump’s Office of Management and Budget. He is seeking to dismantle the 66-year-old National Center for Atmospheric Research, a university-managed institution in Colorado that partners with NOAA. That effort has been blocked by legal challenges.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Artificial intelligence enthusiasm and energy needs clash on Healey’s docket
description: Gov. Maura Healey is all-in on artificial intelligence, but she's also trying to get a handle on soaring energy costs and a growing backlash to the very structures supporting the AI boom — data centers. This week on The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon reporters Jennifer Smith and Jordan Wolman discuss the governor's new executive order trying to make data cente[...]
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Jennifer Smith
GUEST: Jordan Wolman







GOV. MAURA HEALEY stood at the dais of the state House of Representatives and pledged to go big on artificial intelligence. And she explicitly acknowledged the energy costs that could come with that. 
“AI is where the internet was 30 years ago, and it’s going to change everything,” she said. “States will either help steer AI’s impact, or they will struggle to keep pace.”  
A recently signed climate law would speed the permitting and siting process for clean energy, Healey said. “We are building new homes, labs, data centers, and manufacturing plants,” she said. “We need this power, and we’re going to go get it.” 
It was mid-January 2025, still on the early end of what would become a surging bipartisan backlash against the core infrastructure supporting the AI boom — data centers. Donald Trump would return to office just days later, almost immediately signing the first of a series of executive orders aimed at rolling back the clock on green energy projects like solar and wind. 
This week on The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon reporters Jennifer Smith and Jordan Wolman look at how the Healey administration is trying to juggle the governor’s AI enthusiasm with an energy landscape hitting residents squarely in the pocketbook. 
“It makes sense that she’s clearly now trying to thread this needle, trying to sort of have it both ways,” Wolman said. The pitch, he noted, is: “Yes, we can have the competitive, innovative AI economy that the governor wants, while keeping in mind that we don’t want to further exacerbate our energy system [issues].” 
Halfway through her first term, Healey was mostly enthusiastic about AI and publicly mild on data centers. In an economic development bill the summer before, the governor touted $100 million for a new AI Hub. But the 2024 bill also included a 20-year sales and use tax exemption for qualified data centers, so “these two things were very much in the worldview at the time,” Smith noted.  
There was little attention paid to the tax exemption for about two years, until it went into effect in May 2026 and slammed into a Healey order pausing the exemption less than two months later. Meanwhile, lawsuits roiled around proposed data centers in areas like Lowell. Holyoke became the first Bay State community to vote in a ban on new data centers, even as residents are generally supportive of the longstanding eco-conscious data center there that supports computing from the AI Hub and local universities researchers. 
As she announced a new executive order last week, subjecting proposed data center projects to local approval and new green energy regulations before developers can get state permits, Healey was pushed on the tax exemption about-face. 
“The sales tax exemption was not my idea,” she said. “You’d have to ask the Legislature why they included it in the economic development bill package. I signed the economic development bill package, but I did not include that sales tax exemption in there.” 
The governor’s office declined to elaborate on Healey’s stance at the time she signed the bill, simply referring CommonWealth Beacon back to the comment from Tuesday’s press conference.  
“As I’ve seen things, I just didn’t think that it was right for that sales tax exemption to apply in the midst of what we’re dealing with right now,” she said at the event, “which is a lot of concern across communities in Massachusetts in this country about the impact that data centers are having or could have.” 
State Sen. Michael Moore, a Democrat representing areas in and around Worcester who co-chairs the joint technology committee in the Legislature, filed and then withdrew an amendment to the 2026 economic development bill that would have imposed a one-year moratorium on new data centers in the state. 
Moore supported the 2024 bill that included the tax credit, but now, as he’s seen the data center issue play out, he says he feels like the state needs to adapt. He’s not a fan of the governor taking shots at lawmakers on a bill she signed, either, he told CommonWealth Beacon. “Obviously, no one wants their branch of government getting blamed for something,” he said. 
But Moore feels vindicated by Healey’s executive order on data centers after Senate leadership blocked his push for more scrutiny of these facilities – and even texted the governor following her announcement to congratulate her. Moore said the new rules would help ensure that if a community is weighing the energy, water, sound, and aesthetic tradeoffs that may come with a data center, it “has all the facts — the true facts — on making that decision.” 
On Monday morning, Healey put out a statement calling for federal oversight on AI regulation, as leading industry developers openly fret about how rapidly the technology is evolving. She reminded reporters at the recent press conference that “every time you ask a question [of an AI tool], know that you’re consuming energy.”  
Thousands of Massachusetts executive branch employees are using a state ChatGPT-partnered AI assistant across every secretariat, a headlong embrace of the AI revolution that just seven months ago both Healey and Moore were touting. 
On the episode, Smith and Wolman discuss the data center backlashes (2:00), the intertwined AI and energy question (9:30), and the labor angle into artificial intelligence and data center politics (29:00).

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Greenwich resident sues town over automated speed cameras
description: A Greenwich resident has filed a class action lawsuit against the town over its controversial automated speed camera program.
text:
A Greenwich resident has filed a class action lawsuit against the town over its controversial automated speed camera program.
In a complaint filed on September 8, Stephen Lockton, alleged the town of Greenwich failed to hold a public hearing over the speed camera program before the town approved them.
Lockton’s attorney, Timothy Cowan, said his client is looking for a refund.
“The demand is essentially that those individuals be compensated,” Cowan said. “So, ultimately if they had one speeding ticket, they paid $50 plus a surcharge. We’re looking to recover that amount for each person who was subject to that.”
The lawsuit comes as Greenwich and other communities across the state have faced public outcry over the speed cameras. Some residents have characterized the cameras as a way for municipalities to extract money from residents, which Greenwich First Selectman Fred Camillo denies.
[RELATED: As CT speed cameras bring in millions and towns sign up, concerns linger]
Camillo declined to talk about the lawsuit on Monday. But he said the town followed the rules.
“We had the public hearing,” Camillo said. “In fact, some towns had it much later than we did. This is a very new program, so obviously, all lots of towns have had to go back and amend because it’s new, and you have to understand that, and I certainly understand that.”
Greenwich ended up pausing its speed camera program last April, due to public outcry.
Camillo previously told Connecticut Public the town voted to resend a plan for state approval earlier this year. CT Department of Transportation (DOT) spokesperson Eva Zymaris said the town last resubmitted the plan in August.
Zymaris said the DOT’s Office of the State Traffic Administration (OSTA) provided feedback.
“The plan needs further revisions to incorporate updated guidelines that specify additional signage approaching the school zones and flashers on school zone speed limit signs,” Zymaris said. “The application remains pending until comments are addressed by the town.”
Zymaris said since the automated speed camera programs are administered by municipalities the DOT did not have any information on ongoing lawsuits over the program.
Lockton is currently the only plaintiff named in the lawsuit, Cowan said.
The complaint itself states residents found out through a Freedom of Information Act filing earlier this year and the town didn’t hold a public comment section for a Board of Selectmen meeting in 2024. The board later approved the Automated Traffic Enforcement Safety Devices (ATESD) plan.
The lawsuit says the lack of a public hearing before the plan was eventually approved by the Board of Selectmen in 2025, violated state law. It also states the town later held a public hearing – earlier this year. The complaint also states the town’s contractor, Blue Line Solutions, based in Tennessee, collected payments and fees without setting up a Qualified Public Depository, before sending payments to Greenwich.
Blue Line Solutions did not answer Connecticut Public’s request for comment. Cowan said more than $1 million have been collected so far.
“Through public filings, it looks to be at least $ 1.4 million from the few months that it was operating, but there could be late payments that we don’t know of,” Cowan said.
The lawsuit states the funds raised by ticket payments have to be used to fund public safety or roadways. But the complaint stated the town violated those requirements by directing ticket revenue to what it titled, “3 E’s” fund, engineering, Enforcement and Education instead of infrastructure or camera improvements.
Camillo did not answer the particular lawsuit claims but defended the speed camera program.
“It was never about revenue,” Camillo said. “If it was about revenue, we’d have them up 24/7, and we’d have them at every school zone. Not about revenue. It’s about public safety. It always has been, and it always will be.”
This story was first published Sept. 14, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Walking toward clarity
description: The foundational promise of this country— life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness— feels increasingly fragile.
text:
My days begin with a walk in nature, whether through my historic New England town or along the Connecticut shoreline. With my 9‑year‑old English Lab trotting beside me, I move through familiar paths, taking in the quiet choreography of the natural world. 
This morning, that calm was interrupted by a family of three deer crossing the road ahead. Two slipped across effortlessly, but the third froze—ears up, eyes wide—startled by my dog’s insistent barking. We continued on, giving her space to rejoin her family, who waited anxiously on the other side.

Marisa Calvi-Rogers

As I walked, I found myself thinking about how many human families experience far deeper, more lasting separation. Families divided by political decisions. Parents and children torn apart by ICE enforcement quotas. Service members stranded on ships without adequate accommodations. U.S. citizens trapped overseas in war‑torn regions. Children lying in ICU beds with diseases once eradicated by vaccines but now resurging. Families fractured by ideological rifts so deep that reconciliation feels impossible.
The deer’s momentary fear cannot compare to the pain people endure daily. Yet the encounter made me wonder: Why aren’t we seeing more collective outrage? 
The foundational promise of this country— life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness— feels increasingly fragile. Our elected representatives often seem compromised, constrained by fear of retribution or fear of losing their considerable income. Misinformation has become both a political strategy and a media business model, making factual understanding a laborious task requiring vigilance and discernment. Are we becoming numb? Are we too paralyzed to act?
The deer eventually reunited once they sensed safety. That small moment stayed with me. It reminded me that fear can immobilize, but connection restores movement.
My daily walks will continue. They ground me, challenge me, and remind me of what is worth protecting. I will do my part: staying factually informed, supporting candidates who safeguard fundamental freedoms, participating in my community —including local elections— speaking out against injustice, and holding onto the belief that our current state of affairs can improve. 
Perhaps sharing these reflections will encourage others to take their own contemplative walk, to notice what nature reveals, and to consider how we might move—together— toward a safer, more united future.
Marisa Calvi-Rogers lives in Woodbury.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas legislators compete in cattle showmanship, learn about beef industry at state fair
description: HUTCHINSON — Rep. Brooklynne Mosley stepped into the Prairie Pavilion arena at the Kansas State Fair Saturday, leading a heifer around the ring while smiling broadly  Mosley, a Lawrence Democrat, had never spent time with cattle until she began working with two 4-H participants, Genayla Warnken of Manhattan and Makenzie Fishburn of Lawrence to learn […]
text:
Rep. Brooklynne Mosley celebrates a first-place win in the Kansas Legislative Showmanship event at the State Fair on Sept. 12, 2026. She learned how to show the heifer from 4-H members Genayla Warnken, left, and Makenzie Fishburn. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)HUTCHINSON — Rep. Brooklynne Mosley stepped into the Prairie Pavilion arena at the Kansas State Fair Saturday, leading a heifer around the ring while smiling broadly 
Mosley, a Lawrence Democrat, had never spent time with cattle until she began working with two 4-H participants, Genayla Warnken of Manhattan and Makenzie Fishburn of Lawrence to learn about how to show a halter-broken heifer. 
Mosley and four other Kansas legislators were participants in the annual Legislative Showmanship competition. 
“This is the closest I’ve ever been to cattle in my whole life,” Mosley said. “I was really looking forward to doing this as something different. I had great teachers, Makenzie and then Genayla. They were really patient, and they taught me everything that I know. Literally.”
Sen. Cindy Holscher took to the Prairie Pavilion Arena Sept. 12, 2026, as part of a legislative showmanship competition. Behind her were Josie Heter, left, and Ryder Heter, from Reno County, two 4-H participants who helped her prepare for the event and who trained the halter-broken heifer. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Warnken said they begin working with cows when they are young, teaching them to adjust to wearing a halter. 
“That can take some time because they’re pretty stubborn,” she said. “We start getting them on a regular feed diet, and then working with their hair, which makes them look really big and fluffy.”
Fishburn said she loves being part of 4-H because the community is large and she can meet people from across the state. 
Their work with Mosley paid off, as she took first place and earned a traveling trophy that will be engraved with her name. Competing against Mosley were Sen. Cindy Holscher, Rep. Mike King, Rep. Heather Meyer and Rep. Gary White. Meyer, who was also handling a cow for the first time, won second place. 
Monte Ball, a third-generation rancher, and Rylee Hayes, of Jacam Catalyst, judged the event. They examined how well the legislators handled the cows and asked questions about general beef animal knowledge. 
While legislators walked the heifers around the arena, Ball spoke about the event, which he said gives Kansas leaders a chance to learn about the field. 
“These are exciting times in the ag industry right now, particularly in the beef industry,” he said. 
“We’re experiencing record high prices. Unfortunately, we’re also experiencing record high inputs. So these are very stressful times for farmers and ranchers.
Rep. Heather Meyer takes second place in a Legislative Showmanship competition at the Kansas State Fair on Sept. 12, 2026. She had never worked with cattle before learning how to handle the heifer from 4-H members. Monte Ball, middle, judged the competition and Todd Lindquist, left, represented the Kansas Fairs and Festivals Association, which sponsored the event. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
“We need our legislators to understand what the beef industry means to us and what it means to Kansas,” he added.
Ball said young 4-H members represent the future of the beef industry, and the program prepares them for the future. 
“They’re learning about taking care of an animal and being responsible for that animal,” he said.
Ball described himself as a “leadership junkie,” pointing to 28 years in public education as a teacher and coach and then in his current position heading up human resources at Conklin Automotive Group. 
“I thought I knew what leadership was. I thought leadership was having titles. I thought leadership was about position, having people in your charge,” he said. “What I’ve learned is leadership is a long way from that. Leadership is about doing hard things and building relationships, and getting other people to buy in and invest in the places that you want to go.”
It’s also, Ball said, about asking questions, which he encouraged from legislators at the event. 
“We need to eat, and the best way for us to have a secure food source is to raise our own,” he said. “We have to do a better job in the U.S. of taking care of our farmers and ranchers because they’re the ones that are going to feed us in the future.”
After the event, Ball said the market volatility is concerning. 
“You get a headline each day, the markets turn and run, so to speak,” he said. “Volatility is at an all-time high right now in a lot of markets, but the beef industry in particular is experiencing that and uncertainty.”
In January, the U.S. cattle herd was at its smallest size in about 75 years, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Ball attributed the decrease to normal cyclical changes, and also to four-plus years of drought conditions in many areas.
When prices are high, herds tend to grow in size and then as prices fall, they shrink, he said. But drought leads ranchers to make tough decisions. 
“Cattlemen have had to sacrifice part of their herd in order to keep it going,” Ball said. “Drought’s been a big factor in this. It’s been a perfect storm almost.”
Monte Ball, a third-generation rancher, judges the Legislative Showmanship competition at the Kansas State Fair on Sept. 12, 2026. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)

A Department of Natural Resources Type 5 wildland engine is pictured on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026 in Missoula, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)MISSOULA — One of the most common trucks in the State of Montana’s vehicle fleet — the Department of Natural Resources Type 5 wildland engine — is, in part, built in Missoula by some of the very same people who operate them.
The trucks, which are often equipped with water tanks and hoses and carrying initial response crews, arrive at the DNRC’s Equipment Development and Communication Center in Missoula as a cab and chassis. They leave as a fully operational wildland fire vehicle. 
This saves the state money and helps them put vehicles into service suited to Montana’s landscape, said A.J. Angelo, a DNRC program manager for the Equipment and Development and Communication Center.
It’s also a key component of the state’s wildfire strategy, which combines county and state resources on larger incidents.
There are currently 257 Type 5 engines associated with the County Co-op program spread throughout the state. The direct work with the counties is important for the DNRC, programming it highlights often, and Angelo calls it the “backbone” of the state’s wildfire program.
The trucks and the crews who use them are often some of the first responders to wildland fires, and are responsible for helping tamp down hundreds of small fires per year. 
“The basis behind our design and what we do is to keep the engines as simple as possible,” Angelo said. “And the reason we do that is so they can be used in our County Co-op Program and by rural fire departments across Montana.”
A.J. Angelo, a DNRC program manager for the Equipment and Development and Communication Center, is pictured at the program’s facility on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026, in Missoula, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
Many of the people who work in the Equipment Development and Communication Center program also are wildland firefighters themselves, Angelo said, meaning they’re using the same equipment they build.
That was exactly where Angelo started — as a part-time firefighter with the state.
“Very much like a lot of our mechanics, I grew up on a ranch and just am very much into building my own stuff,” Angelo said. “I’m very big into the off-road, four-by-four type of world. That just kind of drew me in. And now I’m here.”
Angelo added that a number of his coworkers have some pretty neat rigs and hot rods, and the job attracts people who hold a wide variety of technical skills.
“I think it’s more of a passion than anything,” Angelo added.
The fire program builds around 20 new trucks per year and works on a great deal more, servicing DNRC vehicles throughout the state. The facility in Missoula is large, connected to a broad swath of land the state has for several programs off Spurgin Road. 
It’s funded and supplied through the federal government and money from the state. In 2025, the Legislature passed House Bill 833, which was signed by Gov. Greg Gianforte and funneled more than $60 million into firefighting operations in the state, including $800,000 into the Equipment Development and Communication Center.
It’s cheaper to build trucks this way than to buy a more expensive vehicle that might not specifically suit the needs of the state, DNRC staff said. A Type 5 wildland fire engine can run up to $300,000 and the state can build one for a third of that, with Angelo saying the cost is about $100,000 per vehicle.
“Everything we do in house really keeps those costs down,” said Brian Hall, who is the shop foreman for the Equipment Development and Communication Center.
Different vehicle bays throughout the facility are used for different stages of work. For starters, a custom bed is fabricated, storage is added, and the rig is painted. If a water tank is being put in the vehicle — the state uses 500 gallon water tanks in its Type 5 vehicles — the water system is also added.
A Department of Natural Resources Type 5 wildland engine — before it has its bed put on it — is pictured on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026 in Missoula, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
Start-to-finish, a truck can be built and put in service in about two work weeks.
The vehicles are also tested by the DNRC before being sent out around the state. Importantly, the state also works with all 56 counties through its County Co-op Program, lending and repairing state fire vehicles that are strategically spread throughout the state. 
Maintenance on the vehicles is no small task either. Four staff members are spread regionally throughout the state for repairs and maintenance, but the trucks are designed with grabbing car parts at the nearest available automotive store in mind.
“The parts and pieces can almost all be acquired at your local hardware place or something like that,” Angelo said.
There are, of course, exceptions and some parts do have to be specially ordered, but they keep a pretty good parts stock, DNRC staff said, and offer the repair at no cost to whatever county the truck is in.
Welding safety gear is pictured at the Equipment Development and Communication Center in Missoula on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
Generally, wildfires are first fought at the county level and if the incident becomes more severe, counties ask the state for help.
Those same counties are also eligible for two federal programs that the Equipment and Development Communication Center also runs that transfer excess federal equipment to states who then can divide it among fire agencies throughout the state.
Those two federal grants are the Forest Service Federal Excess Personal Property program and the Department of Defense Fire Fighter Program. The Department of Defense program has transferred more than $100 million in federal equipment to Montana, according to the DNRC.
The defense program — referred to as “FFP” — has sent the state military trucks, which they turn into Type 2 tactical water tenders with large water reserves.
More than two dozen of those Type 2 trucks are spread throughout the state, and several more military-style trucks were parked outside the DNRC’s building earlier this month, ready to be turned into more Montana wildland fire equipment.
“Our biggest focus is staying made in Montana,” Angelo said, “And saving the taxpayers as much money as we can.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Business group abandons Lombardo in favor of Ford
description: The Retail Association of Nevada, which represents stores and restaurants in Nevada, is endorsing Democrat Attorney General Aaron Ford for governor, a turnaround from the 2022 election when it endorsed now-Gov. Joe Lombardo, a Republican.  “This is the first time in recent history that RAN has endorsed a Democratic candidate for governor,” the association sa[...]
text:
Attorney General and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Aaron Ford acknowledging the endorsement from the Retail Association of Nevada at a Las Vegas restaurant Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo: Dana Gentry/Nevada Current)The Retail Association of Nevada, which represents stores and restaurants in Nevada, is endorsing Democrat Attorney General Aaron Ford for governor, a turnaround from the 2022 election when it endorsed now-Gov. Joe Lombardo, a Republican. 
“This is the first time in recent history that RAN has endorsed a Democratic candidate for governor,” the association said in a news release. 
“We don’t endorse often,” RAN President Bryan Wachter said at a news conference Monday announcing the endorsement. He noted the association “had talks with the governor’s campaign” about talking with Lombardo “but that didn’t go beyond staff.” 
Speaking directly with the candidate, as RAN did with Lombardo in 2022, is part of the association’s endorsement process. 
“It’s usually very helpful to make sure we understand what their thought process is, and sometimes things get filtered through staff,” Wachter said, adding the endorsement decision is made internally. 
Lombardo’s campaign issued a statement noting he has been endorsed “by the Latin Chamber, Vegas Chamber, and Asian Chamber of Commerce, organizations that represent thousands of businesses across Nevada’s diverse communities and industries.”
The governor’s campaign statement also credited Lombardo for job and business growth during his administration, adding the governor “lowered taxes, and eliminated or streamlined over 900 burdensome regulations.”
Lombardo’s campaign spokesperson declined to say why the governor did not participate in an endorsement interview with RAN.
RAN represents more than 8,000 businesses. Wachter said he’s aware individual businesses may back Lombardo but said endorsing Ford was the best move for the association. The association cites Ford’s participation in legal action that has overturned some of President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
RAN made the announcement at Firefly, a Las Vegas restaurant near the Strip. Owner John Simmons said business has plummeted by 15% year-over-year since Trump took office and imposed hefty tariffs. 
“Our cost of goods are up. Tourism is down. All of these trade wars and attacks over our former allies in Canada, Mexico, Europe,” Simmons said, noting the resulting slow down of visitation from foreign nations. 
It’s the second time this year that RAN and Ford have teamed up to take on the debilitating effects of Trump’s tariffs on Southern Nevada businesses. 
More than 70 small businesses in Las Vegas have closed since Trump took office, Ford said Monday. 
“The reason I ran is that I felt Joe Lombardo would cower and lie down,” he said. “I knew and unfortunately, I was right.”
Asked if he really expects Lombardo to stand up to Trump and risk the political fallout from Republican voters, Ford noted that as attorney general he “stood up to Biden,” a reference to a handful of lawsuits filed by Democratic attorneys general against the former Democratic president. 
In 2021, Ford joined the attorneys general of Virginia and Illinois in an appeal that sought to have a court recognize the Equal Rights Amendment as the 28th Amendment. Biden finally recognized the ERA as an amendment just days before leaving office in 2025. 
Lombardo asserts that he has Trump’s ear and has taken advantage of the relationship by persuading the president to allow work to continue on a handful of solar projects on federal land, even though such projects have been halted in other states. 
But the governor has downplayed concerns about the effect of tariffs on the Nevada economy, and suggested he can’t do anything to right the economy.
“When we talk about affordability and inflation rates and everything, I can’t control that as a governor,” Lombardo said at veterans gathering this summer. 
Ford notes Lombardo vetoed a record-setting number of bills in both of his legislative sessions, many of which included cost-cutting measures, including legislation that would have limited corporate home purchases that are driving up the cost of housing. 
“Governor Lombardo has told us that Nevadans need to feel pain from tariffs,” Wachter noted. Nevadans, he said, “can’t afford more pain,” given the cost of food, prescription drugs and energy. “He said that he can’t do anything about affordability, and he said that we need to take care of billionaires first because they provide all of the jobs. We don’t recognize that kind of leadership.”
Most jobs, Wachter added, are created by small businesses, not billionaires.
Ford did not rule out the potential for revamping Nevada’s tax structure, which is among the most regressive in the nation. 
According to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, Nevada households with the lowest incomes pay an overall state and local tax rate of almost 12%, while the wealthiest households are paying less than 3%.
“To the extent that the conversation manifests itself, I’m going to be in the midst of it, as well,” Ford said, adding that his priorities are reducing the burden of housing costs, prescription drugs, and medical debt. 
Last week, an Emerson College poll pegged Ford slightly ahead of Lombardo. The challenger, however, lacks the millions of dollars raised by Lombardo’s campaign and political action committees.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: 2,300 immigrants arrested in Operation Metro Surge were deported or left country
description: The winter surge of 3,000 federal immigration agents to Minnesota eventually led to over 2,300 immigrants leaving the country, according to updated federal data from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement obtained by the Deportation Data Project. The figure is a modest increase from the Reformer’s previous tally of 1,760 people who were deported or left […[...]
text:
A driver pinches the bridge of his nose as ICE agents pull him over and detain him and his passenger Wednesday, Feb. 11, 2026 on Bottineau Blvd. in Robbinsdale. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)The winter surge of 3,000 federal immigration agents to Minnesota eventually led to over 2,300 immigrants leaving the country, according to updated federal data from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement obtained by the Deportation Data Project.
The figure is a modest increase from the Reformer’s previous tally of 1,760 people who were deported or left the country after being arrested by ICE in the surge. The new total includes 2,019 immigrants who were explicitly recorded as being deported, as well as 315 immigrants who left the country after being arrested but under circumstances that are unclear from just looking at the data.
Pew Research estimated that Minnesota was home to around 130,000 undocumented immigrants in 2023, up from 100,000 in 2022, making up around 2% of the state’s total population. Undocumented immigrants in Minnesota are most commonly from Mexico.
The 2,300 immigrants deported during the winter surge, in turn, make up around 2% of the state’s undocumented population.


The new analysis is based on data ending in August, whereas the old analysis was limited to data prior to early March. It gives more insight into what eventually happened to the 800 immigrants who were still detained in early March. Overall, ICE recorded around 3,600 arrests from Dec. 1 to Feb. 15, the rough start and end dates of the surge. Most of those arrests happened in January, the chaotic peak, when federal agents also shot and killed two U.S. citizens.
The deportations were mostly from December to February, though over 400 were deported after February, according to the data.
Over 300 immigrants were still detained in May, meaning, if the data is accurate, they were detained for at least two months. Around 140 of those people continued to be detained as of the end of August, and around the same number were eventually deported.


The immigrants were most often deported to Ecuador, Mexico and other Latin American countries, consistent with the earlier data, with two notable additions: More than 80 immigrants were deported to Laos, and 14 to Somalia, higher than the one or two recorded deportations to those countries in the March data.
Many of those deported to Laos were sent there in March and May. Two of them were listed as being citizens of Thailand and Vietnam but were deported to Laos nonetheless, according to the data.
The data roughly lines up with the account of a Hmong man, reported by the Sahan Journal, who was arrested in South St. Paul in February and deported to Laos in May. The man, Zong Yang, told Sahan that he met about 50 other Hmong, Lao and Vietnamese men who were transferred to the El Paso Processing Center and held for two months. ICE’s data lists 44 men who were held for two months, were detained at the El Paso Processing Center, and were eventually deported to Laos.
Over 3,500 people were detained during Operation Metro Surge. Here’s where they went.

All were listed in the data as being convicted criminals. Yang, Sahan reported, was convicted of a felony burglary in 1999 and served seven years in prison. He appeared to be caught in the Trump administration’s targeting of immigrants with past convictions, the so-called “worst of the worst.”
It’s unclear why ICE held the group of men for so long before deporting them. The 14 immigrants deported to Somalia — all of whom are citizens of Somalia — were also all detained for over a month, according to the data.
Immigration arrests in Minnesota returned to pre-Operation Metro Surge levels starting in March, though immigration enforcement is soaring nationwide.
The Deportation Data Project obtained the data from the federal government via a Freedom of Information Act request. It has some limitations — around 5% of arrests do not show where the arrest was made, for example. Still, it is some of the most detailed data on immigration enforcement available.
ICE has previously challenged the accuracy of the Deportation Data Project, even though the figures come from its own internal data. ICE did not respond to an inquiry of how many people arrested in the surge are still in detention.



Methodology notes
For this analysis, the start and end dates of Operation Metro Surge were defined as Dec. 1 to Feb. 15. This is different from the Reformer’s previous analysis, which looked at both arrests and detentions from Dec. 1 to the most recently available data at the time, which was roughly March 10.
This analysis also includes data for people who were arrested but had no recorded detention, in line with the Deportation Data Project’s August release of joined arrests and detention data. The previous analysis was limited to people who had at least one recorded detention stay.
Detention outcomes were defined as before, with the addition of the category Left country (no detention data), which refers to cases where people had a recorded country of departure but no recorded detention. Left country (other) refers to cases where people had a recorded country of departure and a recorded detention, but no listed mechanism for departure (i.e. the variable called “stay release reason,” which refers to the reason a person was released from detention, had an N/A value). Refer to the methodology of the Reformer’s previous analysis of Deportation Data Project data, as well as documentation from the Deportation Data Project, for more information.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri school funding task force nears final recommendations
description: The Missouri School Funding Modernization Task Force is entering the final stretch of its 15 months of meetings, preparing a set of recommendations that could change the way the state funds public education. The group is poised to review a draft of its plan to update the public school funding formula on Oct. 19 — […]
text:
State Sen. Rusty Black, interim education commissioner Stacey Preis and former education department deputy commissioner Kari Monsees lead a meeting of the Missouri School Funding Modernization Task Force in Jefferson City Monday(Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).The Missouri School Funding Modernization Task Force is entering the final stretch of its 15 months of meetings, preparing a set of recommendations that could change the way the state funds public education.
The group is poised to review a draft of its plan to update the public school funding formula on Oct. 19 — the first of just two meetings scheduled before the task force’s report is due to Gov. Mike Kehoe in December.
“We are in that phase of transition from all the research and building recommendations to getting a final product of a recommendation document or a task force report and collecting additional feedback from stakeholders,” Kari Monsees, the state education department’s former finance chief, said during a task force meeting Monday.
If all of the group’s recommendations become law, the cost of the formula would increase by over $600 million, Monsees estimated. The proposal’s impact on individual school districts has yet to be calculated, but the department will publish some simulations “at or around” the October meeting, he said.
Monsees, who has been facilitating the group’s 11 meetings, referred to the group’s work as the first of three steps to update the formula. Next, the governor’s office will have a chance to convey its preferences to lawmakers — who are ultimately responsible for passing a law to replace the old funding model.
The cost of the current formula has risen in recent years, drawing much concern during the legislature’s budget debates. During this year’s legislative session, lawmakers ultimately refused to fund a $190 million increase stemming from a 2024 law that tweaked the formula.
Officials are preparing for tight budgets in the years ahead as the state exhausts its reserve. Wary of the thin margins, even members of the State Board of Education are looking to scale back how much the department is asking for in the formula.
Those fiscal pressures will likely shape whatever changes lawmakers ultimately make to the education funding formula, and the task force’s report will include a number of elements that can be downsized or modified to reduce the price tag associated with the new formula.
Task force members had the political pressures facing lawmakers in mind Monday as they discussed recommendations for a handful of elements.
 Hold harmless

The current formula has two provisions intended to safeguard districts from receiving less in state aid than they had received under the prior model, which was overhauled in 2005.
Districts with more than 350 students are guaranteed funding on a per-pupil basis at or above what they received in the 2004-05 school year with an adjustment for regional wage rates. Small school districts are guaranteed a total state appropriation at or above their 2004-05 state aid, also adjusted for wage rates.
These protections cost the state $150 million annually, according to a study of the formula led by education nonprofit Aligned and reviewed by the task force.
Monsees recommended that the new formula phase out the hold harmless provisions over 20 years, but some members on the task force were hoping for a sooner end.
State Rep. Ed Lewis, a Republican from Moberly who lost his bid for state Senate in the August primary, said any formula is likely to become obsolete in 20 years and recommended a 10-year phaseout.
“Our whole goal is to get to a modern formula,”said Kerry Casey, who also serves on the State Board of Education. “We won’t ever get there if we keep it longer.”
But Monsees pointed to another purpose of the provisions: helping get a formula change through the legislative process.
“Nobody wants to sign off on their districts getting less money,” he said, adding that any phase-out would be “breaking ground” after decades with hold-harmless provisions.
Under his proposal, districts’ baseline amount would change from 2004 levels to funding they receive under the current formula.
“We need to give a recommendation that is founded in logic,” Lewis said. “Then it can meet (the legislative process).”
 Small-schools grant

The new formula could also overhaul the small-schools grant program, which gives districts with 350 or fewer students a chunk of $30 million on a per-pupil basis.
The program gives the most to districts with daily attendance closest to 350 students. If a district has an average of 351 students attending daily, they receive nothing.
The task force hopes to eliminate this “funding cliff” by building a weighting factor into the formula that considers enrollment numbers with an option to also fund districts with few students spread over a large geographic area. 
Monsees charted the proposal, showing a smooth distribution that tapers off at both ends.
The current model incentivizes small districts to keep the status quo instead of merging with neighboring districts, he said.
“It drives unintended consequences,” Casey said. “I am in favor of what we can do to minimize that and allow for bigger considerations to happen, meaning primarily what’s best for the students.”
The group also liked that the suggestion would be incorporated into the formula and would not be a separate line item in the budget.
“I don’t want to keep the small school grant if we can account for it through the formula,” Lewis said, adding that lawmakers do not always understand what the grant means when looking at the line item in the budget.
 Proration

The task force also looked Monday at changing how the formula adjusts to a funding shortfall.
Currently, when state lawmakers appropriate less than the formula calculates to be sufficient, a number called the state adequacy target is adjusted downward, reducing the per-pupil funding districts receive.
This burden is not shared equally among school districts because of the protections barring funding from plunging below 2004-05 levels. Those who fall under the hold-harmless provisions do not see cuts while districts who have grown in the last 20 years receive less than the formula’s calculation.
Monsees presented options including a flat per-pupil cut, a percentage adjustment or a reduction that changes based on a school district’s local funding ability. The group ultimately decided to include all three in their recommendations and eliminate the current method of adjusting the adequacy target from their report.
“Everybody’s got skin in the game when it comes to using the last three approaches,” Monsees said.
Before the next meeting, the department plans on creating an informational presentation to solicit feedback on the recommendations.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Department of Civil Rights charges Waterford law firm with disability discrimination
description: The Michigan Department of Civil Rights announced Monday that it was filing a disability discrimination charge against Booth Patterson, PC, a law firm based in Waterford, alleging that the firm discriminated against a client with a disability by refusing to honor a request for a “reasonable accommodation during several 2023 meetings with the firm.” The […]
text:
A Michigan flag waves in the state Capitol plaza | Susan J. DemasThe Michigan Department of Civil Rights announced Monday that it was filing a disability discrimination charge against Booth Patterson, PC, a law firm based in Waterford, alleging that the firm discriminated against a client with a disability by refusing to honor a request for a “reasonable accommodation during several 2023 meetings with the firm.”
The claimant, whose name is redacted in a copy of the charge document provided to Michigan Advance, first filed the complaint with the department in November 2023, according to a press release. An investigation was launched, and based on that investigation, the department said it “found sufficient grounds to formally charge the firm with Failure to Accommodate in a Place of Public Accommodation.”
“Refusing to make appropriate accommodations prevents people with disabilities from properly receiving the services they need. This is not just wrong, but illegal,” said Michigan Department of Civil Rights Executive Director John Johnson, Jr. “We all have a duty to enforce these standards and make our places of business available to everyone.” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The charging document notes that the claimant had six meetings with a representative of Booth Patterson, whose name is also redacted, between March and May 2023, after entering a binding agreement in December 2022 for representation in a civil case through June 15, 2023. Throughout that time, the client was billed a total of $1,860 for legal services.
The client verbally requested an accommodation — the specifics of which were also redacted — as early as March 15, 2023, which was not provided by the law firm, according to the charging document. When the client took it upon himself to acquire the accommodation, the law firm refused to reimburse for those services, which cost $130.
The charge document goes on to say that, with billable hours between the claimant and the lawyer set at $300 per hour, “there is sufficient evidence that paying for an [REDACTED] would not have been an undue financial hardship” for Booth Patterson, referring to reimbursement for the accommodation service.
David Lee, an attorney at Booth Patterson, told the Advance that the complaint stems from a deaf client who had his mother as an interpreter throughout legal proceedings on a civil case, which Lee was eventually removed from.
“When they say that I fail to accommodate, the only difference is that they say that I had to have a licensed interpreter, and I’d rather have the mother than a licensed interpreter,” Lee said, adding that he believed his client could communicate better with his mother.
Lee said that he completely denies any damage to him as a result of using the client’s mother, and said that he “did absolutely nothing wrong.”
“I served my client, I did everything, and I represented a client well,” he said. 
Now that the charge has been filed, it will be presented at a hearing with an administrative law judge, who will hear evidence from both the firm and the department. If that administrative law judge determines that discrimination had occurred, the matter would be brought to the Michigan Civil Rights Commission for a final ruling.
The department is requesting that the Civil Rights Commission require the firm to undergo disability training and reimburse the client for any time they spent without the necessary accommodation. The department is also requesting that they send certification of the discriminatory incident to the State Bar of Michigan and the Michigan Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: AI data centers are coming for Massachusetts. Gov. Healey’s new guardrails aren’t enough.
description: GOV. HEALEY took an important step last week to protect Massachusetts communities from the unchecked growth of data centers. Her new executive order will require large data centers to meet […]
text:
GOV. HEALEY took an important step last week to protect Massachusetts communities from the unchecked growth of data centers. 
Her new executive order will require large data centers to meet new standards around energy, water, air quality and public health and gives communities a greater voice in deciding whether these projects move forward. Data centers with peak electricity demand above 25 megawatts must demonstrate compliance with the state’s responsible development framework and enter into a community benefits agreement before receiving state permits. 
These new standards are an acknowledgment of what communities across Massachusetts have been saying: AI infrastructure may exist “in the cloud,” but its costs are very real and very local.  
Residents are already facing high energy costs, and the rapid growth of data centers is putting additional pressure on an already constrained regional grid. Wholesale electricity prices are as much as 267 percent higher than five years ago in areas near significant data-center activity. 
New England has little surplus generating capacity during periods of extreme demand, and adding large new electricity loads can further strain the system, increasing costs and reliance on polluting generation. Those impacts are especially concerning in Black and brown communities, which already face higher energy burdens and greater exposure to pollution. 
The governor’s order rightly recognizes this risk. It directs state agencies to ensure large data centers bear the costs associated with their energy needs and support new clean energy rather than shifting those costs onto existing ratepayers. But the environmental footprint of data centers goes well beyond electricity. 
Data centers consume enormous amounts of water and rely on diesel backup generators, creating additional pressures on municipal systems, air quality, and public health. Data centers use our land, consume our resources, and shape the future of neighborhoods across Massachusetts. 
Lowell offers an important warning. In the city’s Sacred Heart neighborhood, which has a large minority population, a major data center has expanded in an area already facing significant nitrogen oxide pollution burdens. Filings show residents have argued that the expansion is contributing to noise and pollution without a meaningful cumulative environmental review. 
The appeal raised concerns that the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection failed to require a cumulative impact analysis, adequately address data center noise, meaningfully involve environmental justice communities in the environmental review process, or consider alternatives to diesel generation. Instead, the facility expanded in stages, with the number of backup diesel generators growing from seven to 27. The residents’ legal challenge was ultimately dismissed on administrative grounds, leaving the substantive environmental concerns unresolved. 
Lowell is unlikely to be the last community facing these questions. As AI companies seek locations with available land, electricity, and water, more Massachusetts communities will be asked to host facilities that place extraordinary demands on public resources. 
The governor’s new requirement for community benefits agreements is an important response to concerns like these. But a community benefits agreement cannot become a substitute for rigorous environmental review or genuine community power. Nor should protections depend on whether a project happens to cross the executive order’s 25-megawatt threshold. 
Massachusetts needs a statewide framework with real enforcement that applies broadly enough to prevent developers from structuring projects in ways that evade stronger oversight. That means cumulative environmental review, protections for ratepayers and water supplies, meaningful community participation, transparency around proposed projects, and accountability for developers. It also means ending public subsidies for an industry capable of financing its own expansion. 
Gov. Healey’s pause on the state’s sales and use tax exemption for data centers is a step in the right direction, but it does not go nearly far enough. Gov. Healey should not resume the exemption, and the Legislature should eliminate it entirely. At a time when families are choosing between food, medicine, and energy, Massachusetts should not be subsidizing the data center industry. 
Other states are already going further. In New York, Gov. Hochul has signed a statewide moratorium on new hyperscale data centers and moved to eliminate their tax exemption. Illinois, Arizona, and Ohio have also moved to end data center tax exemptions. The Commonwealth must not fall behind, leaving our communities vulnerable.  
The governor’s executive order demonstrates that Massachusetts does not have to choose between technological innovation and protecting communities. But rules are only as strong as their implementation, and Massachusetts should not race to approve new projects while state agencies and municipalities are still developing the systems needed to enforce these protections. A temporary statewide moratorium would give Massachusetts the time to do this right. 
It would give the Commonwealth time to implement the governor’s new requirements and the Legislature time to pass additional protections that establish strong cumulative-impact standards, close potential loopholes, permanently eliminate the data center tax exemption, and ensure that communities, particularly environmental justice communities, have the information and power they need before projects move forward. 
Massachusetts has long been a leader in technological innovation. We can continue to lead without allowing Black and brown communities to become sacrifice zones for the next technology boom. 
Gov. Healey has recognized the problem and begun putting guardrails in place. Now she and the Legislature should build on that progress and eliminate the tax exemption, strengthen the protections in law, and press pause on new data center development until Massachusetts can guarantee that the communities hosting these facilities will not be left paying the price. 
Dwaign Tyndal is the executive director of Alternatives for Community and Environment.

title: Clark school district police use of force report raises more questions about tactics, racial bias
description: The Clark County’s School District Police Department’s first legislatively mandated use of force findings, which showed when pepper spray or stun guns were deployed during the 2025-26 school year it was overwhelmingly against Black people, prompts more questions about school police practices which prompted the report’s requirement in the first place. The rep[...]
text:
(Photo: Clark County School District Police Department)The Clark County’s School District Police Department’s first legislatively mandated use of force findings, which showed when pepper spray or stun guns were deployed during the 2025-26 school year it was overwhelmingly against Black people, prompts more questions about school police practices which prompted the report’s requirement in the first place.
The report, which released its findings this month, found that 18 out of 21 times officers deployed force in 11 confrontations, it was against Black people. Of the remaining three instances, two were Hispanic and one was white.
The report doesn’t break down the age or race of the person each of the 11 times use of force was used in the 2025-2026 school year to get a full picture of these tactics. 
Nevada Current requested a breakdown of age and races of the people targeted in those 11 incidents, but a CCSD official said the information wasn’t readily available.
“If school police don’t provide more data on their use of force incidents, the only thing I can suspect is they are again engaging in providing the public with nominal and minimal information to reduce any perception issues that our community has of Clark County School District, police which is not viewed favorably,” said Athar Hasseebullah, the executive director of the ACLU of Nevada. 
Assembly Bill 420, enacted in the 2025 legislative session, requires school districts to track and report use of force data. 
The original ideas for the legislation was “to ban the use of pepper spray,” Democratic Assemblymember Cecelia González, the bills’ sponsor, said in an interview, adding that “folks couldn’t get there on that and that’s how we ended up with the reporting.” 
Community members who question the frequency and manner of how force is used on students, she said, had to file public records requests that school district police “can deny, deny, deny,” she said. 
By having reporting requirements, González said officials could at least obtain better insight on how police in schools operate. 
AB 420 passed with bipartisan support.
The Washoe County School District use of force report for the 2025-26 school year listed no use of pepper spray, chemical agents, or batons.   
CCSD’s report showed 11 incidents in which force was deployed on 21 different people. The report didn’t indicate how many people, in particular students, were involved in each incidents
The report provides an aggregate breakdown of the ages when use of force was used: 12 were younger than 18, eight cases were people were ages 18 to 35 years old and one instance where the person was older than 35.
González said the legislation didn’t require a more robust breakdown of age and race of each student out of concerns from the school districts that it could identify students. 
There is room to improve the reporting requirements, she said. But the findings, while not surprising were still disappointing, González said, adding it confirms racial bias and anti-Blackness
“Believe students when they are talking about their experiences,” she said. “They have been talking about this issue for a number of years and people have brushed it off saying it wasn’t happening. Now we have data to start to show the types of patterns of how often this is happening and to which students.” 
The fact that people of color “are definitely having more interactions with police and use of force than any other demographic” is something elected officials need to reckon with, González said. 
“There definitely needs to be a conversation about why this is only impacted primarily Black students,” she said.
The data found 8 incidents were on campus and three were off property. Though the report doesn’t identify the school, it provides addresses of locations the incident took place. 
The address for Cheynne High School appeared twice. The off-property incident where two officers used a stun gun was near Robinson Middle School.  
In a statement, CCSD warned people to “use caution in drawing conclusions from a relatively small data set of 11 use of force incidents in the 2025-2026 school year.” 
“CCSD has been very transparent about our work to train officers and staff members to provide interventions for all students before behavior escalates, as well as to recognize biases when working with students,” the statement said. 
The district has faced a litany of questions, and lawsuits, around transparency in recent years. 
After 2023 footage of police officers arresting several Black teenage boys at Durango High School, slamming one to the ground, the ACLU of Nevada had to sue to access footage. 
“We all saw what happened on video,” Haseebullah said. “This was an out of control police officer who decided to violate the law and ended up costing the district and our general public a million dollars because of his antics.”
Clark County School District Board of School Trustees approved a $1 million settlement with two teenage students in 2025.  
More recently, the school district has been scrutinized after reporting from the Nevada Independent found that the district had a contract with the automated license plate reader system Flock. 
“The reason they are not viewed favorably is because they have not been transparent with the public on a variety of issues ranging from the use of Flock all the way down to their use of excessive force and racial profiling of our clients at the Durango High School,” Haseebullah said. 
González questions if there are still times officers use force but it’s not reported. 
“Let’s say there is a fight and pepper spray is deployed but then the officer is using force to push a student to the ground,” she said. “Are they only classifying that as pepper spray? Are we getting other aspects of use of force?”

text:
Illustration by Taylor Haynes/VTDigger

VTDigger has launched its 2026 Election Guide ahead of this year’s general election.
There’s no presidential race on the ballot, but all of Vermont’s state and county-level offices, our lone U.S. House seat and two other ballot items are up for Vermonters to vote on. Your vote will determine the balance of power in Montpelier and who occupies Vermont’s highest offices. 

Go to the Election Guide

The race for governor between political newcomer Amanda Janoo, a progressive Democrat, and Republican Gov. Phil Scott — the nation’s most popular governor by many metrics — looks like it could be Vermont’s most exciting top-of-the-ballot race in years. 
But we’ll be watching far more contests across the state. What impact will a groundswell of rural discontent have on Vermont’s electoral politics? Can Lt. Gov. John Rodgers fend off a challenge from his predecessor, Molly Gray? How will national politics — and the decreasing popularity of President Donald Trump — impact state and local races?
Here’s what you’ll find in the guide:

County-by-county ballot information for federal, statewide, legislative and county races.
Candidate details, including individual financial disclosure forms.
Interactive maps of Vermont House and Senate districts.
Campaign finance data showing how statewide candidates are raising and spending money.
Plain-language explanations of what Vermont’s elected offices do and why they matter.
Step-by-step information on registering to vote, voting early or by mail and voting in person.
Key dates and deadlines for the Nov. 3 general election.
Official voter resources from the Vermont Secretary of State.
VTDigger’s latest election reporting, analysis and explainers.


Go to the Election Guide

name: VTDigger
title: How to vote in Vermont’s 2026 general election
description:
Early voting is available through Nov. 2. All currently registered voters will automatically be sent ballots in the mail on or before Oct. 1. If you are not already registered, there are multiple ways to request and submit your ballot. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  How to vote in Vermont’s 2026 general election.
text:
Vermont’s general election is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
There are two ways to vote:

Early voting by mail or in person, from when ballots are available to Nov. 2.
In person at your polling place on Nov. 3. Bring the ballot mailed to you if you have one.

All U.S. citizens who are residents of Vermont and will be 18 or older for the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, are eligible to register to vote in the election.
Voter registration
To vote in the general election, you must be registered to vote in Vermont, though you may still register on the day of the election. All currently registered voters will automatically be sent ballots in the mail.
If you’re not registered, there are multiple ways to do so:

In person at your town clerk’s office in the days leading up to the election.
In person at your polling place. You may register at your polling place on the day of the election (Nov. 3).
You may also register online or by mail using a paper registration form, both available via the Secretary of State’s Office website, but be sure to leave several days for your registration to be processed if you are using these methods.

According to the Secretary of State’s Office, in-person registrants must provide an identification number when filling out their registration applications, often a driver’s license number. First-time registrants will be required to submit a photocopy of a valid form of ID if registering online or by mail. Acceptable documents include:

Valid photo ID (driver’s license or passport)
Current utility bill
Current bank statement
Another government document

First-time Vermont voters must also take the voter’s oath, a short statement one may recite to oneself. 
Early voting
Early voting is available from when ballots are available (by Oct. 1) through Nov. 2. All currently registered voters will automatically be sent ballots.
Registered voters can track the status of their ballot at the My Voter Page of the Secretary of State’s Office website.
Then, submit your ballot by mail or drop it off at your town clerk’s office.
If you register after ballots are mailed, there are multiple ways to request and submit your ballot. 

Request your ballot:

In person at your town clerk’s office, OR
Online or by mail using a paper registration form via the Secretary of State’s Office website. 


Then, submit your ballot:

By mail, OR
Drop it off at your town clerk’s office.



Early ballots must be received at your town clerk’s office by close of business on Nov. 2. If you’re mailing your ballot, allow a week for delivery.
Election Day
To vote in person on Nov. 3: Find your polling place on the Secretary of State’s Office website. Polls open at various times in the morning and close at 7 p.m.
If you have received a ballot in the mail, you should bring it to use, or you will be asked to sign an affidavit stating that you have not previously voted by mail.

title: With demographic dip in sight, Utah universities prepare for budget impacts
description: Universities across the country are preparing for a major threat: a demographic dip in traditional college-aged people and a drop in the public’s confidence in higher education. Utah, according to a new report, is faring better than the national average. Still, that existential hazard persists in the state, and fiscal analysts are bracing for a […]
text:
Utah State University's Old Main is pictured on Oct. 8, 2024. (Photo by Kelly Winter for Utah News Dispatch)Universities across the country are preparing for a major threat: a demographic dip in traditional college-aged people and a drop in the public’s confidence in higher education. Utah, according to a new report, is faring better than the national average. Still, that existential hazard persists in the state, and fiscal analysts are bracing for a future budget impact.
In Utah it’s not only about the decline of fertility rates. The share of students enrolling in a public Utah colleges within three years of high school graduation has also been in decline for the last few years, going from 56.7% in 2019 to 51.7% in 2025, Kem C. Gardner Institute researchers said in a presentation to the Utah Board of Higher Education on Wednesday. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That shrinking enrollment is expected to have a substantial impact on Utah schools’ budgets. But, if that’s happening years into the future, why are analysts looking at adverse economic scenarios now?  
“We’re not talking about 50% declines. We’re not talking about these cliffs that happen instantaneously. That they’re more slow moving, and there is time to navigate it. But it does require being conscious about how you’re going about that,” said Phil Dean, chief economist with the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute at the University of Utah. 
One of the solutions the institute recommends includes keeping an eye on retention and completion rates. 
According to data from the Utah System of Higher Education, Utah universities and colleges lost about 7,000 students out of the 2023 cohort.
“If you were able to retain those students, then that would basically make up what you would lose that year in the demographic dip,” Andrea Brandley, a senior education analyst at the Gardner Institute said. “And then if you retained them for three years, you could multiply these numbers by three as they went on to finish a bachelor’s degree, so there’s a lot of opportunity here to be able to both improve student outcomes and also increase student enrollment.”
Another way to curb the impact of shifting demographics is to find ways to attract students over 25 years old. More than a third of working age adults have no credential at all, Brandley said, citing a study by Lumina Foundation. A larger portion of them have some sort of certificate, but may benefit from continuing education.
Why the Utah System of Higher Education may get redesigned into ‘regions’

“The opportunity, of course, is to find ways to adapt and to lead where higher education may have the same mission, the mission remains constant, but the students it serves may change. How it delivers education may change, and the challenges it helps to solve will likely continue to evolve,” she said. “So, thinking through all of that and trying to approach things in a proactive way will likely reduce the challenges.”
The Utah System of Higher Education can also build on existing efforts, like recently planned systemwide coordination efforts, which could lead to a unified system of courses across institutions, analysts from the institute said.
With colleges and universities throughout the country facing the same struggles, Utah Commissioner of Higher Education Geoffrey Landward said “rethinking about how we’re operating this system became an imperative.”
Especially when competition with other states will be fierce, he said. 
“This data is exactly why this approach is critical now, and that’s why I think you see other states scrambling to try and rethink how their state systems are operating, because they see the same numbers and they see the same data and they see the same problem,” Landward said. “That Utah’s ahead puts us at a strategic advantage for now, if we can capitalize on what we’ve started.”
