name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Police surveillance technology requires rules and public oversight, not just trust
description: San Francisco police accidentally broadcast hours of live drone footage to the internet recently. The video included thermal images, GPS information, and views into private spaces. During one flight, a drone followed a vehicle across the city, zoomed in on its license plate, and tracked the driver until police made an arrest. During another flight, […]
text:
A police officer uses the Flock Safety license plate reader system. The authors argue that where Minnesota cities implement new technologies with surveillance capabilities, they need enforceable rules, internal audits and public oversight. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)San Francisco police accidentally broadcast hours of live drone footage to the internet recently. The video included thermal images, GPS information, and views into private spaces. During one flight, a drone followed a vehicle across the city, zoomed in on its license plate, and tracked the driver until police made an arrest. During another flight, a drone filmed through an apartment window while responding to what records inconsistently described as a welfare check or missing person investigation.
This breach shows what “drones as first responders” — as their boosters have branded them — can become: not simply a faster way to reach emergencies, but a mobile surveillance system capable of following people, reading license plates, and recording homes from above.
The danger becomes even clearer when drones are understood as one component of an expanding surveillance dragnet in Minneapolis and across Minnesota, including automatic license plate readers, facial recognition and other technologies misleadingly presented by law enforcement agencies and private contractors as safe, neutral and protected from abuse. 
What occurs with these surveillance technologies is an explosion in use without commensurate growth in oversight and transparency. Over two years in San Francisco, the drone fleet grew from six drones to 98 drones and officers flew more than 1,400 flights. In the first three weeks of use in St. Paul, officers flew nearly 500 flights. 
Drones aren’t the only surveillance tools that law enforcement uses to excess. Automatic license plate readers — or ALPR — photograph passing vehicles, record their locations and create enormous troves of searchable and shareable data. Current Minnesota law requires that each search relates to a documented active criminal investigation. Current law also requires that prior to sharing ALPR data with an outside agency, Minnesota law enforcement must confirm that the search is related to an active criminal investigation. In many cases, Minnesota agencies are not doing that due diligence. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Without strong guardrails and public oversight and accountability, networks of cameras can reveal to law enforcement where nearly anyone lives, works, worships, receives medical care, attends a protest, or spends the night. 
Public records obtained by the ACLU-MN indicate that some Minnesota municipalities allowed such broad access to their ALPR systems that, in January, nearly 300,000 searches were run against their cameras. Records showed that many searches related to “civil immigration” instead of any active criminal investigation. 
Local law enforcement does not have the time or resources to vet 300,000 monthly searches to ensure compliance with state law. Instead, they trust outside law enforcement agencies and third-party vendors to do that work for them. 
The public should be educated about the potential for misuse. But even when used in compliance with local regulations, research shows that ALPR systems do not make communities safer or prevent crime.
The government is spying on its own citizens — again

One study placed license-plate-reader patrols in 30 crime hot spots across two jurisdictions. Researchers found no statistically significant reduction in crime generally or in vehicle-related crime. A later study found that while ALPRs increased stolen-vehicle recoveries, they did not increase arrests, reduce calls for crime or disorder while officers were present, delay the next incident, or reduce its seriousness. The authors concluded that the study offered little clear evidence that ALPRs improve crime prevention.
Minnesotans should be concerned about expanding the surveillance dragnet using any of these technologies. But where Minnesota cities do implement new technologies with surveillance capabilities, they need enforceable rules, internal audits and public oversight.
Any drone program must restrict flights to defined emergencies; prohibit surveillance of protests and other First Amendment activity; cannot carry weapons, crowd suppressants, or additional data collection devices like stingrays, which mimic a cell tower to capture data; minimize and localize data collection and retention; mandate deletion schedules; require warrants for investigative tracking; mandate independent audits; provide public access to deployment records; and establish enforceable consequences when rules are broken.
The same principles should govern drones, ALPRs, and all other forms of technological surveillance. Minnesota lawmakers must limit data sharing with third parties and outside agencies, require judicial authorization outside narrow emergencies, and ensure that independent bodies — not police alone — review compliance.
Minnesotans should not have to surrender their anonymity, movements or associations merely because technology makes pervasive monitoring possible.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi 2026 midterm elections guide: Who’s running? What are the issues?
description: A guide to who's running and the driving issues of the Mississippi 2026 midterm election.
text:
Senate Race
House Races
Election Topics
Voting Information
Latest News

Key Senate & House Races Explained
Midterm elections in November will determine control of both chambers of Congress. In Mississippi, a U.S. Senate race tops the ticket, which includes contested general elections for all four of the state’s U.S. House districts.
Who’s in the race: U.S. Senate
Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is running for reelection to a second full term. She faces Democratic nominee Scott Colom and Ty Pinkins, who is running as an independent.

Cindy Hyde-Smith (Republican, Incumbent)





Native of Brookhaven, she is a former state agriculture commissioner and previously served as a Democratic state senator. She was appointed to the U.S. Senate by then-Gov. Phil Bryant in 2018, later won a special election, then a full six-year term in 2020. She is the first woman to represent Mississippi in Congress.
Committee roles: Serves on the Senate Agriculture, Appropriations and Energy committees




Scott Colom (Democrat)





Native of Columbus, Colom was elected district attorney for the 16th Circuit serving Lowndes, Oktibbeha, Clay, and Noxubee counties in 2015. Colom is the first Black DA for his district.
Notable: Nominated by President Joe Biden in 2023 for a northern Mississippi federal judicial seat, but his nomination was blocked by Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.




Ty Pinkins (Independent)





Vicksburg-based attorney and military veteran, former White House communications aide and lawyer with the Mississippi Center for Justice. Pinkins ran unsuccessfully as a Democrat for U.S. Senate in 2024 against incumbent Roger Wicker and ran unsuccessfully for secretary of state in 2023.
Focus: Pinkins says partisan politics and big-money influence have caused government to fail Mississippians.



Who’s in the races: U.S. House
1st Congressional District, northern Mississippi


Trent Kelly (Incumbent), Republican


From Saltillo, Kelly is a six-term U.S. representative, a former district attorney in northern Mississippi and a 39-year Mississippi Army National Guard veteran, retiring in 2025 as a major general. He serves on the House Armed Services Committee and is chairman of the Seapower Subcommittee.





Cliff Johnson, Democrat


From rural Lafayette County, Johnson is director of the MacArthur Justice Center and a professor at the University of Mississippi School of Law and is a former assistant U.S. attorney.





Johnny Baucom, Libertarian


From Columbus, Baucom is an Army National Guard veteran, health and safety technician and has managed mechanic shops.



2nd Congressional District, western Mississippi


Bennie Thompson (Incumbent), Democrat


A native of Bolton, Thompson has served in Congress since 1993, and previously served as an alderman, county supervisor and mayor. He is the current ranking member and former chairman of the Homeland Security Committee, served as a co-chair of the January 6 Commission and is dean of the state congressional delegation.





Ron Eller, Republican


From Jackson, Eller is a cardiac physician’s assistant who served 20 years in the Army starting as a combat medic and retiring as a captain. He has previously run for the 2nd District House seat twice.





Bennie Foster, Independent


A Jackson native, Foster is a longtime educator and administrator.



3rd Congressional District, central Mississippi


Michael Guest (Incumbent), Republican


From Rankin County, Guest is serving his third term in Congress and is a former longtime district attorney for Madison and Rankin counties. He is chairman of the House Ethics Committee and serves on the Appropriations and Homeland Security committees.





Michael Chiaradio, Democrat


From Shubuta, Chiaradio is a farmer and entrepreneur. He played college baseball, then in the Empire Professional Baseball League and has launched several small business ventures, including the American Softball Association. He previously worked for a global government contractor that supports Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act.





Erik Kiehle, Libertarian


From Meridian, Kiehle is a real estate owner, manager and investor, a volunteer firefighter and private pilot who previously worked in software and technology.



4th Congressional District, southern Mississippi


Mike Ezell (Incumbent), Republican


A native of Pascagoula, Ezell is serving his second term in Congress and was formerly sheriff of Jackson County. He serves on the Natural Resources and Transportation committees.





Jeffrey Hulum III, Democrat


A Gulfport native, Hulum has served as state representative for House District 119 since 2022. He is a 22-year U.S. Army veteran who reached the rank of sergeant major.





Carl Boyanton, Independent


Boyanton, of Diamondhead, is founder of Farmer Fresh Produce LLC and has worked as a warehouse laborer.




What matters most to you this November?
Before you cast your ballot this November, we want to know what’s driving your decision. Your answers will directly inform the stories we investigate and the questions we ask candidates.

Help us report


Key issues for this election
Most pundits and prognosticators have Mississippi’s midterm federal elections firmly in the “noncompetitive” category, expecting incumbents to sail to reelection in November.
But challengers are putting in the shoe leather, traversing the state, bombarding social media and, at least in the state’s U.S. Senate race, raising significant amounts of campaign cash.
Particularly, the state’s Democratic challengers to the majority Republican congressional officeholders here hope polling across the country showing dissatisfaction with the GOP on consumer costs, the Iran war, tariffs and trade wars and other policies will provide a foothold to flip seats even in one of the reddest states in the country. Plus, conventional wisdom is the incumbent party can face voters’ ire in midterm elections.
Referendum on Trump
The key question for the 2026 midterms: Will voters in Mississippi, a state dominated by Republican politics, stay loyal to the GOP, even after President Donald Trump’s approval ratings nationwide have plummeted? Rising costs of goods and a protracted war in Iran could erode Trump’s popularity even in red states. 
So far, Mississippi’s incumbent Republican members have allowed little daylight between themselves and Trump, generally praising him and continuing to campaign on alignment with most of his policies. 
But the state’s lone Democratic member, Rep. Bennie Thompson, and Democratic challengers for the other open seats this midterm have criticized the Trump administration and campaigned against many of the president’s policies.
Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has aligned her campaign closely with Trump, who has endorsed her, and she has emphasized her access to and support from the current administration. She has been one of Trump’s staunchest allies in the Senate.
That closeness is also the center of the Democratic case against her. Democratic nominee Scott Colom’s campaign has focused heavily on her vote for Trump’s tax-and-spending package, the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which cut health coverage for many Mississippians and delivered tax breaks weighted toward the wealthy. Colom has tried to characterize Hyde-Smith as a rubber stamp for the White House while forsaking average Mississippians.
Affordability: tariffs, trade wars, inflation and imported beef
The cost of living, or “affordability,” has emerged as a central theme of the midterms, with rising prices, tariffs’ effects on farmers and consumers, gas prices and health insurance and healthcare access are all incampaign issues. After Republicans criticized former President Joe Biden’s handling of inflation, prices have continued to rise under Trump, who pledged to get them under control. 
Generally, Mississippi’s incumbent Republicans have supported the Trump administration’s trade wars and tariff policies, or at least held their tongues. 
Hyde-Smith, a farmer and former state agriculture commissioner, has at times been in a tough spot with Trump’s trade wars. She has supported Trump’s use of emergency powers to enact tariffs, but has also urged the administration to protect farmers from some tariff hikes, such as on fertilizer, and has tried to downplay the costs to Mississippi’s farmers and ag markets.
President Trump’s recent proposal to import cheap beef to try to drive down consumer costs as midterm elections near has drawn flak from Mississippi cattle producers, and at least muted dissension from Hyde-Smith and Republican Rep. Michael Guest. Hyde-Smith faced criticism from Colom and others when she commented in February when asked about high beef prices that, “You have so many proteins to choose from and all commodities go through peaks and valleys.”
Democratic U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson has vocally criticized Trump’s tariffs and trade wars, as have Democratic challengers for the midterms. But Thompson’s Republican challenger, Ron Eller, has said more tariffs are warranted because they will spur more domestic manufacturing.
Iran War
The conflict between the U.S. and Iran, which followed strikes ordered by Trump earlier this year, has become an issue nationally and in Mississippi. Congress has been divided over the president’s use of military force without prior congressional authorization, and a War Powers Resolution aimed at curbing that authority passed the Senate with bipartisan support, though it fell short of a veto-proof majority. 
Hyde-Smith and Mississippi’s three U.S. representatives voted against the resolution, consistent with their broader support for the administration’s national security approach.
The war has also become entangled with the affordability debate, as critics have linked the chokehold in the Strait of Hormuz with higher gas and grocery prices and questioned its cost and open-ended objectives.
Lack of national party support, fundraising
The two main national political parties have not invested heavily in Mississippi’s midterm races, which is not unusual, given the state has not been considered very competitive for non-incumbents in general elections for many cycles.
Some candidates have lamented this, saying the GOP has become too complacent in its hold on all but one congressional office, and the Democratic Party has written the state off as a lost cause.
But for candidates to be successful, they have to raise enough money to buy ads to build name ID. They also need the funds to develop a strong campaign infrastructure leading up to the election. Incumbents tend to have the edge in fundraising, as is the case with this election, though some of the challengers have raised enough money to be competitive. 
Colom has outraised Hyde-Smith for two fundraising quarters this election season. Cliff Johnson, the Democratic nominee for the 1st Congressional District, has for at least a couple of quarters bested incumbent Republican Trent Kelly in fundraising. But both incumbent Republicans have far more campaign cash in their coffers than their challengers. 
A recent report showed Hyde-Smith with $2.54 million cash on hand, and Colom with $847,000.
But things could change in short order in Mississippi races, should national parties or big-money interests decide to weigh in. Mississippi’s media market is relatively cheap, so campaign donations or independent expenditures can go a long way in campaign advertising as races enter the final stretch.
When, Where & How to Vote
Mississippi’s federal midterm Election Day is Nov. 3. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. All Mississippi voters are required to present a photo ID. If you do not present an acceptable form of photo ID, you are entitled to cast an affidavit ballot, but must then present an ID in the local circuit clerk’s office within five business days. For voter ID information or help obtaining valid identification, call 1-800-829-6786.
Register to vote. Mississippians can register to vote in the Nov. 3 general election by mail, at their local county circuit clerk’s offices or at Department of Public Safety offices through Oct. 5. All mail-in applications must be postmarked on or before 30 days prior to Election Day. Mail in applications are available here, or from your circuit clerk. For your circuit clerk’s address and contact information, go to the Secretary of State’s County Election Information page here.
Absentee voting begins Sept. 19. Mississippi does not have standard early voting like many other states do, but the state allows for absentee voting in person and by mail under certain circumstances, including for students attending schools away from their homes, people who will be away from their residence due to work or “any qualified elector who is required to be away from his or her residence within the county on election day for any reason.” Those who are 65 or older also can vote absentee by mail or in person. For more information on how to vote absentee in person or by mail, go to this secretary of state’s web page.
Find your polling location. To find your polling location, view sample ballots and see who your current officeholders are, go the the secretary of state’s My Election Day page.

name: Missouri Independent
title: No matter the congressional map, Missouri voters still have the final say
description: Despite having to endure all the judicial filings and appeals about which congressional district map is legal and should be in effect, let us seize the opportunity this chaotic morass has presented. Vote for the person, irrespective of party affiliation, no matter which congressional district you end up in. We can begin with the midterm […]
text:
A polling location in Jefferson City (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Despite having to endure all the judicial filings and appeals about which congressional district map is legal and should be in effect, let us seize the opportunity this chaotic morass has presented.
Vote for the person, irrespective of party affiliation, no matter which congressional district you end up in.
We can begin with the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
No matter what, Missouri voters still have an opportunity to have the final say by not letting anything stop us from voting.
Amid all the congressional map shenanigans, we must focus on voting for the candidate who will best represent and fight for the well-being of our families, communities and state — not some national, self-serving political or personal agenda.
How can we trust someone who supports defying the Missouri Constitution, the laws that have governed our elections, and the rulings of the Missouri Supreme Court and the U.S. Supreme Court?
In this defining moment, whether we identify as Democrats, Republicans or independents, we must ask a few critical questions of those who are in office or seeking office and who are supposed to be representing the people of Missouri and making the best decisions on their behalf.
When it comes to carrying out the responsibilities of governing or leading, what and where is their moral compass?
For those who are currently in office and seeking re-election, who do they work for now, and who will they work for if they remain in office? Let us not ignore their words or past actions.
A fading or selective memory, or being seduced by a false sense of purpose or false promises, will not serve our state or the people of Missouri well.
A stroll down memory lane proves instructive. We need not backtrack too far — just the past 11 months.
During that short period, from the governor to the Republican supermajority in the state legislature, along with the secretary of state, there have been concerted efforts to undermine, marginalize and even render null and void the voices of tens of thousands of Missourians — making it more difficult, if not impossible, to exercise their rights to participate in our state’s democratic process moving forward.
We must ask ourselves: Irrespective of which congressional district we are in, has our current member of Congress represented and fought for our interests and well-being? Have they stood up and exercised the duties bestowed upon them by the U.S. Constitution when it comes to policy decisions and actions that would have been in the best interests of our state?
Whether you are a city dweller, a rural farmer or living somewhere in between, are you pleased with where our economy is and where it seems to be headed?
How are you dealing with the increasing cost of living, from feed and fertilizer to groceries and gasoline, housing and health care? And where are we heading as a nation when it comes to imposing tariffs, participating in wars and defining our role and standing on the world stage?
These are the areas we sent our members of Congress to Washington to address. How have they performed their jobs?
We, as voting Missourians, can vote them in or out, no matter which congressional district we are in.
Whether the current congressional map based on the last census remains in place, the new gerrymandered map takes effect or the people get a chance to decide which map to use, who ends up in Congress to represent us for the next two years and beyond is in our hands.
Now is not the time to be a rabid, card-carrying, forever-loyal Democrat or Republican when both parties are struggling to reclaim their traditional identities, control emerging fringes or reinvent and redefine themselves in light of emerging forces.
While those struggles are taking place, what better time than now to convey our preferences by voting for the people who best represent our values and democratic beliefs?
Amid all the chaos, we have the opportunity to vote for the best person. That, in itself, will help define party principles and alignment moving forward.
The midterm elections are only weeks away. We will not only be voting for who goes to Congress, but also whom we send to Jefferson City and other local offices. The results of those elections will help define what life will be like in Missouri for the next two years and beyond, depending on what policies are passed, what policies are not and what actions are taken.
We have seen and lived through how the policies and actions of one governing party or the other can change the trajectory of what occurs in our state and nation. We all must honestly answer the question: Do we like and approve of what we see and are experiencing?
Our short- and long-term quality of life is not determined in silos, nor by the outcome of a single election cycle.
Our power, our ability to have the last say, is determined by our ongoing engagement and vigilance and by holding those we send to Washington, Jefferson City, city hall and the county seat accountable.
In the current congressional district morass in which we find ourselves, that is more important than ever.
All the more reason we should not cast our votes with blinders on.

title: Effort to honor first Native American physician expands in Walthill
description: WALTHILL — For 37 years, Vida Stabler raised a family and carefully maintained a two-and-a-half story, Folk Victorian home in this reservation town. text:
Dr. Susan La Flesche Picotte clashed with carpenters several times over the construction of her home in Walthill. She wanted to make sure the home had plenty of natural light and circulation — for health reasons — according to Joe Starita, who wrote her biography. (Courtesy of Gary Bowen)
WALTHILL — For 37 years, Vida Stabler raised a family and carefully maintained a two-and-a-half story, Folk Victorian home in this reservation town.
It was a fixer-upper, she said, but ideal for her and her husband, newly married.
“I loved every morning here,” Stabler said. “Sitting out on the porch. Being surrounded by all the trees. We have a multitude of birds.”
But the house also had a presence, she said. Not a ghost, but the original occupant of the home — a physician and leader in the Omaha Tribe — whom Stabler could visualize walking up stairs, holding tribal meetings or seeing patients in the living room.
The first occupant was Dr. Susan La Flesche Picotte, the nation’s first Native American doctor and a fighter for the rights of her tribe. Stabler said knowing that La Flesche Picotte had once lived in the home was an inspiration to her throughout her life.
“I always felt a warmth from this home … a healing,” she said.
Now, the home is, in a way, heading home.
Stabler, now 69, recently sold the 119-year-old residence to the nonprofit that purchased and restored the hospital built by La Flesche Picotte on a high hill in Walthill in 1907.
The purchase of Dr. Susan’s home, according to those associated with the Picotte Center, will help complete the amazing story of the doctor, who insisted on good hygiene and sanitation and quality medical care for hundreds of patients on the Omaha Indian Reservation in northeast Nebraska.
“Once we got the hospital restored, we always had our eye on the house,” said Gary Bowen, a member of the Picotte Center board. “They go together. You can’t leave one of them out.”
The Dr. Susan home was built in 1907 by her family. Until she was able to get a hospital built, the house served as the center of her medical practice. In 2010, the home was added to the National Register of Historic Places due to its role in the physician’s life.
Dr. Susan La Flesche Picotte’s home hosted patients, tribal members seeking help and several social and political gatherings. A Scottish inscription above the fireplace reads “East West – Hame’s the best.” (Courtesy of  Nebraska State Historical Society)
Above the fireplace is an inscription, “East West – Hame’s the best.” (“Hame” is an old Scottish term for “home.”)
“She loved that home,” said Joe Starita, author of the biography of Dr. Susan, “A Warrior of the People.”
He called it the “spiritual comfort center” of Dr. Susan’s life.
“It anchored her emotionally, it anchored her spiritually … it served many purposes for this beloved doctor,” Starita said.
According to his book, which has an entire chapter devoted to the home, “she began leaving a lighted lantern in the window each night, a beacon to guide the sick and the injured and the desperate through storms and darkness, a light to guide them to her door.”
After a long fight with bone cancer, Dr. Susan died in an upstairs bedroom in the home in 1915. She was 49.
Dozens of tribal members visited the home to view her body, which lay in state in the living room, according to Starita.
In one of the closets, Stabler said, she found the inscription “deliver to Dr. Susan’s house” written on one of the boards.
The doctor saw patients at the home before the opening of the hospital, according to Liz Lovejoy Brown, the executive director of the Picotte Center. Surgical procedures were done across the street, in an outbuilding near her sister’s home.
“She had no other place to go,” Lovejoy Brown said.
It also served as a place where fellow Omaha tribal members could seek Dr. Susan’s help in navigating government regulations and programs. She could interpret for those who didn’t speak or read English.
Typical of her help was this entry in her diary: “White Horse came in to see me about the plans for the new house … Dan Wolf and his wife came in. He wanted me to interpret for him in his will. His wife asked me to look after her lands; that she had received no rent for 2 years.”
Other diary entries included “Tended to Noah who is almost well — drafted letter for Emma H. Guitar,” “Nellie Springer wants her heirship interest looked up. Did so,” and “Got baby’s breakfast and gave him his medicine …”
In 1911, over 60 members of the Omaha Tribe gathered to meet with three members of a Nebraska legislative committee to discuss a proposed bill that attempted to protect the inheritance rights of Native American wives and their children.
During the meeting, Dr. La Flesche Picotte chose to address her fellow tribal members in their native language, rather than in English, which reportedly served to avoid interruptions by the committee chairman, who opposed the proposal, the Gallagher Bill.
Her status and abilities as a local leader were highly valued, according to Lovejoy Brown. Dr. Susan was the youngest child of Chief Joseph La Flesche (“Iron Eye”), the last traditionally recognized chief of the Omaha Tribe, and she advocated and testified for the rights of her tribal members.
“When you’re recognized as a resource in your community, people would come to you,” Lovejoy Brown said. “People trusted you.”
Stabler, who heads up the Omaha Nations Public School cultural and language program in Macy, portrayed Dr. Susan, in period dress, in presentations for local schoolchildren for several years.
That role began after the dedication of the Picotte hospital as a museum, at which Stabler presented a play that highlighted the amazing life of the doctor.
“One day, I was at a Sioux City grocery store when a kid came up to me: ‘I know you. You‘re Dr. Susan,’” Stabler said.
For years, Stabler served on organizations dedicated to preserving the story of Dr. Susan. She is currently the treasurer of the Picotte Center Board.
At 69, Stabler said, she was getting to the point that she could no longer maintain her home, thus the sale to the Picotte Center. It’s been hard to leave, she said, but she expects that Dr. Susan would approve.
“I believe what’s to come will be beneficial for all,” Stabler said.
When the Dr. Susan house was built in 1907, there were few trees in its neighborhood in Walthill. The home is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. (Courtesy of  Nebraska State Historical Society)
Just how the Dr. Susan home will be used has not yet been determined. There are plans to hold town hall meetings with local residents to gather their input on possible uses.
A Lincoln architect, Dan Worth, is doing an assessment of the condition of the home.
Lovejoy Brown said maybe it could become a cafe for visitors to the Picotte Center; Stabler wants the home to be a place of “healing”; Bowen said perhaps a caretaker would live there.
A fundraising campaign would be necessary to finance any renovations to the home. Private donations covered the $100,000 purchase of the house.
Whatever is determined to be the future of Dr. Susan’s house, Bowen said it should be something the Omaha Nation can be proud of.
“That’s the whole purpose of this exercise,” he said. “To honor Dr. Susan and the Omaha people.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ bill would give nursing home residents small boost in monthly Medicaid allowance
description: New Jersey lawmakers advanced a bill to add a cost-of-living adjustment to monthly payments to nursing home residents with Medicaid.
text:
New Jersey lawmakers advanced a bill to add a cost-of-living adjustment to monthly payments to nursing home residents with Medicaid. The residents say much more is needed. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)It took a year for Gail Smith, a nursing home resident in Somerset County, to save enough from her monthly Medicaid allowance to afford new clothing when she lost significant weight, and she still had to buy second-hand.
“It hurts to have our personalities squashed and to lose our independence,” Smith told New Jersey lawmakers Monday. “We’re not just waiting to die. We want to thrive.”
Smith is among a growing group of advocates who want the state to increase the $50 monthly “personal needs allowance” provided to nursing home residents who have Medicaid. Residents use the money to pay for their cellphone, cable TV, haircuts, clothing, toiletries, books, and gifts, among other things.
The Assembly Health Infrastructure Committee unanimously approved legislation Monday that would add an annual cost-of-living increase to the monthly allotment starting next year, a change advocates said amounts to a few dollars a month. Many said the bill, introduced late last week by a trio of Assembly Democrats, doesn’t go far enough. There is currently no Senate version.
John Indyk, a vice president with the Health Care Association of New Jersey, which represents nursing homes, testified in favor of the measure and called it “a fair and reasonable approach for the time being.”
“If the state can find money to do more, we should do that,” Indyk said.
Known as PNAs, these personal needs payments range from $30 — the federal minimum — in Alabama and South Carolina to $160 in Florida and $200 in Alaska, according to the nonprofit National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care. Ten states pay less than New Jersey and three others, including Delaware and New York, also pay $50 a month, the group said.
While nursing homes provide care, food, some basic supplies, activities, and a place to live, residents must pay for many things themselves, including stamps, delivery fees, and some transportation. Advocates said residents need more money if they want fresher food options or an occasional treat, better bedding, and toiletries that aren’t watered down.
“It seems like the state always finds money for things that are important. Please show us that we are important and change this bill to raise the PNA by more than just a tiny cost-of-living adjustment,” Smith told lawmakers, her voice cracking.
Smith and other advocates have long pushed for a separate, bipartisan bill that would boost the monthly allotment to $140 and also add an annual cost-of-living adjustment. That measure, sponsored by Assemblyman Christopher DePhillips (R-Bergen), was passed by a different Assembly committee in early May, but has not advanced further, while a Senate version has not been posted for a hearing.
Assemblyman Christopher DePhillips (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
DePhillips, a member of the Health Infrastructure Committee, supported the cost-of-living measure Monday to move it out of committee, but called its proposed increase to the $50 monthly benefit not enough.
“I understand there are different perspectives on this bill. And budgetary concerns are obviously top of mind for all of us,” DePhillips said. “But we are so far behind that doing it incrementally is something that is unworkable.”
Tanette Clegg, a resident at Trenton Gardens nursing home, called the bill heard Monday a “slap in the face” to residents who testified about the issue in May. Others complained that the new bill was developed without their input and was scheduled for Monday’s hearing before nursing home residents could arrange transportation to join.
Clegg said her Trenton Gardens neighbors struggle to pay for used clothing and, at $45, she can barely cover the cost of a shampoo and haircut at the facility. Clegg described the home’s food as “inexplicably bad,” leaving residents desperate for outside options they can’t afford.
“It’s not healthy or tasty and we rarely get fresh fruits or vegetables, if we get them at all,” Clegg said, adding that she is bothered that residents like her must keep coming to the Statehouse to demand action.
Assemblywoman Shanique Speight (D-Essex), a chief sponsor on both bills, assured advocates she and others continue to work to advance the more generous bill.
“Hearing the testimonies that I’ve heard has had an impact on my heart and will never leave my mind,” Speight said.
Assemblyman Sterley Stanley (D-Middlesex), the committee’s chair and a lead sponsor on the bill that advanced Monday, called the legislation a “starting point.”
“I don’t see why both can’t work together,” Stanley said.
Ray DiFrancesco, a former resident at a Princeton nursing home who was able to move into an assisted living facility when his health improved, said he now enjoys benefits his previous neighbors can’t access. A shuttle bus allows him to shop around for food bargains and visit thrift shops or dollar stores, while nursing home residents are forced to order from catalogs, pay delivery fees, or spring for a car service if they must go out.
“When you have only $50 a month, you can only afford the basics,” DiFrancesco said, adding, “That PNA gets eaten up real quickly.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho District 2 congressional candidates say they’re worried about high cost of living
description: Multiple election challengers to longtime incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson say they are focused on lowering the cost of living for Idahoans.  On Nov. 3, Democrat Ellie Gilbreath, independents Tripp Hutchinson and Emre Houser, and Libertarian Will Johanson, will face Simpson, who’s in his 14th term in the U.S. House of Representatives. He represent[...]
text:
From left, Democrat Ellie Gilbreath, independent Tripp Hutchinson, Libertarian Will Johanson, and Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson.  (Photos courtesy of the candidates)Multiple election challengers to longtime incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson say they are focused on lowering the cost of living for Idahoans. 
On Nov. 3, Democrat Ellie Gilbreath, independents Tripp Hutchinson and Emre Houser, and Libertarian Will Johanson, will face Simpson, who’s in his 14th term in the U.S. House of Representatives. He represents Idaho’s 2nd Congressional District, which covers much of southeast Idaho. 
Simpson’s campaign did not respond to multiple emails and voicemails requesting an interview for this story. Houser also could not be reached, and Constitution Party candidate Carta Sierra Law, known as the Idaho Lorax, who registered to run in the race, died in June, the Idaho State Journal reported. 



Meet the candidates 
Simpson, 76, was first elected to the U.S. House in 1998. Previously, he served in the Idaho state Legislature and on Blackfoot City Council. Prior to his political career, Simpson worked as a dentist with his father and uncle at Simpson Family Dental Practice in Blackfoot, where he grew up, according to his congressional website. 
Hutchinson, 28, was elected in 2023 as the youngest member of the Ketchum City Council. Previously, he was director of programming at a local independent movie theater, he said. He was born and raised in Ketchum, he said.  
Gilbreath, 64, works as a lawyer and conflict resolution mediator. She moved to Ketchum 24 years ago, she said. 
Johanson, 33, is an engineer in the semiconductor industry in Boise. He previously served as a nuclear operator in the U.S. Navy. He moved to Idaho in 2020. 



 What are the top issues for Idaho’s Congressional District 2 candidates?

Simpson said on his website his top priorities included stopping illegal immigration, supporting agriculture, and opposing the Biden-era climate initiatives in the “Green New Deal,” which he called “overreaching and ambiguous.” 
Hutchinson said he wanted to run because he saw a “cost of living crisis for the working people of Ketchum” and Blaine County. 
US District 1 candidates: Idahoans face high healthcare costs. Here’s how they want to fix it.

“We work as hard as we can at the municipal level to address the challenges, but having sat in the seat, it became very apparent early on that a lot of these issues are systemic, all the way up to our federal government,” he said. 
Gilbreath said her top priorities would be protecting public lands, lowering costs for Idahoans, and “raising up rural Idaho … Which includes standing with our Idaho agriculture.” 
“I think we’ve abandoned rural Idaho as a country, but also in Idaho,” Gilbreath said. “So we need to expand our federal funding for rural hospitals and healthcare, and then focus on trade school parity.
Johanson said he’s running to “give voters an alternative.” He said Simpson seems to be “out of touch with our concerns over affordability and the endless wars that we’re fighting around the world.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Idaho congressional candidates propose differing healthcare affordability solutions  

Hutchinson said the biggest challenge he hears about from Idahoans is the high cost of healthcare. 
“I’m a strong believer in capitalism and the philosophy of capitalism, but at the same time, I’m a strong believer that some sectors of our economy should be moving away from the profit motive,” he said. 
He said the country’s anti-trust and anti-monoply laws need to be enforced more heavily in the healthcare industry, including against pharmaceutical and insurance companies. He said, eventually, he wants to see the nation move to a single-payer healthcare system, often called Medicare for all. 
“I’m running to represent Idaho for a two-year term, and I don’t think this is manageable in a two-year term, but I think it’s a goal that’s worth having for our country well into the future,” he said. 
State Medicaid budgets will decline by $665 billion under new federal law, report finds

Gilbreath said she wants to restore the cuts to Medicaid implemented in the federal “big beautiful” law approved by Republicans last year, “or find an alternate solution.” She said the bill’s $50 billion Rural Healthcare Transformation Grant, of which Idaho was awarded $186 million in the first year of the five-year program, was “a game of smoke and mirrors, whether intentional or not.” 
“They threw the net so wide, just calling it healthcare, so it was really difficult for our rural hospitals to get any of that,” she said. 
Johanson said a lack of competition and over-regulation have driven up healthcare costs. To address this, he proposed allowing Medicare to negotiate lower pharmaceutical prices. He also said he supports some healthcare deregulation, such as eliminating requirements for needs assessments for opening new hospitals and eliminating requirements on how insurance companies must use premiums they collect from clients.
He’d also like to see an increase in direct primary care, in which patients pay physicians a regular membership fee to access services instead of going through insurance, to “cut out the middleman.” 
Simpson wrote in the Sun’s 2026 Primary Election Voter Guide, that he supports “legislation that offers common-sense, market-based reforms to lower health care premium costs, expands access to quality care, provides every American with more options and flexibility to choose coverage that works for them, and brings greater transparency to America’s health care system.” 
He said he supported “strengthening rural health care access and protecting Medicare and Medicaid for those who rely on them while rooting out waste and improving efficiency. I also support expanding association health plans and reducing costly regulations that burden providers and small businesses.” 
 Immigration reform: Candidates consider legal pathways for migrant workers, ‘amnesty,’ limiting work visas. 

Gilbreath said the immigration issues the country faces are “solvable.” 
“Both sides are guilty of not really attempting to solve the problem,” she said. “It’s become this very convenient tool to battle the Democrats against the Republicans.” 
She said she supported efforts to secure borders as well as expanded migrant work visas. She said the agricultural work visa program H-2A should be expanded so year-round industries, such as dairy producing, could access laborers year-round. The H-2A program is currently only available for temporary, seasonal work and can’t be accessed by year-round agricultural businesses.
Risch v. Achilles may be Idaho’s most active US Senate race in years. Here’s where they stand.

She said expansions to the program should be “industry-specific and job-specific,” limited to only producers that need the different requirements. 
“As I’ve traveled around the state, there seems to be consensus around that sense of strong borders and secure borders, and also a legal pathway for people to be able to to run their ag businesses and have their neighbors here at legal capacity,” Gilbreath said. 
Johanson argued that the H-2A program depresses wages in the industry, despite requirements around minimum wages in the program to try and reduce adverse effects on wage rates. Johanson said the excess labor coming into the jobs keeps the wages low, and said he’d support limiting the number of visas in the program that are administered. He also supports strong border enforcement, he said. 
“It’s often argued that ag workers do jobs that you know native-born Americans don’t want to do, but I suppose the most clear counter is that native-born Americans don’t want to do these jobs or simply can’t do these jobs because they pay wages far below what we would call a living wage,” Johanson said. 
Simpson wrote on his website that he supports stopping illegal immigration and securing the nation’s border and that he’s “deeply concerned over proposals that would grant amnesty to illegal immigrants in the United States.” 
Simpson in 2021 co-sponsored the bi-partisan Farm Workforce Modernization Act, which among its many immigration changes would’ve granted temporary legal status to some longtime undocumented agricultural workers that meet certain requirements. Those who obtained this temporary status would have the ability to eventually apply for permanent legal status. 
This year, Simpson signed on to another legislative package, called the Securing Agriculture’s Workforce Act, which would update the H-2A program, allowing it to be used for year-round work and would create a visa pathway for undocumented agricultural workers. The bill does not include a permanent legal status pathway. 
“I have also worked closely with our farmers and ranchers that depend on guestworker labor to explore options to reforming this program,” Simpson said on his website. “Idaho’s economy depends on agriculture labor, and without a legal means to solve this outdated system, we are doing our farmers a great disservice.” 
Hutchinson said he supports “properly funding” a pathway to full citizenship for migrant workers. He argued the visa system creates “secondary class that is more easily exploited, accepts lower wages, and creates much bigger profit margins for some of the most powerful people in our country.” 
He also supported “a properly funded presence at both of our borders,” because he believes climate change will drive global mass migration and the country should be prepared. 
 Three candidates don’t support transferring federal public lands to state. One does. 

Simpson in 2025 co-sponsored the “Public Lands in Public Hands” Act amid efforts to sell off large swaths of federal public land to pay for extending tax cuts in the big beautiful bill. Simpson told the Idaho Press he didn’t support transferring ownership of federal lands to the state, because the price tag would be too much for local land managers. 
Nearly two-thirds of Idaho’s landmass is federal public land. 
Hutchinson said that much of the federal land that is permitted to ranchers for grazing should be sold to those ranchers and privatized. 
“The vast majority of federal land is not this sort of appealing, pristine natural beauty,” he said. “It’s more of an austere grazing land or land that’s just kind of rocky. Land that people wouldn’t really think twice about.” 
He also supported moving ownership of national forests to the state and “getting that decision making closer to the voters that are affected by it.” 
Gilbreath and Hutchinson also told the Sun they didn’t support transferring ownership or management of the land. 
Gilbreath added that the federal government should enact limitations on putting data centers on public land. 
“… Negotiations need to be transparent and the public needs to be involved, and it needs to be local control and local benefit to that data center,” she said. “Not just some big tech company that thinks that Idaho is a great place to be able to just come in and take some land and exploit it for their own benefit and value, not those of the citizens.” 
Hutchinson said selling off or blocking off access to the land would “be looked back on as one of the biggest mistakes in our country’s history, and a complete slap into the face to the people over 100 years ago, like Teddy Roosevelt, who had the foresight to to protect these spaces with the highest form of government for the future generations of our country.” 
 Simpson and Gilbreath lead in fundraising 

Simpson’s campaign this year has collected over $1.1 million and spent nearly $800,000, through June 30, which is the most recent Federal Election Commission data available. More than $600,000 of his contributions have come from political action committees or PACs, such as the Freedom Fund, National Rural Water Association Political Committee, and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee PAC.   
Gilbreath’s campaign has garnered nearly $107,000 and spent around $35,700, as of June 30 FEC filings. Over $35,000 of that has come from ActBlue, the Democratic National Convention fundraising platform. Her campaign did not report any contributions from other PACs. 
Hutchinson’s campaign has reported just over $7,500 in contributions, and spent about $1,600. All of his contributions come from individual donors, according to the report. 
Houser and Johanson didn’t have reported contributions or expenditures in FEC filings.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming’s incoming leaders must learn the lessons of the past
description:
The statewide rejection of the Freedom Caucus gives the new legislative class a clean slate, but they should not forget what brought about the caucus’ rise in the first place, writes columnist Khale Lenhart.
The post Wyoming’s incoming leaders must learn the lessons of the past appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
There has been no shortage of retrospectives and analyses of this year’s Republican primary election. The Wyoming Freedom Caucus suffered major losses, with incumbents and challengers alike losing. Come next January, this faction that controlled the Wyoming House the last two years will be reduced to 10 or fewer members out of 62 total seats. There is no way to interpret those results other than as the voters’ rejection of the Freedom Caucus.  

Opinion

What is less clear is the reason why Wyoming voters rejected these candidates. Was it their policies? Their apparent unwillingness to accept input? Their reliance on unelected consultants and national organizations to direct their votes? There is no way to really know if a single factor led to the rejection. Most likely, it was a combination of many factors that caused the voters to turn away.
What lessons can we learn from the Freedom Caucus’ time in office and its members ensuing decimation at the ballot box? One takeaway is that our policymakers must understand the real-world consequences of their actions.  Many of the issues championed by the Freedom Caucus were not the topics that genuinely impacted most people’s lives. Voters want a government that is responsive to their needs, not just responsive to storylines.  
In the same vein, even when the Freedom Caucus took on pressing issues, its members tended to move forward with proposed policies without considering outside input, even when presented to them. Their decisions appeared to be made elsewhere, which left no room for the real work of legislating. Citizens felt that their legitimate concerns went unheard, which painted the picture of a group detached from the actual needs of their constituents. It should be no surprise that voters reacted unfavorably.
In just a few months, a new crop of elected officials will be taking office. They will have much to learn. Nearly half of the Wyoming House will be freshman legislators, and most of the rest of the returning House members will be in only their second or third term. The Senate also will see many new faces. Of the 17 senators on the ballot, eight will be new beginning in January. A majority of our statewide officials will be new to the office beginning next year. Cities and counties also will see new officeholders elected. All will be learning on the job.  
In recognition of this learning process, we should be careful to temper our expectations. It takes a long time to turn a ship, especially with an inexperienced crew. Not everything that voters want is going to happen right away. What we should look for instead is, first, whether they are making progress, and second, whether our new leaders are considering input from others, learning the job and engaging in the process that will lead to better outcomes. We can forgive being new and clumsy, but it is much harder to forgive hubris in the face of this inexperience.
Our policymakers, both newly elected and veterans, must be careful to avoid the mistakes of those who are leaving office. Just as there are many reasons the Freedom Caucus lost this election, there are many reasons why the group won the last one. Our leaders should not be blind to the fact that part of the reason Freedom Caucus politicians won in the first place was that they spoke to a need in our society. Something was not right in the way things were being done, so the voters were willing to try something new. Granted, those voters quickly saw that the “something new” they voted for was not the answer, but we should not interpret the most recent results as a mandate to return to the way things were done before. Our leaders should learn and grow from the experience, not revert to the prior methods and status quo that led to their initial downfall.
Lastly, and above all else, those who now find themselves in positions of power or influence should resist the temptation to turn the tables on others who may have wronged them. Turnaround may be fair play, but it is bad governance. We expect our leaders to act in the best interests of the people, even if that means setting aside hurt feelings or even legitimate grievances. Good ideas advanced by your opponents are still good ideas, and the uncollaborative “us vs. them” division will only be further entrenched if the reaction to taking power is to punish those who came before you. Someone must break the cycle, and what better time than now? Our state has a great opportunity in front of it. Now is the time to rise to the occasion and show what the best version of Wyoming can be.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Spoilers or contenders? Two independent candidates for TN governor try to shake up the race
description: In early September, a new website appeared attacking independent Tennessee governor candidate David Hatley for a 1998 felony conviction.  Hatley, a Washington County businessman, has talked extensively about his past mistakes, using them as a catalyst in a book published earlier this year ahead of his gubernatorial run.  “It’s never fun when somebody attacks[...]
text:
David Hatley, left, and Lauren Pinkston, right, are running as independent candidates for Tennessee's governor. (Photos: J. Holly McCall and John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)In early September, a new website appeared attacking independent Tennessee governor candidate David Hatley for a 1998 felony conviction. 
Hatley, a Washington County businessman, has talked extensively about his past mistakes, using them as a catalyst in a book published earlier this year ahead of his gubernatorial run. 
“It’s never fun when somebody attacks you,” Hatley said. “But at the end of the day it’s part of my journey, and they wouldn’t be attacking me if they didn’t have the same internal polling.”
Tennessee’s gubernatorial seat is open for the first time in eight years, as Gov. Bill Lee is term-limited, making him unable to run in 2026. Republicans have held the state’s governorship since 2010 and haven’t lost a statewide race for any office in a nearly two-decade-long stretch.
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn emerged from the Republican primary as the favorite to become Tennessee’s next governor after this November’s general election. The Democratic Party nominated Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green on its ticket. 
But this year Hatley and Lauren Pinkston have emerged as independent candidates for governor, drawing substantial attention and fundraising.
Pinkston, a former Lipscomb University professor, is running as a moderate, arguing that voters are tired of both parties.
“I think the majority of voters are independent now, and they’re pretty unsatisfied with the two options that they have,” Pinkston said. 
These two campaigns come as the Democratic Party in Tennessee appears to be slipping further in statewide popularity, and polling shows Blackburn’s isn’t drawing the same level of enthusiasm from Republican voters as Lee did in past elections. 
Blackburn won the 2026 gubernatorial Republican primary with 43% of the vote in a three-way race. Her vote percentage was more than Lee’s Republican primary victory in 2018. 
But recent polling shows Blackburn garnering between 46-51% of the vote among registered voters. Lee won his general elections by larger margins, grabbing 60% of the vote in 2018 and 65% in 2022. 
Blackburn’s relatively low polling compared to Lee’s has given both independent candidates hope, and her campaign’s attacks show she’s at least thinking that Hatley could be pulling from her overall support.  The website attacking Hatley for the 1998 felony conviction is paid for by Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign.
Hatley running as conservative outsider
Hatley has never run for political office in Tennessee and has spent most of his adult life as a businessman. 
After a felony bank fraud conviction, Hatley said he turned his life around. He became the successful owner of Whisper Outdoor, which started by manufacturing hot tubs and has since expanded to producing golf carts, boats and off-road vehicles.
While running as an independent, Hatley described himself as “a very conservative guy.”
“I’ve always been pro-life and pro-guns,” Hatley said. “I want to be independent because I don’t want to have party pressure.”
A tenet of Hatley’s argument to voters is that he is pushing for the state to have an elected auditor to “figure out where the money is going,” because he doesn’t feel like the state is managing its budget correctly.
He is also touting his willingness to spend at least $7 million of his own money and doesn’t plan to do any fundraising.
“I don’t want anyone in my ear,” Hatley said. “It’s very important that I go in on day one with a clean slate, only thinking about things that make sense for Tennessee.”
Pinkston trying to stake out moderate lane
Pinkston characterizes herself as a moderate alternative for voters who don’t support Blackburn or Green. But her public policy views show she aligns with many Democratic lawmakers on several key issues.
For instance, she supports a full repeal of the state’s private-school voucher program, which is costing Tennesseans nearly $300 million annually to pay for students to attend private schools. 
Pinkston also says the Memphis Safe Task Force was deployed “to aim for a strong headline, not for effective governance.” Instead of sending Tennessee National Guard troops to the city, Pinkston says she would have asked local law enforcement where it needed to fill gaps.
Pinkston says she has studied the state budget and believes Tennessee is “perfectly capable” of repealing the 4% grocery tax. She contends the state is losing revenue because large numbers of people cross into neighboring states to buy groceries, gasoline and big-ticket items such as electronics.
She criticizes Lee’s business tax rebate and reduction, saying she does not support incentives for Silicon Valley companies to move to Tennessee. Lawmakers eliminated the state’s property portion of the franchise tax in 2024, costing $4 billion in state revenue over the next decade and a three-year refund to businesses totaling $1.55 billion, despite criticism that out-of-state businesses would receive the lion’s share of the breaks.
Pinkston is an adoptive mother who has volunteered with women suffering crisis pregnancies. On abortion, she says, she “believes all life is sacred.” But she has criticized the state’s total abortion ban, which criminalizes physicians, as putting women’s lives at risk.
“Ultimately, health care decisions should lie with the patient and the doctor, and the issues of morality need to have social supports around them so we can save as many lives as possible in this state,” she said. “But the way we save lives and we save the lives of the unborn are to better resource mothers and to better resource families.”

text:
William J. Samford Hall at Auburn University in Auburn, Alabama. The Auburn University Board of Trustees Friday voted to raise tuition across both campuses in its system. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The Auburn University Board of Trustees Friday voted to increase tuition for all students in the university system.
Starting in the 2027 fall semester, Auburn University’s tuition will go up $271, or 2% for in-state students, and $1,879, or 5%, for out-of-state students. With the increases, yearly tuition at the school will go from $13,572 to $13,843 for Alabama residents and from $37,596 to $39,475 for out-of-state students.
Auburn University at Montgomery will also have a tuition increase of $350, or 3%, for in-state students and $732, also 3%. The increase will bring  AUM tuition from $11,666 to $12,015 for Alabama residents and from $24,406 to $25,138 for out-of-state students.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kelli Shomaker, the senior vice president for business and administration and the chief financial officer for Auburn, said during Friday’s meeting that the system continues “to incur cost increases due to rising inflation and labor pressures associated with retaining exceptional faculty and staff and providing an exceptional student experience.”
In 2024, the Board of Trustees voted to raise tuition by 3%, citing inflation, impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic and labor pressures. The board voted last year to raise tuition again by 2% for in-state students and 4.5% for out-of-state students to “meet rising inflation and operational costs.”
The Auburn University System received $440.6 million in the fiscal year 2027 Education Trust Fund budget signed by Gov. Kay Ivey in April an increase of $26.4 million from the FY26 ETF budget.
Of the $440.6 million, $309.5 million was appropriated for Auburn University and $36.6 million was appropriated for AUM.
The University of Alabama’s tuition for the 2026-27 academic year is $12,718 for Alabama residents and $36,724 for non-residents. In 2025, the UA Board of Trustees approved system-wide tuition increases by up to 3% and voted to increase tuition costs by up to 4% earlier this year.
The UA System received $810.1 million from the Legislature in the FY27 ETF, up 45.4 million from the FY26 budget. Of that money, UA received $284.8 million, an increase of $18.6 million from FY26; University of Alabama at Birmingham received $439.3 million, up $22.4 million from last year and University of Alabama in Huntsville got $81.7 million, an increase of $4.4 million from FY26.
