name: Michigan Advance
title: Working Families Party joins Michigan Constitutional Convention opposition effort
description: With less than two months until the general election in November, a coalition urging Michigan residents to vote no on a proposed constitutional convention continues to grow. The Michigan Chapter of the Working Families Party on Monday announced it would join a bipartisan coalition made up of business advocates, community leaders, labor unions and other […]
text:
The Michigan State Capitol dome. April 30, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. With less than two months until the general election in November, a coalition urging Michigan residents to vote no on a proposed constitutional convention continues to grow.
The Michigan Chapter of the Working Families Party on Monday announced it would join a bipartisan coalition made up of business advocates, community leaders, labor unions and other political stakeholders in opposition to a constitutional convention, also known as a Con-Con. 
Every 16 years, Michigan’s Constitution requires voters to determine whether the state should hold a constitutional convention. If the measure passes, a slate of 148 delegates would gather and determine what changes, if any, should be made to the state Constitution. Each delegate would be selected through a partisan election process, with one representative for each state House and Senate district.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Changes could range from small tweaks to a complete overhaul, with members of Protect MI Constitution From Special Interests, the opposition coalition, arguing that approving a Con-Con would open up the state Constitution to influence from wealthy special interest groups. 
Changes must be agreed upon by a majority of the delegates, and would need to be approved by Michigan voters.
“Working people in Michigan have spent generations fighting for the rights and protections that make it possible to build a life with dignity,” Branden Snyder, director of the Working Families Party in Michigan said in a news release. “We shouldn’t put those gains on the bargaining table and give corporations, wealthy special interests, and the well-connected another opportunity to rewrite the rules against working families. A Constitutional Convention creates too much uncertainty and there’s simply no reason to take that risk.”
Other members of the opposition coalition include American Civil Liberties Union of Michigan, the Michigan Chamber of Commerce, the Michigan AFL-CIO, the Michigan Education Association and several other organizations and policymakers.
“Working Michiganders can’t afford gas or groceries — and they definitely can’t afford a Con-Con,” Ron Bieber, president of the Michigan AFL-CIO, said in a statement. “Holding a Michigan Constitutional Convention would open up a Pandora’s Box of special interest carveouts that put billionaires and corporations first when we can least afford it. It’s too risky.”
A recent poll of 600 likely voters commissioned by The Detroit News and WDIV Channel 4 and conducted by the Lansing-based Glengariff Group found 47% of voters would support a Constitutional Convention. Thirty-one percent were opposed while 22% were uncertain. 
During the last vote, held in 2010, 67% of voters rejected the proposal.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV local govs spent most opioid settlement funds on police, jail bills, EMS in fiscal year 2024-2025
description: West Virginia localities spent nearly $10 million more of the opioid settlement funds they received between 2024 and 2025 than in the year previously, with a bulk of that spending going toward law enforcement, jail bill payments and support for emergency medical services, according to a West Virginia Watch analysis of a local spending report […]
text:
West Virginia localities gave the highest percentage — about 23.8%  — of their opioid settlement funds to law enforcement in fiscal year 2025.  Police cruisers were the largest single spending category for law enforcement.
(Stock photo by Halbergman/Getty Images)West Virginia localities spent nearly $10 million more of the opioid settlement funds they received between 2024 and 2025 than in the year previously, with a bulk of that spending going toward law enforcement, jail bill payments and support for emergency medical services, according to a West Virginia Watch analysis of a local spending report published by the West Virginia First Foundation earlier this year.
The report covers opioid settlement dollar expenditures made by local governments between July 1, 2024 and June 30, 2025. Per the report, a total of $36.75 million was sent to more than 170 localities over that time. About $16.76 million of those funds were reported as being spent through 393 individual expenditures.
Of the 172 local governments included in the most recent report, 100 reported not spending any money. 
Compared to the previous report,  which covered expenditures from July 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024, about 70 fewer local governments sent spending reports to the First Foundation, meaning payments made by them have not been tracked or included in this analysis.
The allocations to local governments are separate from money being disbursed by the First Foundation, which is the private nonprofit created in 2023 to dole out the state’s share of opioid settlement dollars. 
West Virginia Watch combed through all expenditures reported by local governments, and here we will break down what that spending looked like while providing you with tools to look up your own local government’s spending priorities.
Of the nearly $16.76 million spent by localities last fiscal year, about 23.8% — nearly $4 million — went toward law enforcement, which was the highest spending category for a second year. Jail bill payments made up about 22.6%, or $3.79 million, of the expenditures while support for EMS accounted for about 21% — nearly $3.56 million — of all money spent. 
Treatment and recovery services accounted for nearly $3 million, or about 17.6%, of all money spent while $1.44 million (8.6%) went toward community-oriented programs and services and more than $912,000 (5.4%) was spent on youth-focused services.
Use the table below to search and see all expenditures reported by local governments during fiscal year 2025, then continue reading to see further breakdowns of the spending categories.
Cruisers, mass surveillance and more make up law enforcement spending
Law enforcement, for a second year, received the most money from all opioid settlement spending, according to the report. Police cruisers — including payments to upgrade and service existing vehicles — were the largest single spending category for law enforcement. Per the report, at least 25 new police cars — including a $157,000 armored vehicle for St. Albans police officers — were purchased, totaling more than $1.6 million.

The full breakdown of law enforcement spending was as follows:

$1.63 million on cruisers and cruiser-related expenses
$630,472 on equipment, including guns, tasers, computer software, canine units and more
$606,271 on infrastructure costs, including remodeling police precincts, flood recovery efforts, utility bills and more
$513,810 on police salary, payroll and overtime pay 
$422,619 on surveillance equipment, including automatic license plate readers, AI-powered camera equipment, licensing fees for accessing ALPR and camera databases and more
$190,591 on training and related expenses, like travel and lodging

For surveillance, numerous localities spent thousands of dollars purchasing ALPRs and other contentious surveillance equipment. In Randolph County, officials spent more than $10,000 on Motorola license plate readers and the licensing fees and software subscription to use them. Upshur County spent about $10,000 on an in-car ALPR camera system from Motorola as well as about $4,000 to license four ALPRs.
More than $413,000 in total was spent directly on Motorola equipment or services. A lack of details provided by localities, however, make it difficult to ascertain how many of the cameras purchased — some of which also come from third party vendors — are ALPRs or AI-supported.
Tensions have been flaring across the state and the country as residents have stood up against mass surveillance purchased and installed by governments from companies like Flock Safety and Motorola. While supporters of the technology allege it will help in policing, residents and others worry that it will lead to mass invasions of privacy and constitutional violations.
The largest single law enforcement expenditure came from McDowell County, which put $339,000 in opioid settlement funds into a separate county fund to repair flood damage and replace equipment at the sheriff’s department. 
Other large expenditures for law enforcement include:

$268,600 from the city of South Charleston to its police department to reimburse previous costs for officers assigned to drug enforcement cases
$219,200 from the Wood County Commission to Whiteside Chevrolet to purchase police vehicles, though the number of cars purchased was not reported
$182,800 from the Wood County Commission to Axon Enterprises for law enforcement equipment and training
$176,000 from the Boone County Commission to purchase and utilize a new records management system for law enforcement

Use this table to see all law enforcement spending:
Jail bill spending grows by more than 600%
During fiscal year 2024, just three counties — Grant, Upshur and Clay counties — sent portions of their opioid settlement funds to cover jail bills, totaling about $519,000 total. 
For fiscal year 2025, these expenditures grew exponentially: 10 counties reported spending part of their settlement funds on jail bills, totaling more than $3.78 million, a 630% increase compared to the previous year. 
While Clay County reported spending all of the money it received on the jail bill, the amount of that expenditure was not included in its report and is not reflected in this analysis.
A full breakdown of jail bill spending is as follows:

Berkeley County: $1.16 million
Boone County: $604,000
Putnam County: $547,000
McDowell County: $499,000
Logan County: $366,000
Wyoming County: $261,000
Marion County: $159,700
Taylor County: $83,500

Counties spending money on the jail bills said in their reports that using the opioid funds to offset jail bill costs allows them to provide other governmental services that otherwise would not be feasible due to the large bills.
Jail bills are a recurring fee. Each county pays its jail bill at the same rate, but the totals differ depending on how many people from a county are being held at a regional jail. Until 2023, a cap was in place that limited the amount each county would be charged per an inmate at $48.25 per a day.
Without the cap, the cost for each person held in a regional jail is $54.48 per a day. Many counties report that jail bills are their highest annual expenses each year.
Equipment and infrastructure upgrades make up most EMS spending
Localities spent about 459% more in opioid settlement funds supporting EMS services in fiscal year 2025 compared to the previous year, totaling about $3.59 million compared to fiscal year 2024’s $643,000, per the report.
Most of these expenditures went toward upgrading equipment, stocking ambulances and firetrucks and general infrastructure needed for EMS services to run.
A total breakdown for EMS spending is as follows:

$1.5 million for communications and radio technology for dispatchers and responders
$1.36 million on equipment including new ambulances, medical equipment, medication, fire truck upgrades and more
$614,200 on infrastructure upgrades and expenses for existing and new EMS stations, including utility bills, contract services and more
$83,000 for training responders and dispatchers

Nearly one-third of all EMS spending in fiscal year 2025 came from Wayne County, per the report. There, the Wayne County Commission spent nearly $1.2 million across 64 expenditures, which included monthly payments to Jan-Care Ambulances for contracted EMS services, rent payments for two additional EMS locations, utility bills for those locations and various other associated costs.
In Kanawha County, the Kanawha County Commission paid a combined $1.5 million over two expenditures to replace a radio tower necessary for Metro 911 dispatchers to respond to calls.
Other large individual EMS expenditures include:

$434,000 from the Wayne County Commission to PennCare for the purchase of three new ambulances
$218,000 from the Boone County Commission to purchase two new rapid response vehicles
$168,300 from the Webster County Commission to Webster Memorial Hospital to purchase new ambulance equipment
$137,000 from the Wayne County Commission to ZOLL Medical Corporation for medical supplies, including defibrillators and more

Use this table to see all EMS-related spending by localities:
Programming support and more dominates spending for direct treatment, recovery services
Direct treatment and recovery services received about $2.95 million from local governments in FY2025, about a 161% increase compared to spending from the previous year, per the report.
Nearly one third of that spending went toward general program support for nonprofits and agencies that service people who use drugs and those in addiction recovery.
The full breakdown for recovery and treatment spending is as follows:

$983,000 for general support of nonprofits, including assistance in paying salaries, expanding services and increasing the amount of recovery beds available
$723,818 in specific treatment and recovery services, like offering new kinds of programs, increasing access to existing ones and more
$683,700 in transportation-related expenses for patients in treatment and recovery, including vans and vehicles to take clients to appointments
$234,500 for endeavors related to housing, including building new in-patient and recovery housing and providing placements for people with substance use disorder
$176,200 for harm reduction purchases, like naloxone, and medical assisted treatment for patients

Several localities gave a portion of their funds to helping expand existing services to confront debilitating gaps that can mean long wait times for those in need and few resources. In Monongalia County, the county commission gave $125,000 to help establish a new, 40-bed treatment facility in the community. 
The Harrison County Commission spent more than $110,000 — nearly $36,000 to Highland Hospital and $76,000 to Stars and Strides Therapeutic Equine Center — to establish an equine therapy program for those in recovery and their families. Through June 2025, the Harrison County Commission reported that 232 clients had benefitted from the services.
Other large expenditures for treatment and recovery include:

Nearly $250,000 from the Kanawha County Commission to Union Mission to purchase four vehicles to transport recovery residents and a storage building to secure the vehicles in
$217,000 from the Randolph County Commission to Ally’s Hope, Inc. to purchase and convert a home into a sober living facility
$200,000 from South Charleston to Thomas Hospitals to support existing addiction treatment efforts
$200,000 from Martinsburg to Eastridge Health Systems to pay operational start-up fees for a new eight-bed sober living center
$200,000 from the Berkeley County Commission, also to Eastridge Health Systems to start the new sober living center

Use this table to see all direct treatment and recovery expenditures:

Pickleball courts, flood recovery and more in community-based spending
Localities spent more than $1.4 million in opioid settlement funds on services and expenditures that directly affect whole communities, like equipment for disaster response, public services, infrastructure upgrades and more. 

A total breakdown of community-based spending is as follows:

$464,000 toward community services, including food pantries, support for people struggling and expanded nonprofit services, among others
$366,500 paid by the Berkeley County Commission for debt owed related to the expansion of its Day Report Center
$228,500 toward community infrastructure, including purchasing materials and equipment for local governments, replacing HVAC systems, demolishing homes and more
$209,200 on health services, like dental care and general support for hospitals and health departments
$183,700 for prevention education and programming
$38,300 for recreation-related expenses

Most of the community expenditures went toward nonprofits, which run food pantries, operate community meetings, distribute prevention materials and more.
For community infrastructure, Bluefield paid more than $51,00 to purchase a tandem truck to assist with cleanup efforts from Hurricane Helene as well as almost $8,000 to rent machinery. The city also paid $30,400 to demolish two homes in its downtown.
In the recreation category, Oceana spent $2,100 on a chili fest where city employees including police and firefighters worked to “foster better relationships” with the public. In Gilmer County, the county commission paid $36,200 to Erskine Pavement for the installation of a new pickleball court. The new court, per the report, can provide “therapeutic recreation” for those recovering from addiction.
Other large community-based expenditures include:

$350,000 from Huntington to support the Huntington City Mission. Details on the grant were not provided
$75,000 from the Nicholas County Commission to the Nicholas County Health Department for general support
$75,000 from Huntington to the Cabell-Huntington Coalition for the Homeless for program support
$63,500 from the Harrison County Commission to Healthy Harrison, a community initiative, to collect and disburse addiction impact stories

Use this table to view all community-based spending from fiscal year 2025:

Prevention education and school-based services make up most spending on children
From stage lighting and little league field upgrades to social workers and addiction intervention training, localities across West Virginia spent about 5.4% of funds in fiscal year 2025 on services for children. 
While the amount of money spent on youth-based services increased about 120% between fiscal year 2024 and fiscal year 2025 — up to $912,300 from last year’s $413,300 — the overall share of the spending decreased slightly compared to last year’s 6%.
A total breakdown for spending related to children is as follows:

$345,000 on prevention education efforts, including trainings and materials
$297,000 on school-based activities, including materials for kids, social workers, literacy programs and more
$154,400 on counseling services and other related interventions for children impacted by substance use disorder
$115,800 on recreation-related activities, like extracurriculars, after school programs, student celebrations and more

Last year, the politically-connected GameChanger program received a bulk of all opioid settlement spending related to children. That program was created in 2018 and is based on schools paying varying fees for prevention materials and a curriculum that experts have called questionable and based in fear, which are not conducive to lowering rates of drug use or overdose among students.
In fiscal year 2024, the program received $270,000 from Marion County schools to implement three years of programming at all public schools.
For fiscal year 2025, however, the GameChanger program saw a drastic reduction in payments. The only recorded example came from Harrison County, which gave the program $30,000 to expand programming in 14 of the county’s schools.
In recreation-related spending, two governments — Randolph County and Bluefield —paid $30,500 and $6,300 respectively to upgrade area little league fields. The Hardy County Commission paid $25,000 to the McCoy’s Grand Theater and Museum to install stage lights on the youth theater while Jackson County spent $10,000 to upgrade playground equipment and $20,000 on a children-focused museum.
Overall, the largest single expenditure for youth-related services came from the Mason County Commission, which paid almost $247,000 to the county board of education to hire social workers to work in schools. The social workers, per the report, will help students with counseling and provide connections to community services when needed.
Other large single expenditures for children include:

$130,700 from the Fayette County Commission to the county health department for youth-focused intervention and harm reduction programming
$90,000 from the Barbour County Commission in grants to local organizations. Per the report, 43 organizations received $1,500 grants and payments for transportation, programming, facilities and more.
$50,300 from the Monongalia County Commission to support an addiction intervention project for children
$50,000 from the Mingo County Commission to circulate drug prevention materials in local schools

Use this table to view all youth-based expenditures:
All other spending
While local governments spent more than $350,000 in fiscal year 2024 transferring money out of their opioid funds to cover general spending needs, no such expenditures were reported for fiscal year 2025.
Instead, in the “other” category are only two expenditures, both from the town of Mullens: $31,700 to purchase insurance for the city and $814 to pay dues for the Region 1 Planning and Development Council.
In total, $803 was paid by six localities in bank fees for managing their opioid settlement account or for purchasing checks.
The local opioid spending report is published by the West Virginia First Foundation annually. While this marks the second year of opioid settlement spending, there are still many localities who have not reported using a single dollar.
If you have concerns, comments or tips regarding how your local government is spending its settlement dollars, reach out to West Virginia Watch to speak to a reporter at info@WestVirginiaWatch.com



All the spending disclosed in this report was self-reported by the localities to the West Virginia First Foundation. The First Foundation, which is the private nonprofit that was created in 2023 to disburse the state’s share of opioid settlement dollars, has no control or power over how local governments spend their share of the funds. 
Appropriate uses for the opioid settlement funds are dictated by guidelines that were set through the court system and approved by the state attorney general in the state’s memorandum of understanding for spending the funds in 2023. Read here for more information on that MOU.
The spending detailed in this report is somewhat preliminary. Some localities did not explain their expenditures. Others did not send a report in at all.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Panel sets tentative pay increases for North Dakota lawmakers
description: A legislative planning committee on Monday advanced pay increases of 3% as a starting point for North Dakota lawmakers in each year of the upcoming two-year budget cycle. The Legislative Procedure and Arrangements Committee unanimously approved the numbers, which are for initial budgeting purposes and are not a final decision. That will come in the […]
text:
Sen. Jerry Klein, R-Fessenden, listens during a discussion of the Legislative Procedure and Arrangements Committee on Sept. 14, 2026. 
(Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)A legislative planning committee on Monday advanced pay increases of 3% as a starting point for North Dakota lawmakers in each year of the upcoming two-year budget cycle.
The Legislative Procedure and Arrangements Committee unanimously approved the numbers, which are for initial budgeting purposes and are not a final decision. That will come in the 2027 Legislature. The committee mostly comprises Republican and Democratic-NPL House and Senate floor leaders. 
Senate Minority Leader Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, who will retire before the next legislative session begins in January, proposed the “3 and 3” as “very reasonable,” citing the rate of inflation.
Committee chair Sen. Jerry Klein, R-Fessenden, said, “That number would be adjusted as per whatever the Legislature finally adopts.”
The cost of the 3% increases would be $414,718 for the next budget cycle, including monthly, daily session, interim meeting and leaders’ additional monthly pay, according to a legislative memo.
North Dakota’s state government operates on a two-year budget cycle beginning July 1 of every odd-numbered year. The 2025 Legislature adopted pay raises of 3% and 3% in the two years of the 2025-27 budget cycle. Raises for state employees and lawmakers are traditionally the same rate.
North Dakota lawmakers approve needs, some wants with $20.3 billion budget

The House and Senate appropriations committees usually jointly adopt the rates for what percentage pay increases to make for state employees and lawmakers after hearing financial projections. State revenues and inflation are key factors for budget writers in that decision, said Senate Majority Leader David Hogue, R-Minot.
“You’ve got to put a number in a blank, so we put in 3,” he said of Monday’s decision.
General fund revenues – tax collections that fund the state government’s main operating account – are about 1% below the forecast set by the Legislature one year into the 2025-27 budget cycle, according to legislative and executive branch reports released last month. That means the general fund did not collect about $37 million that lawmakers had projected amid more than $3 billion collected overall so far. 
Sales taxes are the biggest revenue driver of the general fund, which also includes oil tax revenue, individual and corporate income taxes and other revenue types.
Last year, the Republican-led Legislature approved a $6.26 billion two-year general fund. 
In December, Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong will present his state government budget blueprint to the Legislature, which will include his administration’s recommendation for pay increases, governor’s spokesman Mike Nowatzki said. 
Governor proposes cuts to North Dakota budget to prevent ‘slow burning storm’

Earlier this year, Armstrong asked state agencies to trim their budget requests by as much as 10%. His budget guidelines also included a hiring freeze. A round of buyouts earlier this year led 101 state employees in 14 agencies to part ways with the state.
The 2025 Legislature set the following compensation and reimbursement rates for lawmakers: 

$628 for monthly pay
$226 for daily session and daily interim meeting pay
$110 per day plus tax, up to $2,475 per month for session lodging of lawmakers who live outside of Bismarck-Mandan
$110 per day plus tax for interim lodging
76 cents per mile for travel reimbursement, not including out-of-state or private airplane travel
Up to $45 per day for in-state interim meals expenses
$200 per month for a broadband and mobile data stipend

Additionally, legislative leaders and the Legislative Management chair earn $450 per month. Legislative Management is a powerful committee of lawmakers that guides the Legislature between biennial sessions.
Leaders and committee chairs earn $10 to $20 per day. 
Lawmakers’ compensation package is fair, Hogue said.
“I know there are some that would like more, but to them I would say it’s public service,” he said in an interview. 
From 1889 until 1983, North Dakota lawmakers were paid $5 per calendar day during sessions, as well as varying expense reimbursements over the years, according to another legislative memo.

text:
Members of the DSPC, state and federal legislature and Enstructure pose for a photo at the groundbreaking ceremony for the Delaware Container Terminal. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
Members of the state legislature, Enstructure and the Diamond State Port Corporation gathered to celebrate the groundbreaking of the Delaware Container Terminal on September 14.
 
WILMINGTON, DE — Community leaders and members of Enstructure and the Diamond State Port Corporation (DSPC) gathered together at the site of the Delaware Container Terminal, Monday morning, to officially break ground on the port project. 
The Delaware Container Terminal is intended to be a new container port located along the Delaware River at the former Edgemoor industrial site that was home to a DuPont chemical plant, up until its closure in 2015. The new terminal is a public-private partnership venture between Enstructure and the DSPC, and is expected to increase Delaware’s container handling capacity by a significant amount, according to an official press release from Enstructure following the event.
The groundbreaking ceremony took place on the project site and hosted a plethora of speakers integral in the project’s development. The first speaker and host of the day’s program was Delaware Secretary of State and DSPC Board Chair, Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez. Patibanda-Sanchez was followed by Delaware Governor Matt Meyer, United States Senator Chris Coons, a video message from United States Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester and in-person remarks from United States Representative Sarah McBride. 
A project rendering of what the completed Delaware Container Terminal project may resemble. Photo Credit: Enstructure
State Senators Darius Brown and Jack Walsh spoke after Rep. McBride and State Representative Franklin Cooke followed the senators, telling those assembled together that the port project was special to him because of his familial ties to working at port locations, including the Port of Wilmington. State Rep. Cooke said that for four generations a member of his family had worked at the port, including himself. 
The President of the International Longshoreman’s Association 1694, William Ashe Jr., spoke next followed by the Executive Director of the Bellevue Community Center, Daniel Elkins and Co-CEOs of Enstructure, Matthew Satnick and Philippe De Montigny. 
The overarching theme from all the speakers was an optimism of how the project will positively impact Delaware’s economic footprint both in terms of local job creation and global commerce.
“This is really big for our community,” Gov. Meyer said. “This is something that’s going to create thousands of jobs. It takes a whole lot of investment from the private sector, from the public sector. I would anticipate that not everyone’s going to be for it, but we’re going to push forward. We’re listening to the community. My appointments to the port board reflect that we are not just sitting back and listening to what the neighbors have to say, we’re out there actively soliciting. We want to hear them. They’re part of this project too.”
The project is expected to create thousands of jobs in sectors such as maritime, construction, supply chain and logistics, according to Enstructure. The port will be able to welcome in larger ships due to the expected development that will increase water depth to 45 feet and about half a mile in waterfront docking space at the project’s full-scale.
The port is being designed as a “green port facility” in an effort to reduce the infrastructure’s impact on the surrounding environment. The port will use electric powered equipment such as electric gantry cranes to handle cargo and it will also incorporate “low-emission operating practices”, according to Enstructure. The project will use funding from the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Clean Ports Program to support their efforts in “the collection and analysis of operational data to measure results and refine implementation over time.”
The project isn’t supported by everyone in the local community. 
A group of protestors gathered in front of the project site holding signs that asked for a stop to the project. Patibanda-Sanchez acknowledged the group while speaking to the audience assembled at the groundbreaking ceremony, saying that the DSPC will continue working with the local community to try and mitigate the impact on the community as the site cleanup and development proceeds.
“This was a heavily polluted site for a long time,” Sen. Coons said. “It was a titanium dioxide plant under DuPont’s ownership, and dioxin is very dangerous. It’s a contaminating chemical. So, I think there are legitimate community concerns that need to be addressed as the cleanup proceeds, but I also think having a new state-of-the-art container terminal on this river, a dream that’s been invested in and built towards for now 15 years is well worth doing for the high quality union jobs it will produce for generations in Delaware.”
The port is expected to be open in early 2029, according to Enstructure.

title: Some inconvenient truths about an inconvenient subject
description: There are many reasons that a heck of a lot of people in 21st Century North Carolina – a modern, wealthy, high-tech society of more than 11 million – regularly face a harsh reality usually associated with impoverished third world nations: hunger and malnutrition. Topping the list: poverty. More than 12% of North Carolinians live […]
text:
Volunteers box up food donations at the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina. (Courtesy: FBCENC)There are many reasons that a heck of a lot of people in 21st Century North Carolina – a modern, wealthy, high-tech society of more than 11 million – regularly face a harsh reality usually associated with impoverished third world nations: hunger and malnutrition.
Topping the list: poverty. More than 12% of North Carolinians live below the absurdly low official poverty line. When one looks at what it really takes to get by, the number of folks in need is vastly higher.
And then, of course, there are an array of other related and contributing factors,
There’s the fact that a big chunk of the population is either very young or very old and typically dependent upon someone else – family, friends, public assistance, charity – to help them secure the calories they need. At last count, roughly a quarter of the population was either age 17 or younger or 85 or older.
There’s the fact that as many as a third of adults and more than 200,000 children have a disability (i.e., a physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental health condition – many of which make day-to-day living more difficult).
There’s the fact that as many as a fifth of North Carolinians do not live in close proximity to a real grocery store – what the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) classifies as a “food desert.”
There is the fact that many people of modest means – like their wealthier neighbors – find themselves in personal crises. They live in households harmed by a natural disaster, unemployment, a health emergency, or a broken marriage.
There is the undeniable fact that in some households, the situation is made worse by destructive human behavior – be it substance abuse, gambling addiction, domestic violence, or just plain old poor choices.
And arching over all of this – particularly during the last several months — is the fact that prices for all kinds of basic goods have soared at rates far in excess of wage growth.
Together, all these factors and others have combined to create what can only be described as a truly scandalous situation and crisis for one of the wealthiest societies in human history. According to the most recent USDA data – which actually predates the rampant inflation of 2026 – more than 1.5 million North Carolinians, including one of every five children and teens – lived in a “food insecure” home. What’s more, the numbers have skyrocketed in recent years and now exceed where they stood during the depths of the COVID-19 pandemic.
So, what gives? How did we work ourselves into this dreadful situation and what can and should we do about it?
I recently posed these questions to a pair of nonprofit leaders and experts who’ve spent many years on the frontline in the hunger wars – Amy Beros, President of the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina, and Liz Reasoner, Chief Executive Officer of the Food Bank of the Albemarle – and their overarching answer may come as a surprise.
Yes, dramatically increasing public and private support for groups like theirs — food banks, food pantries and other charitable anti-hunger nonprofits — would help. Both Beros and Reasoner told me that their organizations have been struggling mightily in recent months to keep up with soaring demand from people in need even as their costs for things like the fuel that goes into their trucks has forced them to pinch pennies like never before, and in some instances, reduce services. September is Hunger Action Month, so if you can contribute to a food bank, please do so.
But what both leaders also made plain in our conversation (listen to the full interview by clicking here) is that the only remotely plausible source of a real solution to the current hunger crisis is the federal government. For as much amazing and impactful work as the food banks and other charities do, it pales in comparison to the impact of the federal SNAP (formerly food stamps) program.
As Beros told me, “For every one meal a food bank provides, SNAP provides nine.” What’s more, thanks to massive cuts inflicted on SNAP (which takes up a little more than 1% of the federal budget) by the Trump administration and its congressional allies, the situation has gotten much worse of late. Beros reports that more than 100,000 North Carolinians have been dropped from the SNAP program in just the past year.
Now add to this that the federal cuts have cost food banks around 15% of the food they used to receive from the USDA – not to mention the damage inflicted on a lot of farmers and retailers by shrinking their markets – and the connection between the current mess and the situation in Washington becomes even clearer.
The bottom line: Food insecurity in 2026 North Carolina is a vexing and complicated problem, but any meaningful effort to address it simply must involve restoring, and ultimately, dramatically increasing federal funding for SNAP and similar programs. Pretending that we can make any meaningful difference without doing so is simply delusional.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: We can’t stop Idaho from growing, but with more housing options, we can choose how
description: Every week, public hearings across the Treasure Valley and beyond fill up with an emerging voice: residents, many of whom moved here in the last five to ten years, showing up to vote down housing options their communities need. They organize, vote, and pressure local officials to reject more housing. I understand where that instinct […]
text:
In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening, writes guest columnist Ali Rabe. (Photo by Getty Images)Every week, public hearings across the Treasure Valley and beyond fill up with an emerging voice: residents, many of whom moved here in the last five to ten years, showing up to vote down housing options their communities need. They organize, vote, and pressure local officials to reject more housing. 
I understand where that instinct comes from. I just don’t think it’s pointing us toward the right answer.
Idaho leads the nation in housing growth. The data shows it’s still not enough.

I grew up in Middleton, surrounded by farm fields. Those fields are gone now, replaced by one-acre lots with little infrastructure to support them. I’ve watched Idaho change in ways that make me sad, and I understand the anti-growth mindset. Too often growth here has meant sprawl, distant subdivisions, and longer commutes.
But growth itself isn’t the enemy. Communities grow and change, and that change can make a place better, not worse. The Treasure Valley will keep growing. The question is how.
During my nearly seven years leading Jesse Tree, the Treasure Valley’s eviction prevention nonprofit, I watched more and more Idahoans lose their footing here. People who worked full time couldn’t make rent, families were evicted, and some ended up homeless.
In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening. Meanwhile, most of what gets built on our fringe is the same product: large-lot homes pushing half a million dollars, aimed at out-of-state buyers. 
Young Idahoans, our workforce, and longtime locals are left out.
There’s a better path, and it isn’t new. It’s called missing middle housing, and it’s a return to how Idaho used to build.
Missing middle housing means duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes, cottage courts, and small-lot homes woven into existing neighborhoods rather than dropped onto the fringe. It’s gentle, incremental density that adds homes without ruining a neighborhood’s character.
 Look at Idaho’s historic neighborhoods and you’ll find these home types everywhere. This is how our cities grew before exclusionary zoning took hold in the 1970s and made large-lot sprawl the only easy path for developers.
It’s also better economics, for residents and for cities. Land is the single largest cost on a developer’s pro forma. When zoning only allows large-lot product, that cost gets baked into every home, which is why half-million-dollar houses keep getting built. 
Smaller homes on smaller lots bring that cost down and open the door to starter homes again. For cities, more homes per acre means more property value per acre without miles of new pipes, roads, and schools. It’s a better deal for taxpayers on both ends.
None of this requires upending the neighborhoods people love. In my experience, when people see what missing middle housing actually is, rather than what they assume it is, most come around. Even hearing opponents soften once they realize it isn’t a five-story apartment complex next door. It’s a duplex that looks like the house beside it.
I don’t fault anyone for wanting to protect what they love about this place. I love it too, farm fields and all. But protecting Idaho doesn’t mean freezing it in place, and it certainly doesn’t mean a housing market that only works for people who aren’t from here. 
It means asking a better question: how do we grow in a way that gives our young people, our workforce, and our own neighbors a shot at homeownership?
Missing middle housing is one of the clearest answers we have. If you want to help make the case in your community, Gem State Housing Alliance is activating pro-housing voices across the state, and we’d love to welcome you.

text:
Students work in a classroom  in Salt Lake City in 2024. The Alabama Public Charter School Commission Monday approved its first merger application and two charter school renewal applications. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The Alabama Public Charter School Commission Monday approved its first merger application and renewals for two charter schools.
The commission approved the newly-created merger policy in July to allow two or more schools to combine. Invictus Academy, which was set to open in 2027, and Alabama Aerospace and Aviation High School became the first schools to submit an application to merge. The application was approved with minimal discussion. No details about the merger were given during the meeting.
Ruben Morris, founder of Alabama Aerospace and Aviation High School, said during the meeting the merger will ensure the Bessemer area has “viable options” for schooling.
“Bessemer is a small community where I get to share this work with Dr. (Meredith Davis, superintendent of Empower Community School) and she’s doing a great job at Empower, and we want to make sure that students in this community have viable options, and that there’s no unnecessary competition for enrollment, and that when we’ve got great options available around career and technical education, and career connected learning, that we present this in a way that best suits kids,” he said.
The commission renewed a charter school contract for ACCELL Evening and Day Academy, located in Mobile, for another five years with no discussion. Empower Community School’s renewal was also approved, but Commissioner Cynthia McCarty raised concerns about the school’s math scores.
“Their math scores are a little bit disappointing,” McCarty said. “And there are so many supports out there in the Numeracy Act, and with math coaches, with professional development for teachers, and I would just ask that you provide them with a solid plan so that they have the resources that they need the professional development, the curriculum, whatever it might be, that would help them to be able to raise those math achievement scores.”
Empower Superintendent Meredith Davis, agreed that math scores need improvement but said the school is using resources to help push the scores in the right direction.
“We have made some progress over the last couple of years, but we are working with the Office of Math Instruction, the Numeracy Act,” Davis said. “We do have a math coach in place, and we utilize the state curriculum and purchase outside coaching for our teachers in the area of math and professional development to try to close those gaps.”

title: Tennessee families must earn 85%-164% more than federal poverty limit to get by, new study finds
description: The income a Tennessee family needs to pay for necessities such as food, housing and childcare far surpassed the federal poverty threshold, according to an analysis by The Sycamore Institute, a nonpartisan think tank. The analysis found that basic necessities in Tennessee cost significantly more than those living at the poverty line can afford. The […]
text:
A new report by The Sycamore Institute finds Tennessee families who earn more than the federal poverty limit still struggle to pay for basic needs. Food banks across Tennessee and pop-up food pantries work to fill gaps. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The income a Tennessee family needs to pay for necessities such as food, housing and childcare far surpassed the federal poverty threshold, according to an analysis by The Sycamore Institute, a nonpartisan think tank.
The analysis found that basic necessities in Tennessee cost significantly more than those living at the poverty line can afford. The poverty threshold is a metric set by the federal government to establish a minimum “survival budget.” It often forms the basis for determining whether families are poor enough to qualify for certain public benefits.
In Tennessee, more than 40% of households struggled to afford basic needs in 2024, the study found. The report also found the cost of those basic needs – such as housing, childcare and food –  in Tennessee has increased faster than inflation since 2019.
The study relied on Census data and a methodology known as “ALICE” that was designed as an alternative to the federal poverty level metric to account for a broader range of common expenses families incur to get by. 
It found that the estimated costs of basic needs varied widely by county. Families in Williamson, Wilson, Rutherford, Trousdale and Roberton counties incurred the highest costs for necessities; families in Lincoln, Campbell, Claiborne, Clay and Benton Counties incurred the lowest. 
The report also found that wages and income in Tennessee grew faster than inflation. Median household income grew by more than 28% between 2019 and 2024.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Democratic Senate hopeful Jamie Davis avoids GOP talk at LSU voter event
description: LSU students gathered Monday for a standing room-only discussion on the importance of voting with Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Jamie Davis, ahead of National Voter Registration Day.
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Jamie Davis, left, speaks with Malachi Mays, vice president of Geaux Vote LSU, a nonpartisan student organization. The group invited Davis to its event Monday, Sept. 12, 2026, at the Manship School of Mass Communication. (Photo by Julia O'Donoghue/Louisiana Illuminator)LSU students gathered Monday for a standing room-only discussion on the importance of voting with Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Jamie Davis, ahead of National Voter Registration Day. 
“If you don’t exercise your right to vote, you just muffled your own voice,” Davis, a farmer from Waterproof, told students at LSU’s Journalism Building. “You cannot complain when you don’t exercise your right,” 

Davis, 55, who served on the police jury in remote Tensas Parish, faces Republican Congresswoman Julia Letlow of Baton Rouge in an uphill battle on Nov. 3. Incumbent U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy was knocked out of the race in May’s GOP primary and must step down in January. 

The nonpartisan Geaux Vote LSU student organization has also invited Letlow to speak, but her campaign has not committed to an appearance date, said Malachi Mays, the group’s vice president. 

Letlow’s campaign did not answer questions Monday about whether she plans to meet with LSU students on campus ahead of the November election. 

“We hope the [Letlow] campaign will come to LSU,” Mays said in an interview.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 

Davis’ appearance was organized by Geaux Vote, LSU’s Black Student Union and the Black Girls Vote organization. 

Davis went out of his way to remain “nonpartisan” in his remarks to the students. He never criticized President Donald Trump or brought up Letlow’s name, and he rarely talked about Republicans during the event.

Trying to appeal to students, Davis recalled attending LSU himself though he didn’t graduate. Davis said he left school early to work when he found out he was going to be a father. 

The candidate spoke extensively about the need to overhaul the federal student loan system, which the Trump administration recently revamped to be more restrictive. Millions of students who took out student loans will now have to make higher payments monthly for the loans to be forgiven.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Jamie Davis gestures as he speaks Monday, Sept. 12, 2026, during an event hosted by Geaux Vote LSU, a nonpartisan student organization. The group’s vice president, LSU junior Malachi Mays, stands behind Davis, who faces U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, in the Nov. 3 election. (Photo by Julia O’Donoghue/Louisiana Illuminator)
 Rules for borrowers should not change in the middle of the repayment process, Davis said, adding that there should be more generous student loan forgiveness for people who choose to work in rural areas like his home Tensas Parish. 

Davis also said he has “acted a clown” during parts of his campaign in an attempt to reach younger voters. For example, he referenced silly social media videos he’s posted in the hopes that they will resonate with college students.  
Many students who attended the forum said they will vote for the first time in the November when Davis and Letlow are on the ballot. 
Madelyn Broussard, a LSU senior, said she’s worried about rising gas and grocery prices. She said she’s also opposed to recently announced industrial projects in Louisiana, such as the SpaceX launch facility in Vermilion Parish and data centers in rural areas.

Louisiana should not be “selling off our wetlands to be destroyed,” Broussard said. 

Tyler Wood, a freshman, said he worries about the impact of artificial intelligence and corporate spending in politics. More transparency is needed around the enormous Meta data center project being built in Richland Parish, near where Davis lives, Wood said. 

Sarah Bailey, a junior who leads the Black Student Union, said she was looking for a politician with an authentic voice. 

“I don’t want to be sold dreams. I want something that is realistic,” Bailey said. “I just want to know who’s keeping it real.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Taylor aims to rein in private equity in healthcare, restore Medicaid funding and ACA subsidies
description: Shannon Taylor, the Democratic nominee for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District representative, wants to restore healthcare funding and resources slashed by the Republican-controlled Congress over the past year, she said at a roundtable alongside care workers and union leaders in Henrico Monday afternoon. Taylor, who was first elected to her current role as[...]
text:
Democratic nominee for Virginia's 1st Congressional District Shannon Taylor speaks during a roundtable event in Henrico County on Sep. 14, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Shannon Taylor, the Democratic nominee for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District representative, wants to restore healthcare funding and resources slashed by the Republican-controlled Congress over the past year, she said at a roundtable alongside care workers and union leaders in Henrico Monday afternoon.
Taylor, who was first elected to her current role as Henrico County Commonwealth’s Attorney in 2011 and who is vying to unseat longtime Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, said she would also explore ways to more tightly regulate private equity in healthcare, if elected. 
“No private equity should be profiting off of people’s healthcare and their health situation,” Taylor said. “It’s just morally wrong.” 
The issue surfaced in Virginia earlier this year, when Valley Health trimmed services at one of its hospitals and  changed staffing contracts, enabling a private equity firm to take over certain staffing decisions at all six of the health system’s hospitals in Virginia and West Virginia. 
The move is meant to reduce Valley Health’s spending by over $80 million annually. 
Valley Health joined a growing list of Virginian hospitals or clinics that recently reduced services, citing changes to Medicaid and hospital funding mechanisms that will strain their budgets in the months and years ahead due to H.R. 1, the federal spending bill passed last year. 
Taylor cautioned against the hiring-and-firing tactics that can ensue once private equity firms enter healthcare spaces, and said facility staff may be replaced with different positions at lower salaries. 
If Taylor defeats Wittman, who is seeking an eighth term in Congress and has supported the healthcare cuts levied by H.R.1, she will pursue legislation to  “get private equity out of the healthcare equation,” she said. 
“(We should) start from a premise that there should be no one getting rich off people getting sick — period. Then we’ll see what that looks like moving forward,” she added.
 Taylor’s healthcare goals: Unraveling the ‘big beautiful bill’ and restoring ACA credits

Democratic nominee for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District Shannon Taylor listens to area resident Catherine Rey during a roundtable event in Henrico County on Sep. 14, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
Virginia and other states have already invested money into compliance with the forthcoming federal changes and strategized methods to prevent eligible people from losing their assistance. 
Roughly 300,000 Virginians are at risk of losing coverage next year, while 5,800 lawful immigrants will no longer be eligible for Medicaid by October. Hospitals predict a $31 billion loss in Medicaid over the next decade, and 13 rural hospitals will be more vulnerable to closures or service cuts. 
Congress also failed to extend expired Affordable Care Act subsidies that help low-income earners be able to purchase health insurance through state ACA marketplaces. 
Wittman was one of few Republicans nationwide to join Democrats in support of extending the subsidies; the measure failed in the Senate. Prior to that aisle-crossing, Wittman had previously voted 60 times to repeal the ACA.
Wittman voted 60 times to undo the Affordable Care Act, then he backed extending its subsidies

At Monday’s event, Taylor criticized him for these moves and for voting to pass H.R. 1.
A key priority for Taylor if she takes Wittman’s seat will be “to make sure we are putting this funding back in place,” she said. 
Several of Taylor’s would-be constituents shared their personal concerns about healthcare policy at the roundtable.
When Central Virginian Melissa Earley faced a cancer battle, her partner cared for her. Now, her partner can’t work due to a traumatic brain injury and Earley is her caregiver. 
“She tells me everyday ‘I wish I could go back to work,’ but literally she can’t,” Earley said.
Medicaid coverage has helped the couple, but their finances have still been tight. At one point they had to appeal losing their waiver. The couple fears that additional Medicaid cuts could threaten their ability to maintain shelter.
“We almost lost our house. You can’t heal or you can’t stay healthy if you lose a home,” Earley said. 
Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration predicts a $2 billion to $6 billion loss in revenue to the state each year starting in 2028 amid the federal Medicaid changes. 
Catherine Rey had to become a permanent caregiver for her two sons that were born with ATR-X syndrome, which causes physical and intellectual disabilities. Rey’s children will need to live at home with specialized care for the rest of their lives.
“We’re 14 years in, which has felt like a long time, but it’s just a drop compared to a lifetime that we have ahead of us,” she said at the roundtable. 
A specialized Medicaid waiver allows Rey to be reimbursed as a worker for the full-time care, but she called H.R. 1 a “big betrayal bill” due to the financial “pressures” it puts onto states. 
“Every state is going to have to contend with ‘how are we going to make up for the loss of (Medicaid) funding?’” Rey explained.
Rey said she fears support for home care workers or community-based services to help her sons could become “optional” in future state budgets, which must now cover healthcare costs that used to be borne by the federal government.
Spanberger issued an executive order to help state and local social service agencies manage the increased workloads and foster collaboration with community-based organizations. 
The state’s budget has also earmarked hundreds of millions in its state budget over the next two years to support  H.R.1 compliance and a temporary state-level version of the expired ACA subsidies. 
As Taylor traverses the district in the months leading up to Election Day, she said the rising cost of living is a top concern for voters in both Democratic- and Republican-leaning areas. 
She connected spiking gas and fertilizer prices to healthcare costs, noting that none of the issues “exist in a silo.”
“The way I’ve always conducted myself and will continue to conduct myself, is to understand that things are very multifaceted,”Taylor said.
Voters will head to the polls Nov. 3 to elect Virginia’s next slate of congressional representatives. Early voting begins Friday.

description: Federal lawmakers will consider a proposal to reduce congestion around Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, one of the busiest aviation hubs in the nation. No survivors found in crash between military helicopter and jet over Potomac River near DC Virginia’s U.S. Sens. Tim Kaine and Mark Warner, both Democrats, announced the DCA Air […]
text:
Reagan National Airport.  (Photo by Skyhobo / Getty Images)Federal lawmakers will consider a proposal to reduce congestion around Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, one of the busiest aviation hubs in the nation.
No survivors found in crash between military helicopter and jet over Potomac River near DC

Virginia’s U.S. Sens. Tim Kaine and Mark Warner, both Democrats, announced the DCA Air Safety Act on Thursday, after the completion of the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation of the deadly 2025 crash near the airport between an American Airlines Bombardier jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter over the Potomac River.
The crash killed 67 people including the pilots, crew members and passengers, some of whom were from Virginia.
The senators’ proposal would cap hourly arrivals, reduce flight clustering, and the specific time windows for flights to take off or land. 
Kaine said in a statement that Congress must do more to ensure that the “highest level” of safety regulations are in place to prevent future tragedies.
“While I support various proposals to help do that, it’s obvious that any set of reforms that doesn’t address overcrowding at this airport—which sits along restricted airspace and is already operating beyond capacity—is dangerously insufficient,” said Kaine, in a statement. 
He added that his bill lays out a “commonsense plan” to curb hourly arrivals and reduce flight clustering and overall traffic. 
The legislation would cap hourly arrivals by requiring the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to reduce DCA’s Airport Arrival Rate to no more than 28 aircraft per consecutive 60-minute period, thereby decreasing the likelihood of a collision.
Following the crash, the FAA said the rate at the time was 32 and dropped to 30 by the summer.
The legislation would also prevent too many planes from taking off or landing at the same time. Within 180 days, airports would have to set limits for each 30-minute period so flights are spread out more evenly throughout the hour.
The proposal would remove 30 flight slots over five years to reduce overcrowding at the airport. Then, starting in 2028, six slots would be removed each year, including at least 26 flights that are currently allowed to exceed the airport’s 1,250-mile distance limit, with all changes completed by the end of 2032.
A mandatory public process from the FAA  — including publishing a proposed list of slots to be eliminated — a 60-day public comment period, and publishing a final list within 120 days after the public comment period closes are also key requirements stipulated by the bill.
The focus on flights comes from the NTSB’s investigation, which found that on the night of the collision, one air traffic controller was responsible for managing 29 separate aircraft during an 18-minute period.
Since 2000, the senators said the airport has added 64 daily flights.
Congress owes it to the victims of the crash to act and prevent another case from occurring again at one of the busiest airports in the country, Warner said. 
There have been several near-misses close to the airport since last year’s crash, including one occurring a month afterward and a second involving a plane carrying President Donald Trump.
“For years, Senator Kaine and I have been warning that DCA is overcrowded and have fought to reduce the number of slot exemptions at the airport. The risks are now painfully clear, and Congress cannot wait for another tragedy to act,” Warner said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Cybertruck owners take a heavy toll on the Pell Bridge. And pay one too.
description: Gresh Laing’s 2024 Tesla Cybertruck gets plenty of attention on Rhode Island’s roads. Most of it isn’t friendly. “I get more middle fingers and thumbs-downs and just looks of disdain and hate, having this vehicle drive me around Rhode Island, than I have ever experienced in my entire life,” he said in an interview. The […]
text:
Gresh Laing is shown with his Tesla Cybertruck on the Goat Island Causeway in Newport. The Pell Bridge, across which he commutes each workday, is in the distance. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)
Gresh Laing’s 2024 Tesla Cybertruck gets plenty of attention on Rhode Island’s roads. Most of it isn’t friendly.
“I get more middle fingers and thumbs-downs and just looks of disdain and hate, having this vehicle drive me around Rhode Island, than I have ever experienced in my entire life,” he said in an interview.
The West Virginia native who served 23 years in the Navy admits he wasn’t in a rush to buy a Cybertruck when it first hit the market in 2023, saying it looks like “a 6‑year‑old’s drawing of the future.” He wound up buying a pre‑owned one in May after researching EV trucks on the market and quickly came to love the way the Cybertruck drives.
It’s high off the road, packed with safety features, and can self-drive him across the Pell Bridge from his home in North Kingstown to the naval base in Newport where he now helps design training programs for Navy recruits. Laing, 50, also saw the electric truck as a way to help cut emissions, in line with Rhode Island’s lofty climate goals. 
Then his E-ZPass account started refreshing more frequently.
“I noticed that it happened twice in one month,” Laing said. “So I opened up my account to sort of do a forensic analysis of my transponder and saw that it was $4 every time I went across the bridge.”
Rhode Island passenger vehicles with E-ZPasses pay a discounted toll rate of 83 cents to cross the Pell Bridge, a rate the Turnpike and Bridge Authority set when electronic tolling began in 2008. But that discount only applies to vehicles below 8,000 pounds gross vehicle weight. 
“Heavier vehicles (over 8,000 pounds) cause more damage to the bridges so they are not eligible for discounts,” Cara Cromwell, a spokesperson for the Rhode Island Bridge and Turnpike Authority, said in an emailed statement.
Cybertrucks range from 8,199 pounds to 9,169 pounds gross vehicle weight, depending on their configuration. That heft is partly a product of its battery, explained Christian Roselund, a member of Climate Action Rhode Island’s leadership team.
Roselund said the EV industry has largely settled on two types of lithium-ion batteries: nickel manganese cobalt (nmc) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP). NMC batteries are generally more energy-dense, while LFP batteries — which the Cybertruck uses — have historically required more weight to store the same amount of energy.
“Heavier vehicles disproportionately damage and wear out our roads,” Roselund said. “Tolling vehicles based upon weight makes sense.”
One study published October 2025 by New York University’s Tandon School of Engineering found that projected adoption of electric trucks could increase pavement and bridge damage costs in New York City by up to 12%, or about $500,000.
Laing doesn’t dispute the fact that heavier vehicles wear out roads faster and acknowledges the bridge’s road surface is pocked with patches and rough spots. 
But he says it feels backward for a state that’s pushed its residents toward electric cars to continue to charge them extra at the Pell Bridge just because their batteries add more weight — especially since battery-powered EV owners now pay a $200 registration fee as of last year to make up for missing gas tax revenue. Rhode Island’s gas tax is 41 cents per gallon, with proceeds supporting the state’s roads, bridges and mass transit.
Congress is also considering a federal annual fee on electric vehicles, including $130 for battery EVs and $35 for plug-in hybrids.
“If the state really wants to encourage people to have electric vehicles, then there might be a carveout for the fact that the batteries that operate electric vehicles are heavier,” Laing said.
Gresh Laing wipes fingerprints from his computer screen before taking a ride in his Tesla Cybertruck through Newport. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)
Another bridge to cross later?
Over the summer, Laing brought his concerns to his elected officials, who said they would follow up with the Rhode Island Turnpike and Bridge Authority. Rep. Robert Craven, a North Kingstown Democrat who is retiring at the end of the year, said he would like to see the quasi-governmental agency review whether its toll structure makes sense for noncommercial EV trucks.
“He shouldn’t be charged more than you and I for crossing the bridge,” Craven said. “Yes, it probably weighs considerably more, but there are so few of them that this seems to be discriminatory in nature.”
Robert Craven Jr., won the Democratic primary for the House District 32 seat his father has held since 2013 and is unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election. Craven Jr. said state transportation officials should consider whether its tolls are discouraging people from buying electric vehicles.
“There has to be a conversation about ways we incentivize people to purchase green vehicles,” Craven Jr. said.
Registration data provided by the Rhode Island Division of Motor Vehicles show 289 electric passenger trucks in the state, of which 24 are Tesla Cybertrucks.

Roselund argues there may be a stronger case for exempting electric trucks that are used by tradespeople, rather than passenger vehicles such as the Laing’s Cybertruck.
“I don’t have a lot of sympathy for Cybertruck owners,” Roselund said. “They bought a very large, heavy vehicle that is frankly dangerous because of its inability to see over the dash — it’s dangerous to children.”
Laing says he understands why critics worry about the size and weight of vehicles like his, but safety is the very reason he chose to buy a Cybertruck. It has nine cameras and two artificial intelligence “brains” that constantly scan its surroundings and can handle most of the driving, even detecting when a pedestrian waves it through an intersection.
“It will make the roads much safer when there’s greater adoption,” Laing said.



Quotation







I don't have a lot of sympathy for Cybertruck owners. They bought a very large, heavy vehicle that is frankly dangerous because of its inability to see over the dash — it's dangerous to children.


– Christian Roselund, energy policy analyst and leadership team member of Climate Action Rhode Island


Laing believes a lot of the anti-Cybertruck sentiment has less to do with how the truck actually performs on the road than with what it looks like and what people think it represents: Tesla CEO Elon Musk’s foray into partisan politics and work with the Trump administration.
But Laing said buyers like him aren’t necessarily thinking about Musk’s politics when they buy one. He said he “was not really pleased with” Musk’s political involvement because he believes the controversial CEO has “a fiduciary responsibility to remain out of that kind of business.”
“They want a large vehicle that’s capable of towing 11,000 pounds with 3,000 pounds in the bed, and going zero to 60 in 2.9 seconds, and having an autonomous chauffeur,” he said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: New commission works to untangle challenges at health licensing boards
description: After state audits reported inadequate response times by some health licensing boards to complaints about licensees, and other boards behind on healthcare facility inspections, lawmakers set up a new commission to address the issues causing those oversight issues.
text:
Del. Anne R. Kaiser (D-Montgomery) is co-chair of a new commission tasked with helping health occupations boards  improve administrative challenges. A Senate co-chair has yet to be named. (Photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)When Marylanders go to the doctor or see a nurse, they expect the professionals treating them have been properly vetted by state officials, and their facilities meet health and safety standards.
But after state audits reported inadequate response times by some licensing boards to complaints about licensees, and other boards that were behind on annual inspections of healthcare facilities, lawmakers responded with a new commission to iron out the challenges contributing to those oversight issues.
After an organizational meeting this summer, and a second where board directors laid out the issues they are facing, the Maryland Health Centralization Commission met virtually Monday to discuss the first of those issues, information technology challenges.
The commission has until Dec. 1 to report on ways to improve “efficiency, transparency and accountability” of the occupational licensing boards, a report that will be required annually thereafter.
“Everyone comes into these commissions with the end goal of doing good and right … so far in our two meetings, I’ve learned a lot of positives,” said Del. Anne Kaiser (D-Montgomery), co-chair of the commission, which includes members of the state health department and executive directors of of a number of licensing boards.
Health officials, auditors at odds over millions in Medicaid payments to inmates

“I hope to get to a point where people are willing to share maybe some of the negatives … so there could be opportunities to learn best practices from each other,” she said. “But that will never happen if someone doesn’t say, ‘Hey, we’re struggling with this or that.’”
There are 20 state occupations boards overseeing health professions in Maryland, each operating differently and each facing their own set of problems and possible solutions. But there are common challenges involving informational technology, inadequate staffing levels and other issues will help guide the commission’s work going forward.
Kaiser is currently the sole leader of the commission, as the Senate has not named a senator to serve as the other co-chair.
The commission was created this year under House Bill 1372 to improve operations at the state’s 20 health occupation boards, ensuring that boards issue licenses, respond to complaints and conduct required facility inspections in a timely manner. It’s related to a larger legislative push to crack down on audits that repeatedly identify the same issues in oversight and fiscal documentation of state agencies.
The fiscal note for HB 1372 cites a 2025 report by the Office of Legislative Audits that found several issues at various occupational boards, including delayed investigations of complaints against licensees and backlogs of annual inspections at various healthcare facilities.
The boards’ focus spans healthcare fields and related industries, overseeing the licensing of physicians, dentists, long-term care facility administrators, psychologists, morticians and funeral directors. Other boards cover fields such as social work, acupuncture, and occupational therapy, among others.
Over the next few meetings, commission members will discuss issues with staffing levels, bureaucratic hurdles and inadequate funds to address known problems.
During Monday’s meeting, Board of Nursing Executive Director Rhonda Scott noted that high educational requirements in Maryland, while important to ensuring that healthcare professionals create safe environments, can also slow down licensing approval.
Scott also referenced the FBI investigation of Project Nightingale, a Florida-based fraud scheme, announced in January 2023 by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General. That probe said three Florida nursing schools were tied to bogus nursing degree diplomas and transcripts that were sold to aspiring registered nurses and licenses practical/vocational nurses so they could qualify for the national nursing board exam. More than two dozen nursing license applicants in Maryland were implicated.
Board of Nursing has cleared hundreds of cases of questionable documentation for nurses

“Yes, timeliness is important, but safety is paramount,” Scott said. “We have to make sure our review is conducive of public protection and ensuring these people are actually qualified to be licensed.”
Christine Farrelly, executive director of the Board of Physicians, said that communication challenges from the Maryland Department of Information Technologies has also contributed to delays in the computer systems, which can be “very, very frustrating.”
Tiffany L. Smith-Williams, executive director for the Maryland Board of Acupuncture, noted that some boards are working to improve their legacy computer systems, but need more funding to improve those antiquated technologies.
“Sometimes we stretch the dollar or the value of what we have, because it helps us control cost” Smith-Williams said.
Kaiser said in an interview last month that the work of the commission is needed.
“These professional boards have a great responsibility to ensure that our licensed medical professionals across the state meet certain standards,” she said in an August interview. “They also deal with discipline and other measures…. We, the legislature, can’t sit on the side when we’ve been told for years that he board needs better oversight.”
The issue of funding for occupational licensing boards and stagnant fee increases for licensing will be the focus of the next commission meeting slated for mid-October.
“Hopefully, I have a Senate co-chair by then,” Kaiser joked at the end of Monday’s meeting.
