name: Daily Montanan
title: Secretary of State responds to legislative subpoena, with pushback
description: Montana Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen responded to a legislative subpoena to disclose voter roll information her office provided to the federal government, but also objected to the demand and described it as “political theater.” For months, members of the State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee have been trying to find out exactly[...]
text:
The Secretary of State’s office in the Montana State Capitol in Helena on Wednesday, April 26, 2023.  (Photo by Mike Clark for the Daily Montanan)Montana Secretary of State Christi Jacobsen responded to a legislative subpoena to disclose voter roll information her office provided to the federal government, but also objected to the demand and described it as “political theater.”
For months, members of the State Administration and Veterans’ Affairs Interim Committee have been trying to find out exactly what information Jacobsen, a Republican, provided to the federal government in response to the U.S. Department of Justice’s demand for voter records.
Earlier this month, the committee voted 10-1 to approve the subpoena for the information.
“The subpoena was an unnecessary encroachment on the separation of powers that wasted taxpayer dollars, could have been avoided, and lacked warranted scrutiny,” said the letter from Montana Secretary of State Chief Legal Counsel Austin James.
But the response also outlined the categories of information the Secretary of State’s Office provided to the Department of Justice — to varying levels of satisfaction from members of the committee.
The Secretary of State’s Office did not share driver’s license or state identification numbers with the federal government, but it did share the last four digits of Social Security numbers — generated by the federal government — for the fraction of voters who use their Social Security numbers to register to vote, according to the response letter.
The DOJ has demanded states turn over voter lists to ensure ineligible voters are not included and has sued 30 states and Washington, D.C., for the records. It has lost 23 of those lawsuits to date, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.
Some state legislators have worried the Secretary of State didn’t protect Montanans’ privacy in responding to the federal government, but Jacobsen has largely been absent from legislative meetings and unresponsive to the committee.
James previously told the committee the office protected the privacy of Montanans, but he declined to provide specific information to lawmakers, citing the threat of litigation.
The Sept. 11 letter in response to the subpoena said in August 2025, the Secretary of State’s Office provided the U.S. Department of Justice the public statewide voter registration list “available to any member of the public.”
It stated the type of data provided, and it included voter ID numbers, names, voter status, addresses (minus those protected from disclosure), phone numbers, birth years, precinct, other political districts, and “absentee indicator.”
“While demanded by the Department as empowered by Congress, the list provided did not contain any Montana driver’s license number or state identification card number,” the letter said.
In December 2025, the office again sent the voter registration list, but “this time with the addition of a federal identifier for a portion of voters where that information was provided as part of their voter registration application,” the letter said of partial Social Security numbers.
The Secretary of State’s Office said “a fraction” of voters who don’t have a driver’s license use their “federal identifier” instead, or the last four digits of their Social Security numbers, and in those cases, the office provided the last four digits. (The letter did not state how many voters that encompassed.)
The letter said the office keeps partial Social Security numbers “from general public distribution.”
But it said the last four digits aren’t considered a Social Security number by the U.S. Privacy Act, the federal government “routinely receives” those identifiers “that the federal government itself provided,” and they were provided under “nondisclosure requirements.”
The letter from the Secretary of State’s Office also said it did not consider the subpoena valid for a number of reasons, and it warned that such actions set up a confrontation between branches of government.
The Secretary of State’s Office cautioned legislators against any further subpoena for voter registration records. It said it considers the subpoena answered and will not produce additional information “absent a court order.”
Monday, Manzella said she is satisfied with the response from Jacobsen and believes the Secretary of State protected Montanans’ privacy.
“I believe that she is obligated to, under federal law, do what she did, and I think she both did what she could to protect our citizens’ privacy and also honor our request,” Manzella said.
Manzella said she approves of where Jacobsen drew the line because she protected state information, the driver’s license numbers, but she shared partial information the federal government itself generates.
“I personally don’t have a problem with the federal government requesting driver’s license numbers simply because we are a citizenry that moves across state lines on a daily basis,” Manzella said. “And I believe that the priority on elections needs to move from privacy to transparency and auditability.”
Rep. Kelly Kortum, a Bozeman Democrat, raised the idea to issue the subpoena, and he said he is not satisfied with the response from the Secretary of State.
However, Kortum also said he is likely to be the most aggressive voice on the committee on the issue, and he said it would be important to hear from Manzella and Rep. Marc Lee, a Democrat and committee vice chairman.
Kortum said the letter describes the information the Secretary of State says it sent the DOJ, but it does not provide the actual portion of the data file showing the categories.
He said the Secretary of State still is avoiding “showing us the top line on that spreadsheet.”
“I do believe the will of the committee is being thwarted,” Kortum said.
Lee said the letter was full of legalese, and he believes it fell short of the demand in the subpoena. He said he was anxious to speak to legislative staff to see if they could shed light on the response.
Lee also said Montanans value their privacy, and he doesn’t believe the idea that the federal government already has information is a justification for turning over data.
“Why would the federal government ask for stuff that they already have?” Lee said. “There has to be some sort of information that was provided to the federal government that they are not privy to.”
The Brennan Center for Justice, which has a mission to defend democracy, has described the demands by the Department of Justice as unprecedented and an encroachment on states’ authority to run elections.
Lee said legislative staff earlier indicated the committee was on solid ground in issuing the subpoena. He said his interest is in transparency from the Secretary of State’s Office.
“The Secretary of State forced us into this position because they weren’t willing to answer what I would consider a very basic question,” Lee said.
Manzella said the committee has a planned meeting in October, and if needed, it would schedule a special meeting about the subpoena.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Confidential records sitting in empty charter school building are now secured, state officials say
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Private records from a shuttered Oklahoma City charter school are now in state hands after months of delay and dispute. Proud To Partner Leadership Academy, a charter high school known as PTPLA, formally closed on June 30, but for months afterward, paper copies of students’ educational records and financial documents needed for […]
text:
Proud To Partner Leadership Academy, pictured May 19 in Oklahoma City, closed at the end of June. Obtaining hard-copy student records and financial documents from the school became a monthslong dispute. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Private records from a shuttered Oklahoma City charter school are now in state hands after months of delay and dispute.
Proud To Partner Leadership Academy, a charter high school known as PTPLA, formally closed on June 30, but for months afterward, paper copies of students’ educational records and financial documents needed for a closing audit remained in its former building in southwest Oklahoma City.
The Statewide Charter School Board canceled the school’s founding charter contract and cut off its state funding over financial, operational and academic quality concerns. Board staff then sent repeated requests that PTPLA turn over the records or allow state officials entry to retrieve them, according to email correspondence Oklahoma Voice obtained. 
Disagreements with the school turned into a legal fight with the building’s landlord. The state board on Wednesday sought an emergency court order demanding access to the records, online court documents show.
A day later, the landlord, Cameron Kaspereit, voluntarily allowed board staff to enter the property, where they picked up eight to 10 boxes of paper documents, officials said during a Statewide Charter School Board meeting Monday.
Kaspereit did not immediately return a request for comment Monday.
The landlord had until then refused to release the school documents because PTPLA owed him back rent, damages and a penalty for early lease termination, the board’s court filing states. The records were his “only leverage,” and he said he wouldn’t release them without court intervention, the board claimed in its legal filing.
Further stressing the “emergency nature” of the situation, the former school building had recently been broken into, but “according to (Kaspereit) nothing appeared to be removed,” court documents state.
State board staff are now preparing to sort through the records, said Skyler Lusnia, the state board’s director of school performance. 
“We knew it was going to be challenging, and it has been challenging,” Lusnia said of the closure process. “If and possibly when this ever happens again, we’ll be ready.”
Skyler Lusnia, director of school performance for the Statewide Charter School Board, speaks to the Proud To Partner Leadership Academy board during a meeting Nov. 18 at the charter school in southwest Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Board staff on Monday presented a host of potential changes to administrative rules governing charter school closures. Among them is added clarity that the school, not the state, is responsible for completing closure tasks like document transfers.
The state has had electronic copies of students’ academic transcripts for several weeks, which allowed PTPLA students to transfer elsewhere unimpeded, board staff have said. 
The paper records are necessary to assemble hard-copy transcripts for students and ensure they receive proper credit for their scholastic efforts, according to the board’s court filing.
The financial records are needed to finish a legally required closing audit of PTPLA, Lusnia said. The state hired a third-party audit firm, which will be able to complete its review once the hard-copy records are in hand.
PTPLA “intentionally abandoned any attempt to comply with state and federal law regarding those documents,” the board contended in its court filing. 
Representatives of the school previously told Oklahoma Voice they no longer had access to the building after turning in the keys in July. They advised state officials to coordinate with the landlord to gain access, email records show.
PTPLA Board President Sharri Coleman alerted news media and state leaders last month that the documents had been sitting in the empty facility for weeks.
“I am pleased to hear (state board) reports that the records have been retrieved and secured,” she said Monday.

title: RI elections board rejects Pelino’s recount request in Republican gubernatorial primary
description: The close contest between Rhode Island’s Republican gubernatorial primary is not close enough to justify a manual refeeding of every ballot into a tabulating machine, the Board of Elections determined Monday. The unanimous vote by the election panel came after an hourlong back-and-forth with trailing candidate Elaine Pelino, who protested a lack of public no[...]
text:
The Rhode Island Board of Elections rejected a recount request by GOP gubernatorial candidate Elaine Pelino, seated before the panel. (Screenshot)The close contest between Rhode Island’s Republican gubernatorial primary is not close enough to justify a manual refeeding of every ballot into a tabulating machine, the Board of Elections determined Monday.
The unanimous vote by the election panel came after an hourlong back-and-forth with trailing candidate Elaine Pelino, who protested a lack of public notification and transparency by election administrators. Pelino acknowledged the 259 votes separating her from likely primary winner Aaron Guckian was slightly wider than the 231-vote margin needed to justify a recount under state law. 
But the determination does not cement Guckian as the GOP nominee. The margin is still close enough to allow election administrators to cross-check the memory sticks from ballot machines against the final tally.
Pelino seeks recount in close GOP gubernatorial primary

Pelino, 72, of North Smithfield, insisted the elections board should recount every ballot, rattling off a litany of problems with meeting notice requirements and details of how election administrators counted ballots.
The information Pelino presented during her 30-minute soliloquy Monday afternoon did not show any evidence of election impropriety — the only way the elections panel can agree to a recount when the race is not close enough to justify a recount based on the margin of victory.  
“These are more arguments than actual evidence, there’s no evidence,” board member David Sholes told Pelino, who was accompanied by 2022 GOP gubernatorial nominee Ashely Kalus.



Who gets a recount under Rhode Island General Laws § 17-19-37.1
20,000 or fewer total votes: trailing candidate must be down by 2% or 200 votes, whichever is fewer
20,001 to 100,000 total votes: trailing candidate must be down 1% or 500 votes, whichever is fewer
More than 100,000 total votes: trailing candidate must be down .05% or 1,500 votes, whichever is fewer  



Election administrators defended the transparency of the ballot counting process, which includes public notice and observation of mail ballot certification, opening of envelopes and correcting of potentially deficient ballots, among other steps.
“The entire process is open to the public, it is open to the representative of a candidate, and it’s the burden of the candidate to be part of that entire process from beginning to end,” Ray Marcaccio, the board’s legal counsel said.
Marcaccio later said, “Now is the time to proffer the evidence, not to say, ‘I want to start looking to see if something suspicious was happening.’” 
Pelino, a political newcomer and proud MAGA candidate, said she did not receive any communication from the elections board regarding any element of the tabulation process, and was unaware of it happening.
“Noted, and heard, and this information is also publicly available,” Chairwoman Jennie Johnson told Pelino. 
In her final plea to the elections board, Pelino stressed the importance of having all ballot information available to her.
“We’re just asking to look at the data,” she said, to which Johnson responded, “What data?”
Guckian, 50 of East Greenwich, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The self-described “compassionate conservative” gave what appeared to be a victory speech on the State House steps Monday afternoon, despite the pending recount request, The Providence Journal reported. 
Providence City Council primaries 
Separately, the board authorized a full recount in one Providence City Council Democratic primary. Councilor Juan Pichardo and his Democratic challenger Carmen Castillo each asked for the review after the tally showed Castillo trailing Pichardo by nine votes in the Ward 9 primary. The ward spans south Elmwood, Elmwood and Roger Williams Park. Castillo and Pichardo both attended the meeting but declined to comment when asked by the board.
A second Democratic Providence City Council primary, for the Ward 4 seat, qualified for a rereading of the memory sticks but not a full recount of every ballot. The initial tabulation shows Councilor Justin Roias beating challenger Joseph Casoli by 55 votes for the seat representing the Charles and Wanskuck neighborhoods. The margin would have needed to be no more than 29 votes to qualify for a recount.
Casoli attended the meeting but declined to comment.
Recounts and memory stick rereadings will begin at 9 a.m. Tuesday, and are expected to conclude by noon. The elections board will certify final results from all state primary races, including those subject to recounts, at a scheduled meeting at 5 p.m. Tuesday.
Election board members Louis DeSimone, Randy Jackvony and Michael Connors were absent from the meeting.

title: Lars Herseth, former South Dakota governor nominee from prolific political family, dies at age 80
description: Lars Herseth, a Democratic former South Dakota legislator and 1986 nominee for governor, died Saturday of cancer at age 80.  Herseth grew up in a politically active Democratic family in rural Houghton, where he returned to be a farmer and rancher after graduating from the University of South Dakota. His father, Ralph Herseth, was the […]
text:
Lars Herseth, a Democratic former legislator and 1986 nominee for governor, died Sept. 12, 2026, at age 80. He's pictured here in a 2023 oral history interview. (Screenshot courtesy of South Dakota State Archives/YouTube)Lars Herseth, a Democratic former South Dakota legislator and 1986 nominee for governor, died Saturday of cancer at age 80. 
Herseth grew up in a politically active Democratic family in rural Houghton, where he returned to be a farmer and rancher after graduating from the University of South Dakota. His father, Ralph Herseth, was the state’s 21st governor from 1959 to 1961, and his mother, Lorna Herseth, was South Dakota’s secretary of state from 1973 to 1979. 
Lars Herseth’s daughter, Stephanie Herseth Sandlin, served in the U.S. House from 2004 to 2011 and is now the president of Augustana University in Sioux Falls.
Republican Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen paid tribute to Lars Herseth and the Herseth family Monday in a post on Venhuizen’s personal website.
“Few South Dakota families can match that record of public service across three generations,” Venhuizen wrote.
Lars Herseth served in the state House of Representatives from 1975 until 1986, when he won the Democratic nomination for governor but lost in the general election to Republican George Mickelson, who was also the son of a former governor. Herseth then served in the state Senate from 1989 until 1996. His legislative leadership positions included House minority leader, Senate president pro tempore and Senate minority leader.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
During his time in the state Senate, Herseth served with Mike Rounds, a Republican who would go on to become governor and is now a U.S. senator. Rounds wrote about Herseth in a post Monday on the social media platform X.
“Lars was a statesman and a problem solver who was willing to work with anyone if it meant bettering the lives of South Dakotans,” Rounds wrote. 
Herseth’s obituary said he focused his political career on issues including agriculture, transportation, economic development and healthcare. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, he worked with Republican Gov. Bill Janklow to preserve abandoned rail lines that were critical for transporting agricultural products.
“Lars was known for his legislative acumen, command of the issues, collegiality that knew no partisan bounds, and being true to his word,” his obituary said. “He was exceptionally fair-minded and a steadfast advocate for women’s rights and Native American issues. During his final legislative term, he spoke passionately in opposition to a bill that sought to prevent recognition of same-sex marriage.”
In his later years, Herseth was president of the American Coalition for Ethanol.
A memorial service will be at 2 p.m. Central time on Oct. 4 at the Johnson Fine Arts Center on the campus of Northern State University in Aberdeen. South Dakota Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden has ordered flags at the state Capitol in Pierre to be flown at half-staff in honor of Herseth that day.

title: Kenosha County DA’s law license suspended
description: Kenosha County District Attorney Xavier Solis had his license to practice law suspended Monday.  A memo issued by the state court system’s Office of Lawyer Regulation states that Solis’ suspension was for “willfully failing to cooperate with one or more OLR investigations into alleged misconduct.”  The memo also states that Solis violated a Wisconsin Supreme[...]
text:
Xavier Solis (photo courtesy of Xavier Solis)Kenosha County District Attorney Xavier Solis had his license to practice law suspended Monday. 
A memo issued by the state court system’s Office of Lawyer Regulation states that Solis’ suspension was for “willfully failing to cooperate with one or more OLR investigations into alleged misconduct.” 
The memo also states that Solis violated a Wisconsin Supreme Court rule that states that lawyers can have their licenses suspended if they’re under investigation by the OLR and don’t comply with deadlines to provide information. 
Solis, a Republican, was elected DA of Kenosha County in 2024 and had previously worked as a private defense attorney. 
Stephen Kelley, a spokesperson for the state court system, told the Wisconsin Examiner the only information available to the public is the rule Solis is alleged to have violated. 
State law requires district attorneys to have a valid law license, so Solis cannot currently perform the job. It’s not clear what the suspension will mean for Solis’ future in the seat. Under state court rules, an attorney suspension can be lifted if the suspended lawyer discloses what happened and cooperates with the investigation to the “reasonable satisfaction” of the regulators within 18 months. 
Deputy District Attorney Rosamaria Delgado is now serving as interim DA in Solis’ office. 
“Administrative staff of the Kenosha County District Attorney’s Office and I will continue to oversee the day-to-day operations of the office,” Delgado said in a statement to 620 WTMJ. “We have reached out to the State for direction. I will take over management and/or reassignment of District Attorney Solis’ caseload until such time as District Attorney Solis’ license to practice law is reinstated or, until further direction is received from the Governor’s Office.  At this time, no other information is available.”
Solis, who had no experience as a prosecutor when he was elected in 2024, has been the subject of criticism since taking office and has struggled to fill vacancies after experienced prosecutors resigned. He was previously sanctioned by a judge for filing briefs written using the assistance of artificial intelligence which “hallucinated” fake citations.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland leaders must fight to restore climate justice funding
description: The effects of climate change are being felt in Maryland, and the impact is even greater in Black and brown communities, writes Sacoby Wilson, which is why our lawmakers need to fight to restore the climate justice grants the Trump administration stripped away.
text:
Effects of climate change are felt more severely in Black and brown communities, writes Sacoby Wilson, which is why lawmakers need to fight to restore climate justice grants eliminated by the Trump administration. The smokestack of the WIN Waste incinerator in Baltimore. (File photo by Joe Ryan/Capital News Service)Flooding. Heat waves. Brutal storms. Power outages. Thanks to the Trump administration’s clawbacks of approved grant funding, Maryland residents are less prepared for these and other impacts of a changing climate. Low-income communities and people of color — who are hit first and worst by climate disaster — will suffer the most.
Back in 2024, I served on a team that won a $20 million grant for a program to improve climate resilience in Prince George’s County. The competitive application process was rigorous, involving extensive planning and mountains of paperwork. The evidence-based program included tree planting to keep neighborhoods cool; stormwater management to reduce flooding; and weatherization efforts to lower bills and reduce emissions while building a skilled trade workforce.
We were thrilled in the fall of 2024 when the Environmental Protection Agency announced that our project, BrightFuturres, was the winner for the state of Maryland. We began the precertification process during the winter of 2024/2025 — filling out more mountains of paperwork. Then the new administration came in, stopped the process, and BrightFuturres never received a dime.
We were not alone. Last year, the Trump administration canceled nearly $3 billion in environmental and climate justice block grants awarded to cities, nonprofits and tribes, along with another $20 billion in clean energy grants. All of these grants were approved by Congress as part of the Biden-era Inflation Reduction Act.
Of course, Congress still holds the “power of the purse,” as granted by the Constitution. Accordingly, federal courts recently ruled that the administration’s clawbacks of appropriated funds were illegal. But, when ordered to reinstate the funds by Sept. 30, Trump’s EPA argued in court that it lacks the staffing and money to do so. That is, the EPA lacks staffing and money because the administration itself has eliminated them.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Putting aside the administration’s shenanigans, our state needs this money and should fight for it.
Climate change is now a daily reality, in Maryland and around the globe. Human activity has raised atmospheric carbon dioxide to levels not seen in 2 million years, raising global temperatures by more than 2 degrees Fahrenheit. We could see the planet warm by 5.6 degrees to 7.9 degrees by the end of this century.
Already, the impacts are severe: In 2024 — the last year the federal government collected such data — Americans endured 27 major weather disasters, which killed 568 people and cost at least $182.7 billion.
Here in Maryland, rising temperatures mean more heat waves and air pollution. Flooding is a growing concern, both from sea level rise and increased rainfall. Along our nearly 3,200 miles of coastline, tidal marsh has swallowed nearly 30,000 acres of forest and farmland since 1984. While storms are more intense and rainfall is heavier, we are also seeing more droughts and wildfires.
Climate change does not affect all Marylanders equally. The legacy of redlining and other racist policies has left Black and brown neighborhoods more vulnerable to climate impacts. Crowded with polluting industries and lacking parks and green spaces, these neighborhoods are hotter and more flood-prone than their wealthier, whiter counterparts. In Baltimore, low-income Black neighborhoods can be up to 17 degrees hotter than the leafy enclaves of the affluent. Partly as a result, the rate of heat-related deaths among Black Americans is about 200% higher than for non-Hispanic Whites.
Climate impacts are layered atop other environmental injustices and the health impacts they cause. Black communities in Maryland and across the U.S. already bear a disproportionate burden of industrial pollution. Cancer risk from air pollution is more than twice as high in majority-Black census tracts as in majority-white tracts. That’s one reason Black Americans are 40% more likely to have asthma than white Americans, and Black children are eight times more likely to die from asthma than their white peers. The heat and wildfire of climate change is worsening these disparities.
Building climate resilience — especially in hard-hit parts of our state — is one way to address this generational injustice. It’s also a practical solution that makes good fiscal sense. A report by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the Allstate insurance company found that every dollar invested in climate resilience strategies saves saves $13 in economic costs, damages, and cleanup.
That’s why our elected officials must fight — in the courts, and in Congress — to restore the climate grants that were lawfully appropriated to our state. We won that $20 million fair and square. And those resources are essential to help prepare Marylanders for a hotter, wetter, more dangerous future and ensure equity in climate mitigation, adaptation, and resilience.

text:
The Arkansas Department of Health is laying off several dozen people.
(Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)The Arkansas Department of Health will lay off more than three dozen people and eliminate unfilled positions in November, a spokesperson confirmed on Monday.
In total, 71 positions within the 2,100-person department will be eliminated. Thirty-eight of those positions are currently filled, while the rest are unfilled.
The reduction in force will align the department’s resources with “budget priorities and long-term goals,” said department spokesperson Sarah Morris in a statement.
The health department is responsible for programs such as food safety inspections at restaurants and illness surveillance. It is also in charge of issuing birth certificates and licensing healthcare professionals.
The reduction will go into effect on Nov. 1 and will affect various divisions within the department. Morris said the reductions won’t affect services offered by its health units or other department services. The Division of Health Advancement will lose the most people, with 14 filled positions set to be eliminated.

name: Missouri Independent
title: JD Vance uses Missouri visit to announce new crackdown on COVID loan fraud
description: KANSAS CITY — The federal government is going after thousands of people suspected of stealing millions of dollars from taxpayers through their participation in a COVID-19 pandemic program meant to protect small businesses and workers, Vice President JD Vance said Monday. The government is permanently suspending 870,000 people from receiving federal governmen[...]
text:
Vice President JD Vance speaks about the administration’s crackdown on fraud during a Monday news conference at the FBI field office in Kansas City (Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector).
KANSAS CITY — The federal government is going after thousands of people suspected of stealing millions of dollars from taxpayers through their participation in a COVID-19 pandemic program meant to protect small businesses and workers, Vice President JD Vance said Monday.
The government is permanently suspending 870,000 people from receiving federal government loans after defrauding the Paycheck Protection Program and other federal programs, Vance said in a news conference at the FBI’s Kansas City field office.
“We’re going to make it impossible for them to get loans from the federal government,” Vance told a small gathering of law enforcement and local officials on the first leg of two stops, one in Missouri and another in Kansas.
The Paycheck Protection Program was set up to give loans to small businesses so they could rehire employees and keep their doors open during the pandemic.
“As happens with so many of the programs that are born out of the generosity of the American taxpayer, we had many, many people who took advantage of those programs,” Vance said.
“If you screw the American taxpayer, the federal government is now going to say you’re cut off, no more,” he added.
William Kirk, inspector general for the Small Business Administration, said a national program will launch Tuesday with demand letters going to “suspected fraudsters in Kansas and Missouri.”
“It does not matter when the fraud happened. If you stole from the taxpayers by claiming … any SBA loan that you are not entitled to, answer the demand letter you’re going to receive from the SBA,” he said. “If you do not, you will face consequences. We know who you are and where you live.”
Vance criticized President Joe Biden’s administration for failing to initiate anti-fraud efforts with the Paycheck Protection Program loans, calling it an “open secret” that the program was rife with fraud.
PPP started issuing loans in 2020, under President Donald Trump. It quickly ran out of its first allocation of funding by April, after issuing more than 1.6 million loans, according to the U.S. Treasury.
More funds were allocated, and another round of loans were issued in 2021, under Biden.
Vance said that in the past three months, a fraud enforcement partnership made nearly 90 decisions to prosecute.
“Decisions that are making clear and sending a message to the fraudsters that if you defraud the American people, if you steal money from the American taxpayer that should go to American workers, we’re actually going to prosecute you, and we’re going to try to send you to prison,” he said.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that from mid-June through Sept. 1, the administration uncovered $245 million in losses and charged more than 80 people in a summer focus called Operation No Doze.
In a Missouri case, Jamie W. Gray attempted to steal more than $55 million by filing for hundreds of Paycheck Protection Program loans, claiming to own dozens of businesses in operation before the pandemic, Blanche said.
“But in every instance but one, these businesses didn’t even exist,” Blanche said. “The only business that he claimed to own that did exist was a business called Fur Lives Matter.”
That Texas business, though, hadn’t heard of Gray, Blanche said. Gray was indicted on money laundering and wire fraud charges, according to a Department of Justice news release.
“For years, fraudsters got the message that Washington would look the other way. That era is over. We’re charging more defendants,” Blanche said. “We’re convicting more. We’re taking the money back. We’re working with every single federal agency to use every tool in our toolbox to go after these fraudsters.”
Operation No Doze was a coordinated effort between SBA’s Office of Inspector General, federal prosecutors and more than 40 U.S. attorney offices, the DOJ news release said.
The operation involved more than 160 criminal defendants and about $245 million in intended losses to American taxpayers, the news release said.
U.S. Attorney for Kansas Ryan Kriegshauser announced Monday that four people in the state were charged with Paycheck Protection Program-related fraud with losses of about $182,000.
Vance said a review process was put in place for anyone who believes they have been “wrongfully tagged as a fraudster.”
The 870,000 people who can’t apply for loans from the federal government were “tagged as having a high likelihood of committing fraud for other actions that they’ve engaged in,” he said.
“This actually sets up a system whereby, if you have a high suspicion of having defrauded the government, we’re not going to make it easy for you to apply for these loans anymore,” he said. “We certainly appreciate that some people, you know, mistakes sometimes happen. So we’ve set up a process to ensure that people can actually challenge whether they’ve been accurately tagged as a fraudster.”

name: VTDigger
title: Directed by voices or acting on his own? Mental state of man accused of shooting Palestinian students is focus of trial
description:
Attorneys presented opening statements Monday in the case of Jason Eaton, followed by the testimony of the three men Eaton allegedly shot.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Directed by voices or acting on his own? Mental state of man accused of shooting Palestinian students is focus of trial.
text:
Jason Eaton watches as Hisham Awartani arrives to testify in Eaton’s trial inChttenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Monday, September 14, 2026. Eaton is accused of shooting three Palestinian students, including a now-paralyzed Awartani, in November of 2023. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
BURLINGTON — An attorney said his client was hearing voices directing him through the radio and was legally insane when he is alleged to have shot and wounded three Palestinian students in Burlington nearly three years ago. 
A prosecutor described Jason Eaton as an arrogant man who always wanted to be the smartest guy in the room and knew what he was doing was wrong when he allegedly pulled the trigger on his handgun multiple times that night.
Those were two differing views presented Monday to jurors during the opening statements in Eaton’s trial in Chittenden Superior criminal court. The trial is expected to run through the week. 
Eaton faces three counts of attempted second-degree murder accusing him of shooting three college students visiting Burlington over the Thanksgiving holiday in 2023. If convicted of even one of the charges, Eaton, 51, faces up to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Eaton has raised the insanity defense, putting a focus during the trial on the testimony of experts for each side who are expected to offer competing views on whether he should be held criminally responsible for the shootings.
The arguments 
“This is a case about reasoned conclusions,” Sally Adams, Chittenden County chief deputy state’s attorney, said as she began her roughly 30-minute address to the jury.
Adams told the jury that Eaton emerged from a porch on his apartment building on the evening of Nov. 25, 2023, and shot the three students — Hisham Awartani, Kinnan Abdalhamid and Tahseen Aliahmad.
“He doesn’t say a word,” Adams said of Eaton as he allegedly fired the shots and then fled. 
“He has a sense of entitlement. He takes advantage of others,” Adams said, adding that Eaton had a “grandiose” sense of self-importance.
“We believe Mr. Eaton did not suffer from a mental disease or defect,” the prosecutor said. 
Adams told jurors to consider the information that experts for the two sides relied on to reach their conclusions, as well as their own observations and other witness testimony throughout the trial.
Investigators encountered Eaton at his apartment building a day after the shooting, Adams said. She said that Eaton reportedly told those investigators, “I’ve been waiting for you.”
Eaton made no further comments or answered any questions, Adams said, saying he wanted to talk to a lawyer.
Later testing revealed matches between a gun found inside Eaton’s apartment and casings found at the shooting scene, Adams said.
Joshua O’Hara, one of Eaton’s attorneys, countered during his opening statement that the evidence would show that his client met the legal standard for insanity at the time of the shootings. 
“This case is going to be hard. This case is going to be difficult,” O’Hara said to the jury. 
The defense attorney told jurors they will hear expert testimony about the complicated topic of mental health.
O’Hara said Eaton had lost his job at a credit union shortly before the shootings and was suffering from delusions. As Eaton listened to public radio, the defense attorney said, Eaton had begun hearing voices he believed were coming from a government intelligence agency. 
Initially, the voices were validating, offering praise, O’Hara said. But eventually, O’Hara said, those voices began directing Eaton, including telling him to shoot somebody by 6 p.m. on the night of Nov. 25, 2023. Eaton, the defense attorney said, believed that a nearby Jewish family needed his protection.
“He prays,” O’Hara then said of Eaton, before the shooting took place.
Community turns out
A standing-room-only crowd packed the courtroom for the trial’s opening day, including many supporters for the three students. 
Joe Murphy, a University of Vermont student, said he was there to show solidarity for the three men shot.
“It was a terrible tragedy when it happened, and I think it was a moment where the community was kind of all that we had,” Murphy said. “So you know, I think our presence here today is really important to keep up that community support.”
Murphy said he was most worried about the effects of the violence, regardless of Eaton’s motives.
“You had three boys who were wearing keffiyehs and speaking Arabic and were shot,” Murphy said. “I don’t know what was going on inside Jason Eaton’s head when it happened, but I know that when that kind of thing happens, the impact kind of speaks for itself.”

Onlookers pack the courtroom during Jason Eaton’s trial in  Chttenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Monday, September 14, 2026. Eaton is accused of shooting three Palestinian students in November of 2023. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Several of the people in the gallery were wearing keffiyehs, a traditional scarf that is a symbol of Palestinian identity. Two of the three students were wearing keffiyehs when they were shot. 
Judge John Pacht, speaking before jurors entered the room, told people in the gallery they could not visibly wear keffiyehs in the courtroom, fearing that it could taint the jurors as they considered the case. 
People in the crowd wearing keffiyehs either took them off or covered them up with other clothing. 
Pacht did say that he would allow the three students to wear keffiyehs as they testified, and later Monday each of them did take the witness stand with a keffiyeh draped over his shoulders.
Testimony begins 
Eaton, dressed in a blue suit with white shirt and blue tie, leaned back in his chair at the defense table between his two attorneys as he listened to the testimony of the three students.
Awartani testified from his wheelchair, telling the jury his injuries from the shooting left his lower body paralyzed.
Awartani said he had traveled to Burlington over the Thanksgiving holiday with two of his friends to visit relatives, including his grandmother and uncle. 
He said that on the day of the shooting they had gone to a bowling alley as part of a birthday party for a relative and when they returned early in the evening he and his two friends went outside for a walk and to smoke cigarettes. 
As they walked back to the home where they were staying on North Prospect Street, Awartani told the jurors, they were speaking to each other in a mix of English and Arabic. A man then approached them, Awartani said.
“He pulled a handgun and started shooting at us,” Awartani said of that man, whom he did not know.
Awartani said he fell to the ground and called 911, reporting the shootings and that the gunman had fled. At one point on the 911 call played in court Monday for the jury, Awartani told the dispatcher, “I think I’m gonna die.”
Awartani, like his two friends Abdalhamid and Aliahmad, who also testified Monday, told jurors that the man did not say a word before the shootings or afterward.
Abdalhamid said he ran after the shooting, trying to find a place to hide before going to a residence where he found people to call 911. He said it wasn’t until he sat in a chair at that residence that he realized he had been shot in his right buttock. 
Aliahmad told jurors he wasn’t immediately sure what happened when the shooting took place.
“I heard some gunshots and I was on the ground,” Aliahmad said, adding he kept still, fearing that a shooter may still be out there. “I was playing dead.”
Emma White contributed reporting.

title: Trump EPA to strip greenhouse gas limits for power plants, a key Biden climate policy
text: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency will revoke limits on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants that run on coal and natural gas, according to regulatory documents Administrator Lee Zeldin signed Monday.The administration framed the action to repeal 2024 limits on greenhouse gas emissions from virtually all power plants other than wind, solar or hydro-powered as lowering energy costs, which the war with Iran has driven up, as energy producers will save at least $310 million on compliance. The move could produce a tenfold increase in coal power, the agency said.“Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning,” Zeldin said in the release. “We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices, and a more prosperous America.”Environmental groups and elected Democrats blasted the move, which would roll back regulations set by Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, for hastening climate change and increasing air pollution. Some called the action a corrupt favor to an industry that boosted President Donald Trump’s campaign.“It's simple. Big Oil & Big Coal give millions to help get Trump elected. He lets them pollute more. You get dirtier air, extreme heat, flooding, & droughts,” Maryland U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat, wrote on social media. “Trump's trading away your health & safety to pad his donors' pockets. Polluters win, Trump wins, you lose.”Repeal of Biden carbon pollution standardsThe EPA published two regulations in the Federal Register in a single effort Monday that it said would reduce energy costs and boost availability, while complying with judicial rulings in recent years that restricted the agency’s power to regulate climate change.A final rule would partially repeal the Biden-era Carbon Pollution Standards, which the agency said was not achievable by their 2032 target date and would lead to power plants shutting down. And a supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking considered stripping all greenhouse gas limits on fossil-fuel power plants since 2015.U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, a West Virginia Republican who leads the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, applauded the move.“Finally, under President Trump’s leadership, we are ending the Biden-era Clean Power Plan 2.0, which was designed to eliminate coal and natural gas power generation, drastically increasing Americans’ electric bills,” she said in a statement. “I have long opposed this rule and warned of the devastating economic impacts it would have in West Virginia.”Zeldin laid the groundwork for the move last year by repealing the agency’s “endangerment finding” that formed the basis of federal regulation targeting climate change.Monday’s release called concerns about greenhouse gas emissions’ effect on climate change overblown, while elevating “baseload power” generation as a much more important issue for Americans.“Models continue to show that (greenhouse gas) emissions from power plants have no material impact on global climate change,” the release said. “In fact, if all carbon dioxides were eliminated tomorrow, there would be no meaningful climate impact.”That finding is disputed, including by an EPA webpage, the climate advocacy group Evergreen Action noted. “Electric power generation is the second largest emitter of carbon dioxide pollution, contributing to climate change, which is threatening public health and affecting ecosystems at multiple levels,” the EPA webpage, which was last updated in December, says.“The EPA’s own publicly available analysis contradicts the administration’s laughable claims that the U.S. power sector doesn’t meaningfully contribute to climate change or harm public health,” Pete Wyckoff, Evergreen’s vice president for policy, said. “If the U.S. power sector were its own country, it would rank as the world's fifth-largest emitter of climate pollution.”Regulation moving to statesRhode Island U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, blasted the move and rebutted the EPA’s cost-saving rationale, saying the agency’s “own analysis” showed a 2024 Biden rule would have saved about $20 billion annually in “prevented climate disasters and health care costs.”“The fossil fuel-captured EPA’s decision to end its regulation of greenhouse gas emissions from power plants is a tragic and expensive mistake,” Whitehouse said. “In refusing to address this national crisis, EPA is shifting the costs of climate change onto every family in America.”More frequent natural disasters driven by climate change cost lives as well as billions in damage to buildings and infrastructure, property insurance, agricultural losses and more “long-term destabilization of the national economy,” he continued. “But the Trump EPA refuses to measure these costs and is only interested in tabulating, and inflating, the alleged costs to industry.”Whitehouse added that the decision could backfire on fossil fuel energy producers, as more states and local governments would seek to fill the void left by federal regulators and place their own limits on fossil fuel energy generation.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming’s governor cheers Trump administration move to repeal power plant rules limiting planet-warming emissions
authors: Dustin Bleizeffer and The Associated Press
description:
Local advocates say curtailing greenhouse gas emissions is more important than extending the life of coal-fired power plants at or beyond their functional retirement age.
The post Wyoming’s governor cheers Trump administration move to repeal power plant rules limiting planet-warming emissions appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
WASHINGTON (AP)—The Environmental Protection Agency said Monday it is repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas and announced it is taking a separate but related step to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.
The rule change, first proposed last year, represents a fundamental shift from efforts by Democratic Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama to address climate change and clean up industrial pollution.
Gov. Mark Gordon welcomed the move to eliminate “onerous restrictions regarding greenhouse gases,” he said in a prepared statement. “Under my administration, Wyoming litigated over the ability of the Biden Administration to regulate greenhouse gases and this is just further good news for our fossil fuel industry and our economy.”
Environmental groups decried the change, saying it would come at a cost to Americans’ health and further degrade the environment.
“Instead of prioritizing lowering energy prices, the Trump administration is set on raising them by locking in expensive, volatile fossil fuel markets that leave states like Wyoming with higher costs and fewer opportunities for jobs, investment and tax revenue,” Sierra Club Wyoming Chapter Climate and Energy Organizer Emma Jones said. “Meanwhile, wind and solar have consistently kept our rates lower and reduced risk for customers. This repeal absolutely stacks the deck to the benefit of the fossil fuel industry.” 
Revoking the Biden-era power plant rule would save industry more than $300 billion in costs and help “unleash” American energy, the EPA said. The change will allow utilities to make the best decisions for their ratepayers rather than be forced to close aging or inefficient plants, said EPA Assistant Administrator Aaron Szabo.
The power plant rule, to take effect soon after publication in the Federal Register, is expected to face immediate legal challenges.
David Fotouhi, left, nominated to be Deputy Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, and Aaron Szabo, nominated to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation of the EPA, are sworn in before the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on Capitol Hill in Wednesday, March 5, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana)
Environmental groups also are likely to challenge the separate rule proposed Monday that could prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants. The proposal, expected to be made final next year, follows on EPA’s action earlier this year revoking a scientific finding that long has been the central basis for U.S. action to regulate greenhouse gas emissions and fight climate change.
The February action eliminated all greenhouse gas emissions standards for cars and trucks. The new plan would apply similar logic to a broader undoing of climate regulations on stationary sources such as power plants.
In addition to health and human-caused climate warming implications, Wyoming has much at stake. 
Unlike other coal-producing regions in the U.S. that sell a different type of coal to steelmakers around the globe, Wyoming coal production is dependent almost entirely on U.S. customers that burn the commodity to generate electricity, making Wyoming’s industry particularly vulnerable. Though the administration’s rollback could help extend the life of some aging coal-fired power plants in the Equality State, like the Dave Johnston plant outside Glenrock, Gordon and other local coal proponents have been fighting the Biden-era rules because Wyoming coal mines serve nearly half the nation’s coal-fired power plants.
A truck hauls coal at the Belle Ayr mine in Campbell County in June 2025. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Yet, a University of Wyoming analysis suggests the average age of power plants served by Wyoming coal is 41 years. That makes retiring greenhouse gas-emitting coal plants the obvious option rather than “permanently” stripping the EPA’s authority to do so in the face of a dangerously warming plant, according to Sierra Club’s Wyoming Chapter.
“While wildfires rage, floods devastate communities and families struggle to afford skyrocketing electricity bills and insurance premiums, the Trump administration is handing the fossil fuel industry a license to keep polluting,” Sierra Club Chief Program Officer Holly Bender said. “This is full-throated climate denial while the climate crisis happens in real time and a shocking betrayal of the American public.”
The Obama- and Biden-era rules were intended to push coal plants to retire before technology could catch up to eventually commercialize carbon capture throughout the fleet, Wyoming Mining Association Executive Director Travis Deti said. Eliminating the rules gives the industry the opportunity to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions while still meeting booming electrical demand.
“We’re going to need all the energy we can produce in this country in the coming years, and we’ve got to have coal as part of the mix,” Deti said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: End Citizens United group hosts roundtable supporting Turek’s Senate campaign
description: Iowans supporting Josh Turek’s U.S. Senate campaign said at a Monday roundtable they believe the Democratic candidate would be more effective than Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson at limiting corporate influence in politics. The event, hosted by End Citizens United in Des Moines, brought in community members and advocates for Turek’s Senate campaign to spe[...]
text:
Tiffany Muller, right, president of End Citizens United, alongside Nathan Sage, left, and other Iowans, held a roundtable discussion cohosted by Rep. Josh Turek's U.S. Senate campaign on corporate political spending at Smokey Row Coffee in Des Moines Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowans supporting Josh Turek’s U.S. Senate campaign said at a Monday roundtable they believe the Democratic candidate would be more effective than Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson at limiting corporate influence in politics.
The event, hosted by End Citizens United in Des Moines, brought in community members and advocates for Turek’s Senate campaign to speak about the need to elect someone to Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat who will advocate for working and middle class Iowans during a time of rising costs.
Turek was not at the event in person, but in a news release said he supported ECU’s work to tackle money in politics in the Iowa U.S. Senate race.
“It’s working class Iowans that are bearing the cost of Washington’s corruption,” Turek, a state representative from Council Bluffs, said in a statement. “Congress has refused to crack down on these powerful interests for too long because politicians like Ashley Hinson are bought and paid for by billionaires and corporations. We have far too much money being poured into our political system, and our communities are getting left behind. I’m grateful to End Citizens United for taking on Big Money and hosting this roundtable to center the voices of everyday Iowans.”
Tiffany Muller, the president of End Citizens United, said their organization was formed in the wake of the 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United v. FEC. She said many of the higher costs Americans are seeing at the grocery store, gas pump and in healthcare are caused by the “unlimited and undisclosed money flooding into our system” allowed by the 2010 ruling, which removed limits on corporations’ direct spending in support of a political campaign.
“What we see right now is a pay-to-play government where we have basically legalized corruption, and this wasn’t inevitable, right?” Muller said. “These are policy choices, but right now in Washington, we have far too many people who won’t stand up to the corporations who are gouging consumers, and instead just allow that to continue to be passed on to the people. So that is why we are here.”
Mandy Newton Rosenow, a Democrat running for Iowa House District 46, said she does not believe Iowa voters, or most Americans, are “anti-corporation” — she said instead, she believed most voters were “anti-‘being ripped off.”
“We’re anti-being the product, right? Like, I don’t like that corporations are able to mine whatever I click and look at, and then sell that to someone else without my permission. And I’m guessing most people feel that way, but someone is paying to allow that to continue to happen because … it’s productive for them. And you know, I think Iowa does great, and we’ve got a wonderful business sense and a business history. But it gets to the point where the big guys get big, and then they squash everything else. And when people take donations in large amounts, they feel beholden to that, obviously. And I think that’s where the balance is off. And when this court case of Citizens United went through and changed how those were funded, we saw those big changes.”
ECU endorsed Turek in June. As people at the roundtable discussed what would make Turek an effective legislator in Washington, D.C., to tackle issues related to corruption, they also criticized Hinson, his general election opponent. Muller said Hinson is an example of a politician who benefits from corporate spending in politics, pointing to a criticism levied regularly by Democrats that her personal wealth grew significantly since she first entered the U.S. House in 2021.
“Iowans have been squeezed by rising cost, but her own personal wealth has grown up to 10 times since going to Congress,” Muller said. “That’s not a coincidence. That is a rigged system working exactly as it’s supposed to.”
Muller said Hinson has taken more than $2 million in funding from corporate political action committees, “including over $600,000 from big pharma and the healthcare industry.” She also criticized Hinson for her husband retaining private stock in an business he formerly owned, meaning the business’ stock is not traded on public exchanges.
Hinson has said she does not trade stocks, and she would support banning all members of Congress from stock trading. She voted in July in support of the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would ban lawmakers in Washington, D.C. and their families from purchasing stocks while serving, but still includes certain exemptions for stocks owned before taking office and for private stock.
Hinson and supporters argue the increase her family’s increase in net worth is because her husband sold his insurance business in 2021.
Nathan Sage, a former U.S. Senate Democratic candidate who has endorsed Turek, said “at the end of the day, actions speak louder than words.”
“Iowans want to see things done,” Sage said. “And you know we’ve seen Ashley Hinson, we’ve seen our (legislators) being in Washington make more money. She’s increased her net worth 10 times. … We want people that are that are actually not just going to say the words, but live by those words, and that’s what we’re talking about with Josh Turek, because that’s who Josh is.”
Billy Fuerst, Hinson’s campaign communications director, criticized Turek in a statement responding to the event for getting support from a super PAC during the Democratic primary.
The VoteVets super PAC, which supports Democratic veterans and is affiliated with Senate Democratic leadership, spent money on ads supporting Turek during his primary election campaign facing Iowa Sen. Zach Wahls.
“Chuck Schumer spent more than $10 million to buy the Democrat nomination for Turek,” Fuerst said. “Now suddenly Josh wants limits on spending? What a hypocrite.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Threats to our outdoor way of life present a test for South Dakota’s US senators
description: The Trump administration is moving on two fronts to weaken protection for South Dakota’s wetlands and streams. One proposal could remove most seasonal streams and wetlands from the Clean Water Act. The other could permanently certify old and potentially inaccurate maps associated with the Swampbuster program, which is supposed to discourage farmers from conv[...]
text:
U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, center, and Sen. Mike Rounds, right, Republicans from South Dakota, speak with an attendee, left, at the Daakotafest agricultural trade show in Mitchell on Aug. 19, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)The Trump administration is moving on two fronts to weaken protection for South Dakota’s wetlands and streams.
One proposal could remove most seasonal streams and wetlands from the Clean Water Act. The other could permanently certify old and potentially inaccurate maps associated with the Swampbuster program, which is supposed to discourage farmers from converting wetlands to cropland.
Together, they threaten prairie potholes, waterfowl, fishing, flood protection and South Dakota’s outdoor economy. They also present a defining test for Sens. John Thune and Mike Rounds, who portray themselves as hunters and defenders of South Dakota’s outdoor heritage.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture is accepting comments on its Swampbuster rule through Sept. 28. Comments on the Environmental Protection Agency and Army Corps of Engineers’ supplemental “waters of the United States,” or WOTUS, proposal are due Oct. 9.
Sometimes the best crop is grass

This matters beyond environmental organizations and federal regulators. South Dakota sold more than 317,000 habitat stamps to hunters and anglers last year, with revenue used to support wildlife habitat and public access projects. A statewide survey, commissioned by the National Wildlife Federation, found that 53% of South Dakota voters consider themselves hunters, anglers or both. About 59% camp, half watch birds or wildlife, and 47% boat, canoe or kayak.
Those numbers describe how South Dakotans spend time with their families, teach children about the land and remain connected to this place.
The EPA proposal would limit Clean Water Act jurisdiction to relatively permanent rivers, lakes and streams, and wetlands directly connected to them. Under its narrowest alternative, streams would need to flow continuously except for predictable dry periods totaling no more than about one month a year.
That could eliminate federal protection for seasonal streams, including many streams in western South Dakota. Wetlands would need to be “indistinguishably part” of another protected water, with surface water present for at least 11 months of a typical year.
Waters excluded from the Clean Water Act could be polluted, filled or destroyed without federal review under that law. EPA estimated its original 2025 proposal would leave only about 19% of the nation’s wetland acreage federally protected. The September alternative could reduce that estimate further.
The Supreme Court had already narrowed Clean Water Act protection in its 2023 Sackett v. EPA decision. The administration is now deciding how aggressively to extend that ruling — and whether to adopt an interpretation leaving only a sliver of wetlands and seasonal streams protected.
The separate USDA interim rule concerns Swampbuster determinations issued between November 1990 and July 1996. Swampbuster does not prohibit farmers from draining wetlands. It conditions eligibility for crop insurance subsidies, commodity payments, farm loans and other federal benefits on protecting them.
But in a February 2019 memo, The Association of State Wetland Managers Inc. reminded everyone that of the 3 million pre-1996 wetland determinations about 60% were inaccurate. Over 90% in North Dakota were deficient. 
A prairie pothole missed by both the Clean Water Act definition and an old Swampbuster map could effectively disappear from federal protection.
Those shallow potholes produce the insects that breeding ducks and other birds need when they return in spring. The Prairie Pothole Region produces more than half of North America’s waterfowl.
Wetlands also hold runoff and trap sediment and nutrients. Losing them can mean more flooded property, damaged roads and additional water treatment.
A study prepared for South Dakota Game, Fish and Parks found that hunting, fishing, wildlife viewing, boating and trapping generated more than $1.4 billion in annual spending based on 2021 activity. That spending supported more than 14,500 jobs and $123 million in state and local tax revenue.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Thune and Rounds are not spectators in this debate.
Rounds has written about pheasant hunting with his children and grandchildren and acknowledged that habitat supports rural businesses. Thune has described pheasant hunting as an economically significant and treasured part of South Dakota’s heritage.
Thune is Senate majority leader, a longtime Agriculture Committee member and a past defender of conservation compliance and the Sodsaver program, which discourages the conversion of native prairie to cropland. He has the influence to challenge the administration and protect policies he previously championed. If those protections are dismantled on his watch, silence cannot credibly be called neutrality.
Rounds has advocated for stronger landowner discretion over wetlands on their property. Landowners deserve a fair process. But automatically certifying potentially inaccurate determinations is not fairness. It accepts possible errors permanently, with wildlife, downstream landowners and the public bearing the consequences.
Both have the standing and influence to demand changes.
Wearing blaze orange, attending pheasant openers and celebrating outdoor heritage are easy. Protecting the habitat that makes those traditions possible — particularly when that requires confronting an administration of one’s own party — is the meaningful test.
Thune and Rounds have made South Dakota’s outdoor heritage part of their public identity. If these protections disappear and they decline to intervene, that will become part of their legacy.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Racing Commission to seek $8.4M from state budget in upcoming legislative session
description: The New Mexico Racing Commission, which regulates horse races at non-tribal casinos across the state, plans to ask for $8.4 million in state funding during the next legislative session, NMRC Chief Financial Officer Amber Trujillo told a panel of state lawmakers last week. Fires and floods in Ruidoso are among the many challenges facing the state's horse raci[...]
text:
Mud and debris cover the track at Ruidoso Downs Casino and Racetrack on July 10, 2025. A panel of industry officials recently told state lawmakers that New Mexico horse racing faces significant economic challenges. (Danielle Prokop/Source New Mexico)The New Mexico Racing Commission, which regulates horse races at non-tribal casinos across the state, plans to propose an $8.4 million budget during the next legislative session, NMRC Chief Financial Officer Amber Trujillo told a panel of state lawmakers last week.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Trujillo acknowledged that the figure “seems like an alarming number,” when speaking to the interim Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee in Las Cruces on Sept. 9, but went on to explain some of the factors restricting how the commission’s funding works. 
While the commission has the cash on hand to support much of its annual budget of about $8 million, it’s limited in how it can spend much of the money it generates through its programming, Trujillo explained.
For example, when the state racing commission makes money by charging a racehorse owner a registration fee, that fee goes into one of several commission funds and can only be spent on specific purposes. One such fund has a balance of more than $3 million, but state law dictates that the commission can only spend that money on certain uses, such as jockey insurance. Another fund, with some $700,000, can only be used on drug testing athletes. When the state Legislature appropriates money to the commission, however, it is typically for general use.
“A lot of our funding is restrictive,” Trujillo said, adding that more than half of its money can only be spent on specific uses.
Trujillo spoke alongside New Mexico Racing Commission Vice Chair John Buffington and Sunland Park Racetrack and Casino President Fred Heinrich. Their remarks came as the state has seen a shifting landscape in the sport.
After fires and floods impacted Ruidoso in recent years, the local racetrack relocated several of its lucrative races. The Ruidoso track held its 2026 racing season in Albuquerque, and more recently track officials have proposed holding its 2027 races in Texas.
To illustrate the challenges facing the industry statewide, Buffington pointed to the drastic decline in the number of thoroughbred racehorses born in the state each year. In 2008, he said there were 1,078 thoroughbreds foaled in the state. In 2023, it was just 269, he said.
He said that decline concerns him, because the industry has historically produced hundreds of millions of dollars of revenue annually. A report from the New Mexico Horse Breeders Association found that it supports about 10,000 jobs statewide each year.
New Mexico tribe and pueblos wrap up case that Kalshi sports betting hurts their sovereignty

“Besides the role in the culture and history of New Mexico, it’s also an economic machine,” he said.
Many of the “racinos” — racetracks with adjacent non-tribal casinos — have a uniquely challenging business model. Under New Mexico law, non-tribal casinos are only allowed to exist in conjunction with a racetrack and are prohibited from offering many of the attractions found in a tribal casino, including table games like poker or roulette. But the casinos have become what’s subsidizing the horse races.
“Our hands are tied. The casino probably funds 95% of our operation,” Heinrich said. “We are not allowed sports betting. We are not allowed to have live table games. We cannot even have alcohol on the gaming floor…New Mexico is the only state where you can drink a beer, you can play a slot machine, but you can’t do both at the same time.”
One state lawmaker, Republican Senate Leader Bill Sharer of Farmington, told the panelists that he wanted to see the industry thrive, but was concerned by a lack of specific information regarding the causes behind the industry’s decline.
“We’ve got to go backward now. How do we rebuild the industry? How do we get more horses? If we have more horses, we have more race days,” Sharer said. “What I fear is we don’t know why it’s broken, and since we don’t know why it’s broken, we don’t know where to go.”

name: VTDigger
title: New tech policy takes shape at Lamoille South Supervisory Union
description:
The new approach scales back the use of digital devices and essentially prohibits the use of artificial intelligence.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  New tech policy takes shape at Lamoille South Supervisory Union.
text:
Buses pick up students at the end of the day at the Westford School in Westford on Thursday, April 17, 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Liberty Darr was first published in the News & Citizen on Sept. 10, 2026.
When Stowe parent Molly Triffin Gaines attended “meet the teacher night” for her daughter’s third grade class just ahead of the new school year, she was surprised and thrilled to find that cursive writing was back on the curriculum.
Parents across the Lamoille South Supervisory Union — which oversees schools in Elmore, Morristown and Stowe — can likely expect a lot more pencil scribbles and eraser shavings this year thanks to a new technology policy and associated plan that scales back the use of devices across the schools and essentially prohibits the use of artificial intelligence.
“We had one teacher the other day that came down to the office at the middle school and said they needed to purchase a bunch of pencil grips because the kids have been doing so much handwriting that they’re complaining about the cramps in their hands,” Lamoille South Superintendent Ryan Heraty said just days into the new school year.
Those in the office at the time, he said, all but cheered.
In a letter to families ahead of the school year, Heraty outlined just a few examples of the extensive plan regarding electronics:

Kindergarten students will no longer have devices in the classroom — excluding assistive technology.
Middle school students will no longer take devices from school home.
Students will no longer have access to artificial intelligence tools.
YouTube is blocked for student use.
Apps and platforms need independent research to support their use. Exceptions will be made on a case-by-case basis.

And, yes, homework at the middle school level is going analog.
The intersectionality of technology and its use in the classroom has hit an inflection point across the country and in Vermont in recent years. This year, for the first year, new state legislation is in effect that prohibits students from using cellphones and other personal electronic devices during the school day.
Lamoille South has arguably been ahead of the curve when it comes to studying the effects technology has on the cognitive and emotional well-being of its student body. Two years ago, the schools began limiting cellphone use.
“Overwhelmingly, over 80% of families said get rid of the phones,” Heraty said. “Teachers were saying, ‘Let’s get rid of the phone.’ So, we did it, and it was pretty seamless.”
That work essentially set the stage for a broader discussion around the overall usage of technology in the classroom — including Chromebooks and other tools.
The use of such devices really ramped up during the Covid-19 pandemic, Heraty said, as the switch to digital learning took precedence.
“There started to be this groundswell of public sentiment or discussions around technology and Chromebooks and screen time and mental health awareness,” he said.
The supervisory union performed an audit of how many minutes a day — both in classrooms and at homes — students were looking at screens on their laptops. Although the numbers across all the schools weren’t particularly overwhelming, in some cases, they were still high, especially nighttime usage among older students.
“One of the things we were finding at the middle school that pushed us in this direction was that students were doing a lot of gaming on their Chromebooks at home, and parents were feeling like they had another screen to monitor,” Heraty said.
Earlier this year, the supervisory union formed a technology working committee composed of students, teachers, administrators and parents that ultimately proposed the new two-page policy, adopted by the combined Lamoille South board at a July 14 retreat. And the research that they found wasn’t really all that convincing that using computers is better than doing something on paper, he said.
One of the policy’s main directives requires administrators to present a technology plan annually to the school boards for feedback and review.
The working group met three times over the summer and created the first plan, a 12-page, detailed document that sections specific grade-level bands and developmental levels. The role of technology and the associated guidelines are clarified specific to that unique level.
Heraty said it’s meant to be a living document, updated annually to meet the demands of the rapidly changing environment while balancing the need to prepare students for the world that exists.
Triffin Gaines, a parent of three and a member of the committee, said the work is a step in the right direction, at least in her perspective.
“My kids don’t have smartphones or iPads or anything, but then it was hard when they would go to school and they would be given a device of their own,” she said.
The plan, Heraty said, won’t be perfect, but it is an attempt to strike the balance between responsible tech use and students’ health.
“We’re going old school in some ways,” he said. “It’s just proven strategies and not wanting to get away from the things that we know work.”
