title: Curt Crowell Peterson
description:
Curt will be remembered as a beloved father and friend, and a devoted husband to Jennifer, his wife of 43 years and the love of his life. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Curt Crowell Peterson.
text:
Born: 02/05/1943
Plainfield, New Jersey
Died: 09/01/2026
Windsor, Vermont
Details of service:

Curt Crowell Peterson of Hartland, Vermont, formerly of Weston, Massachusetts, passed away from prostate cancer on September 1, 2026.
Born in 1943, he was the son of Carl Peterson and Gladys Crowell. He is survived by his wife, Jennifer Cross Peterson; his children, Jennifer, Mark, Gretchen, Heather, and Erik Peterson; his grandchildren, Ruth Peterson, Owein Labarr, Mae Peterson, and Parker Rowley; his sister, Chip Miles; and many cousins, nieces, and nephews. He was predeceased by his granddaughter, Zoe Peterson, and his sister, Diane Mundy. 
Curt was born in Plainfield, New Jersey, and grew up in Watchung. He attended the Pingry School and Washington & Jefferson College, and graduated from Rutgers University. Most significantly, he was a faithful and proud alumnus of Proctor Academy (’62) or, as he called it, “the school of last resorts,” where he served on the board of trustees. 
Everywhere he lived, whether in New Jersey, New York, New Hampshire, or Weston, Mass, he was an active leader in community organizations, including the Swedish-American Chamber of Commerce, the Scandinavian Living Center, and Trout Unlimited, where he made many lifelong friends. 
Nowhere was this more true than in Hartland, where Curt was on the board of Aging in Hartland, delivered Meals on Wheels, wrote for the Mountain Times and Valley News, and raised Icelandic sheep, while also forging many deep and loyal friendships in the area, especially with the “usual suspects”: Moira and Tom Ripley, Carol and Howard Trachtenberg, Carol Stedman and Marty Banak, and Helen and Bob Stocker. 
Curt will be remembered as a beloved father and friend, as well as for the cards he made for family and friends, his irreverent sense of humor, his entertaining stories, his love of dogs and sheep, his gruff kindness, and his appreciation for food, particularly pork roll. As his mother-in-law once said, “Curt never met a meal he didn’t like.” This was also true of people. Curt was genuinely interested in everyone he met, with whom he’d inevitably find points of connection, whether through family, friends, fishing, golf, Sweden, New Jersey, or his many professional endeavors. His family came to expect errands to take twice as long because of all the friends he’d run into along the way, especially at BG’s, where he was a regular fixture, often stopping by multiple times a day for coffee, a treat, and a chat. 
Most of all, Curt will be remembered as a devoted husband to Jennifer, his wife of 43 years and the love of his life. He never stopped marveling at how lucky he was that she agreed to marry him, and he expressed his gratitude for her every day.
Donations in Curt’s memory may be made to Aging in Hartland or the Rutland County Humane Society.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Amy Beros and Liz Reasoner discuss the growing food insecurity during Hunger Awareness month
description: Thanks to soaring prices and big cuts to federal food assistance, hunger is quickly growing worse across North Carolina. The latest conservative estimate is that one out of seven North Carolinians is “food insecure” – a number that’s way up in just the last five years and now even higher than during the pandemic. […]
text:
Amy Beros and Liz Reasoner (Courtesy photos)  
Thanks to soaring prices and big cuts to federal food assistance, hunger is quickly growing worse across North Carolina. The latest conservative estimate is that one out of seven North Carolinians is “food insecure” – a number that’s way up in just the last five years and now even higher than during the pandemic. How did we get into this situation, how are food aid organizations trying to respond, and what more should all of us be doing? Recently, as part of Hunger Awareness Month, Newsline explored those questions and more in a special extended conversation with a pair of experts: Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina President Amy Beros and Food Bank of the Albemarle CEO Liz Reasoner.
In Part One of our recent extended conversation with North Carolina food bank leaders Amy Beros and Liz Reasoner we explored the remarkable and unhappy fact that – thanks to the toxic combination of rising prices and big cuts to federal funding for food assistance, the scourge of hunger is on the rise in North Carolina, and is now worse even than during the COVID-19 pandemic.
In Part Two of our chat, we dug deeper into the scope of the crisis, the huge practical challenges that many struggling households face in acquiring healthy food, the daunting problems that food banks and pantries face in serving the growing number of people in need, and how ultimately, it’s incumbent upon all of us to ask and expect more from elected leaders – particularly in Washington – if we’re going to see any meaningful improvement in the situation.

title: U.S. Senate Dems disclose Trump administration operation dug through state voter rolls
text: WASHINGTON — Department of Homeland Security officers may have broken state laws carrying out the Trump administration's orders to find noncitizens voting illegally in federal elections, Democratic senators alleged Monday following a whistleblower complaint.U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said the whistleblower detailed the department’s “Unlawful Voter Initiative," in which U.S Citizenship and Immigration Services immigration officers combed through state voter rolls, sometimes pretending to be the voter to access records. U.S. citizens were also swept up in the efforts due to faulty data and pressure from top officials to meet a quota of five investigations per hour, or 12 minutes per inquiry, according to the whistleblower’s account. “We just got more proof of (President Donald) Trump’s vile schemes to rig our elections,” said Schumer, a New York Democrat. “A DHS whistleblower warns that the department is pulling hundreds, hundreds of federal agents from national security roles, and sending them on a wild goose chase. The goal: to try and prove Trump’s sad, tired and long debunked election conspiracy theories.”The New York Times was the first to report the existence of the DHS operation.California Sen. Alex Padilla, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration that oversees federal elections, said the president “will go to extraordinary lengths to try to interfere with the midterm elections.”Padilla said the whistleblower came forward last week.  Padilla and Schumer called for DHS to shut down the operation. The department did not immediately respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment. “Donald Trump knows his record has been so bad,” Padilla said. “His only chance at keeping Republican majorities in Congress is to interfere with the elections.”Noncitizens are not allowed to vote in federal elections, and cases are extremely rare. Some localities have passed laws to allow for noncitizen voting in local elections. But the topic is a priority for the president, who has directed DHS to investigate voter rolls for illegal voting by noncitizens. On Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced two noncitizens from Kansas and Louisiana illegally voted in federal elections.“Voter fraud is already a serious problem, but non-citizens voting is even worse,” Mullin said. “Every time a non-citizen casts a ballot, it steals a vote from an American citizen.”

title: Iowa Utilities Commission to decide on hearing dates for Summit pipeline changes
description: The Iowa Utilities Commission proposed hearing dates Monday for a permit on segments of a carbon sequestration pipeline project proposed in Iowa.  Supporters of the Summit Carbon Solutions pipeline said the early 2027 hearing dates should be moved up to before the end of 2026, while opponents said the proposed hearing schedule interferes with harvest, […]
text:
Parties for and against a carbon sequestration project shared opinions with the Iowa Utilities Commission Sept. 14, 2026 about a potential hearing schedule for the pipeline. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) The Iowa Utilities Commission proposed hearing dates Monday for a permit on segments of a carbon sequestration pipeline project proposed in Iowa. 
Supporters of the Summit Carbon Solutions pipeline said the early 2027 hearing dates should be moved up to before the end of 2026, while opponents said the proposed hearing schedule interferes with harvest, winter holidays and calving season. Opponents of the pipeline also argued that the hearings on the company’s second phase of the project should not be heard until the lawsuit over the permit for the pipeline’s initial route has concluded. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
IUC proposed hearing schedules for two segments of pipeline – both less than 5 miles in length – and heard comments from Summit Carbon Solutions’ SCS Carbon Transport, corn, ethanol and labor groups in favor of the project and from landowners and environmental groups opposed to the project. 
Summit Carbon Solutions is planning to build a carbon sequestration pipeline that would connect to biofuel facilities across Iowa and other surrounding states and transport carbon dioxide captured at the plants to be sequestered underground. 
Originally, the company planned to sequester the liquified gas in geological formations in North Dakota, but a law change in South Dakota and additional incentives for enhanced oil recovery have led to a change in plans. The company filed a request to amend its original permit, which was already approved by the IUC, to the new route which reduces the overall number of impacted landowners.
The dockets in discussion Monday were part of Summit’s second phase of the project to add more laterals to the pipeline across Iowa. One docket centered on a 2.98 mile stretch of pipe through Ida County and the other on a 4.08 mile stretch through Floyd County. 
Landowners who have been fighting against the pipeline for several years now questioned Monday how a hearing for the pipeline’s second phase could proceed when Summit’s permit – giving the company the right to eminent domain – is the subject of a lawsuit currently in district court. 
Deborah Main, a participant at Monday’s hearing, said the dockets in discussion were “not self-sustaining” as they are “dependent” on the first phase of the pipeline project. 
“We shouldn’t even be here today,” Main said. “We have the proverbial cart before the horse.”
IUC Chair Sarah Martz reminded participants at the hearing Monday that it was a “procedural” scheduling conference set to establish a hearing schedule and not to discuss the merits of the pipeline project. 
Because both segments were less than 5 miles in length, Martz explained the hearings did not need to take place in the counties and would instead take place in Des Moines. Opposing participants in the scheduling hearing also argued the hearings should be held in the counties so locals can easily participate. 
Under IUC’s proposed hearing schedule for both docket entries, the Ida County segment hearing would be Feb. 23, 2027, with various filings due in the months preceding. For the second docket, IUC proposed a March 23, 2027 hearing.
Brant Leonard, representing SCS Carbon Transport, said the evidence the company planned to present at the future hearings would be “very similar if not identical in many respects” to information the IUC has heard from the “original docket.” 
Leonard said there were five landowners on the Ida County segment and eight on the Floyd County segment that had yet to sign easements with the company. 
Leonard said he anticipated it was “not likely to be a lengthy hearing process” and the company felt the hearings should be held in mid-December, for both segments. 
Representation for Iowa Corn Growers Association, Iowa Renewable Fuels Association and Great Plains Laborers District Council also pushed for earlier hearing dates.
“Again, this has been five years, and we would like to see the hearing or schedule moved and expedited in any way possible,” Richie Schmidt with Great Plains said. 
In filings on the docket, Summit asked the schedules for the two dockets be combined, or to run parallel. 
Christina Gruenhagen, representing Iowa Farm Bureau Federation, asked commissioners if that motion was being denied since the commission proposed two separate schedules. She also asked if there were issues within the docket that would be considered as already decided on by the IUC and therefore not heard again. The answer to this, she said, would “influence” the anticipated length of the hearing and the evidence presented by involved parties. 
Landowners who spoke in opposition to the project said if a hearing is held, it should be later in the year, some suggested June 2027. 
“The deadline there, a lot of that takes place over the holiday season, calving season, early harvesting in the fall,” Don Johannsen, a Cherokee County landowner, said Monday. “This is obviously a schedule that’s for the convenience of the pipeline and not for the landowners and people who would try and talk up against this project.” 
Wally Taylor, legal chair with the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, questioned why these two dockets were being separated from the other phase two filings.
Martz said the commission would take the input shared into advisement and that the body will issue orders for procedural schedules on the dockets. Martz did not say when the orders will be issued.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont says ‘rain bomb’ overwhelmed parts of Fairfield County
description: There were no known injuries or deaths from the storm. Officials will tally damages to see whether CT qualifies for federal disaster relief.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont said on Monday that a “rain bomb” was to blame for severe localized flooding in parts of Fairfield County over the weekend that covered roads and stranded dozens of motorists. 
There were no immediate reports of injuries or deaths from the storm, but officials said they were in the process of tallying damages to determine whether the costs would qualify for federal disaster relief funds.
During a press conference at the State Capitol Monday, flanked by emergency management and transportation officials, Lamont explained that rain bombs differ from other severe storms in their unpredictability and ability to quickly overwhelm local infrastructure.
“It’s how sudden the intense rainfall is — five, seven, nine inches in a very limited period of time. That’s what causes severe flooding that overwhelms our stormwater drainage systems,” Lamont said. “And you saw that yesterday, especially down in Fairfield County.”
More than 7 inches of rain fell Sunday in Stamford, Darien and Westport, according to data collected by the National Weather Service.
The most severe impacts were felt in Westport, where several downtown businesses were flooded and local fire crews conducted 13 water rescues. Floodwaters also covered several lanes of Interstate-95 between exits and 18 and 19 on Sunday, according to NWS reports.
More than six feet of water was measured in the yard at a state Department of Transportation regional maintenance facility in Westport, according to Deputy DOT Commissioner Laoise King. Officials are evaluating how many vehicles at the yard were damaged and whether they can be repaired, King said.
Other instances of localized flooding and water rescues were also reported in Bridgeport, Fairfield and New Haven.
In Stratford, 4.25 inches of rain had fallen as of 7:52 p.m. yesterday according to Sikorsky Memorial weather station data. Sunday’s rainfall is among the top 25 heaviest rainfall days dating back to the 1940s, according to historical data from the weather station.
But some of the hardest rains in Connecticut fell over the course of just a few hours, prompting several meteorologists to label it a one-in-200-year flood event.
This metric is determined by the probability that an area will see a certain amount of rainfall in a given time period. A 200-year flood has a one in 200, or 0.5% chance, of occurring. Gary Lessor, a meteorologist at Western Connecticut State University, said such historic rainfalls are happening more frequently than the odds would suggest.
“A 200-year flood occurring is not that usual, and it is seemingly happening quite often,” Lessor said.
This photo provided by Westport Fire Department shows flash flooding in Westport, Conn., Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. Credit: Jennifer Petrosinelli / Westport Fire Department via AP
Emma Cimino, the acting commissioner of the state Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, said climate change is contributing to the severity of the storms and the costs to rebuild.
“Climate-induced extreme rainfall is increasing, even without a comparable increase in annual rainfall,” Cimino said. “And as we’ve heard, as we’ve seen, when intense rain falls quickly, local drainage systems, roads, streams, and other infrastructure can be overwhelmed. It is hard to build infrastructure that can withstand rain like what we saw yesterday.”
Several officials, including Lamont, compared the weekend’s storms to the catastrophic floods that struck the Naugatuck River Valley in 2024, breaking rainfall records and causing an estimated $206 million in damages. While the impacted areas of the state were largely spared that level of devastation, officials were working to determine whether the damage would qualify for a major disaster declaration.
State Emergency Management Director Bill Turner said the threshold to qualify for federal public disaster assistance in Fairfield County is around $5 million, along with $7 million in total statewide damages.
“We’re doing our due diligence and surveying the whole coastline, all the coastal communities, to make sure we’re not missing anything,” Turner said. 
King, the deputy DOT Commissioner, said there was no “permanent” damage reported to any state roads. Rail operations along Metro-North Railroad and CT Transit lines had also returned to normal schedules on Monday, she added.
Also on Monday, the Federal Emergency Management Agency approved more than $350,000 in federal disaster aid to pay for repairs to Darien’s Gorham Pond Dam, which was damaged in flooding caused by Hurricane Ida in 2021.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Pacheco wins Dartmouth-area primary as 14-vote margin holds
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
description: Pacheco claimed a 14-vote win with 2,493 votes to Medeiros' 2,479 after the recount, according to results from the secretary of state's office.
text:
AFTER A RECOUNT, Edward Pacheco has narrowly secured victory over Stephen Medeiros in the Democratic primary for the Ninth Bristol District House seat. 
Pacheco claimed a 14-vote win with 2,493 votes to Medeiros’s 2,479 after the recount, according to results from the secretary of state’s office. Last week, results from The Associated Press showed Pacheco up by the same number of votes with 2,469 to 2,455 for Medeiros, a Dartmouth real estate agent.
Pacheco, a Dartmouth resident, works as a bartender and transportation manager for a nonprofit in Fall River and is a former security guard at Dartmouth High School. He has said he wanted to run to bring a “working class person’s perspective to the State House.”
Pacheco told the News Service on Friday his campaign is “very glad that the democratic process worked the way it was supposed to.”
“We have the utmost confidence in the process and the technology that’s used for these, you know, balloting systems,” he said. “So, you know, was very grateful for all of the work that all of the election workers did and all of the volunteers, the poll workers … grateful obviously for the other people that participated in the process as well.”
Looking ahead to November’s general election, Pacheco said he plans to continue speaking about the issues affecting residents “with substance rather than just slogans.”
Pacheco’s campaign has focused on housing, public safety and local aid. He said his priorities include addressing the district’s wastewater system issues, noting that Dartmouth’s system has almost reached 80% of its capacity. Pacheco said he wants to support public safety services, including fire stations, which he said have been closing across the district. Pacheco’s website outlines several other issues including opposing large-scale data centers, curbing rising utility costs and promoting more transparency from the Department of Public Utilities, recruiting and retaining educators, establishing universal early childhood education, preserving open spaces and farmlands as well as sealing eligible juvenile criminal records.
In a Facebook post on Wednesday, Medeiros congratulated Pacheco on his win. He also called for more voters to cast ballots and to research each candidate.
“An educated, participating community is the backbone of our democracy,” Medeiros said in the post.
Pacheco is set to face Republican and political newcomer Chester Tam in November’s general election for the seat that Rep. Christopher Markey is vacating. The district, which covers Dartmouth and parts of New Bedford, was the only one in the state where both parties had contested primaries this cycle.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: State revenues climb 2.8% in August, remain ahead of forecast
description: Virginia’s general fund revenues rose by $58 million in August compared with the same month last year, keeping collections slightly ahead of the state’s forecast despite signs of weakness in Virginia’s labor market.  Collections increased 2.8% for the month and totaled nearly $4.61 billion during the first two months of fiscal 2027, according to the […]
text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger's administration reported that Virginia’s general fund revenues rose 2.8% in August and remained ahead of the state’s forecast through the first two months of fiscal 2027. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Virginia’s general fund revenues rose by $58 million in August compared with the same month last year, keeping collections slightly ahead of the state’s forecast despite signs of weakness in Virginia’s labor market. 
Collections increased 2.8% for the month and totaled nearly $4.61 billion during the first two months of fiscal 2027, according to the August revenue report released by Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration on Friday. 
Through Aug. 31, revenues were up 5.4%, or $236.5 million, from the same period last year and were running 1.8%, or $81.5 million, ahead of the official forecast. 
“Revenue remains generally in line with our forecast through the first two months of the fiscal year, though continued national economic uncertainty means we must stay vigilant,” Spanberger said in a statement. 
“With high costs driven by the president’s reckless war and an uncertain labor market remaining areas of concern nationwide, particularly given persistently high inflation, we will continue to responsibly manage the commonwealth’s finances.”
Sales and use taxes provided much of the early growth. Collections increased 4% in August from a year earlier and were up 9.1%, or $77.3 million, for the fiscal year to date. That put sales tax revenue 5.6%, or $49.2 million, ahead of projections. August collections reflect sales made in July. 
Individual income taxes, which account for about 70% of general fund revenue, showed a different picture. Net collections fell 1.2%, or $18.8 million, in August. They remained up 2.1% for the fiscal year but were $22.4 million below projections.
Payroll withholding taxes declined 1.9%, or $27.9 million, compared with last August and came in $37.3 million below the monthly forecast. Through August, however, withholding collections were up 2.3% from the same period last year and only $9.6 million below projections. 
“August is a light month for revenue collections, with no major quarterly deadlines affecting sources like nonwithholding or corporate income tax,” Secretary of Finance Mark Sickles said. 
“Withholding collections came in $37.3 million below forecast for the month, though that is well within the normal range of monthly variance for that source. Sales and use tax collections continued to outperform, growing 4% for the month. We are concerned by persistently high core inflation and the resulting increased likelihood of a Federal Reserve rate hike.”
The report noted that monthly withholding collections typically vary from the forecast by $70 million to $90 million. 
Nonwithholding income tax collections, which include estimated and final payments, rose 17.2%, or $19.9 million, in August. They were up 7.4% for the year and running $11.2 million ahead of the forecast. August is not typically a significant month for those payments. 
Virginia also issued $92.6 million in individual income tax refunds during August, up from $81.8 million a year earlier. Refunds totaled $204.4 million through the first two months of the fiscal year, an increase of 12.4%. 
Corporate income tax collections totalled $7.2 million for the month and were $35.2 million ahead of projections for the fiscal year to date. 
The $114.8 million year-over-year increase largely reflects an accounting adjustment that recategorized some corporate revenue in August 2025, producing an unusually negative total that month.  
 Recordation taxes and related collections increased 4.1%, or $1.7 million, in August and were up by 8.4% for the fiscal year. Despite that growth, collections remained $6.6 million below the forecast.
The revenue projections came against a mixed economic backdrop. The nation added 162,000 jobs in August while the unemployment rate held at 4.1%. Virginia’s unemployment rate dipped from 3.8% to 3.7% in July, the latest month for which state figures were available.
The state’s labor market showed more signs of strain. 
Virginia lost 9,600 jobs in July, and the state’s June employment estimate was revised downward by another 1,900 jobs. Labor force participation slipped to 63%, continuing what the report described as a sustained multiyear low. 
U.S. gross domestic product grew at an annualized rate of 1.5% during the second quarter, according to the report. Oil prices remained elevated, while the Federal Reserve’s preferred measures of underlying inflation were unchanged in July. 
Virginia’s official forecast calls for general fund revenue to reach nearly $34.7 billion during fiscal 2027, an increase of 4.1% from the previous year.

title: Vermont’s new homelessness policy abandons people in crisis
description:
Emergencies don't stop happening just because the state stops answering the phone.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s new homelessness policy abandons people in crisis.
text:
Dear Editor,
I read Carly Berlin’s recent story in VTDigger about Vermont’s new homelessness assistance policy with sadness. Apparently both our Republican governor and the Democratic Legislature are complicit in this. My familiarity with the subject derives mainly from the dozen years I spent in the Vermont attorney general’s office representing the Department for Children and Families in administrative hearings, often concerning denials of assistance to people in housing emergencies. 
I have this to say about the new policies: Needs do not arise only during normal business hours. Emergencies do not stop occurring merely because you stop viewing them as such. It is long, long past time that we as a society stopped making people prove they deserve a roof over their heads as a prerequisite for helping them obtain it. Everybody deserves it. Especially children. 

READ MORE

This state’s treatment of people who lack that basic human right is, and long has been, shamefully inadequate. I am sad to see it getting worse.
Seth A. Steinzor South Burlington, Vt.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Eyeing copper, mining giant BHP returns to Alaska
description: This story was originally published in the Anchorage Press. Subscribe here. The world’s largest mining company is back in Alaska. More than a decade after abandoning a search for coal in the western Arctic, Australia-based BHP quietly staked new mineral claims this summer in a remote part of Southcentral Alaska — with an eye for […]
text:
A sample of copper — a metal that one of the world's largest mining companies is now targeting in Alaska. (U.S. Geological Survey)This story was originally published in the Anchorage Press. Subscribe here. 
The world’s largest mining company is back in Alaska.
More than a decade after abandoning a search for coal in the western Arctic, Australia-based BHP quietly staked new mineral claims this summer in a remote part of Southcentral Alaska — with an eye for copper.
The company, which owns huge iron, coal and copper mines around the world, also conducted sampling and aerial surveys in Alaska in recent months, a BHP spokesperson told the Anchorage Press.
The project is still in the earliest stages of exploration, likely many years if not decades away from becoming an active mine. Most claims that mining companies stake never actually get developed; a subsidiary of a different mining giant, Rio Tinto, abandoned claims in 2013 in the same area that BHP is now showing interest, according to state records.
But BHP’s foray into Alaska is still notable given the company’s deep pockets and global reach, and as the latest example of the mining industry’s surging interest in the state.
Unlike the small, cash-strapped companies that do much of the claim-staking and early-stage exploration work in Alaska, BHP has the financial horsepower and expertise to turn a prospect into a mine.
“They are not going to farm it out to anyone if they find what they’re hoping to find,” said Dave Szumigala, a state mineral exploration geologist with decades of industry experience. “They’ve got the resources to take it all the way through development.”
BHP’s interest in Alaska comes amid high commodity prices, increased global demand for metals like copper and an intense push by the Trump administration to spur resource development in the state.
The company’s return to the state also reflects an uptick in new mining claims across Alaska, and it could contribute to a backlog in the Dunleavy administration’s processing of those claims.
The number of claims staked this year statewide is on track to double from last year, according to Steve Buckley, head of the mining section at the Alaska Department of Natural Resources.
Buckley’s team, which reviews and approves state mining claims, has reported a backlog of more than 10,000 claims this summer. The department has transferred three employees — more than doubling typical capacity — to help work through the backlog, Buckley said.
“It’s unprecedented,” he added.
Buckley declined to comment on BHP’s claims because they are still pending review. But he said large new claim blocks make up “a good portion” of the state’s backlog, which could take months for officials to clear.
State land managers have not yet reviewed and approved BHP’s claims, meaning they don’t appear on the state’s public mining claims database.
But documents filed with the state recorder’s office show that BHP staked dozens of claims across thousands of acres in the heart of the Alaska Range at the beginning of the summer.
Many of the claims appear to be deep in the mountains near the northern edge of Lake Clark National Park and the upper reaches of the Skwentna River, a tributary of the Susitna River, about 100 miles west of Anchorage and the state’s road system.
Szumigala called that region “very prospective” for massive, low-grade copper concentrations known as porphyry deposits.
He also noted that BHP’s interest in the area could draw more investment from other companies. Small exploration firms often stake claims next to majors, he said.
“One way juniors will get investment in their company is to say, ‘Well, we staked right next to BHP’s property,” Szumigala said.
BHP confirmed that it’s assessing the area’s copper potential.
“Through the summer months we commenced non-disturbing studies as part of a first, early-stage exploration program to better understand the area’s geology and resource potential,” the company said in a statement provided to the Anchorage Press. “As we advance this work, we are meeting with local stakeholders to learn more about the region.”
BHP has not applied for permits to conduct more intensive exploratory work like drilling.
“Exploration is inherently a long-term process,” the company said, noting that “the vast majority of exploration programs do not advance beyond the early stages.”
BHP has met with representatives from the region’s Alaska Native corporation, CIRI, to review maps and discuss cultural training, a CIRI spokesperson said.
Environmental groups, meanwhile, say they’re working to ensure that new mining in the state doesn’t come at the cost of public lands and wildlife.
The broad uptick in state mining claims is a “real cause for concern, especially when DNR can’t even keep up with them,” said Mary Catharine Martin, communications director at the conservation organization SalmonState, using an acronym for the Alaska Department of Natural Resources.
In an email, Martin cited four principles about development espoused by the late Alaska governor Jay Hammond.
“Do Alaskans want it? Does it pay its own way? Is it environmentally sound? Does it meet our constitutional mandate to manage our natural resources for the maximum benefit of all Alaskans?” Martin said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Some Oklahoma airport visitors will be able to greet family, friends at airport gates again
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – For the first time in more than two decades, some non-ticketed airport visitors will be able to greet and say good-bye to airplane passengers at the gate. The Transportation Security Administration will now allow PreCheck members to accompany family members and loved ones to the gate, greet arriving passengers and use airport […]
text:
Travelers stand in a long line at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on Monday, March 23, 2026, the same day federal immigration officials started assisting with airport security. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)OKLAHOMA CITY – For the first time in more than two decades, some non-ticketed airport visitors will be able to greet and say good-bye to airplane passengers at the gate.
The Transportation Security Administration will now allow PreCheck members to accompany family members and loved ones to the gate, greet arriving passengers and use airport facilities and restaurants without taking a flight at 13 airports, including Will Rogers International Airport in Oklahoma City. The program is called Gateside.
TSA PreCheck members must request a pass to go beyond the security checkpoint one to three days before the visit.
Applicants must enter their TSA PreCheck Known Traveler Number and select a participating airport.
After completing the online process, approved participants must present a REAL ID or other acceptable form of identification, such as a passport, at the TSA checkpoint. Visitors  will be subject to TSA screening.
Those enrolled in TSA’s prescreening program, who pay a fee of $85 or less, are given quicker access through security lines to get to airport gates. They are allowed to leave electronics in a bag and don’t have to remove jackets, shoes and belts when going through airport security checkpoints.
TSA said the new initiative will make “the airport experience more seamless, convenient and family friendly” while maintaining security.
Airport visitors were last allowed at the flight gate without a ticket 25 years ago. That access was halted following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.
Other airports participating in the Gateside program include:

Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport, Little Rock
Dallas Fort Worth International Airport
Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport
Harry Reid International Airport, Las Vegas
Indianapolis International Airport
John Glenn Columbus International Airport in Ohio
Los Angeles International Airport
Mesa Gateway Airport in Arizona

text:
The Department of Corrections Broad River complex houses death row, among other prisoners, in Columbia, S.C. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A death row inmate who previously asked to drop his appeals and be executed is suing the state for medication he says will make him want to continue living.
James Robertson, who was convicted in 1999 of killing his parents in what prosecutors said was a bid to get part of a $2.2 million inheritance, would no longer want to face execution immediately if he were on the right medication, his attorneys argued in the lawsuit filed last month.
The legal challenge came after multiple requests from Robertson to drop his appeals and face execution as soon as possible. That led to a year’s worth of mental evaluations, including two private hearings in May, to determine whether the 52-year-old was mentally fit enough to fire his lawyers and withdraw the pending appeals in his case.
SC death row inmate asks to drop his appeals and face execution

An expert determined Robertson’s mental health would likely improve with the right combination of medications and consistent access to the same therapists and psychiatrists. When Robertson had long-term relationships with counselors and the right medications, his symptoms improved, according to the lawsuit
Under changed policies, the Department of Corrections started rotating mental health counselors and removed Robertson’s medications from the list approved in the prison’s pharmacy, according to the lawsuit. Robertson is housed on death row at the agency’s Broad River campus in Columbia.
“As a result, Robertson suffers from deteriorating mental health that has caused him to take actions which harm his material interests and threaten to cause Robertson to suffer permanent injury,” his lawyer, Jeremy Hodges with Nelson Mullins, wrote.
Spokespeople for the Department of Corrections and the attorney general’s office, which is representing the agency in the case, declined to comment. Neither has filed a response in the case.
The lawsuit doesn’t specify the diagnoses Robertson used the medication to treat. In previous court filings, attorneys have said he has a history of depression and suicidal thoughts, as well as bipolar disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
Robertson previously took Pristiq, an antidepressant often used for major depressive disorder, and Seroquel, an antipsychotic medication often used to treat bipolar disorder, according to the lawsuit.
James Robertson. (Provided/SC Department of Corrections)
In February 2025, the Department of Corrections changed its policy to bar pharmacists from prescribing the exact type of medication Robertson used, which was released into the bloodstream immediately. Instead, Robertson was prescribed a slower-acting, longer-lasting version of the medication.
The lawsuit doesn’t explain why the agency removed the medication from its pharmacy, or why Robertson stopped taking his accompanying medication. Quick-release Seroquel has become associated with drug abuse, especially among prisoners, researchers have found.
The slower-acting version of the medication caused unwanted side effects and didn’t work as well, according to the lawsuit. Robertson stopped taking his medications altogether.
This was the third time Robertson lost access to medications that helped control his mental health symptoms during the 27 years he’s spent in prison, his lawyers wrote. The Department of Corrections similarly removed previous medications that helped manage his symptoms, according to the lawsuit.
Robertson’s attorneys are arguing the denial of the medications amounts to cruel and unusual punishment under the U.S. Constitution. The lawsuit asks a judge to order the prison system to give Robertson access to any of the medications he’s tried in the past that worked for him.
With the right mental health treatments, Robertson would likely want to continue pursuing his appeals instead of opting for execution, his attorneys wrote.
Robertson first asked to fire his attorneys and withdraw his appeals in spring of 2025. In a letter to a federal judge, Robertson said his attorneys declined to do so, a decision they later said in court documents was a breach of their ethical obligation to do what is right for their client.
Robertson only wanted to face execution because he was depressed, his attorneys at the time wrote. His depression was caused in large part by the execution of several of his closest friends on death row, they wrote.
In May, following two private hearings evaluating his mental health, Robertson wrote again to the magistrate assigned to his case, Judge Mary Gordon Baker, asking for help getting access to one or both of the mental health medications he had previously taken.
Robertson was sentenced to death in 1999 for killing his parents, Terry and Earl Robertson, two years prior. The murders took place two days before Thanksgiving. Robertson, who was 24 at the time, used the claw end of a hammer, a baseball bat and a knife, prosecutors said.
Robertson’s attorneys said he had a psychotic episode after crushing and snorting too much Ritalin, a drug he was prescribed for ADHD. Prosecutors said he had planned his parents’ deaths, and the jury, which recommended death, agreed.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Amateur sports the latest frontier in NJ independent contractor fight
description: Business groups and sports officials are pushing for a law declaring referees and umpires independent contractors amid a broader worker classification fight.
text:
Business groups and sports officials are pushing for a law declaring referees and umpires independent contractors amid a broader worker classification fight. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/Oklahoma Voice)Umpires, referees, and other amateur sports officials urged Assembly lawmakers to pass legislation that would exclude them from a state test that weighs whether they are employees or independent contractors.
More than one witness told the Assembly Labor Committee, which did not vote on the bill Monday, that labor regulations set to take effect in October would push them out of the industry, raise costs for school districts and sports leagues, and rob workers of flexibility.
“When my wife and the thousands of sports officials across New Jersey take the field, they are not looking for a traditional W-2 job,” said bill co-sponsor Assemblyman Anthony Angelozzi (D-Burlington). “They choose when and where they work, which leagues they serve, and how many games they accept.”
Sports officials’ push for an exception comes amid a broader furor against the state’s move to codify into regulation its interpretation of New Jersey’s independent contractor test, called the ABC test. The test’s three prongs measure whether a worker is free from their employer’s control, performs work outside a firm’s regular course or place of business, and engages in business independent of a given firm. Workers who meet all three prongs are independent contractors.
In New Jersey, amateur sports officials typically work piecemeal, selecting games from lists proffered by sports official associations at their leisure, multiple officials told the panel. They pay dues to join those associations and are paid at rates negotiated beforehand between the associations and the school districts or leagues that hold the events.
Officials argued that arrangement, which the bill’s proponents said allows individual umps and refs to select or reject assignments without consequence, leaves sports officials free from the control of a single employer, a key leg of the ABC test.
John Gallante, president of the New Jersey Umpire Alliance, said the state Department of Labor is moving to classify some sports officials as employees of the associations, though that determination is now the subject of a court challenge.
The nature of the department’s determination is unclear. The agency examines individual employment relationships for misclassification and does not issue industrywide classification rulings, though some of its decisions — like determinations that Uber and Lyft drivers are employees — can be applied that way. It does not comment on individual cases.
Sports officials on Monday questioned how they would even become eligible for some benefits. Classifying sports officials as independent contractors could, for example, require that they pay for unemployment benefits it’s unclear they could ever claim, Gallante said.
“How would the unemployment system realistically apply to someone who officiates one or two games a week and is paid by the game? When does that little league umpire become quote-unquote unemployed? When their Saturday game is canceled? When they choose not to accept an assignment? When their baseball season ends?” he said.
Official associations are also largely staffed by volunteers, lack the infrastructure for payroll withholdings, and would need funds to gain those capabilities, said Gallante, who is president of the Tri-State Elite Umpires Association, which supplies umpires to youth, adult, and little leagues.
Those costs would eventually be passed onto school districts and sports leagues, he said.
Others cautioned a change in their classification would deprive sports officials of the ability to deduct spending on uniforms, trainings, and safety gear from their taxes.
“If we were employees, we wouldn’t be able to file that. That, sometimes, can add up to a lot of money,” said Sam Robinson, an umpire and football referee.
Classing officials as employees would “take away the very autonomy we treasure,” Robinson added.
Though New Jersey in May moved to adopt regulations outlining the state’s interpretation of the ABC test, those regulations’ effective date was delayed until Oct. 1. Senate President Nicholas Scutari (D-Union) has urged Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) to move the date to July 1, 2027. Spokespeople for the governor did not return a request for comment.
Business groups have echoed Scutari’s call and seized on the push for exceptions to rail against the rule entirely, arguing lawmakers would need to make many more to calm disquiet over worker classification and lack the time for such changes.
“Do we realistically have time in 17 days to deal with every single industry that’s going to be affected?” said New Jersey Business and Industry Association policy analyst Jack Kelly.
Others have urged the administration to maintain its course on the rule, arguing it would ensure workers would receive overtime and sick leave benefits the law entitles them to.
“We need this rule to stop companies from cheating their workers, plain and simple,” said Nedia Morsy, director of immigrant advocacy group Make the Road New Jersey.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘Dear William,’ a book chronicling a family’s struggle with addiction, will be feature film
description: David Magee, in forefront, at the University of Mississippi's Ford Center with his family at the launch of his book, "Dear William," about his son's struggles with addiction.
text:
David Magee’s memoir is inspired by the last conversation he had with his late son.
“The last thing my son William had told me, like literally the last words, were, ‘Dad, you know, I hope you’ll tell our story one day,’” he recalled. “I didn’t really understand what that meant, and then I never saw him again.”
“Dear William,” a bestselling book, is about their family’s intergenerational struggles with addiction and mental illness. Now a feature film based on the book is being shot in Mississippi with help from an $800,000 grant from the Mississippi Attorney General’s Opioid Settlement Fund.
Magee is an author, speaker and Mississippi native. His oldest son and the book’s inspiration, William, died from an overdose. David Magee and his younger son Hudson are both in recovery from addiction, and his daughter struggled with an eating disorder. Magee and his wife live in Oxford. 
Magee explained that the grant money will go toward research and the film’s production. The rest of the film’s funding comes from in-kind donations from Magee and The Magee Foundation and from private investors. Donations and grants will cover the screenings.
Oxford’s David Magee, author of “Dear William,”  speaks at Boys State about addiction. Credit: Courtesy photo
“The film is a tool to (reach) the hearts and minds and students and families of Mississippi, and then beyond,” he said.
Principal photography began in Greenwood, MS on Sept. 8. Greenwood was previously a filming location for “The Help,” “Mississippi Masala,” and the miniseries “Women of the Movement,” among others.
Additional filming will take place at the University of Mississippi in Oxford. Magee said filming should wrap within seven to nine months, and that talks with distributors have been promising.
He previously told the Clarion-Ledger newspaper that the Delta region would be a pilot community for the educational component of the project. He previously worked there as an editor.
Last year, Mississippi Today investigated how the state had spent less than 1% of the tens of millions of dollars it received from the opioid settlement lawsuits on directly addressing addiction and overdose deaths.
Most of that money – 85% –  is now managed by the Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council and the Mississippi Legislature. The council reviews applications for projects that address Mississippi’s opioid crisis and makes recommendations to the Legislature on which ones to fund. 
Last year, the Legislature passed a bill expanding its ability to fund projects outside of the council’s recommendations.
Cover of David Magee’s book about his son’s struggles with addiction.
Magee believes there should be more resources of all kinds for people impacted by addiction, and strongly believes in the power of storytelling to make an impact. 
“We’re not standard, and I own that,” he said of settlement funds being used to help produce the film. 
“But I think students and families need us, and the AGs and all these people who fought for the opioid settlement, they need somebody and some people to jump out there and try something new and different – also that happens to have a lot of evidence around it supporting that it just might work.”
The plan is to show screenings of the film to K-12 students across Mississippi, followed up by panel discussions and directing people to addiction abatement resources.
There are plans to expand screenings to college students, establish storytelling workshops in the Delta and set up an online hub with prevention resources.
Magee added that the Center for Research Evaluation at the University of Mississippi will also be doing research on the project.
“The opioid funds, if they don’t belong to making this movie, to take to students and taking this education to them, then I don’t know where it belongs,” he said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Prison heat may have contributed to Iowa inmate’s July death, his sister says
description: On one of the hottest days of the summer, with temperatures in the 90s, Robert Buel, 57, died at the Anamosa State Penitentiary.  The official cause of death was arteriosclerotic and hypertensive cardiac disease, or chronic heart disease, according to the State Medical Examiner. But Buel’s sister, Kerensa Buel, of Sioux City, believes the lack […]
text:
Robert Buel's sister said she believes his July 15 death at the Anamosa State Penitentiary was related in part to excessive heat at the prison. (Photo of Buel courtesy of Kerensa Buel; photo of Anamosa courtesy of the Iowa Department of Corrections)On one of the hottest days of the summer, with temperatures in the 90s, Robert Buel, 57, died at the Anamosa State Penitentiary. 
The official cause of death was arteriosclerotic and hypertensive cardiac disease, or chronic heart disease, according to the State Medical Examiner. But Buel’s sister, Kerensa Buel, of Sioux City, believes the lack of air conditioning in the prison contributed to her brother’s July 15 death.  
“I think that he probably wouldn’t have died of a heart attack if he would have been in an air-conditioned prison,” Kerensa Buel said. 
For 15 years, the Iowa Department of Corrections has been asking state lawmakers for money to install air conditioning at the Anamosa prison and at the Mount Pleasant Correctional Facility – prisons that house more than 1,000 men each. 
The Iowa Legislature has never funded the proposals and, so far, the Corrections Department has prioritized other major infrastructure projects over adding A/C to the aging limestone lockups. 
Climate change is causing more and longer durations of extremely hot weather across the country and in Iowa. Eastern Iowa was under a heat advisory much of early September with heat indices topping 100 degrees, according to the National Weather Service. 
The air temperature at 8:30 p.m. in Living Unit C of the Anamosa State Penitentiary was 80 degrees or higher 21 days in July and 10 days in August, according to data collected by an inmate from a Corrections Department digital clock with a temperature display. 

Another inmate, Shawn Crowley, 55, said the hot, wet air at night makes it hard to breathe. 
“I’m having some pain in my chest, but it has not gotten to the point of going back to the hospital,” he said. 
Crowley, of Cedar Rapids, serving 32 years for second-degree kidnapping and voluntary manslaughter, had a heart attack in May 2025 and was airlifted from Anamosa to the University of Iowa Health Care in Iowa City, he said. 
“About a month and a half after returning from Iowa City, the weather was getting hot and the temp in the unit was hovering in the high 80’s to low 90’s every day and all night long,” Crowley said. “I began to get pains in my chest again, but not like the heart attack.”
Corrections medical staff diagnosed Crowley with pericarditis, an inflammation of the sac around the heart, he said. Doctors installed a defibrillator implant later in 2025, he said.  
“Because of the heart damage, being in the heat and humidity really takes a toll on me, to the point that I cannot do much, as in any form of exercise,” Crowley said. “I’m relegated to spending most of my time trying not to get overheated and pass out. Luckily the pericarditis has not flared up to the point of sending me to the hospital yet, but I’m in fear every day that it will, or worse.”
Kerensa Buel said she did weekly video calls with her brother, convicted of second-degree murder in Sioux City in 2022. Robert Buel often talked about struggling through summer heat waves in a prison without air conditioning in more than half the cells, she said. He said the cafeteria was the only place with air conditioning, but staff required inmates to leave soon after they’d finished eating. 
The night he died, Buel called his wife, Hilda, and said he felt like he was having a heart attack, Kerensa Buel said. 
“Instead of saying anything to anybody, he went and laid down and died,” she said. Robert Buel’s time of death was 11:36 p.m. July 15, according to the news release the Corrections Department sent out July 22. 
The Corrections Department did not respond to several emails and a voicemail message seeking comment for this story. 
About 1,700 people a year died from heat-related causes from 2018 to 2025, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But the actual number of U.S. deaths affected by heat may be as high as 9,000, according to a new analysis by Boston University and National Public Radio.
Heat causes the body, especially the heart, to work harder to keep cool. It can also exacerbate other chronic health conditions, like asthma. Because heat doesn’t leave marks on a body, it often isn’t noted on death records, Dr. Sameed Khatana, of the University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine, told NPR. 
Robert Buel was overweight, his sister said. Their father had died of a heart attack when he was 54. But Kerensa Buel believes if Robert hadn’t been incarcerated, he would still be alive. 
“He was a wonderful brother. He was a wonderful person,” she said. “He should not have been in prison and this should not have been the end of his life.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC AG Jackson requests new Duke rate class for data centers
description: Jackson argued the separate class would prevent data centers from shifting energy costs to residential consumers.
text:
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson on August 26, 2026. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson is asking the state Utilities Commission to make a new rate class for Duke Energy’s data center customers, his office said on Monday.
Jackson argued the separate class would prevent data centers from shifting energy costs to residential consumers.
“Duke Energy is onboarding an unprecedented number of data centers without a clear plan on how to protect ratepayers from higher rates and unacceptable risk,” Jackson said in a statement. 
NC AG Jackson, DEQ reach $590M settlement with chemical firms over PFAS

The proposal is part of a process the Utilities Commission began in Duke Energy’s rate cases after Jackson asked for a separate proceeding to consider the impact of new data centers and other large-load energy users. 
Jackson’s proposal asks for Duke Energy to make public the template contract it uses with data centers and other large energy users and submit regular reports about any agreements with large energy users that are different from those templates. 
“These data centers are upending our energy system, and we need to know that the Utilities Commission is making sure data centers pay for the strain they put on the grid and don’t unfairly burden ratepayers,” Jackson said in a statement. 
It also suggests that Duke Energy should make projections about energy load forecasts every 90 days, instead of its current schedule of every six months, so that the utility’s energy infrastructure reflects demand. 
Jackson’s proposal includes a request for Duke to pause new natural gas plant development so stakeholders can fully evaluate the company’s load forecast. 
State Sen. Natalie Murdock said her constituents are concerned about rising energy costs on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
“Duke Energy’s focus is straightforward: data centers and other large-load customers must pay the costs required to serve them,” Duke Energy spokesperson Craig Wilson told NC Newsline. “We’re committed to protecting existing customers from the costs to serve data centers while enabling responsible growth that strengthens our communities.”
State Sen. Natalie Murdock, a Democrat representing Chatham and Durham counties, said at a press conference Monday that she hears from constituents every day saying they’re concerned about rising costs due to rapidly expanding data centers. 
“North Carolina families simply cannot afford it,” Murdock said. “They cannot afford these higher bills that are higher for no reason.”
Over the past few months, the attorney general has consistently pushed back on Duke Energy.
Last month, Jackson accused the utility of providing incorrect information about its rate hike under oath. In July, he fired back against Duke’s proposed rate increase.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Woonsocket vows to close its sewage incinerator. For now, a new company  holds promise.
description: A new private contractor already well known in Rhode Island is on track to temporarily take over Woonsocket’s sewage treatment plant while city officials look for a long-term solution for the regionally vital but locally unwelcome incinerator. A resolution and accompanying draft contract on the Woonsocket City Council’s Monday night agenda call for a six-mon[...]
text:
The Woonsocket Wastewater Treatment facility is poised for new management under an agreement between the city and Veolia North America. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)A new private contractor already well known in Rhode Island is on track to temporarily take over Woonsocket’s sewage treatment plant while city officials look for a long-term solution for the regionally vital but locally unwelcome incinerator.
A resolution and accompanying draft contract on the Woonsocket City Council’s Monday night agenda call for a six-month agreement with Veolia North America to run the 16-acre Cumberland Hill Road sewage plant overlooking the Blackstone River. The contract covers all aspects of the wastewater treatment services and general oversight the accompanying sludge incineration arm. 
Veolia would replace Texas-based Jacobs Engineering Group, which is cutting ties with the city 14 years into its 20-year contract over a late payment dispute. The six-month agreement with Veolia, with up to six one-month extensions, calls for a $251,250 monthly payment for 15 full-time Veolia employees and repair costs. There is also a one-time $270,000 startup and transition fee, according to the agreement.
The contractor change comes as city officials continue their quest to shutter the controversial sludge-burning service, fed up with the odor, truck traffic and operational and legal woes piling up after 50 years of treating dried sewage for many of their municipal neighbors. 
The Cranston Wastewater Treatment Facility, also operated by Veolia, is the only other treatment plant in Rhode Island with an incinerator. The Boston-based company also provides water and wastewater treatment services for East Providence, South Kingstown, Narragansett, Jamestown, Newport and Providence, making it the obvious choice to step in for Jacobs, said Council President Dan Gendron, who is sponsoring the resolution
“The closing of the incinerator, in my mind, is absolutely the biggest factor of all this,” said Gendron, who is running in the nonpartisan city mayoral race against Mayor Chris Beauchamp. “That is absolutely a goal for the city.”
But an earlier plan to shutter the incinerator and sell off the wastewater treatment arm of the plant to the quasi-public Narragansett Bay Commission is no longer on the table. Negotiations fell off sometime this summer, felled by controversy over a separate project for a high-heat sludge processing plant in North Kingstown’s Quonset Business Park. Narragansett Bay Commission was planning to use the proposed Quonset pyrolysis plant to treat its wastewater byproducts, including from Woonsocket, but the Quonset project is now on hold amid community backlash, a pair of lawsuits, and a soon-to-begin legislative study panel.
“When that rug was pulled out from under NBC, so too was the ability to unconditionally shut down our incinerator,” Gendron said.




Quotation







The closing of the incinerator, in my mind, is absolutely the biggest factor of all this. That is absolutely a goal for the city.


– Woonsocket Council President Dan Gendron



A spokesperson for Narragansett Bay Commission did not respond to requests for comment Monday.
Meanwhile, a years-old payment dispute with Jacobs had reached its limit. 
Jacobs claims the city broke its contract by failing to make several of its monthly service payments on time in 2024, using the alleged breach of contract to justify severing the agreement entirely. The 20-year contract, signed in 2012, would have kept the wastewater operator in Woonsocket until 2032.
Jacobs, which also runs Westerly’s sewage plant, did not respond to multiple requests for comment on Monday.
The city acknowledges it failed to make at least two of the monthly payments within the mandated 90-day time frame due to what city solicitor Michael Lepizzera called a “clerical error.” But Lepizzera does not agree that the city’s late payments — rectified as soon as Jacobs notified city officials in December 2024 — constitute a breach of contract.
“The whole point of that clause was to make sure someone is not held hostage, that our financial problem does not become their financial problem,” Lepizzera said in an interview on Monday. “We had the money. That’s not the issue.”
Running out the clock 
Lepizzera claims that Jacobs intentionally waited out the late payment window because the company wanted out of the contract. Two 2023 lawsuits filed by state regulators and residents over environmental pollution and odor, respectively, along with the very public city position to shutter the plant, made it financially and legally unappealing for Jacobs to continue operations in Woonsocket, Lepizzera said.
Jacobs still hasn’t left, maintaining a 13-person crew running 24/7 operations and submitting mandated monthly odor reports to the city as recently as Aug. 14. But the company indicated they are “winding down,” and will be on their way out soon, Lepizzera said.
The date of Jacobs’ departure was not immediately available. 
“We have an obligation to make sure that the plant is being operated,” Lepizzera said. The wastewater arm treats 10 million gallons of sewage a day, from its host city as well as for North Smithfield and Bellingham and Blackstone, Massachusetts.
Gendron acknowledged it will be more expensive for the city to bring on Veolia than if it had retained Jacobs, which receives around $250,000 a month under the escalating payment framework laid out in its 2012 contract.
The city’s approved fiscal 2027 budget featured higher sewer fees to cover its expected payments to Veolia, with a $556 annual charge for city residents compared with roughly $440 the year before, Gendron said. The city’s independent wastewater treatment fund is expected to generate $13.5 million in revenue in fiscal 202, nearly $4 million more than the $9.6 million balance as of June 30, according to city budget documents.
The incinerator burns the dried sewage byproduct from these municipalities, along with another 30+ municipal and commercial customers that pay to have their sludge trucked to Woonsocket from across southern New England. Synagro, based in Baltimore, oversees the sludge operations, but Jacobs acted as Synagro’s supervisor and was the designated backup if Synagro breaks or ends its contract.
Sophia Salis, a spokesperson for Veolia in Rhode Island, acknowledged requests for comment but could not provide details immediately on the company’s interest in the work.
The Woonsocket City Council meets at City Hall at 7 p.m. Its meeting will also be streamed in the city YouTube page.
This story will be updated.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Nearly 150 Allina hospital doctors walk off the job in historic 4-day strike in Minnesota
description: Nearly 150 unionized doctors at two Twin Cities area hospitals began a four-day strike on Monday in what’s believed to be the first walkout by private-sector hospital doctors in U.S. history. Doctors clad in their white coats walked picket lines outside Allina Health’s Mercy Hospital in Coon Rapids and Unity campus in Fridley, carrying signs […]
text:
Doctors Council-SEIU members at Allina picket during a historic four-day Unfair Labor Practice strike at Allina Mercy Hospital in Coon Rapids, Minnesota Monday, Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Nearly 150 unionized doctors at two Twin Cities area hospitals began a four-day strike on Monday in what’s believed to be the first walkout by private-sector hospital doctors in U.S. history.
Doctors clad in their white coats walked picket lines outside Allina Health’s Mercy Hospital in Coon Rapids and Unity campus in Fridley, carrying signs that read “patients over profits” and “burn out hurts.”
Union leaders say the strike — and potential disruption to patient care — is a necessary last resort after negotiating for more than three years for a first labor contract governing wages and working conditions.
Their fight, they say, goes beyond pay and benefits: It’s a fight against profit-focused hospital executives who demand workloads so punishing that doctors are burning out, with patients’ care at risk.
“We need to be able to stand up for ourselves,” said Dr. Amber Galarowicz, an Allina hospitalist and bargaining team member for the union Doctors Council SEIU. “The voice that we’ll be able to have for our patients far outweighs the next four days.”
Allina Health, one of Minnesota’s largest health systems with 12 hospitals and over 60 primary care clinics, downplayed the potential impact of a strike by a “small portion of physicians,” noting the union represents only about 10% of the physicians who can provide care at both facilities.
In a statement on Thursday, Allina Health said that both hospitals “will continue normal operations, with no disruption to services.”
“A strike does not benefit anyone. It only adds pressure for patients, families, care teams and the broader community who rely on Mercy Hospital, a Level 2 trauma hospital and one of the busiest hospitals in the metro,” the health system said in a statement on its website.
Allina Health, which had more than $6 billion in revenue in 2025, has seen significant labor unrest in recent years. More than 60 Allina hospice nurses began a seven-day strike on Friday, after failing to reach a deal that addresses their concerns about low staffing levels.
“We have spent so much time caring for our patients and not feeling that we matter,” said Allina hospice nurse Susie Smerz at a Monday news conference outside Mercy hospital.
Last November, hundreds of Allina doctors, physician assistants and nurse practitioners across its primary and urgent care clinics went on strike for a day in what was believed to be the first by doctors in state history and the largest in U.S. history. The advanced care providers then voted to strike indefinitely this spring before reaching an agreement on a three-year contract.
The doctors at Mercy and Unity hospitals voted to unionize in 2023 and have met more than 60 times with health system leaders to negotiate a first contract, including on Sunday night. They voted to authorize a strike with 90% support in July and gave 10-day’s notice before beginning the work stoppage.
One of the top issues is paid sick leave, said Dr. Alia Sharif, a hospitalist and bargaining team member. While state law entitles all workers to paid sick leave — six days a year for full time workers — Allina hospital doctors say they aren’t able to take paid time off when sick.
“It’s become unsustainable for us to continue working like that,” Sharif said. “Doctors get sick.”
The union and the health system are also stuck over pay raises, with doctors complaining they haven’t received cost of living adjustments amid high inflation.
And, the two sides continue to be at odds over which doctors can be covered by a union contract because doctors often work across various Allina hospitals. While doctors must spend at least 20% of their time working at Unity and Mercy hospitals to be included in the union, how that time is calculated is disputed.
Hanging over the negotiations is the proposed merger between Allina and the far-larger California-based Sutter Health to create a combined $26 billion system with 39 hospitals serving more than 5 million patients in California, Minnesota and Wisconsin.
The merger, which is fiercely opposed by labor unions, is under review by the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office.
Unions and health care advocates warn the increasing consolidation in healthcare is driving up costs for patients, hurting care and suppressing wage growth for workers.
Sharif said she doesn’t expect her union to stop the merger, but does hope to see a community benefits agreement to shield against immediate service cuts and layoffs like the one recently reached between the state and Sanford Health in acquiring North Memorial’s Robbinsdale hospital.

Doctors Council-SEIU members at Allina picket during a historic four-day Unfair Labor Practice strike at Allina Mercy Hospital in Coon Rapids, Minnesota Monday, Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Unionized doctors at two Twin Cities area hospitals began a four-day strike on Monday in what’s believed to be the first walkout by private-sector hospital doctors in U.S. history.
Doctors clad in their white coats walked picket lines outside Allina Health’s Mercy Hospital in Coon Rapids and Unity campus in Fridley, carrying signs that read “patients over profits” and “burn out hurts.”
Union leaders say the strike — and potential disruption to patient care — is a necessary last resort after negotiating for more than three years for a first labor contract governing wages and working conditions.
Their fight, they say, goes beyond pay and benefits: It’s a fight against profit-focused hospital executives who demand workloads so punishing that doctors are burning out, with patients’ care at risk.
“We need to be able to stand up for ourselves,” said Dr. Amber Galarowicz, an Allina hospitalist and bargaining team member for the union Doctors Council SEIU. “The voice that we’ll be able to have for our patients far outweighs the next four days.”
Allina Health, one of Minnesota’s largest health systems with 12 hospitals and over 60 primary care clinics, downplayed the potential impact of a strike by a “small portion of physicians,” noting the union represents only about 10% of the physicians who can provide care at both facilities.
In a statement on Thursday, Allina Health said that both hospitals “will continue normal operations, with no disruption to services.”
Blois Olson, a spokesperson for Allina, said only about half of the nearly 150 doctors represented by Doctors Council SEIU walked off the job: 37 crossed the picket line and 40 are not scheduled to work this week, he said.
Allina Health, which had about $6 billion in revenue in 2025, has seen significant labor unrest in recent years. More than 60 Allina hospice nurses began a seven-day strike on Friday, after failing to reach a deal that addresses their concerns about low staffing levels.
“We have spent so much time caring for our patients and not feeling that we matter,” said Allina hospice nurse Susie Smerz at a Monday news conference outside Mercy hospital.
Last November, hundreds of Allina doctors, physician assistants and nurse practitioners across its primary and urgent care clinics went on strike for a day in what was believed to be the first by doctors in state history and the largest in U.S. history. The advanced care providers then voted to strike indefinitely this spring before reaching an agreement on a three-year contract.
The doctors at Mercy and Unity hospitals voted to unionize in 2023 and have met more than 60 times with health system leaders to negotiate a first contract, including on Sunday night. They voted to authorize a strike with 90% support in July and gave 10-day’s notice before beginning the work stoppage.
One of the top issues is paid sick leave, said Dr. Alia Sharif, a hospitalist and bargaining team member.
While state law entitles all workers to paid sick leave — six days a year for full time workers — Allina hospital doctors say they don’t have dedicated sick days. Allina says doctors can take sick leave as part of their paid time off that includes vacation and personal days, and it is in compliance with state law.
“It’s become unsustainable for us to continue working like that,” Sharif said. “Doctors get sick.”
The union and the health system are also stuck over pay raises, with doctors complaining they haven’t received cost of living adjustments amid high inflation.
And, the two sides continue to be at odds over which doctors can be covered by a union contract because doctors often work across various Allina hospitals. While doctors must spend at least 20% of their time working at Unity and Mercy hospitals to be included in the union, how that time is calculated is disputed.
Hanging over the negotiations is the proposed merger between Allina and the far-larger California-based Sutter Health to create a combined $26 billion system with 39 hospitals serving more than 5 million patients in California, Minnesota and Wisconsin.
The merger, which is fiercely opposed by labor unions, is under review by the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office.
Unions and health care advocates warn the increasing consolidation in healthcare is driving up costs for patients, hurting care and suppressing wage growth for workers.
Sharif said she doesn’t expect her union to stop the merger, but does hope to see a community benefits agreement to shield against immediate service cuts and layoffs like the one recently reached between the state and Sanford Health in acquiring North Memorial’s Robbinsdale hospital.
*This story has been updated with comment from Allina Health on the number of doctors who crossed the picket line.

title: Rare wolverine documented in Idaho’s central mountains
description: An outdoor recreationist recently captured video of a rare wolverine in Idaho’s central mountains, Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials said. The sighting occurred recently at a high altitude lake in the Pioneer Mountains, Idaho Department of Fish and Game Southwest Regional Wildlife Biologist Jamie Utz said.
