title: New report explores barriers and possible improvements to state childcare assistance program
description: The New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute published a new report Monday analyzing the state’s childcare tuition assistance program and its problems, and offered potential expansion strategies and improvements for providers and families.  The New Hampshire Child Care Scholarship Program helps families afford childcare by subsidizing tuition costs and paying c[...]
text:
This chart shows how New Hampshire's Child Care Development Fund, which pays for the state's childcare assistance program, is funded. (Screenshot)The New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute published a new report Monday analyzing the state’s childcare tuition assistance program and its problems, and offered potential expansion strategies and improvements for providers and families. 
The New Hampshire Child Care Scholarship Program helps families afford childcare by subsidizing tuition costs and paying childcare programs directly for services. The program is designed to reduce the cost of child care services for working parents, so long as they are working, in school, or in a training program.
Children must be under 13 years old, or 18 years old if they have a disability, and families must meet work and financial eligibility requirements to enroll. As of July 2026, more than 5,800 children were enrolled in the scholarship and connected to a childcare program. 
The report, written by senior analyst Dow Drukker, explores how the scholarship program works for families and childcare programs, how it is funded using state and federal dollars, and its impact on Granite State families and the economy, as well as its fiscal toll on the state. 
“We want folks to recognize New Hampshire has expanded the scholarship program substantially in recent years. We’re seeing increased demand and enrollment, but I think the system is constrained in a lot of ways,” Drukker said in an interview with the Bulletin. “We (want) to be able to provide policymakers with sort of a lay of the land of how other states are looking at expanding or strengthening their program, so then we could start to think a little bit more about how can we apply or think about our own scholarship program in similar or differing ways.” 
For young families, access to childcare is crucial to allowing them to go to work and contribute to the state’s economy. Provider shortages and a lack of available, affordable childcare cause families and the state to lose out on revenue. 
Between 2023 and 2025, the state’s childcare workforce declined by 6%, representing a loss of about 330 educators and staff. Research suggests that in 2023, the state’’s childcare shortage may have cost businesses up to $56 million and state and local governments up to $14 million in lost revenue. Overall, from 2017 to 2025, the number of licensed childcare programs in New Hampshire declined by 16%. 
“The program serves as both an early childhood support and a financial support, helping families access care while supporting labor force participation and provider stability,” Drukker wrote.  
The report also examines the recent shift in New Hampshire’s reliance on federal funds, instead of state general funds, for the program. 
From the 2020-2021 biennium to the current 2026-27 biennium, state general fund appropriations for early childhood education have declined by 11%, including a 19% reduction in funding for the scholarship program. In the same time period, reliance on federal funding, primarily coming from transferred Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF, dollars has increased by 62%. 
Enrollment in the childcare scholarship program has increased substantially since 2021, with a large increase in 2024 after the state expanded financial eligibility. As a result, the state is spending more on the program to prevent a waitlist, but with less state money to do it. If TANF funds run out, a waitlist may be needed anyway. 
The report also explores policy approaches and lessons that other states employed to stabilize their childcare tuition assistance programs and maximize their ability to work within the broad federal rules. Drukker gives examples of states that have employed tactics to improve affordability, strengthen provider participation in the scholarship program, and enhance program administration, and how those tactics could be used in New Hampshire. 
Potential considerations include broadening family income eligibility requirements to prevent parents, specifically mothers, from leaving the workforce and risking future economic and employment instability; targeted eligibility waivers to childcare professionals so they can have access to the scholarship and continue to work in the workforce; embracing the flexibility that the federal government gives states in designing their scholarship programs; and more. 
The scholarship program, provider shortages, and affordability are all interconnected and directly related to New Hampshire’s and families’ economic well-being. The report suggests that a well-funded scholarship program with a reimagined design could improve the lives of families and childcare programs alike. 
“It can’t just be about affordability. It needs to be about investments in provider capacity, the workforce, administratively, from a funding perspective,” Drukker said. “New Hampshire families need both affordable care and a sufficiently large financially sustainable provider network that can serve them, and that there are levers that can be pulled within the scholarship program design that can get at that.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Michigan wins coal plant case, but Indiana’s plants still remain open under federal order
description: Two Indiana coal-burning power plants remain open under an order from the Trump administration. But a federal appeals court ruling could change that in the future. The U.S. Department of Energy has repeatedly extended the lifespan of coal plants in five states, arguing the electricity generated at the facilities is needed to help address a national […]
text:
A new federal court ruling threw out a federal order keeping a Michigan coal plant open. (Stock photo by Monty Rakusen via Getty Images)Two Indiana coal-burning power plants remain open under an order from the Trump administration. But a federal appeals court ruling could change that in the future.
The U.S. Department of Energy has repeatedly extended the lifespan of coal plants in five states, arguing the electricity generated at the facilities is needed to help address a national energy emergency.
However, a three-judge panel at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, in a ruling issued Friday, said it was unpersuaded by the department’s justifications for keeping the J.H. Campbell Coal Plant online in Michigan, determining that the department had exceeded the emergency authority granted by the Federal Power Act.
“There is no dispute that for almost a century states have exercised authority, preserved by the Federal Power Act, to regulate in-state power plants for the economic and environmental benefit of their citizens,” Judge Cornelia Pillard wrote for the panel. “It is the states — informed by federal, regional, and load-serving entities’ assessments of available supply and reliability needs — that bear the responsibility to plan for and avert reliability risks on an ongoing basis. To that end, states decide which generation resources must be built, expanded, reduced, or shut down.”
Trump administration renews order keeping Indiana coal plants open for the third time

The panel ultimately vacated the order.
The Campbell plant’s owner, Consumers Energy, announced a plan to retire the facility in 2021. The Michigan Public Service Commission, which oversees energy companies within the state, and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, the energy grid operator for the central United States, each signed off on the plant’s retirement, with MISO determining the move would not violate its reliability criteria.
In addition to the Campbell plant, the Trump Administration extended the operation of five other plants in Indiana, Pennsylvania, Colorado and Washington.
The U.S. Department of Energy first issued the orders in December — days before CenterPoint Energy and the Northern Indiana Public Service Co., or NIPSCO, were set to retire the coal-powered F.B. Culley and R.M. Schahfer generating stations in Indiana.
The latest renewal runs through Sept. 19
CenterPoint Energy released a statement saying it is committed to prioritizing affordability and reliability for its southwestern Indiana customers.
“We are reviewing the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit’s decision involving Consumers Energy’s J.H. Campbell plant and evaluating its potential implications for Culley 2 generating unit in Warrick County,” CenterPoint said. “This decision does not change the U.S. Department of Energy’s direction for Culley 2, and we will continue to comply with that direction.”
CenterPoint said there are no direct bill impacts to customers — “Going forward, we will continue to work collaboratively with federal, state and local stakeholders and remain focused on delivering reliable electric service to our southwestern Indiana customers and their families.”
The company has filed requests with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission regarding compliance with the DOE’s order and subsequent cost recovery.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
NIPSCO said “We are reviewing the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit’s decision regarding the Department of Energy’s Section 202(c) order for Consumers Energy.  Our focus remains on serving customers safely and reliably while continuing to comply with applicable legal and regulatory requirements.”
In a February letter urging the administration not to renew the order, CenterPoint Indiana Region President Michael Roeder described the coal-fired Culley plant as an “inefficient and increasingly unreliable asset,” accounting for less than 1% of the region’s installed electric capacity.
The following month, NIPSCO and CenterPoint executives told the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission that the fuel, chemicals, staffing and upgrades needed to keep the units operational are costly.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission authorized MISO to adopt tariffs so NIPSCO and CenterPoint can recover those costs.
The Michigan ruling was the result of the attorney general there challenging the federal order.
An analysis from the Sierra Club, which filed a lawsuit challenging the emergency orders, estimates it could cost consumers a net of $174,000 a day to keep NIPSCO’s Schahfer plant online, while CenterPoint’s Culley plant could cost consumers $21,000 a day.
Michigan Advance reporter Kyle Davidson contributed to this report.

name: VTDigger
title: It’s time to close Vermont’s tax loopholes for the wealthy
description:
State tax laws let privileged property owners dodge proposals that could fund healthcare for everyone else.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  It’s time to close Vermont’s tax loopholes for the wealthy.
text:
This commentary is by Dan Jones, who has worked for many years on sustainability and resilience in Montpelier and was the founder and director of the Sustainable Montpelier Coalition.
Recently, I received an interesting lesson on how privileged Vermonters will use our state’s protective tax laws to shield themselves when I got into a conversation with a woman who is a member of what I will call the “well-to-do” class.
“This whole idea of taxing second homes more to pay for health insurance is stupid,” she said. “If you have a home here and live in another state, it’s easy to get around this. All my husband and I have to do is register our home in Florida as his primary residence and our home here as mine. We are protected from this higher tax rate, and no one can do anything about it.”
I protested, “But the whole idea is to give all Vermonters primary healthcare and lower all our health insurance costs. What is so wrong with that? Why shouldn’t those with greater wealth help pay their fair share?”
“Most people you are talking about are on Medicaid and just game the system to get more extra care,” she said. “They use the system to get cheap drugs. We don’t need any more of these healthcare scams.”

READ MORE

The exchange left me wondering how we will manage in an increasingly threatening future. It seems that at least one person who can support houses in Florida and Vermont finds a proposal to provide for the larger social good an imposition to be gamed away. Our government and tax systems have been supporting such privileged selfishness for too long.
Rather than protecting Vermonters from the threat of deteriorating affordability, Gov. Phil Scott has opposed efforts to raise taxes on Vermont’s highest earners, arguing a wealth tax would drive well-to-do residents out of the state. He has resisted broader property tax increases, framing them as a burden ordinary Vermonters can’t afford.
Now I don’t know about you, but as I watch the South become insufferably hot and the West burn up, Vermont’s moderate climate looks more and more attractive. I’m pretty sure that, even with increased taxes, our well-to-do property owners won’t be going anywhere as the larger climate collapses. The arguments against fairer taxation seem to me to be part of current Vermont policy to protect the privileged.
Without big changes to tax laws and political will to support the public good, such reasonable innovations as universal basic healthcare will be impossible to create. Instead, Vermont’s citizens will have to anticipate ever higher taxes and insurance costs just to keep things in place. 
While I’m not a tax expert, it is clear there are several loopholes for evading taxes, such as the example I mentioned above. We could tighten the tax laws that now allow different marriage partners to own different properties and trick the tax authorities, and authorize ways of seeing through such dodges. If one partner claims Vermont residence, then the couple’s total income should be subject to Vermont income taxes. Oh, and let’s make our income taxes truly progressive on incomes over $500,000 per year.
The simple fact is that privileged property owners have protections built into Vermont’s tax laws. This has to change, or the rest of us will see our futures eroded by constant inflation, failing healthcare systems and lost prospects of future prosperity. 
The privileged have been protected for way too long. They have sucked up the resources the rest of us need and taken more from our state than they should. It is time for them to pay their fair share.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  It’s time to close Vermont’s tax loopholes for the wealthy.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Morrisey requests major disaster declaration for three WV counties
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey has requested federal disaster assistance for three counties affected by heavy rains and flooding last month.
text:
Many streets on Charleston, West Virginia's West Side, including Greendale Drive, experienced severe flooding on Sunday, Aug. 16, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)Gov. Patrick Morrisey has requested federal disaster assistance for three counties affected by heavy rains and flooding last month. 
The state has requested individual assistance for Kanawha, Fayette and Harrison counties and statewide hazard mitigation for storms and flooding that occurred Aug. 14 through 18. 
“Our communities have been hit hard by repeated storms and flooding, and too many West Virginia families are still trying to put their homes and lives back together,” Morrisey said in a news release Sunday. “Our state, local communities, first responders, and volunteers have stepped up from day one. Now we are asking President (Donald) Trump to approve this declaration so we can bring additional resources to the families and communities working to recover.”
More than 600 homes were damaged in the flood, Morrisey’s office said Monday. One woman was killed in the Pax area of Fayette County when her vehicle was swept away.
According to the National Weather Service, more than four inches of rain fell at Yeager Airport, leading to high water throughout Kanawha County. Three to six inches fell over 48 hours in Fayette County, according to the Weather Service. 
Speaking to lawmakers Sunday, Matt Blackwood, director of the emergency management division for the state, said the August weather events broke “many rain records across the state.”
“Charleston and other areas here in Kanawha County, isolated areas in Fayette County and Harrison County saw extensive damage to homes and roads,” Blackwood said. 
According to preliminary damage assessments, 624 residences were affected by the storms in Fayette, Harrison and Kanawha counties, the governor’s office said. Of those, 22 homes were destroyed, 60 had major damage, 261 had minor damage and 281 were otherwise affected.
The state estimates that $4.8 million in housing assistance and other needs assistance is needed. Only about 9.5% of affected households had flood insurance, the governor’s office said. 
“When families lose their homes or face repairs they cannot possibly afford on their own, government should work together to help them recover,” Morrisey said in the news release. “This is exactly why federal disaster assistance exists. We will continue fighting to make sure these communities have the resources they need to rebuild.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Republican Ty Masterson concentrates gubernatorial campaign on generational change
description: Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson, the GOP nominee for governor, shares thought about his life and campaign to become the state's next governor.
text:
Senate President Ty Masterson, the Republican Party's nominee for governor, says on the Kansas Reflector podcast that he's eager to transform the state into a place that generations of Kansans find fulfilling.  In this image from Sept. 12, 2026, Masterson speaks at the Kansas State Fair. (Photo by Jill Hummels for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A little-known fact about Kansas Republican gubernatorial nominee Ty Masterson is that he could be a real contender in a dairy cow milking contest.
“I know how to milk a cow by hand,” said Masterson, who grew up on a farm in Butler County with brothers assigned duties by his father. “We were the labor force out there.”


What’s well known is Masterson’s skill at snagging the pivotal endorsement of President Donald Trump. That campaign reality prompted former Gov. Jeff Colyer to drop out of the GOP primary. In August, Masterson leaned into the alliance with Trump to land 43.2% of the Republican vote in a field of seven candidates. He doubled the take of his closest rival, businessman Philip Sarnecki, who claimed 22.3%. He easily outperformed Insurance Commissioner Vicki Schmidt’s 13.6% and Secretary of State Scott Schwab’s 10.9%.
In the general election Nov. 3, he’s up against Democratic nominee Cindy Holscher, a Johnson County state senator who secured a 48.7%-to-38.6% victory over fellow Democrat Ethan Corson in August.
“The stakes couldn’t be any higher, the choice any clearer,” Masterson said on the Kansas Reflector podcast. “We’re clearly in different positions on all the big controversial things and we have records that show that.”
Masterson, 56, of Andover, started in politics in early 2005 as a member of the city council. He was eager to reform the city’s reliance on impact fees assessed for residential construction. His company built homes, but it didn’t survive the recession that crashed the global economy in 2008. He filed for bankruptcy in 2011, a process that left a lasting impression.
“It’s made me more relatable to a lot of people because I’ve been there,” he said. “I’ve been down. I’ve been up.”
He’s on leave as director of GoCreate, a community workshop located on the campus of Wichita State University. He said he was recruited to lead the Koch-funded initiative because it was interested in hiring a director who made it through life without a college degree.
“We go after what they call nontraditional kids, kids that aren’t typically aimed for college,” he said. “It’s a shop, and we have things like water jets and 3D printers and laser engravers and things that you wouldn’t have in a typical garage. We try to get the kids excited about learning about making things. It’s been incredibly successful.”
Masterson transitioned to state politics after being appointed to a vacancy in the Kansas House in 2005. He won election to the Kansas Senate in 2008. The conservative lawmaker has served as president of the Kansas Senate for five years.
“When I came up, I was I think a little intimidated, honestly, thinking I needed to be an attorney, right, because you’re dealing with statutes,” he said. “I realize this is just … about relationships, and you want everyday people there. I do like that we’re a citizen Legislature.”
He said the decision to run for governor stemmed from a desire to reshape government and build a stronger foundation for his six children and eight grandchildren, and others like them, so they could remain and prosper in Kansas for generations. Part of that involved pivoting from policies advanced by two-term Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, he said.
“I just have a deeply vested interest in this state,” Masterson said. “I’m very conscious of the fact that my clock’s going to time out, and I’ve got little clocks that haven’t even started yet that I care about deeply. I want to make this the greatest state in the nation to live, work and raise a family. It’s pretty much that simple.”
 
State tax proposals
Kansas voters have been eager for the state to do something about rising property taxes, but the task has proven challenging.
The Legislature in 2025 eliminated the 1.5 mill property tax used to fund building maintenance at public universities. But the heart of the matter remains local residential property taxes. Action by the Legislature would step into the jurisdiction of officials elected to city councils, county commissions and school boards. Politically, not even the House and Senate have reached consensus.
“It is the one tax that taxes people on an unrealized gain, all because your house may or may not sell for more in the market,” Masterson said. “You’re paying on that higher number, right? That doesn’t mean you have more money in the bank. They’re counting that as an asset, and you’re paying on that. And the result of that is we’re taxing people out of their homes, particularly the fixed-income people.”
Masterson sought a constitutional amendment in the 2026 legislative session that would cap annual increases in assessed valuation of property at 3% per year to avoid big leaps in property taxes due to surging valuations. Other state legislators favored a mandatory cap on increases in property tax mill levies.
In 2024, the Legislature agreed to create just two state income tax rates — 5.2% on income up to $23,000 for an individual, 5.58% for income above that threshold — and raised standard deductions and personal exemptions. That amounted to an estimated $2 billion in state revenue reductions over a five-year period. Future growth in state income tax revenue has the potential of chipping away at the state’s income tax rates.
“That’s what’s missed by a lot of people. It’s if the growth growth is there, the tax revenue growth, then it buys it down,” Masterson said.
State lawmakers also eliminated the income tax on Social Security benefits and agreed to drop the state sales tax on groceries.
Reductions in revenue have been significant, but the state started a rainy day fund that holds more than $1.5 billion. During the past two years, lawmakers approved spending about $700 million more than the state collected annually in taxes. That deficit was covered by the state’s cash reserves, but burning through that rainy day fund could take Kansas back to a budget crisis similar to the one beginning in 2012, when then-Gov. Sam Brownback slashed state income taxes without similarly reducing spending.
Masterson opposed repeal in 2017 of the Brownback’s program to eliminate the state income tax in Kansas.
 
Other key issues
Loud opposition has emerged in Kansas to construction of data centers. A 2025 state law grants a 20-year state and local sales tax exemption for construction, remodeling and equipment acquired for qualified data centers in Kansas. Some residents don’t want the facilities near the homes, and the tax break served to fuel their opposition.
Masterson defended the tax incentive, but he said people failed to acknowledge the law required data center developers to purchase electricity rather than build their own power plants. Parts for data centers cannot come from China.
“I think we do need to add some additional guardrails,” Masterson said. “Make sure that it’s not possible to use eminent domain. I don’t think they can now, but that might need to be clarified.”
In the end, he said, decisions about individual projects should be made at local levels of government rather than at the state Capitol.
Masterson has opposed abortion rights and objected to the 2019 decision by the Kansas Supreme Court that the Bill of Rights in the Kansas Constitution created a fundamental right to bodily autonomy, including the right to end a pregnancy. Kansas voters rejected an amendment to the constitution in 2022 that would have nullified that Supreme Court ruling.
In August, Kansas voters defeated a constitutional amendment that would have mandated direct election of Supreme Court justices. Advocates of that amendment said, in part, that elections for Supreme Court justices would change composition of the court to more easily restrict abortion.
Masterson supported both amendments, but he argued the most recent measure wasn’t about forcing conservative decisions from the Supreme Court. He said the state’s nonpartisan nominating commission responsible for interviewing, vetting and suggesting finalists for the Supreme Court — governors make the actual appointment — was unfairly controlled attorneys on the commission. The amendment would have killed the nominating commission.
“It was about changing the system to put the people back in charge of that branch of government, because it has become the most powerful branch,” Masterson said.
Masterson, who attended Kansas State University for two years before moving to Wichita to start a business, said he supported the idea of using state tax dollars to support private schools because public school students deserved the opportunity to get away from underperforming schools.
“We have kids that in effect are trapped by their ZIP code,” he said. “We cannot leave those kids like that. They just learn to be on generational welfare or they learn crime pays.”
He said Kansas should mirror the Mississippi requirement that third-grade students demonstrate proficiency in reading before advancing to the fourth grade. The policy helped Mississippi rise from 49th to ninth in NAEP standardized testing of fourth graders, he said.
“We have to do things inside public education to get … serious about literacy. Because no matter what you do on school choice, the public system is going to be the way most kids are educated,” Masterson said.

title: Yellowstone National Park superintendent departs America’s first national park
description: After nearly eight years leading Yellowstone National Park, Superintendent Cameron “Cam” Sholly will join the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, said a news release Friday from Yellowstone park and the Department of the Interior. The announcement said Sholly will conclude nearly 30 years with the National Park Service later this month. He will join the [[...]
text:
Steamboat Geyser eruption seen through the trees in Yellowstone National Park on September 17, 2018. (Photo by Jacob W. Frank/ National Park Service)After nearly eight years leading Yellowstone National Park, Superintendent Cameron “Cam” Sholly will join the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, said a news release Friday from Yellowstone park and the Department of the Interior.
The announcement said Sholly will conclude nearly 30 years with the National Park Service later this month.
He will join the foundation as its chief operating officer. The news release said the foundation was chartered by Congress in 1984 and is the nation’s largest conservation foundation.
The National Park Service has already started a search for the next Yellowstone superintendent and will announce an interim leader separately, the news release said.
In a statement, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum thanked Sholly for his service to the parks.
Yellowstone National Park Superintendent Cam Sholly speaks Monday, May 4, 2026, while attending the Cody Country Chamber of Commerce’s 74th Annual National Parks Day Luncheon. (Photo by Victoria O’Brien/Cody Enterprise)
“Cam is an exceptional leader who delivered extraordinary results for Yellowstone National Park and the American people,” Burgum said. “His dedicated leadership leaves Yellowstone stronger, safer and better prepared for the future.”
The news release said Sholly led “one of the nation’s largest and most complex national park operations,” and it outlined some of his achievements since 2018 as follows:

In his tenure, Yellowstone put more than $1.5 billion to work in conservation and infrastructure projects,
The park made “historic investments” in native fisheries, wildlife conservation and infrastructure,
It expanded bison transfers to tribal nations, and
Yellowstone launched one of the largest public-private employee housing initiatives in National Park Service history.

“Sholly also guided Yellowstone through the Covid-19 pandemic, record visitation and the historic floods of 2022,” the news release said.
It said following the floods, the park reopened 93% of Yellowstone within 20 days and restored access through the damaged northern entrance in less than four months.
“Serving as superintendent of Yellowstone has been the greatest professional honor of my life,” Sholly said in a statement. “Everything we accomplished was made possible by an extraordinary team of employees and partners who care deeply about this park.”
Sholly began his career with the park service as a seasonal employee in Yellowstone in 1990, according to the news release. He also directed the National Park Service’s midwest region, with 61 national parks in 13 states, and helped lead “the $380 million public-private transformation of Gateway Arch National Park.”
He has received the Presidential Rank Award, the federal government’s highest recognition for members of the senior executive service, and a meritorious service award from the Department of the Interior, among other leadership awards, the news release said.
“I look forward to joining the NFWF team and continuing important conservation work on a national scale,” Sholly said in the news release.

text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments

Dearborn City Council gave its first reading to an ordinance that would halt data center construction for six months, allowing city officials to develop regulations around the facilities, Fuad Shalhout reports for MLive.
Warren City Council voted to approve its own 12-month moratorium on data centers. The moratorium, which passed unanimously, stemmed from concerns raised by Council Secretary Mindy Moore over the strain that large scale data centers would place on the city’s electrical infrastructure, Brian Wells writes in Warren Weekly.

Legislative Action

Members of the Sierra Club’s Michigan chapter, Clean Water Action and the Michigan Environmental Justice Coalition stood upon the east steps of the Michigan Capitol as the state Senate returned for session on Wednesday, calling on state lawmakers to act on legislation setting regulations for data centers and establishing a statewide moratorium on their development.

News of Note

State Rep. Jennifer Wortz (R-Quincy), who led the introduction of a bipartisan bill package to place a one-year moratorium on data center development joined Robyn Vincent on WDET’s the Metro to discuss who gets to say no when a data center comes to town.
State officials have declined to identify companies who applied for tax breaks for data center equipment, MLive’s Danielle James and Lucas Smolcic Larson report. While a spokesperson for the Michigan Economic Development Commission cited the 2024 law creating the tax break as the reason for its secrecy, one of the lawmakers who crafted the bill said that was not its intent.
A poll conducted by WDIV and The Detroit News found that nearly two-thirds of Michigan residents oppose the construction of data centers in the state, with 64.3% in opposition, 18.9% in support and 16.9% uncertain.
Some attendees at a Saginaw panel discussion hosted by the organization Michigan for Responsible Data Centers, left with more questions than answers, Blace Carpenter writes for WCMU. The panel was intended to create awareness around data center development, and featured panelists from Saginaw Future, Consumers Energy, Public Sector Consultants, Citizens Research Council and the University of Michigan Center for EmPowering Communities.
University of Michigan officials faced an outpouring of anger and frustration from Ypsilanti Township residents during a town hall meeting it held to discuss its $1.2 billion computing center planned for construction within the Washtenaw County community. Residents said the university had show a lack of respect for the community, and destroyed the respect residents had for the university, Planet Detroit’s Brian Allnutt reported.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Congress returns before midterms sprint, but no action expected on AI
description: Both chambers of Congress return to Capitol Hill this week for a brief session before heading back to the campaign trail until mid-November.
text:
WASHINGTON — Both chambers of Congress return to Capitol Hill this week for a brief session before heading back to the campaign trail until mid-November. 
The House will be in for one week and the Senate for three, giving Republicans little time to enact any laws or confirm nominees before voters decide whether to give them another two years in power. 
Lawmakers have already agreed to fund the government through Dec. 11, pushing off any need to reach bipartisan agreement on the dozen annual appropriations bills or risk a government shutdown. 
But they haven’t reached compromise on several other measures and are unlikely to do so until at least the lame-duck session, which spans five weeks in November and December. 
Left undone
Congress has so far opted not to approve legislation that could provide tens of billions in additional funding for the Defense Department amid the war in Iran. 
The two chambers haven’t brokered compromise on the different versions of the annual defense policy bill known as the National Defense Authorization Act, or NDAA. 
There’s no sign of significant progress on the years-delayed farm bill that is supposed to authorize agriculture and food aid programs. 
Republicans had discussed approving a third party-line package through the complex reconciliation process they used to enact their “big, beautiful” law and three years of funding for immigration enforcement. 
But the Senate needs to adopt a budget resolution before that process could begin and that doesn’t appear to be on the horizon this September. 
President Donald Trump’s insistence lawmakers approve nationwide voter registration and identification requirements is also not expected to become law, lacking the votes in the Senate to advance. 
AI stalemate
Lawmakers aren’t expected to make any progress on how to place guardrails on artificial intelligence amid increasingly dire warnings the technology could “kill us all” before the end of the decade.
Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union with Jake Tapper and Dana Bash” that he wanted tech company executives to work with lawmakers on striking the right balance. 
“We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us, and that’s the challenge,” he said. “It’s national security balanced with the immediate security of making sure the models are safe.”
Johnson said he and others in Congress understood the possible ramifications of letting AI run as it is now, but added that “the people who are creating these models have to have to ensure that their products are safe.” 
“But we also at the same time have to resist Congress jumping in and imposing some sort of emergency moratorium,” he said. “It’s got to be done right, safely, wisely.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., had a different take on AI, writing in a statement released Monday that administration officials should brief senators in a classified setting. 
“The American people deserve better from their government at such a consequential moment. I have long argued that we must keep the U.S. as the global leader in AI innovation and security. But that innovation must be coupled with serious guardrails that earn the trust of the American public,” Schumer said. 
“Warning bells are ringing louder than they ever have – and the Trump administration is looking the other way. Well, if they won’t hold themselves accountable, we will. And if Trump does not act, Congress must.”
Nominees on tap
The Senate does have several pending nominees on its list that it could push through in the coming weeks, including Keith Sonderling for labor secretary, Sean Kaufman for assistant secretary for preparedness and response, and numerous judges. 
How much Congress accomplishes following the midterm elections will likely depend on what those results show. 
Democrats are unlikely to negotiate major policy or spending bills with Republicans if voters give them control of both chambers come January. 
A mixed result, possibly Democrats regaining the House but Republicans keeping control of the Senate, could lead to some deal-making later this year. 
This story was first published Sept. 14, 2026 by States Newsroom.

title: Congress returns to session before midterms sprint, but no action expected on AI fears
text: WASHINGTON — Both chambers of Congress return to Capitol Hill this week for a brief session before heading back to the campaign trail until mid-November. The House will be in for one week and the Senate for three, giving Republicans little time to enact any laws or confirm nominees before voters decide whether to give them another two years in power. Lawmakers have already agreed to fund the government through Dec. 11, pushing off any need to reach bipartisan agreement on the dozen annual appropriations bills or risk a government shutdown. But they haven’t reached compromise on several other measures and are unlikely to do so until at least the lame-duck session, which spans five weeks in November and December. Left undoneCongress has so far opted not to approve legislation that could provide tens of billions in additional funding for the Defense Department amid the war in Iran. The two chambers haven’t brokered compromise on the different versions of the annual defense policy bill known as the National Defense Authorization Act, or NDAA. There’s no sign of significant progress on the years-delayed farm bill that is supposed to authorize agriculture and food aid programs. Republicans had discussed approving a third party-line package through the complex reconciliation process they used to enact their “big, beautiful” law and three years of funding for immigration enforcement. But the Senate needs to adopt a budget resolution before that process could begin and that doesn’t appear to be on the horizon this September. President Donald Trump’s insistence lawmakers approve nationwide voter registration and identification requirements is also not expected to become law, lacking the votes in the Senate to advance. AI stalemateLawmakers aren’t expected to make any progress on how to place guardrails on artificial intelligence amid increasingly dire warnings the technology could “kill us all” before the end of the decade.Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union with Jake Tapper and Dana Bash” that he wanted tech company executives to work with lawmakers on striking the right balance. “We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us, and that's the challenge,” he said. “It's national security balanced with the immediate security of making sure the models are safe.”Johnson said he and others in Congress understood the possible ramifications of letting AI run as it is now, but added that “the people who are creating these models have to have to ensure that their products are safe.” “But we also at the same time have to resist Congress jumping in and imposing some sort of emergency moratorium,” he said. “It's got to be done right, safely, wisely.”Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., had a different take on AI, writing in a statement released Monday that administration officials should brief senators in a classified setting. “The American people deserve better from their government at such a consequential moment. I have long argued that we must keep the U.S. as the global leader in AI innovation and security. But that innovation must be coupled with serious guardrails that earn the trust of the American public,” Schumer said. “Warning bells are ringing louder than they ever have – and the Trump administration is looking the other way. Well, if they won’t hold themselves accountable, we will. And if Trump does not act, Congress must.”Nominees on tapThe Senate does have several pending nominees on its list that it could push through in the coming weeks, including Keith Sonderling for labor secretary, Sean Kaufman for assistant secretary for preparedness and response, and numerous judges. How much Congress accomplishes following the midterm elections will likely depend on what those results show. Democrats are unlikely to negotiate major policy or spending bills with Republicans if voters give them control of both chambers come January. A mixed result, possibly Democrats regaining the House but Republicans keeping control of the Senate, could lead to some deal-making later this year.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trump EPA to eliminate rule limiting greenhouse gas emissions from power plants
description: The EPA is expected to repeal rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Environmental Protection Agency is expected to repeal rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas, an action that Administrator Lee Zeldin has said would remove billions of dollars in costs for the industry and help “unleash” American energy.
The rule change, proposed last year, could be announced as soon as Monday, according to two people familiar with the proposal, and represents a fundamental shift from efforts by Democratic Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama to address climate change and clean up industrial pollution, often in low-income and majority Black or Hispanic communities.
The rule, which is expected to face immediate legal challenges, also could prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, the people familiar with the proposal said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because the rule had not yet been made final.
The EPA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The plan to make the rule final was first reported by the New York Times.
The rollbacks are meant to fulfill Republican President Donald Trump’s repeated pledge to “unleash American energy ” and make it easier for utilities to supply electricity for homes and businesses.
The power plant rule is among nearly three dozen environmental regulations that Zeldin targeted in early 2025 when he announced what he called the “most consequential day of deregulation in American history.”
Zeldin said in proposing the new rules last year that they were meant to end the Biden and Obama administrations’ “war on so much of our U.S. domestic energy supply.”
Environmental and public health groups called the rollbacks dangerous and vowed to challenge the rules in court.
“Tearing down our national protections against climate pollution from power plants will have enormous costs for the health, safety and well-being of families across the country,” said Vickie Patton, general counsel for the Environmental Defense Fund. “Americans everywhere are already suffering from record-breaking heat, more dangerous floods and storms, and skyrocketing insurance costs.”
The EPA has a legal responsibility to protect the public from harmful pollution, Patton said, adding that “clean, affordable and reliable technologies are widely available to power our homes and businesses.”
Coal, gas and oil-fired power plants are responsible for about one-quarter of the nation’s total climate pollution, second only to the transportation sector. Pollution from power plants is one of the largest sources of climate-changing pollution in the world.
The rules targeted by Trump’s EPA could prevent an estimated 30,000 deaths and save $275 billion each year they are in effect, according to an Associated Press examination last year that included the agency’s own prior assessments and a wide range of other research.
Even a partial dismantling of the rules would mean more pollutants such as smog, mercury and lead — and especially more tiny airborne particles that can lodge in lungs and cause health problems, the AP analysis found. It would also mean higher emissions of greenhouse gases, driving Earth’s warming to deadlier levels.
Biden, a Democrat, had made fighting climate change a hallmark of his presidency. Coal-fired power plants would have been forced to capture smokestack emissions or shut down under a strict EPA rule issued in 2024. Those rules are now being upended.
In its proposal last year, the Trump EPA argued that carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases from fossil fuel-fired power plants “do not contribute significantly to dangerous pollution” or climate change and therefore do not meet a threshold under the Clean Air Act for regulatory action. Greenhouse gas emissions from coal and gas-fired plants “are a small and decreasing part of global emissions,″ the EPA said.
Zeldin, a Republican and former New York congressman, said the Biden-era rules were designed to “suffocate our economy in order to protect the environment,” with the intent to regulate the coal industry “out of existence” and make it “disappear.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Anti-ICE coalition asks Slotkin to help end ICE use of county jails for detention in Michigan
description: A Michigan-based group of organizations working to end immigration detention has sent a letter to U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) calling on her to help end the practice of Michigan county correctional facilities and jails being used as detention centers for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The letter from The Coalition to Shut the Camps, […]
text:
Melody Simmons, chair of the Coalition to Shut the Camps, speaks to demand that Gov. Gretchen Whitmer use executive action to stop the development of an ICE detention facility in Romulus. June 11, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. A Michigan-based group of organizations working to end immigration detention has sent a letter to U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) calling on her to help end the practice of Michigan county correctional facilities and jails being used as detention centers for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
The letter from The Coalition to Shut the Camps, sent on Aug. 20, makes three specific requests and for Slotkin to take the lead on at least one. That includes a congressional oversight visit to all four facilities, as well as a demand for the release of specific withheld records from Calhoun County. The records were the subject of litigation starting in 2019 from the American Civil Liberties Union, including detainee-level records and inspection reports of the facility.
The group also asks that Slotkin and her fellow federal elected officials help work towards the passage of a law banning that practice, specifically by hosting a convening in Lansing or Battle Creek to build support for state legislation that would end county jail contracts with ICE. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The coalition has requested Slotkin’s staff to respond by Sept. 18, and have said that if she will not take the lead on any of their three requests, they intend to coordinate with other federal elected leadership.
Slotkin spokesperson Josh Steweart told Michigan Advance that the senator was reviewing the letter, and her team has been in touch with the group.
“The Senator is deeply committed to providing strong oversight over ICE in Michigan and has recently done just that in a visit to the Baldwin ICE detention facility and in her work with local leaders to stop the proposed ICE facility in Romulus,” Stewart said. “That work continues as Michiganders look for accountability and oversight of this Administration.”
Currently, four county detention facilities in Michigan — Calhoun County, Chippewa County, Monroe County and St. Clair County — are being used by ICE. 
Based on a Michigan Advance analysis of government data provided by ICE in response to a Freedom of Information Act request, processed by the Deportation Data Project and spanning data between January 2025 and early August 2026, the four facilities collectively held on average 398 ICE detainees daily.
Calhoun County holds the most ICE detainees on average, with its highest daily population last year being 232 detainees. 
Melody Simmons, the chair of the Coalition to Shut the Camps, cited an April 21 sworn declaration from Shawn L. Byers, the deputy director of ICE’s enforcement and removal operations field office in Chicago, presented in litigation over a proposed ICE detention facility, in her calls for Slotkin to act on these county facilities. 
Byers wrote that because ICE has no “for-certain reliable or dedicated detention capacity in the Detroit area and therefore relies on local law enforcement partners in nearby counties to provide space for detainees,” that without increased detention capacity in Michigan, ICE might be forced to make decisions including “forgoing arrest of some individuals who would otherwise be apprehended.”
Simmons said in a press release from the coalition that, “ICE told a federal court that without these county jails, its officers may have to forgo arrests.”
“Four counties are giving ICE the detention space it needs to scale violence into our communities,” Simmons said. “People in Detroit, Dearborn, and Ypsilanti never voted for the sheriffs who made these deals. We are asking Senator Slotkin to visit the jails, demand the records, and bring together the people who can pass a state law.”
Ale Rojas, a member of No Detention Centers in Michigan, said in a news release that the importance of a state law is to prevent ICE from simply seeking out another county to contract with if one of the four currently contracted counties cancels its agreement. 
“We get calls after someone has disappeared into the system. A father can be picked up Tuesday and held in an internment camp hours from his children by Wednesday,” Emily Duthinh, co-founder of Community Aid for Empowerment in Oakland County, said in the press release. “He may be prevented from calling his wife, and his family may not know where he is. His wife and children lose their husband and father, breadwinner and transportation, and sense of safety.”
Duthinh added that “People miss medication, lose jobs, and fall behind on rent while their families search for them.”
“His family may be unable to afford an attorney and document that they are complying with our laws,” Duthinh said. “The result is a child who does not know where his father is because a county agreed to rent ICE a bed.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska sues North Slope oil and gas operators over three almost-abandoned wells
description: Acting like a waiter presenting a divided restaurant dinner table with the bill, the Alaska Department of Natural Resources filed suit against nine different North Slope oil and gas operators last month, seeking to determine who is financially responsible for three semi-abandoned wells. The state’s voluminous 59-page complaint, filed in Anchorage Superior Co[...]
text:
The logo of the Alaska Department of Natural Resources is seen on Tuesday, June 14, 2022 outside the office of the commissioner in Juneau, Alaska. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)Acting like a waiter presenting a divided restaurant dinner table with the bill, the Alaska Department of Natural Resources filed suit against nine different North Slope oil and gas operators last month, seeking to determine who is financially responsible for three semi-abandoned wells.
The state’s voluminous 59-page complaint, filed in Anchorage Superior Court, represents an extraordinary act by DNR, which typically resolves well-ownership disputes short of a courtroom.
But the former Beechey Point Unit, a small oil and gas field north of Prudhoe Bay, has been a regulatory headache for more than 15 years now, and the three wells named in the complaint were the subject of a record $6.3 million fine by the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission last year.  
That fine was levied against Brooks Range Petroleum, a firm is one of the nine named in DNR’s lawsuit. The other eight are AVCG, Brooks Range Development Corp., CaraCol Petroleum, MEP Alaska, Nabors Drilling Technologies USA, Ramshorn Investments, TG World Energy and TP North Slope Development. 
The nine represent the operator and working interest owners of Beechey Point, and the suit asks a state judge to order the nine to assume financial responsibility for the plugging and final closure of three still-open wells in the coastal region defined by Beechey Point. 
Under the state’s lease agreement, the users of Beechey Point were required “to restore and rehabilitate the land to the satisfaction of the Department of Natural Resources within six months after lease termination.”
That hasn’t happened, the suit claims, making the former operator and leaseholders financially responsible for the state.
Across the country, orphaned oil and gas wells are a significant environmental and safety hazard. Louisiana alone had almost 5,000 documented orphaned wells in 2024.
As of 2024, Alaska had 45 such wells, one dating to 1901. Several were part of the Katalla oil boom that took place east of Cordova in the first decade of the 20th century.
In 2024, the state seized a $200,000 bond from a bankrupt oil and gas company to seal an orphaned well in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough.
The three wells identified in last month’s lawsuit are not formally orphaned, DNR said, and the suit amounts to an attempt to prove paternity. 
Online court records show the case has been preliminary assigned to Judge David Roghair; no proceedings have yet been scheduled.

title: Journalism is essential to democracy. AI can’t replace it.
description: The news Thursday that 13 skilled journalists in Lexington were laid off was heart-breaking but also frightening. The suggestion that AI can replace reporters who are trained to observe, interpret, and ask the tough questions is unrealistic. AI is a tool and a resource, but it cannot replace a human reporter. The real danger here […]
text:
AI cannot replace local news. (Getty Images)The news Thursday that 13 skilled journalists in Lexington were laid off was heart-breaking but also frightening.

The suggestion that AI can replace reporters who are trained to observe, interpret, and ask the tough questions is unrealistic. AI is a tool and a resource, but it cannot replace a human reporter.

The real danger here is the declining number of journalists in the field. It is not just newspapers. We have witnessed veteran broadcast journalists who have been sidelined as TV goes through its own shakeout.

So, what are we losing? What is the real value of journalism?


Journalism gives citizens the facts they need to make informed decisions. This information is about our schools, taxes, governments, businesses, medicine, and it is information that shapes our lives. A skilled journalist gathers the information, verifies and presents it in in a way that can be understood.


Journalists hold government entities accountable. The most important responsibility of a journalist and media company is to ask the tough question — the question an elected official may not want to answer. This skill takes courage and patience as it has become common for officials to deflect attention by insulting or criticizing the reporter rather than answer the question.


Journalism is a historical record. Births, deaths, milestones, new businesses and tragedies are all part of a community’s record. Much of the history we know of our past is because of the journalists who have gone before us.


Local journalists tell stories that would otherwise be untold. Find any local media, be it a newspaper or a TV station, and you’ll find stories the national media are not covering.


Journalism and local media connect communities in a way no other entity can do.


We have more information at our fingertips than ever before. In the age of social media, blogs, rumors and artificial intelligence, the ability to separate misinformation has gotten more and more difficult. Local journalists are the filter who report the stories through verification, attribution and with accountability.


Journalism gives people a voice. Their stories are not just about those holding elected office or the powerful. Stories of teachers , farmers, small-business owners, young people and veterans fill the pages of good community newspapers.


Journalism is part of the bedrock of democracy. People participate in their communities when they understand the issues. Coverage of public meetings, local debates and elections provides the information people find necessary for participation.


Journalists serve as witnesses. Major events are documented by journalists  who provide information about what happened and how the community responded. This role is especially important during emergencies and disasters.


Journalists create accountability. Good journalists acknowledge mistakes, correct the record and explain how they obtain information. This transparency builds trust.


The value of a journalist is in their presence. Whether it is at a city council meeting, a sporting event, or community event, the actual presence of a journalist cannot be reproduced. Each time they build relationships and knowledge of the community they serve.


A good journalist is a good journalist because they know the community.

title: Democrats adopting the socialist term may distract voters from the issues these candidates support
description: Political observers are predicting a big year for Democrats in congressional elections. This is expected given the dynamics of midterm loss, where the president’s party loses seats in Congress in non-presidential election years. This has been the pattern in all but two elections going back to 1938. Common explanations for midterm loss center on how […]
text:
How will democratic socialism impact the midterm elections? (Getty Images)Political observers are predicting a big year for Democrats in congressional elections. This is expected given the dynamics of midterm loss, where the president’s party loses seats in Congress in non-presidential election years. This has been the pattern in all but two elections going back to 1938. Common explanations for midterm loss center on how the frustration from losing the presidential election fires up out-party partisans and invites many ambitious congressional candidates. 
This energy is positive for mobilization but can encourage newer candidates to blame their party’s establishment for not standing up to the other party’s president. For example, in 1974, the so-called “Watergate baby” Democrats criticized their own party leaders lack of post-Watergate reforms. In 2010, Tea Party Republicans ran against Republican incumbents for not stopping the Affordable Care Act and Great Recession regulatory reforms. 
In 2026, Democratic Socialists accuse establishment Democrats of not doing enough to halt President Donald Trump.
While similar to previous midterm elections, this year’s dynamic could end up differing because of the adoption of the historically loaded “socialism” term. Academically, the socialism term is misplaced in theory and in practice, but the pressing problem for this year’s election is that the term could distract from the issues that the Democratic Socialists are championing.  
As far as political theory, using the term socialism is off. No one running for office for the Democrats in 2026 is an actual socialist, which by definition is when the people, through government rather than the private sector, own the means of production. These candidates also do not resemble the similarly named European Social Democrats due to our distinct American political history. 	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US




Our historical experience has created different political values than other democracies where socialism emerged. The Declaration of Independence borrowed directly from John Locke’s argument that a legitimate government would not take away any individual’s right to life, liberty, or property without due process. This made the U.S. a liberal democracy, which is not leftist, but rather a governing system that limits government to protect liberties in society and the marketplace. 
This predates the socialist movement that democratized most European social democracies with the right to vote for the working class and a focus on the common good being superior to individual rights. Our Constitution highlights negative rights, those that the government cannot take away but does not define many rights the government must provide its citizens. In contrast, due to social democratic ideals, other democracies emphasize positive rights, or those that the government must provide people the common good like universal rights to work, leisure, environmental equality, gender equity, and social welfare. 
As a result, American Democratic Socialists might push for marginally higher taxes and regulation compared to Republicans, but they are not emphasizing positive rights or policies that are central to European constitutional democracies like mandating a 32-hour work week or that private-sector companies have to provide weeks of paid vacation and paid maternal and paternal leave. American Democratic Socialist are not calling for a massive overhaul of the tax code that would match European democracies, where on average over 40% of the overall economy is taxed, compared to 25% in the US.  
Americans often do not recognize how commonly held our admiration of our liberal democracy is. American exceptionalism scholars have written about our confined, shared belief system throughout our history. Alexis de Tocqueville loved American democracy but was shocked at how narrow American political thought and debate were in our very early republic. Philip Converse argued that Americans do not have any real divides in our ideological beliefs, but rather made up “folk ideologies.” 
Other scholars like Louis Hartz and Richard Hofstadter have pointed to the danger of our collective liberal tradition because we do not recognize that views slightly out of the norm are not drastic threats to our democracy. It makes us prone to overreactions or paranoia like McCarthyism and the red scare.  
Consequently, if the past patterns hold, the self-named Democratic Socialists may set off unwarranted panic among some who fear they are challenging the American way of life even if their positions are not far from the mainstream. 
How would they govern?
This is not just mistaken political theory, in practice Democratic Socialists would likely not govern that dramatically different from establishment Democrats. The person most associated with the Democratic Socialists is U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, who has endorsed many Democratic Socialist candidates. Sanders’ brand has been clear: establishment Democrats act too much like Republicans. But how different is Sanders’ behavior than other Democrats? 
Congressional Quarterly’s 2024 Senate party unity scores – the percentage of times each Senator voted in agreement with their party when a majority of the other party voted in the opposite direction – are instructive because it was the last time Democrats controlled the Senate agenda. The average Democratic Senator had a party unity score of 98.5%. Bernie Sander’s party unity was 93%. This is not a massive chasm between Democratic Socialists and Democrats. 
This is not to say that Democratic Socialists would not push new issues relative to other Democrats. It’s just that by adopting the socialist term, it may distract voters from the issues these candidates advocate. Voters will likely see more threatening name-calling ads about Marxism or communism than substantive issue positions. The paradox to this likely backlash is that the U.S. has moved rightward on taxation, redistribution, and regulation in recent decades but if these candidates are caricatured, the threat will be seen as shifting too far to the left and the important issues they raise will be ignored.   
For example, many of the Democratic Socialists have taken distinct positions on the Israeli-Palestinian issue compared to many mainstream Democrats. This is a needed debate following October 7, 2023m and the response in Gaza and Lebanon, especially when there are accusations of antisemitism or Islamophobia in debates on the topic within both parties. We will not have this national discussion if we are calling each other Marxists and fascists.
Democratic Socialists also emphasize policies to address growing inequality in American society, which fuels resentment among voters and increases incivility and polarization in American politics according to the political science literature. These and other thorny issues deserve a full debate this year but may not emerge out of the reflexive name-calling and negative political environment we are in.

name: Nevada Current
title: Republicans face tall task in effort to erode Democratic state Senate majority
description: Despite an election year forecast that’s less than encouraging for Republicans in states across the country, Nevada Republicans hope to flip control of the state Senate by ousting three Democratic incumbents, all in Southern Nevada. It’s a tall order. All the Democratic candidates have significantly out-raised their Republican challengers according to the mo[...]
text:
(Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Despite an election year forecast that’s less than encouraging for Republicans in states across the country, Nevada Republicans hope to flip control of the state Senate by ousting three Democratic incumbents, all in Southern Nevada.
It’s a tall order.
All the Democratic candidates have significantly out-raised their Republican challengers according to the most recent state campaign finance reports through July.
Democrats currently hold 13 of the 21 seats in the Senate, and have held both legislative chambers since 2016. If Republicans can beat three Democrats, and don’t lose any seats, Republicans would have 11 senators to the Democrats’ ten.
Conversely, if Democrats were to not only hold their own but pick up an additional seat currently held by a Republican, they would have a veto-proof majority in the state Senate.
A Democratic supermajority however seems unlikely. Incumbent Republican state Sen. Danielle Gallant, who represents Senate District 20, is seeking reelection, but in a heavily red district with 52,612 registered Republican voters compared to 30,077 Democratic voters. There are 50,489 nonpartisan registered voters in the district. 
Democratic candidate Calvin Sandoval, a union pipefitter endorsed by AFL-CIO and the Culinary Union, is challenging Gallant. 
He has not been endorsed by the NV Senate Democratic Caucus. Sandoval has raised $5,577 through the July 15 cycle compared to Gallant’s $73,942.
Supermajority scare takes a back seat this year
During the 2024 campaign cycle, Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo was not on the ballot. But in conjunction with the Lombardo-aligned Better Nevada PAC, the governor made blocking Democratic supermajorities in the Legislature a campaign priority, so as to assure Democrats could not override his vetoes. A veto override requires a two-thirds vote from both houses.
The year before, in 2023, Lombardo had set the state’s record for the most vetoes by a governor in a single legislative session, with 75. 
Democrats did not win legislative supermajorities in either chamber in the 2024 election. In the ensuing 2025 legislative session, Lombardo smashed his previous veto record, rejecting 87 bills.
Focusing instead on Lombardo’s reelection, neither Lombardo nor the Better Nevada PAC have mounted a high-profile effort warning against legislative supermajorities this year. 
Meanwhile, state Senate Democrats, hoping Attorney General Aaron Ford ousts Lombardo from the governor’s mansion, are focusing on tying Lombardo and Republican Senate candidates to the Trump administration.
“Republicans nominated a slate of candidates who will double down on failed policies that are raising costs for Nevadans,” Brandon Errer, a spokesperson for the NV Senate Democrats. “Their candidates support Trump’s tariffs and oppose going after out-of-state corporations that are buying up housing and driving up the cost of health care and groceries.” 
The Senate Republican Caucus didn’t respond to requests for comment. 
Potential Democratic leadership shake-up
Assuming Democrats stave off the Republican challenge and maintain the Senate majority, they could also be seeing a new era of leadership. 
Senate Majority Leader Nicole Cannizzaro, who has led since 2019, is running for Nevada Attorney General. If she wins the statewide election it will lead to an opening in Senate Democratic leadership with no clear successor. 
Senate District 12, located in the southeast part of the Las Vegas Valley, is currently held by Democratic incumbent. Julie Pazina. She is being challenged by Republican Rafael Arroyo-Montalvo, a small business owner.
Pazina raised roughly $125,000 in the second quarter of the year and has raised a total of $419,000 as of July 15. Arroyo-Montalvo raised $59,000 in the second quarter with a total of $99,000.
Pazina was first elected in 2022, which flipped the district to Democratic control after several years being held by Republicans. 
Former Republican state Sen. Joe Hardy was first elected to the seat in 2010 and held it for 12 years. Prior to winning a state Senate seat in 2012, Ford unsuccessfully tried to flip SD 12 in 2010. 
As of August there were 34,328 registered Democratic voters in the district, compared to 30,168 registered Republicans, according to the Secretary of State’s office. As they do statewide, nonpartisans account for the largest share of the district’s electorate, with 51,835 registered voters.
Arroyo-Montalvo ran in Assembly District 41 in 2024 but narrowly lost against Assemblymember Sandra Jauregui. 
SD 8, which is located in the Summerlin area, has also bounced back and forth between the parties. 
Democratic state Sen. Marilyn Dondero Loop, who is seeking re-election for her third and final term representing the district, will face Republican George Harris, an Army veteran and entrepreneur. 
Dondero Loop raised $132,000 in the second quarter and has raised a total of $506,000. Harris raised roughly $77,0000 during the same period and raised nearly $92,000 total.
Democrats have an edge in the district with 32,734 registered voters compared to 30,972 Republicans. Nonpartisans make up the biggest portion with 47,511 active voters.
Dondero Loop was first elected in the blue wave election year of 2018, when Democrats in Nevada won a trifecta — both houses of the Legislature and the governor’s office.
Two-term incumbent Democratic Sen. Melanie Scheible will face Republican Maria Thompson, a former broadcast journalist, in SD 9 in the southwest part of the valley. 
Like the two other districts, Democratic voters outnumber Republicans, with 33,456 registered Democrats compared to 25,934 registered Republicans. There are 51,485 registered nonpartisan voters.
Scheible was first elected to the seat in 2018 during the blue wave, flipping the district from Republican control.
Republicans were able to claim the district during the 2014 Republican wave, which ousted then Democratic state Sen. Justin Jones. 
Scheible raised $119,000 in the second quarter of the year while Thompson raised $91,000. Scheible has raised $340,000 in total campaign contributions while Thompson has nearly $173,000.

 Catching Our Eye

• Flooding. The Ohio Newsroom’s Erin Gottsacker is reporting, “As flooding gets more frequent in central Appalachia, streamgages could offer advance warning.”
A small stream in eastern Ohio’s Harrison County looks shallow and slow, as it winds past banks of yellow flowers and humming summer bugs.
But Natalie Kruse Daniels, a professor and director of the environmental studies program at Ohio University, says the peaceful scene can be deceiving.
“Little streams can flash flood really, really quickly,” she said. She recently visited another one in Athens. “It’s maybe ankle deep right now, but it flooded the road and multiple businesses on August 11th.”
Similar scenes played out across the state last month: Floodwaters submerged basements and highways, as severe storms caused major damage to hundreds of properties across 23 central and southern Ohio counties.
• Immigration. Politico’s Myah Ward, Eric Bazail-Eimil, and Jessica Piper are reporting, “Mullin seeks to win over immigration hardliners with messaging blitz.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has launched a PR blitz to save his floundering reputation among immigration hardliners who think he’s soft on deportations. So far, it’s not working.
The Department of Homeland Security chief, who has faced an onslaught of attacks from MAGA activists and immigration hardliners in recent months, has grown alarmed by the blowback and is looking to shore up support with a key part of the Trump coalition, according to an administration official and another person familiar with the messaging effort, both granted anonymity to discuss internal thinking.
“Mullin is very concerned about the criticism, so the effort to hammer stats and ‘tough talk’ is intentional,” said the official.
