title: Drought leads to ‘unprecedented’ black bear conflicts in Wyoming
description:
Wildlife officials plead with homeowners to secure food and trash as black bears range into cities, campgrounds looking for sustenance.
The post Drought leads to ‘unprecedented’ black bear conflicts in Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The 5-year-old black bear had a routine. At nightfall, she would climb down out of one of Laramie’s many cottonwood trees, spend the night searching for tasty morsels in city and residential garbage cans, then by 6 a.m. she would find another tree, climb back up, and sleep off all that garbage while 60, 80 or even 100 feet off the ground. 
Pictures show her legs free floating on either side of a branch, dangling like a cartoon bear near the city’s historic train depot and across town by baseball fields. Wyoming Game and Fish Department biologists received regular reports of her whereabouts, but she was either 80 feet up a cottonwood tree — too high to dart with no branches to catch her fall — or she’d already moved on, said Lee Knox, Laramie’s Game and Fish’s regional wildlife coordinator. 
He’s guessing she spent nearly a month in Laramie before one night in late August she climbed up a spruce tree instead of a cottonwood and someone called Game and Fish in time. Knox requested help from a tree trimming service who arrived with a truck and bucket and hoisted another biologist into the air. The biologist shot the chubby bear with a tranquilizer dart and watched as she tumbled out of the spruce tree like a ball in a game of plinko, the branches slowing her fall before coming to rest in a tarp held slightly off the ground. 
This black bear spent weeks in Laramie this summer. It would sleep in trees during the day and descend at night to eat garbage. (Lee Knox)
He then checked her for injuries, gave her an ear tag to show she’d been captured and drove the sleepy bear to the nearby Snowy Range, where he released her deep in the woods hoping he wouldn’t see her again.
A black bear spending a month loitering in a town of 35,000 people was strange enough. Even weirder was that she wasn’t a young, dumb male bear — she was a 5- to 6-year-old female who had previously reared cubs. Adult females tend to be known more for their caution than recklessness, Knox said. But that’s a reflection of how bad this summer has been for bear and human conflict, not just in southeast Wyoming, but across much of the Mountain West.
“To find a bear in town once or twice a summer wouldn’t be crazy, but this summer was unprecedented,” Knox said. “There’s been an unheard-of number of conflicts. It’s at least three times as bad as the last bad year, and the majority of the conflicts have been more aggressive bear behavior.”
Why, exactly, is anyone’s guess, but one of the biggest drivers is likely an extreme drought causing a decided lack of food. And summer is not over yet.
Black bears in trouble
The Laramie region, which encompasses half of the Sierra Madre range all the way to the Nebraska border, regularly deals with black bear conflict. Several years ago, Game and Fish advised people in the Saratoga Valley and Centennial areas to lock their vehicles because black bears figured out how to open car doors for tasty rewards inside. 
This year they’re not only breaking into vehicles but also houses and cabins. Game and Fish has received at least 20 reports of black bear thieves sneaking in through screen doors and sometimes windows. They’ve also wedged themselves through doggy doors, though one bear realized too late it couldn’t get back out the doggy door and ran away with the contraption around its waist.
A black bear pads through the forest near Yellowstone National Park’s northeast entrance in May 2015. (Neal Herbert/National Park Service)
The issue is even more serious in Colorado, where portions of the state have seen a 219% rise in bear conflicts in the first seven months of the year. And in late August, a black bear broke into a home in Estes Park, Colorado, rooted around in the kitchen and then scratched and knocked over an 80-year-old woman. The woman is recovering from her wounds, according to Denver7, and the bear escaped back through the window. 
Northern Wyoming also has been struggling with problem bears, though so far they’ve largely spared houses, opting instead for chicken coops, bird feeders and garbage, said Tim Thomas, Game and Fish’s Sheridan regional wildlife coordinator. In the Bighorn Mountains, a black bear tried climbing in a tent with campers after harassing other campers a few miles away. Game and Fish caught the bear, ran DNA tests to determine it was the same one trying to steal food in campgrounds, and killed it to prevent it from an inevitably more serious conflict. 

John Hebberger Jr. submitted this photo of a black bear in Jackson to the Jackson Hole News&Guide’s “Field Notes” section in September 2024. Last year was a deadly year for Teton County black bears, which get much less attention than their cousins, the grizzly bears. (John Hebberger Jr./Jackson Hole News&Guide)

“We’re seeing issues across both gender and age classes,” Thomas said. “It’s not just young ones getting kicked off mom, they’re all looking for food resources.”
In Muddy Mountain near Casper, the Bureau of Land Management temporarily closed a campground in July after it was visited by a black bear. Because the bear had returned multiple times for food rewards, Wyoming Game and Fish made the decision to euthanize it, an agency spokesperson told Oil City News.
Colorado wildlife officials have killed nearly 300 black bears this year, according to reporting from the Colorado Sun, including an 18-year-old bear whose intestines were completely blocked by plastic garbage bags and “at least 10 nonflushable cleaning wipes.”
Looking for food in all the wrong places
Dan Thompson, Game and Fish’s large carnivore supervisor, figures he’s fielded dozens of calls from journalists this summer wondering why black bear conflict is so much higher than normal. 
The simplest answer in regions like Laramie and Sheridan is likely tied to drought and few natural foods. They’re popping up looking for food in places as far away from mountains as Torrington and Pine Bluffs, Knox said, which is not typical bear habitat.
“Hot dry conditions and lower than normal berry abundance and other things like that are contributing factors,” Thompson said. 
Berry crops failed in the Sheridan region because of a late frost, and grasses and wildflowers peaked much earlier than normal this year. But lack of food isn’t fully to blame for increased conflict. Fewer bears came into Lander this year, for example, than last year when berry bushes bowed their heads under the weight of their fruit. Last year, Thompson said, bears followed that berry abundance right into the urban-wildland interface. 
Trash overflows from a dumpster at Rob Roy Campground in the Snowies. Wildlife officials are asking the public to secure their food and trash to avoid bear conflicts. (Christine Peterson)
A larger part of the problem is the combination of scarce wild foods and more readily available human foods. If a hungry bear can’t find anything to eat, it will keep moving. If it discovers trash or other snacks, it will stick around. That’s why Game and Fish asks people year after year to bring bird and dog food into secure places, keep garbage in bear-proof cans and lock down those chicken coops. Because once a bear discovers a cache of easy, tasty food, it won’t forget, Thompson said. 
“People should let us know as soon as possible, especially if there’s any conflict activity, if they’re seeing a black bear in an area where they aren’t expecting to,” he said. “People are reluctant to call because they think we will show up and kill a bear.”
And Game and Fish has killed more black bears than normal this year, though Thompson said he wouldn’t know how many exactly until closer to winter when bears are finally in their dens. If people call early, before a bear is habituated to finding human food, Game and Fish has more luck hazing or moving the bear and helping homeowners secure food and other attractants.
“We really need people to give wildlife some grace and be as bear aware as possible,” Knox said. “If you live out of town, especially, anything is possible. It’s Wyoming and it’s a rough year.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Mixed-status immigrant households expected to lose benefits under new public charge rule
description: The rules may lead people without lawful status to forgo enrollment in public benefits for their U.S. citizen kids and other dependents.
text:
A 10-year-old Honduran immigrant who came into the United States as an unaccompanied minor carries her baby cousin in 2021 in Indiana. A new federal rule expands public charge considerations in immigrants’ applications for lawful permanent residency, a policy that could contribute to more than a million people disenrolling from public benefits. (Photo by John Moore/Getty Images)New rules going into effect this week allow immigrants’ enrollment in safety net resources to be taken into account for lawful immigration status applications, the latest in the Trump administration’s immigration overhaul.
The rules will have wide implications for mixed-status households, as people without lawful status may forgo enrollment in public benefits for their U.S. citizen kids and other dependents out of fear.
The new U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) guidance goes into effect Sept. 18 and affects people applying for a green card, certain visas or admission into the United States. It rescinds the Biden administration’s 2022 public charge regulations, which restricted immigration officers from considering immigrants’ use of non-cash public benefits, including many benefits for low-income families such as Medicaid, housing programs and food stamps.
When an immigration officer determines a person could become dependent on government benefits, that “public charge” is a ground for inadmissibility under federal law.
Trump’s new policy broadens immigration officers’ discretion, allowing them to consider enrollment in non-cash public benefits as public charge. That includes Medicaid, Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the country’s largest food assistance program.
Those subject to public charge consideration are immigrants seeking adjustment of immigration status to lawful permanent residency, and includes those who are spouses, siblings, parents and children of U.S. citizens; widowers and widows; foreign medical school graduates; U.S. armed forces personnel; certain workers such as those with advanced degrees, and others.
USCIS specifies certain immigrant groups and classifications that are not subject to public charge. Those include asylees, refugees, Afghani and Iraqi interpreters or such nationals who worked for the U.S. government, people seeking temporary protected status, human trafficking victims, self-petitioners under the Violence Against Women Act, Indigenous people born in Canada who aren’t U.S. citizens, among other groups.
Health research group KFF this summer estimated that between 1.4 million and 4.1 million Medicaid and CHIP enrollees living in a household with a noncitizen could disenroll due to the public charge rule or another immigration-related fear.
Last November, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security acknowledged this, saying that the rule would affect U.S. citizens in mixed-status households. The agency said that federal and state spending could be reduced by almost $9 billion annually “due to disenrollment or forgone enrollment in public benefits programs by members of households that include aliens who may be receiving public benefits.”
It also acknowledged “downstream and upstream” effects for states and their economies.
“For example, the rule might result in reduced revenues for healthcare providers, such as hospitals and nonprofits, participating in Medicaid, companies that manufacture medical supplies or pharmaceuticals, grocery retailers participating in SNAP, agricultural producers who grow foods that are eligible for purchase using SNAP benefits, or landlords participating in federally funded housing programs,” the agency wrote in its proposed guidance.
Previous studies found that under the first Trump administration’s public charge rules, families were less likely to apply for food assistance or seek healthcare, a point emphasized by the American Academy of Pediatrics this week.
“When a child is hungry, it can affect every aspect of their development and lead to chronic conditions like heart disease and diabetes, even into adulthood,” said Dr. Sural Shah, chair of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ Council on Immigrant Child and Family Health, during a news conference Thursday.
“Without accessing WIC, babies and young children will miss out on critical nutrition supports that are important for brain development in the first 1,000 days of life. Medicaid and CHIP are lifeline programs.”
In an executive order he signed a month after his inauguration, President Donald Trump wrote that his administration would “uphold the rule of law, defend against the waste of hard-earned taxpayer resources, and protect benefits for American citizens in need, including individuals with disabilities and veterans.”
Health clinicians say immigration activity has been leading to fear and isolation among families, causing delayed care and illnesses to advance among children. They also say those with disabilities and complex needs will be among those hit hardest.
The Autism Self Advocacy Network, for example, said immigrants with disabilities will be disproportionately affected, as they tend to use public benefits more than other immigrants.
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming families are struggling to afford healthcare. Here are two solutions.
description:
The state must be a good steward of rural health dollars while making 12-month postpartum care permanent, writes the Healthy Wyoming Board of Directors.
The post Wyoming families are struggling to afford healthcare. Here are two solutions. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming health care is at a pivotal crossroads. With the arrival of federal Rural Health Transformation  funding, the work of state task forces, and a primary election that demonstrated voters’ clear demand for constructive governance, healthcare is dominating public debate.

Opinion

The central takeaway from all this discussion is clear. Wyoming families are paying too much for care, and healthcare costs remain among voters’ top concerns heading into the fall. Among all the difficult proposals to address this problem, two are clear and available now: Focus new federal funding on rural healthcare access, and permanently extend Medicaid care for new moms to a full year after giving birth.
For more than a decade, Healthy Wyoming has advocated for policies that make healthcare affordable and accessible. Over that time, we consistently urged lawmakers to make our state Medicaid coverage available to all low-wage citizens. That is a policy that has strengthened rural hospitals and public health in neighboring states.
Practically speaking, what can state leaders do to meet challenges as they exist today? Those challenges include new federal work-reporting rules under 2025 federal bill H.R. 1 — the so-called Big Beautiful Bill Act — shifting administrative burdens, and evolving federal budget guidelines. Broad Medicaid expansion faces real implementation and fiscal hurdles. However, Wyoming cannot afford to stand still. We must focus on tangible, immediate steps that protect access and stabilize our communities right now.
In the coming months, Healthy Wyoming will focus our advocacy on two urgent, high-impact priorities:
First, safeguarding rural investment. As Wyoming begins allocating more than $200 million in federal Rural Health Transformation dollars, Healthy Wyoming will serve as a watchdog for patients and local communities. These funds must directly protect essential local services — including rural emergency rooms, EMS transport, clinic staffing and mental health services — so families in frontier counties can access care close to home.
Second, making 12-month postpartum care permanent. In 2023, the Wyoming Legislature demonstrated genuine pro-family leadership by approving a temporary extension of postpartum Medicaid coverage from 60 days to a full 12 months. That extension is set to expire in March. When lawmakers convene in Cheyenne this winter, Healthy Wyoming will ask them to remove that sunset and make 12-month care a permanent fixture in state law.
The medical and economic case for permanent postpartum care is overwhelming:

Clinical necessity: Nationwide, more than half of pregnancy-related complications and maternal deaths occur after the initial 60-day window, driven by cardiovascular conditions, chronic disease flares and behavioral health struggles.
Mental health in our frontier state: Between 13% and 20% of new mothers experience postpartum depression, with symptoms frequently emerging or peaking between three and nine months after delivery — long after the old 60-day cutoff. In a state facing an acute mental health provider shortage and tragic suicide rates, no new mother should be dropped from care when she is most vulnerable.
Good governance and fiscal sense: This policy does not expand eligibility to a single new group; it simply ensures mothers already enrolled receive uninterrupted care through their baby’s critical first year. The federal government covers half the cost through regular matching funds, and permanent authorization gives rural hospitals and state administrators the certainty they need to plan budgets and keep clinic doors open.

Pro-family policy is not just a slogan — it is the commitment to ensure mothers and babies survive, recover and thrive. Making 12-month postpartum coverage permanent and responsibly stewarding rural health investments are common-sense steps Wyoming can achieve together right now.
Healthy Wyoming will continue working with lawmakers, providers and local communities to build a health care system that works for every Wyomingite.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Trump gives feds 90 days to consider removing endangered species protections for wolves
description: President Donald Trump signed an executive order Sept. 4 giving the U.S. secretary of interior 90 days to decide whether to remove Endangered Species Act protections for gray wolves and Mexican wolves in the United States. The Supporting America’s Ranchers executive order calls for Secretary of Interior Doug Burgum to decide within 90 days whether […]
text:
A gray wolf in snow. (File photo courtesy of Eric Cole/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)President Donald Trump signed an executive order Sept. 4 giving the U.S. secretary of interior 90 days to decide whether to remove Endangered Species Act protections for gray wolves and Mexican wolves in the United States.
Carter’s Hope: After U.S. government killed off Western wolves, a bold experiment brought them back

The Supporting America’s Ranchers executive order calls for Secretary of Interior Doug Burgum to decide within 90 days whether gray wolves and Mexican wolves have met their recovery criteria and to begin the process of delisting or downlisting them. 
The executive order also calls for Burgum to prepare a legislative recommendation for Trump to fully delist or downlist wolves and, upon determination that recovery criteria have been met, encourage states to delist wolves and revise state standards for the killing of wolves in order to help ranchers.
 The history of the near extermination of wolves in the U.S., and their recovery

Wolves are a native species that was almost completely eliminated in the Western United States by the 1940s through a widespread government extermination campaign backed by congressional bounties and the extensive use of poisoning.
After they were nearly killed off, wolves became one of the first animals added to the Endangered Species List in 1974. Then, the U.S. government reintroduced wolves into Idaho and Yellowstone National Park in 1995 and 1996 using wolves captured from Canada. 
Wolves were removed, or delisted, from the Endangered Species Act in Idaho, Wyoming and Montana beginning in 2011, where they can be hunted and trapped. 
U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins delivers remarks on May 27, 2026, at the USDA’s headquarters in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Christophe Paul/USDA)
But wolves are still protected under the Endangered Species Act in other parts of the United States. Those Endangered Species Act protections prevent hunting in places where wolves are still protected, but those protections could go away if wolves are removed from the Endangered Species Act as a result of Trump’s new executive order.  
“While the Biden administration chose to villainize ranching and the rural way of life under the guise of radical environmental mandates, the Trump Administration continues to focus on rebuilding the Great American Cattle Herd,” U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said in a written statement. “For the past 19 months, USDA has worked tirelessly to defend and promote our nation’s ranchers. Through our Beef Plan and the Ranchers First Initiative we are working to continue increasing our nation’s heifer retention rate. Today, the President laid out tools to better equip farmers and ranchers to deal with dangerous predators threatening their livestock, provide more transparency for consumers on where their meat originates, and expand market opportunities while maintaining our world class food safety standards. President Trump is focused on delivering an America First agenda and will do that by continuing to put our Ranchers First.”
 Wolf advocates worry Trump’s order is premature, and that wolves have not fully recovered in the U.S. 

Trump administration officials and several Republican elected officials support the executive order. 
On the other hand, wolf advocates and some conservation groups oppose the move, which they say is premature because wolf populations have not met their recovery goals across the U.S.
Collette Atkins, senior attorney and director of the carnivore conservation program at the Center for Biological Diversity, said removing wolves from Endangered Species Act protections could be devastating because wolf populations have not yet received after nearly being completely wiped during the 20th century.  
Atkins said also the Center for Biological Diversity would challenge any misguided delisting attempts in court. 
Cattle Battle: How wolves and livestock collide – and how one Idaho project offers solutions

“Trump’s new push to prematurely remove wolf protections will lead to yet another court decision that reinstates those protections while doing nothing to help ranchers,” Adkins said in a written statement. “Smart ranchers coexist with wolves by using commonsense measures like guard dogs and fencing to protect livestock. Trump should be funding these tools, not wasting taxpayer money trying to kill or illegally strip wolves of lifesaving protections.”
Carter Niemeyer, a former government trapper turned wolf advocate, called Trump’s executive order on wolves “a distraction,” saying it won’t help ranchers in Idaho, Montana and Wyoming – where wolves have already been removed from the Endangered Species List protections and can already be hunted and removed by government agencies for harassing livestock. 
“This executive order, to me, is just a distraction from other bigger issues farmers and ranchers have,” Niemeyer told the Idaho Capital Sun on Thursday.
Niemeyer, who is retired in Idaho but previously worked for the U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Services, said wolves kill about 200 livestock animals a year between the states of Idaho, Montana and Wyoming, where there are more than 6 million cows and cattle. 
More livestock are killed in accidents and by vehicles each year. 
“I remind people that livestock losses to wolves are less than one-tenth of 1% for cattle and sheep,” Niemeyer said. “I would think tariffs, the cost of gasoline and diesel and the lack of access to fertilizer and things like that should be way higher up the list of concerns for ranchers and farmers than wolves.”
Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials estimated that Idaho’s wolf population decreased to an estimated 1,129 wolves in 2025, a decrease of about 100 wolves compared to the year before. State officials attributed the decrease to aggressive hunting and trapping, and said the number of livestock killed by wolves is trending downward, the Sun previously reported. 
 



  Learn more about wolf recovery and wolves in the West

Check out Howl, a 2025 longform written series and podcast created by the Idaho Capital Sun and Boise State Public Radio to learn about wolf reintroduction, recovery and controversy in Idaho.

title: Molder and Hatcher discuss positions on renewable energy, nuclear power ahead of November election
description: District 5 candidates Charlie Hatcher, a Republican farmer and former Tennessee agriculture commissioner, and Chaz Molder, the Democratic mayor of Columbia, share pride in Tennessee’s nuclear energy work and see renewable energy sources as tools for powering the state’s future. But they take different approaches on federal government involvement and dealing[...]
text:
Charlie Hatcher, left, and Chaz Molder, right, are campaigning to serve Tennessee's 5th Congressional District. (Photos: John Partipilo)District 5 candidates Charlie Hatcher, a Republican farmer and former Tennessee agriculture commissioner, and Chaz Molder, the Democratic mayor of Columbia, share pride in Tennessee’s nuclear energy work and see renewable energy sources as tools for powering the state’s future.
But they take different approaches on federal government involvement and dealing with nuclear waste.
The contenders are vying for a district that spans some of the state’s most and least populated areas, including counties where local economies have ties to renewable energy sources.
The majority of the 54 solar farms in Tennessee are concentrated in West Tennessee. The 5th Congressional District includes several solar farms, including the state’s largest in rural Lake County. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The district is also home to some of Tennessee’s top agricultural counties, where corn and soybeans remain among the leading commodity crops. About 46% of Tennessee’s corn yield is used to make ethanol fuel, according to Tennessee Corn, a coalition of farmer-funded corn promotion groups. The majority of Tennessee’s soybean yield is used for animal feed, but oil extracted from the beans is also used to make biodiesel fuel.
Here’s what Molder and Hatcher told the Lookout about their positions on renewable and nuclear energy.
Federal involvement
Hatcher’s primary election campaign saw a boost from outside spending by the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a political action committee funded by renewable energy investors that spent $2 million opposing incumbent U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles for his actions against renewable energy development. After Ogles’ defeat, President Donald Trump endorsed Hatcher to win the general election.
But what does Hatcher think of federal support for renewable projects?
Federal subsidies or grants can and should be used to help fledgling industries get off the ground, he said, but these should be limited in time frame.
“The federal government doesn’t need to create an artificial demand for a certain renewable energy,” Hatcher said. “It’s just not sustainable, and that’s where you get into (being) not good use of taxpayer money. If you have to subsidize renewable energy for a long period of time, I don’t like that.”
Hatcher points to agricultural subsidies as an example.
“Commonly, the USDA gives grants for value-added products, and they’re grants, but the expectation is once that project or that industry gets off the ground, then that’s … termed out,” he said. 



Quotation







The federal government doesn’t need to create an artificial demand for a certain renewable energy. It’s just not sustainable, and that’s where you get into (being) not good use of taxpayer money. 


– Charlie Hatcher, Republican nominee for the 5th Congressional District 


Hatcher also acknowledged the agriculture industry’s positive relationship with renewable fuels, which provide another use case and revenue stream for the country’s most prominent row crops.
“I’m for all forms of energy that make sense,” he said. “They have to stand alone themselves once they get off the ground.”
Molder said federal incentives for renewable energy need to be consistent, referring to the Trump administration’s abrupt reversal of Biden-era tax credits and other federal support for renewable energy programs.
“Federal policies need to be consistent and steady enough for utilities and businesses, small businesses particularly, to plan around it,” Molder said. “Constantly creating these incentives and then turning around and abruptly eliminating them makes it harder and harder for businesses to really participate in these types of renewable energy options, and frankly, make it more expensive to build and more expensive to borrow for.”
Solar power and other renewable energy can help lower costs and strengthen the grid long-term, Molder said. 
Gov predicts Tennessee will be a finalist for nuclear campus

“This is an opportunity where government can be put to work to do good by incentivizing the private sector to be innovative with respect to renewable energy opportunities instead of creating inconsistencies and causing confusion,” he said.
Going nuclear
The U.S. Department of Energy announced in early August that Tennessee is one of five states under consideration for a federal nuclear energy partnership. The state has a long history in nuclear research at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and Gov. Bill Lee created a $70 million investment fund for nuclear projects and a nuclear advisory council.
The federal government is proposing a $50 billion investment in a nuclear campus involving both production and nuclear waste storage. The announcement stirred concern over where and how nuclear waste might be stored in Tennessee if the state is selected for the project.



Quotation







We’ve got to make sure we understand what we’re doing in our own state relative to nuclear energy and waste that’s being produced in our own state before we start becoming a storage site for other states’ waste.


– Chaz Molder, Democratic nominee for the 5th Congressional District 


“Nuclear energy is already our state’s biggest source of electricity,” Molder said. “We should be proud that Tennessee is leading the nation in this regard.”
Molder emphasized the growing need for electricity and said “having reliable, low-carbon power around the clock is important,” and nuclear energy will be a part of meeting that demand.
But he’s concerned about the possibility of Tennessee becoming a storage site for other states’ nuclear waste.
“We’ve got to make sure we understand what we’re doing in our own state relative to nuclear energy and waste that’s being produced in our own state before we start becoming a storage site for other states’ waste,” Molder said. “And I think, you know, being a mayor, having local control on these issues is very important for me.”
Hatcher said he’s proud of Tennessee “leading the country on nuclear energy,” including Lee’s focus on the industry. Lee appointed Hatcher to his position in the state’s agriculture department, and endorsed Hatcher’s campaign to represent the 5th District. 
Regarding nuclear waste, Hatcher said he would “just let the experts deal with that.”
“We’ve had nuclear waste in the past. I expect, as technology advances, there will be less nuclear waste and a better way to store it,” he said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama grocery tax repeal, once on the margins, becomes bipartisan campaign issue
description: Repeal of Alabama’s grocery tax, once an effective political impossibility, has become a bipartisan issue in the fall campaign. Long touted by anti-poverty groups and championed by Democrats, Republicans have sponsored efforts to reduce the tax over the past four years. John Wahl, the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor, made the issue central to his[...]
text:
A WIC child participant takes a WIC-approved product off the shelf in a grocery store in Seattle in September 2024. Alabama is one of eight states that still taxes groceries, and several statewide candidates are calling for it to be repealed. (Photo by U.S. Department of Agriculture) Key Points




Several candidates campaigning for statewide office pledged to support repealing the grocery tax in Alabama. This includes both the Democratic and Republican candidates for Governor and Lieutenant Governor.
Lawmakers in the past three years passed legislation to reduce the statewide portion of the grocery tax from 4% to 2%.
Anti-poverty advocates called the tax “immoral” because of its regressive nature. Households in the lowest income brackets pay more of their income to the tax than wealthier households.
Rep. Danny Garrett, R-Trussville, said he drafted a bill to repeal the grocery tax for the coming legislative session.




Repeal of Alabama’s grocery tax, once an effective political impossibility, has become a bipartisan issue in the fall campaign.
Long touted by anti-poverty groups and championed by Democrats, Republicans have sponsored efforts to reduce the tax over the past four years. John Wahl, the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor, made the issue central to his primary campaign this spring and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones has centered it in his pitch to voters.
Last week, Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville, who had largely ignored the issue during his primary campaign, endorsed it in his first ad of the general election, saying “elimination” of the tax would be the first step in a broader tax-cutting program.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As of early Friday afternoon, Tuberville’s campaign website did not explicitly list cutting the grocery tax among his priorities. Messages seeking comment were left with Tuberville’s campaign on Thursday and Friday.
One of a handful
Alabama has taxed groceries since the sales tax was introduced in 1939. The state is one of eight that still imposes a levy on food, and until 2023 was one of an even smaller number that fully taxed it.
Efforts to eliminate the tax were complicated by the fact that it brought hundreds of millions of dollars into the state’s Education Trust Fund, which pays for most public education in the state, and disagreements over how to replace the lost revenue.
According to the Legislative Services Agency, in 2025 the sales tax rate on food brought $393.5 million to the Education Trust Fund. Through August, sales tax collections on food this year totaled $207.6 million. LSA expects total collections from the grocery tax for the year will be about $230 million, artificially lower because of a two-month sales tax holiday on food in May and June, which overlapped with state primary and runoff elections.
The cost to fully eliminate the remaining 2% state sales tax on food would be approximately $270 million.
“From an economic perspective, grocery taxes are effective at raising revenue because groceries are what we call inelastic goods in elasticity,” said Benjamin Meadows, an assistant professor of economics at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. “When we say that a good is inelastic in price, what that means is that when you change the price a little bit, people don’t change their behavior much.”
Alabama House attaches grocery tax holiday to overtime pay deduction bill

Anti-poverty advocates have long said the tax, which could rise up to 10% of a grocery bill in many parts of the state, hit low-income households particularly hard and contributed to food insecurity.
“Someone of limited means is going to pay more out of their paycheck proportionally than someone who is of adequate means,” Meadows said. “As you have less and less income, more of the income is devoted to that tax.”
But as other states have begun reducing or eliminating grocery taxes, the state has taken steps to do so. The Republican-controlled Legislature in 2023 reduced the state tax on groceries from 4% to 3%, and cut it to 2% in 2025. Local grocery taxes have been frozen but still remain in place.
Republicans have touted the move as a means of fighting inflation.
“I think the first thing we need to do on a state level is eliminate the rest of the state grocery tax,” said Sen. Andrew Jones, R-Centre, who led efforts to reduce the tax in the Alabama Senate.
Democratic counterparts said they had always supported eliminating the grocery tax. Former Rep. John Knight, D-Montgomery, a former chair of the House Ways and Means General Fund committee, fought for years to reduce the levy.
“Democrats have been advocating for eliminating the grocery tax for well over 20 years,” said Jones in an interview on Friday. “Republicans have been in control of the Legislature for 16 years, and they could have done it at any point.”
Jones, whose platform calls for fully eliminating the grocery tax, added that “there are people in this state that really need the break.”
Phillip Ensler, the Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor, said he has advocated for eliminating the grocery tax while he was a member of the House of Representatives and voted to reduce it in both 2023 and 2025.
“Everywhere I go in the state, it doesn’t matter if it is a bigger city or smaller town, Republican area or Democrat, there is overwhelming support to cut it because people are having a hard time, and we know that those few extra dollars on the grocery bill, it adds up,” Ensler said.
Though the lieutenant governor has little power to address the tax, the issue is one that Ensler and Wahl, the Republican lieutenant governor nominee, broadly agree on.
“I really have a heart for the people of Alabama, and I think there are a lot of people out there right now who are struggling to make ends meet,” Wahl said. “You have young families just working to put food on the table, seniors on fixed incomes who are having trouble just paying for basic necessities.”
‘A tax on survival’
Chris Sanders, a spokesman for Alabama Arise, an anti-poverty group that has long fought to eliminate the grocery tax, said the group was excited that “there is widespread, bipartisan support for untaxing groceries.”
“This is not a partisan issue,” he said. “It is a human issue, a moral issue, everybody has to eat to survive, and that makes the grocery tax a tax on survival.”
Rep. Danny Garrett, R-Trussville, who chairs the House Ways and Means Education Committee, which oversees levies like the grocery tax that go into the ETF, said in an interview Friday that a bill has been drafted to eliminate the remaining state portion of the grocery tax.
“What we said when we eliminated the first 50% that we thought we would be on a path to eliminate the remainder of it at some point,” Garrett said. “We have already drafted a bill; we have had a bill drafted a couple of months ago that would do that.”
Grocery tax cut may have had smaller-than-expected effect on Alabama education budget

Garrett’s plan to repeal the grocery tax altogether, however, does not include a provision to replace the lost revenue.
“We know the revenue growth, the projections on the budget,” Garrett said. “We can also look at expenses and things we have in the budget, so we have the wherewithal to repeal it.”
A constitutional amendment to fully eliminate the state grocery tax passed the Alabama House of Representatives in 2008, but failed to attract the necessary votes in the Senate. Both chambers were controlled by Democrats at the time.  Subsequent efforts to address the issue got little traction until 2023.
Others have expressed concerns about the potential impact it would have on the ETF budget and proposed some alternatives. Alabama Arise, for example, wants to eliminate the federal income tax deduction, a longtime proposal from Democrats who called for eliminating the grocery tax.
“That is a highly skewed, highly upside-down tax break that overwhelmingly benefits the wealthy households in our state,” Sanders said. “For most people in Alabama, it is worth $100 or less, but for people at the very top of the income scale, it can be tens of thousands, potentially even hundreds of thousands of dollars, per year.”
Democrats, on the other hand, want to eliminate the CHOOSE Act, which provides tax credits of up to $7,000 per child to be spent on non-public school activities, including private school tuition.
“When we lift the caps off of the ability to have taxpayer money going to private schools for the wealthiest people in this state, I think we can offset this a good bit,” Jones said.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: ​Police cooperation with ICE to appear on Colorado ballot
description: Colorado voters will weigh in on a constitutional amendment this fall that would require law enforcement to more closely cooperate with federal immigration authorities. If passed, Amendment 81 would compel law enforcement to figure out if a person charged with a crime is “lawfully present” in the country, and tell the U.S. Department of Homeland […]
text:
Denver District Attorney John Walsh speaks against Amendment 81 at the Colorado Capitol on Sept. 10, 2026. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)Colorado voters will weigh in on a constitutional amendment this fall that would require law enforcement to more closely cooperate with federal immigration authorities.
If passed, Amendment 81 would compel law enforcement to figure out if a person charged with a crime is “lawfully present” in the country, and tell the U.S. Department of Homeland Security within three days if someone in their custody lacks proper legal status or if they are unsure after attempting to find out. It would apply to people charged with violent crimes or if the person has a previous felony conviction.
As a constitutional amendment, it needs 55% of the vote to pass.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The text of the amendment does not lay out how a police officer, sheriff’s deputy, correctional officer or district attorney should determine if someone is in the country legally. State and local authorities don’t track how many immigrants who lack permanent legal status are charged with violent crimes.
It is one of six measures backed this year by Advance Colorado, a conservative “dark money” group that does not disclose its donors. Last August and September, national dark money group A Common Sense America spent about $460,000 gathering signatures to get the amendment on this year’s ballot.
In an August 2025 post about so-called immigration “sanctuary policies,” the organization highlighted Colorado’s existing laws that limit cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration authorities.



Quotation







Today, state and local law enforcement can truthfully tell victims and witnesses that we do not participate in federal, civil immigration enforcement ... If this passes, we would no longer be able to do that.


– John Walsh, Denver district attorney


Those laws “have stripped law enforcement of the ability to notify or assist federal immigration authorities—even when dealing with repeat felons,” the unattributed post says. “These policies shield offenders and deepen Colorado’s public safety crisis.”
Colorado law currently bars law enforcement officers from participating in civil immigration enforcement, and they cannot detain people based on a civil U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainer request. State and local government agencies and employees are also prohibited in many cases from sharing certain personal information with federal immigration authorities.
Opponents launch campaign
A poll earlier this year from the Colorado Health Foundation found that 61% of Coloradans view the mistreatment of immigrants as a serious problem and 65% think misconduct from federal immigration officials is a serious issue.
Two issue committees are registered in favor of Amendment 81: the Eagle County Republican Women Club and A Brighter Colorado, which was registered in July to support all of Advance Colorado’s ballot measures. To date, A Brighter Colorado has received $250,000 from A Common Sense America and $20,000 from Advance Colorado, according to financial disclosures with the secretary of state’s office.
There is virtually no public-facing campaign in support of the amendment. Advance Colorado did not respond to a request for an interview. Opponents launched their campaign, however, Thursday with a rally at the state Capitol.
“Unless a person charged with a crime happens to be carrying their passport, or unless local law enforcement can verify their immigration status within 72 hours, Amendment 81 would require us to report that person to ICE,” Denver District Attorney John Walsh said. “It inevitably means that law enforcement will be forced to report to ICE people who ultimately turn out to be American citizens and people who are lawful permanent residents of the United States. It is a recipe for abuse and racial and ethnic profiling.”
He said the amendment would erode trust in immigrant communities throughout the state and reduce their confidence to report crime.
“Today, state and local law enforcement can truthfully tell victims and witnesses that we do not participate in federal, civil immigration enforcement,” he said. “If this passes, we would no longer be able to do that.”
Three issue committees are registered in opposition to the amendment: Colorado Communities First, The People’s No, and Vote Common Sense. Those committees are financially supported by groups including ACLU Colorado, the Colorado Immigrant Rights Coalition and the Colorado Organization for Latina Opportunity and Reproductive Rights.
The Colorado Association of Chiefs of Police is neutral on the amendment and the County Sheriffs of Colorado has not taken a position on any ballot measures.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Why Idaho needs more women like me in the cockpit
description: One of my earliest memories is sitting behind my dad in his airplane, pressing my face to the window, watching the big buildings shrink to look like Lego sets. I remember thinking: I want to fly a plane one day. The memories of flying with my dad – a fixed wing and helicopter pilot who repaired […]
text:
An Alaska Airlines jet lands at Newark Liberty International Airport. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)One of my earliest memories is sitting behind my dad in his airplane, pressing my face to the window, watching the big buildings shrink to look like Lego sets. I remember thinking: I want to fly a plane one day.
The memories of flying with my dad – a fixed wing and helicopter pilot who repaired power lines – stayed with me for years of raising three wonderful children and working in sales. It wasn’t until my early 40s that I completed my private pilot license, the first step in my pilot career. I’m currently completing my instrument rating while working toward my commercial certificate, both needed to achieve my long-term goal of building a career in corporate aviation.
My story matters now because women don’t need to wait until mid-life to become pilots. If the calling comes in childhood, follow it. Girls in Aviation Day returns to Boise on Saturday, Sept. 19, and I want as many people as possible, especially girls who may assume a cockpit isn’t for them, to see what’s possible.
Women hold only about 5.5% to 6% of U.S. airline pilot jobs. This number has barely moved in decades, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Meanwhile, North American airlines expect to be 30,000 pilots short of what they need by 2032, despite the U.S. government projecting that there will be roughly 18,000 new airline and commercial pilot openings this decade.
My timeline was unusual and now I’m training while balancing significant family responsibilities that don’t pause for flight lessons. Training is expensive, and self-funding my dream has meant real sacrifice for myself and my family.
I’ve asked myself more than once whether it made sense to keep going. My answer has stayed the same: yes. I credit that to the mentorship I’ve received from other women in aviation. A scholarship through Women in Corporate Aviation last year helped me pass my instrument written exam and keep training toward my checkride.
I pay it forward by mentoring girls through our local chapter of Women in Aviation and volunteering with events like Girls in Aviation Day, because I wouldn’t be here without seeing the many women before me who have made it to the rank of captain.
Girls in Aviation Day brings around 250 girls ages 8 to 18 to Western Aircraft in Boise for a free day of aircraft tours, hands-on activities, and one-on-one time with women working across aviation and aerospace: pilots, engineers, mechanics, dispatchers, air traffic controllers. For many of these girls, it may be the first time they see someone who looks like them doing this job.
Representation changes what a kid believes is possible for herself. While I didn’t have many women pilots to point to when I was younger, those in my life are instrumental in keeping me on my career path. I want the girls in the Treasure Valley community to have that now, not decades later. I want women considering aviation later in life, like I did, to know their timeline doesn’t have to look a certain way.
Please bring the girls in your life to Western Aircraft at the Boise Airport between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. Registration is free at bit.ly/GIAD2026. Come see what’s possible when the cockpit door is actually open.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Rural Americans wait after judge delivers mixed ruling on digital equity dollars
authors: Sarah Jane Tribble, KFF Health News
description: A federal judge in July gave digital equity advocates a partial victory against President Donald Trump, stopping his attempt to unilaterally kill a multibillion-dollar grant program Congress created. But U.S. District Judge John D. Bates, in a 35-page opinion, also agreed with the administration that it was unconstitutional for the government to use race or[...]
text:
(KFF Health News illustration; Getty Images; court documents)A federal judge in July gave digital equity advocates a partial victory against President Donald Trump, stopping his attempt to unilaterally kill a multibillion-dollar grant program Congress created.
But U.S. District Judge John D. Bates, in a 35-page opinion, also agreed with the administration that it was unconstitutional for the government to use race or ethnicity as the basis to award money under a program created to expand internet skills and access.
“It was definitely disappointing,” said Angela Siefer, executive director of the National Digital Inclusion Alliance, a nonprofit that filed suit last year after not receiving a nearly $26 million award meant to bolster digital and internet skills nationwide. “With this administration it’s really worrisome.”
Congress passed the $2.75 billion Digital Equity Act in 2021 as the skill development component of a multilayered “Internet for All” initiative under President Joe Biden’s signature infrastructure law, which included a bigger pot of money for expanding internet infrastructure.
A few months into his second term, Trump directly attacked the Digital Equity Act on social media, pledging “no more woke handouts” and calling the program “illegal.” The language echoed two Trump executive orders characterizing diversity, equity, and inclusion programs as illegal.
Joe Burgei (left) helps Shaunta Harris Jr. with an online digital literacy course at a soup kitchen and homeless shelter in Defiance, Ohio. Burgei is a grant-funded digital navigator for the Northwestern Ohio Community Action Commission, which operates the shelter. (Northwestern Ohio Community Action Commission)
The National Telecommunications and Information Administration, which oversees implementation of the law, responded by abruptly halting Digital Equity Act grant programs, leaving states and organizations like the National Digital Inclusion Alliance in limbo.
In response to Bates’ decision, federal attorneys said the government would reinstate the NDIA-related competitive grant program without racial classification. The government aims to release a new grant application in December, according to a joint status report filed in the case.
The NDIA now must reapply for the grant award, which was slated to be disbursed among more than a dozen organizations and tribes, including the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma, El Centro Hispano in Arkansas, Portland Community College in Oregon, and Community Service Programs of West Alabama. The grants are meant to go toward digital navigator programs, in which community workers teach technology and internet skills, according to the NDIA.
In western Ohio, Jamie Huber said her organization was a subrecipient of the NDIA grant funds. Huber, director of community services at the Northwestern Ohio Community Action Commission, said that without the funding, she is left searching for money to continue navigator programs such as one she runs for people who are unemployed, homeless, or both.
“How do you find a home? Well, you got to look online. And how do you find a job? You have to look online,” Huber said.
Huber’s digital navigators also teach internet skills at 10 senior centers in rural counties stretching along the corner of Ohio bordering Michigan and Indiana. They help active older adults learn how to go online to pay bills and get healthcare, so they “continue having agency over their own life,” Huber said.
Rural residents live sicker and die younger on average than people in the rest of the country when they live in counties lacking high-speed internet access and healthcare, an analysis by KFF Health News found.
At Computer Reach in western Pennsylvania, Executive Director Dave Sevick said his organization has cut staff and programs. He said the nonprofit, which started in 2001, has refurbished more than 24,000 computers, giving them away to families it finds through schools and churches.
“We’re aware that affordability is the biggest issue around, and this doesn’t make it any better for folks,” Sevick said. “We’re helping a little bit by getting a free computer out to people.”
The Digital Equity Act lists exactly whom the money should benefit, including low-income households, older people, some incarcerated people, rural Americans, veterans, and members of racial or ethnic minority groups.
According to 2025 polling by the Pew Research Center, people in rural communities were less likely to have internet subscriptions compared with their urban and suburban counterparts.
Megan Hahn teaches class attendees how to use an online health portal at the Swanton Senior Center in Swanton, Ohio. Hahn is a digital navigator with the Northwestern Ohio Community Action Commission. The group’s work is supported by local, state, and federal grants. (Northwestern Ohio Community Action Commission)
The Pew Research polling also revealed that home broadband use among Black and Hispanic adults lagged that of white and Asian adults. While 81% of white adults surveyed said they subscribed to broadband at home, only 71% of Black adults and 68% of Hispanic adults said the same.
In court, lead federal attorney Patrick Butler argued that Congress failed to prove a compelling government interest when including the racial or ethnic criteria. Congress did not “identify anything close to” a specific instance of discrimination in the broadband industry, Butler said, according to the transcript.
Butler then surprised the court, saying that if the racial or ethnic status could be severed from the law, “we would obviously apply the grant program without considering race.”
In his opinion severing the race factor, Bates wrote that the court agreed that “the President lacks the power to cancel laws passed by Congress based on his bald disagreement with Congress’s policy determinations.”
Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), a primary sponsor of the law, said she will be “watching very carefully to ensure this administration does what Congress intended.”
“It is indisputable that these challenges are particularly pronounced in low income, rural, and Tribal communities — and there’s a reason Democrats and Republicans across the country support this program so strongly,” Murray said in a statement to KFF Health News.
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) voted against Biden’s infrastructure bill in 2021 and sent a letter to the National Telecommunications and Information Administration in late 2024 asking the agency to pause the $1.25 billion competitive grants program, arguing the use of racial classifications “does not serve a compelling governmental interest.” Cruz did not respond to requests for comment.
Arielle Roth, administrator of the agency, previously worked as the telecommunications policy director for the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee’s majority staff under Cruz. She was appointed by Trump to lead the agency.
Joe Burgei (left) gives Paul Helbling tips for using his smartphone during a session at the Henry County Senior Center in Napoleon, Ohio. Burgei’s job as a digital navigator with the Northwestern Ohio Community Action Commission has been supported by local, state, and federal grants. (Northwestern Ohio Community Action Commission)
In June, during a House committee hearing, Roth had tense exchanges with Democrats who took issue with changes to the Biden-era infrastructure law’s internet deployment program, which now allows more satellite services rather than prioritizing fiber-optic cable lines.
Lawmakers also asked about the Digital Equity Act’s grant programs.
“Communities across the country deserve a clear answer and a path forward,” Rep. Nanette Barragán (D-Calif.) said during the hearing. While the National Digital Inclusion Alliance’s lawsuit does not include the state grants, Barragán asked how those grants would be rolled out, considering the federal judge’s decision on race.
California was awarded a $70 million state capacity grant. Early this year, the Justice Department sent a letter to Congress asserting that the state grant and the competitive grant program both are illegally based on race, citing the Supreme Court’s decision invalidating affirmative action in higher education admissions. Roth declined to answer Barragán’s question, noting there is active litigation.
Barragán said she was “extremely” frustrated by “some of the responses or nonresponses.”
Stephen Yusko, a spokesperson with the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, declined to comment or respond to questions for this article.
The government and the National Digital Inclusion Alliance agreed to pause court proceedings to give the agency time to reinstate the competitive grant program. The NDIA has also proposed that the agency provide status reports every 30 days during the court pause “to ensure prompt attention to reinstatement,” according to the most recent court filing.
“We need to make sure it’s all moving forward,” Siefer said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Environmentalists push lawmakers to forge ahead on moratorium and regulations for data centers
description: As data center developments remain top of mind for Michigan residents, and with Election Day soon on the horizon, environmental advocates continue to push lawmakers to enact a statewide moratorium and establish better protections for communities. Members of the Michigan Senate returned to Lansing last week. In turn, members of the Sierra Club’s Michigan chap[...]
text:
A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images)As data center developments remain top of mind for Michigan residents, and with Election Day soon on the horizon, environmental advocates continue to push lawmakers to enact a statewide moratorium and establish better protections for communities.
Members of the Michigan Senate returned to Lansing last week. In turn, members of the Sierra Club’s Michigan chapter, Clean Water Action and the Michigan Environmental Justice Coalition stood upon the Michigan Capitol’s east steps for a news conference meant to remind lawmakers of their responsibility to act on data centers.
Lawmakers in both the House and the Senate have introduced policies to block permitting for new data center projects for a full year, arguing that the state needs to hit the pause on data center development to give local governments time to determine how one of these facilities could impact their residents. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A group of Democratic state Senators in June put forth a series of proposed regulations on data centers, including water-use permit requirements, protections for water and electrical customers, community benefit requirements and a ban on public officials entering into non-disclosure agreements tied to data center deals.
However, the bills have not seen any movement in the Senate Energy and Environment Committee since their introduction. 
While Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) has expressed interest in taking up some regulations on data centers, another slate of proposals put forth by House Democrats has similarly sat dormant in the House Government Operations Committee since June. The committee is generally considered as the committee where bills go to die.
During the group’s press conference on Sept. 9, Chris Gilmer-Hill, policy manager for the Michigan Environmental Justice Coalition, noted how a lack of strict regulation on data centers in other states had contributed to pollution in Black and working class neighborhoods. Gilmer-Hill is also the Democratic Party’s nominee for the 8th Michigan House District.
Chris Gilmer-Hill, policy manager for the Michigan Environmental Justice Coalition, speaks out about the environmental impacts data center have had on communities in other states during a press conference at the Michigan Capitol on Sept. 9, 2026. Gilmer-Hill is also a candidate for the Michigan House of Representatives in 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance.)
In addition to the health of our communities, data centers have also impacted the health of our democracy, Gilmer-Hill said.
“Data centers have already corroded trust in our government, and have shown real flaws in transparency at the state and local level all over our state,” Gilmer-Hill said. “We’ve seen people in communities across the state be surprised to find out that a data center was coming to their community, potentially an enormous project that was going to have direct impacts on their lives in their neighborhoods, and they didn’t know about it because of a non-disclosure agreement.”
Marta Johnson, legislative and political organizer for Sierra Club Michigan, said that a moratorium is a critical piece in addressing Michiganders concerns around data centers, but is not the solution on its own.
Johnson called the Senate’s package of data center regulations “an excellent start” but stressed that the state should move toward a moratorium regardless, as there is no guarantee that lawmakers and the governor will be able to agree on data center regulations. 
“We have an excellent start, let’s see it get moving,” Johnson told reporters after the press conference.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Women’s Health Center of West Virginia launches campaign promoting abortion pills
description: A Charleston women’s clinic has launched an ad campaign letting West Virginia residents know that despite the state’s near total ban on abortion, they still have options.
text:
The Women’s Health Center of West Virginia and Shout Your Abortion have placed billboards in Beckley and Huntington as part of their new ad campaign to let residents know they can still access abortion pills. This billboard is on Interstate 77 in Beckley. (Photo courtesy of the Women's Health Center of West Virginia and Shout Your Abortion)A Charleston women’s clinic has launched an ad campaign letting West Virginia residents know that despite the state’s near total ban on abortion, they still have options.
The Women’s Health Center of West Virginia has teamed up with Shout Your Abortion to promote the abortion pill with a new PSA campaign, billboards, mailers and digital advertising targeting the core demographic for abortions. 
“There’s still, to this day, so much misinformation circulating about reproductive healthcare, and our responsibility for being a trusted partner for 50 years in West Virginia as a healthcare provider is to make sure patients can access accurate information and compassionate care,” said Danielle Maness, a provider and clinician at the Women’s Health Center of West Virginia. 
Maness added that the health center doesn’t promote any certain healthcare for patients, but makes sure they have accurate information to make decisions themselves.
The PSA depicts a woman facing an unwanted pregnancy that’s not an emergency because she has abortion pills on hand, said Amelia Bonow, director of Shout Your Abortion. The ads refer people to the website https://www.youalwayshaveoptions.com/, which lists reproductive health resources, including where people can access abortion pills. 
“We want to elevate that in order to sort of kind of move people into this future of abortion access that we’re currently in, where laws and, like, legality and access are no longer interchangeable,” Bonow said. “And we also want to make sure that folks in places like West Virginia know that they have incredible community healthcare in their states that are ready to meet them where they are and offer compassionate, non-judgmental …options (like) counseling. So not promoting any path with any person, but helping them based on their needs and circumstances and desires to understand what their options are.”
The campaign launched Sept. 7 and will run through October. 
The West Side clinic stopped providing abortion in September 2022, after state lawmakers passed a ban on the procedure with narrow exceptions. A law prohibiting abortion in West Virginia state code became effective after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Roe v. Wade and the federal right to an abortion.
Shout Your Abortion is a public education campaign that started in 2015 when Bonow’s personal story went viral, leading to tens of thousands of women sharing their own reproductive health stories. 
“(Shout Your Abortion) was initially really just about normalizing abortion, creating places to talk about our experiences and art and media and events all over the country,” Bonow said. “And then as the legal landscape has changed, and as we’re now in the midst of our second Trump administration, SYA has shifted to be really about helping people understand their options for abortion access, and also sort of how to activate people to be resources for that information in their community.”
While abortion, including by telehealth, is mostly illegal in the state, it’s still happening. Last year 780 medication abortions took place in West Virginia, according to data from Guttmacher Institute, a research and policy organization that aims to advance “sexual and reproductive health and rights worldwide.” 
West Virginia’s Republican lawmakers in recent years also have pushed bills that would target out-of-state health providers and organizations that mail abortion drugs into the state, though prosecuting out-of state-agencies may be difficult. 
Twenty-two states and the District of Columbia have enacted shield laws that protect against out-of-state investigation and prosecutions, according to KFF, a nonprofit health policy research, polling, and news organization.
Since 2023, 1,680 medication abortions have taken place in West Virginia — all through clinicians in states with shield laws, according to Guttmacher. 
“We see time and time again that West Virginia legislators and politicians are repeatedly putting policies in place that are directly in opposition for what our population, our communities and what Appalachians actually need,” Maness said of bills that would target out-of-state abortion pill providers. “…They’re trying to put policies in place that are directly in opposition to what Appalachians are actually wanting.”
The Women’s Health Clinic and Shout Your Abortion aren’t the first organizations to promote the abortion pill in West Virginia. Last year, Mayday Health ran a campaign promoting the medication at gas stations in Kentucky and West Virginia. Last week Kentucky sued the organization over the advertisements, alleging they broke state law. 
This year marks the 50th anniversary for the Women’s Health Center, which was West Virginia’s first provider of elective abortion. 
After the abortion ban took effect, the clinic pivoted to add new services, Maness said. Now, the health center offers gynecological and annual wellness exams, gender-affirming hormone therapy, harm reduction, HIV testing and PrEP and more. Maness said the partnership with Shout Your Abortion allows the Women’s Health Center to let people know they’re still there, providing health care for everyone. 
“Essentially, what Women’s Health Center of West Virginia does is look to our community to determine gaps in care, and then we pivot to say, ‘How can we fit how can we fill those gaps? How can we meet those needs?’ We’re going to continue to do that.” 
“Something that’s really important and unique to independent clinics, specifically abortion care providers, is we’re used to providing care to people who are often marginalized and underserved, and we treat people with respect and without judgment,” she said. “And those clinics are unique, and we have people who drive across state lines just to come and get care. And we’ve been providing this care for 50 years, and I hope that we’re going to be providing it for 50 more.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: First tribal police recruits set to graduate from basic training in North Dakota
description: Basic law enforcement training for tribal police officers expanded to North Dakota this year, offering tribes in the northern region a training option other than the U.S. Indian Police Academy in New Mexico. Twelve recruits from nine tribal law enforcement agencies participated in the first 14-week class of Camp Grafton’s Indian Country Police Officer Traini[...]
text:
Tribal police recruits participate in the Indian Country Police Officer Training Program at Camp Grafton near Devils Lake, North Dakota. (Photo courtesy of the Bureau of Indian Affairs)Basic law enforcement training for tribal police officers expanded to North Dakota this year, offering tribes in the northern region a training option other than the U.S. Indian Police Academy in New Mexico.
Twelve recruits from nine tribal law enforcement agencies participated in the first 14-week class of Camp Grafton’s Indian Country Police Officer Training Program, with graduation set for Tuesday.
Camp Grafton Training Center, a North Dakota National Guard base near Devils Lake, previously offered advanced law enforcement training for the BIA. But the only basic training option was in New Mexico, which leaders in North Dakota and other northern states have said is a barrier to recruiting new tribal police officers.
Tribal law enforcement academy to be located in North Dakota

Charles Addington, principal director for justice services and law enforcement for the Bureau of Indian Affairs, said in a statement that the response to the new program has been “overwhelmingly positive.” 
“This pilot offering has provided renewed hope for many agencies across the northern region by giving them a closer, more accessible option for training their officers,” Addington said.
One North Dakota tribal police recruit joined the pilot program from the BIA Turtle Mountain Agency. Other participants are from tribal nations in Washington, Nebraska, Wyoming and Wisconsin. The program also was promoted to Idaho, Montana, South Dakota, Minnesota and Iowa, Addington said.
The training at Camp Grafton is closer to home and easier on family life, said Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians Chairman Jamie Azure.
“You’re not having to displace yourself and go all the way across the country just to receive training to come back and provide a service in our own communities,” Azure said. “It provides more opportunity to more people, being closer.” 
Sgt. Mike Roy, a school resource officer for the Three Affiliated Tribes, said he would have preferred to have a training option closer to home. He attended the tribal law enforcement academy in New Mexico while his wife and kids were home in North Dakota.
“Being away for like five months, that’s hard,” Roy said. “Had I been here, I could have been coming home on the weekends.”
The Indian Country Police Officer Training Program at Camp Grafton in North Dakota offers tribal police recruits from northern states a training option closer to home. (Photo courtesy of the Bureau of Indian Affairs)
The program features nearly 600 hours of training across different disciplines, such as report writing and court testimony, federal and tribal criminal law, emergency vehicle operations, firearms fundamentals and arrest and control techniques, according to the bureau.
Addington said the goal of the pilot program is to assess the capabilities of Camp Grafton as a training site and ensure adequate resources, facilities and the number of instructors are in place to provide the basic law enforcement course into the future.
The bureau is planning to offer multiple tribal basic law enforcement courses over the next year that will include 24-36 officers in each class. 
In addition to basic law enforcement training, the bureau will also feature basic training for tribal correctional officers and additional specialized training for tribal police and corrections officers in missing persons, defensive techniques, child and elder abuse and high-risk traffic stops, according to the bureau’s website.
“All academy programs are taught by subject‑matter experts who have extensive experience working in tribal communities and handling the complex and sensitive investigations often encountered in Indian Country,” Addington said. 
North Dakota Monitor journalists Jack Dura and Amy Dalrymple contributed to this report.
